stories.Headline: Warsh leads San Francisco Fed conference on how AI could reshape productivity and jobs
stories.Summary:
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh opened a conference at the San Francisco Fed on Monday at 9 a.m. Pacific with 15 minutes of remarks, then led panels for most of the morning. The panels featured Stripe co-founder Patrick Collison, Stanford economist Nick Bloom, and venture capitalist Marc Andreessen, according to the published agenda. The topic was how artificial intelligence, which the Fed calls superintelligence, will change productivity and jobs. Warsh was sworn in as Federal Reserve Chair on May 22 under pressure from President Donald Trump to lower interest rates.

The conference took place as the $31 trillion Treasury market sent Warsh a signal. The Fed lifted the upper bound of its target range to 4.00% in September, from 3.75%. Real GDP grew at a 3.4% annualized pace in the third quarter, above the 2% to 3% range considered healthy trend growth. In the week ending November 13, the 10-year Treasury yield rose from 4.86% to 5.15%, and the 30-year reached 5.47%. Data centers could use up to 12% of U.S. electricity demand by 2028, according to Energy Department projections.

Core Personal Consumption Expenditures prices, the Fed's preferred inflation measure, rose 0.3% in September. Warsh said at Jackson Hole in August that "We've come to a hinge point in history" and called AI "potentially a new factor of production." He asked whether AI would "cause a significant, sustained rise in productivity across the economy" and who ends up with the gains. At his October 28 press conference, he said "Productivity growth is strong and capital investment robust" while noting inflation has run above target "for close to six years." He asked whether AI would bring a rapid productivity miracle or gradual gains, and whether it would make price stability easier or harder.

Warsh said capital spending sits "at a historically high share of GDP," led by high-tech investment. The independent market monitor for PJM Interconnection, which runs the largest U.S. power grid, concluded that "data center load growth is the primary reason" for its tight supply and high prices. Inflation-adjusted average hourly earnings were $11.26 in October, a preliminary figure, down from $11.38 a year earlier. The University of Michigan's consumer sentiment index fell to 48.1 in September, a level associated with recessions.

Unemployment sits at 4.1%, so AI has not caused mass layoffs, and it has yet to show up in paychecks. Warsh has said the task force's findings will inform future policy judgments, not dictate immediate decisions. Bond investors are betting against an AI productivity miracle, with the 10-year Treasury yield jumping and the 30-year hitting 5%. If AI lifts productivity fast enough, the Fed could hold or cut rates, easing mortgage costs and supporting stocks well beyond NVIDIA.

If spending keeps outpacing efficiency gains, the Fed is dealing with a classic overheating economy, and long-term yields above 5% could stick. Data centers compete with everyone else for power, chips, and electricians, which pushes prices up well before any productivity return. The efficiency gains come later, but the construction bills are due now. Monday is unlikely to bring a rate signal, so two things are worth tracking instead.

The first is whether Warsh presents strong productivity as a reason for patience on rates. The second is the next reading of core Personal Consumption Expenditures prices. Cooler readings alongside 3% growth would be the first real evidence of an AI productivity boom. The articles leave open whether AI will deliver a rapid productivity miracle or gradual gains, and whether it will make price stability easier or harder to achieve.

stories.Headline: Amazon cancels data center plans for Virginia campus after county dispute
stories.Summary:
Amazon withdrew its plan for four data center buildings totaling more than 800,000 square feet on its 122-acre Ashburn campus, the former George Washington University campus, under an October 20 deal with Loudoun County, Virginia. Amazon had purchased the campus for around $427.3 million in March 2026 and in July filed a site plan called Bridgefield Tech Center with four two-story data center buildings and three parking garages. Amazon sought a by-right approval, an administrative process with no Planning Commission, public hearing or Board vote. On July 30, Supervisor Juli Briskman vowed to fight it every step of the way, and in early October county staff told supervisors Amazon would need additional county approval because data centers were not a permitted primary use. Board Chair Phyllis Randall later announced the agreement, Project Potomac Promise, on October 20.

Under the county's terms, Amazon cannot construct data centers or host their supporting infrastructure on the Ashburn campus, will convey about 25 acres to the county and will seek to rezone the rest, mainly for housing. On November 17, supervisors will take a final vote on pausing new legislative data center applications for up to 12 months, the maximum Virginia law allows, a resolution deferred from October 20 to give staff more time. On September 15, supervisors voted 7-1-1 to pause Board consideration of rezonings and special exceptions for data centers and electrical substations. The pause does not cover administrative applications, including at least 17 grandfathered applications totaling over 11 million square feet, and the Board can still consider grid reliability substations. The county hosts about 233 data center buildings and 56.5 million square feet built or under construction as of March 1, 2026, plus 35.7 million square feet approved but not yet built, and in 2025 it issued permits for over 10 million square feet.

Randall said the campus was just the wrong location for a data center, owing to the infrastructure it would need and residents' opposition. Amazon's Josh Weissman said the company had heard the community's pointed concerns and took them seriously, and that while Amazon and the county had differing views on the site's legal potential, it chose a shared vision over costly litigation. Neither Amazon nor Randall cited power supply as the reason for calling off the planned construction. Amazon called staging finished equipment near deployment sites best business practice and disputed that it lacked a path to bring the racks into its data centers. AWS CEO Matt Garman cautioned that over 100 data center moratoriums are being considered across the U.S.

Business Insider reported that some AWS sites had space for Nvidia GB300 racks but not enough power to run them, so finished racks were held in warehouses, a story that broke on October 20 but was based on internal emails from August. One email projected around $5 billion of GB300 racks in August, followed by around $3 billion a month for the foreseeable future, and the report gave no detail on how many racks were stored, at which sites, or for how long. Governor Abigail Spanberger said the decision on approving or blocking data center projects should rest with the community and not the state, and State Senator Russet Perry drafted a three-year statewide moratorium on data center approvals. Dominion Energy, the utility for Northern Virginia's data center cluster, said on its Q3 earnings call that it has more than 54 GW of data center capacity in various stages of contracting, including over 12 GW under electric service agreements. Dominion also told CBS 6 that new data centers sign 14-year contracts with minimum demand charges and post collateral of $1.5 million per MW, so residential customers do not pay for stranded infrastructure if a project falls through.

A 2000 zoning ruling assigned data centers as office buildings, letting companies build them by right in office-zoned areas, and since March 2025 new data centers have required a special exception approved by a Board vote, though projects grandfathered under the old rules can still proceed administratively. The county's data centers generated $1.2 billion in real and personal property tax revenue in fiscal 2026, 39% of its total budget, and fiscal 2027 estimates project around 40%, at $1.3 billion. In Amazon's April shareholder letter, CEO Andy Jassy said AWS added 3.9 GW of power capacity in 2025 and expected to double this capacity by the end of 2027, but still had capacity constraints that yield unserved demand. In August, AWS and Nvidia shared a joint announcement detailing plans to deploy over 2 million more Nvidia GPUs on AWS in 2027 and 2028. On September 24, Oracle issued a force majeure notice to Blue Owl Capital, owner of STACK Infrastructure, over Project Jupiter, its 2.45 GW Stargate campus in Doña Ana County, New Mexico, with planned investment of up to $165 billion, after the state land office denied a gas pipeline route and the Green Chile pipeline's in-service date slipped to February 1, 2027.

AWS reported a $578 billion backlog and $46 billion in Q3 sales, up 39%, while Amazon purchased $77.3 billion of property and equipment and its leases signed but not yet started rose to $164.9 billion in Q3 from $137.2 billion in Q2 and $96.4 billion at the end of 2025, up 71%. Amazon's Q3 filing also lists $159.6 billion of property and equipment commitments, separate from the leases, and Amazon plans to spend meaningfully more in 2027 than the roughly $220 billion planned for 2026. On October 2, Garman pledged more than $1 billion to support communities near its data centers over five years and confirmed Amazon would stop using NDAs with government agencies. South Korea's Electronics and Telecommunications Research Institute said on the 19th that EMP, its in-house cross-server memory sharing software, is being piloted at the University of Southern California's Center for Advanced Research Computing, which operates an HPC cluster of about 500 servers. A server with only 448GB of its own memory completed a genomic analysis requiring about 1.8TB after EMP was applied, borrowing roughly three-quarters of the memory it needed from other servers, while performance per unit of memory improved by as much as 2.3 times. Ko Kwang-won, head of ETRI's AIDC Research Division, said the significance lies not so much in raising the efficiency of a single memory as in sharing memory across multiple servers, and that from a hyperscaler's perspective it amounts to gaining a temporary stopgap before new memory arrives.

stories.Headline: ECB vice president Boris Vujčić warns rapid AI expansion threatens financial stability
stories.Summary:
European Central Bank Vice President Boris Vujčić warned on Monday, November 16, 2026, that rapid artificial intelligence expansion could threaten financial stability. He spoke at Euro Finance Week in Frankfurt about how stretched stock market valuations for AI increase the risk of a repricing. Vujčić noted that a correction following America's mid-term elections serves as a reminder for the region to remain cautious. The bank also published research on November 18 regarding the stability implications of AI adoption in the real economy. This research found that reliance on a small number of AI providers could amplify risks across the entire financial system.

The research paper suggests that banks and asset managers use AI for portfolio management, fraud detection, and credit scoring. Eurostat data shows about 20 percent of European Union enterprises used AI in 2025, an increase of 6.5 percentage points. Adoption was higher in northern European countries than in the south and east, and higher in finance than in manufacturing. Anthropic's index on Claude.ai showed automation rose from 27 percent in January 2025 to 39 percent in August 2025. The ECB now requires better data on AI use, stronger oversight of providers, and changes to supervisory capabilities and safeguards.

Boris Vujčić stated that system-wide stability risks now stem from quickening AI adoption, concentration of exposures, and potential cyberattacks. He said that external funding is expanding from equity to debt markets, which adds to the current financial stability risks. Vujčić argued that it is critical to have a resilient banking sector while maintaining supervision over non-banks and private credit. He noted that private credit warrants close monitoring due to limited transparency, liquidity mismatches, and growing interconnectedness with insurers. The official believes that geopolitical headwinds further elevate the risks that the European Central Bank must currently manage.

The International Monetary Fund reported that AI can accelerate vulnerability discovery and exploitation across shared technologies to create correlated disruptions. This report suggests that AI cyber risk is now an enterprise governance issue for merchants, FinTechs, banks, and critical infrastructure operators. The IMF noted that the main question is how much autonomy systems should receive and if organizations can contain them. Other affected parties include companies in information technology and finance, which the ECB found have high exposure to AI risks. These institutions are vulnerable through their reliance on a concentrated group of cloud service providers and AI model providers.

The ECB research drew on emerging research, evidence from investment funds, and recent surveys of banks and various industries. The authors examined how financial firms are exposed to changes at other businesses that are adopting new AI technologies. US survey data indicated that professional services, finance, and information technology used AI more than the manufacturing sector did. The authors admitted that survey results were not directly comparable because the populations, questions, and definitions differed across sources. The research focused on how AI helps asset managers process information and how banks assess borrowers and detect activity.

The European Central Bank will continue monitoring the rapid growth of private credit and the concentration of AI model providers. Future efforts will focus on improving market safeguards to address emerging risks and increasing the oversight of critical AI providers. The articles leave open how exactly the ECB will implement these new supervisory capabilities to manage the identified systemic risks. They do not specify the exact timeline for the requested changes to data collection regarding AI use across the union. It remains unclear how the bank will balance AI autonomy with the need to contain systems when things fail.

stories.Headline: Anthropic's Claude Code team uses verification loops so Claude writes and reviews about 90% of its code
stories.Summary:
On the Claude Code team at Anthropic, about 90% of code is written and reviewed by Claude, Addy Osmani wrote in a claude.dev blog post published Nov 16, 2026. The post described how the team equips its agents to verify their work with evidence. Verification loops let the team delegate more work to Claude, Osmani wrote. Without them, you can really only run one or two Claudes at a time, because you have to check everything yourself, he wrote. With them, you can run dozens or hundreds in parallel, he wrote.

In internal testing around structured file generation, a separate grader checking Claude's work against a rubric improved task success by up to 10 points over a standard prompting loop, with the largest gains on the hardest problems. The post recommended end-to-end tests, property tests and differential tests. Property test libraries named were fast-check for JS/TS, Hypothesis for Python and proptest for Rust. The team maintains a reliability checklist with 39 items, each with a trigger readable from a diff, a check, and the incidents or PRs behind it. Claude reads the diff and checks only the items whose trigger matches, usually 3 to 10.

If a check is still failing after three rounds, Claude stops and brings in a human, the post said. Code owners write their own checks and refine them until they flag what the owner would flag, it said. Code Review reads the REVIEW.md file from the base or default branch, never from the pull request's changes, and the team ensures the rules that gate changes are on a branch the change can't modify. The team stamps each commit with how it was verified, including "none," and created a commit gate with off, observe and enforce modes that can block a commit if the session did not contain /code-review or /verify. If commits have been blocked twice in the session, the next one will be allowed through so Claude doesn't get stuck.

The team tracks how many merged changes were reverted, how many changes a maintainer rejected before merging, and a size-matched subset of changes that have stayed clean. Code Review tags findings as Important, Nit or Pre-existing, where pre-existing means the reviewer shouldn't hold the author responsible for something that was already a bug. The team tunes recall up to the point where the next improvement would be overfitting to the eval rather than actually catching bugs. In the Claude Code repo, the team has two methods of turning missed cases into rules, the first being extracting patterns in human code review comments and PR reverts. These must occur in at least two PRs and be identifiable from a diff to be considered a potential rule, and three agents will try to di, where the article ends.

The post said the team has previously written about how code review works at Anthropic, and this article aimed to go deeper on how the team verifies its work. It said running the app end to end matters more than tests, and that this is how nearly all changes are tested at Anthropic. It advised creating a skill called verify in a .claude/skills/ folder in your repo, as close to the relevant code as you can, and said Claude knows to use the verify skill before committing changes. It said Claude can test the whole app the way a human or QA engineer would, using the Claude Chrome extension for web changes, an iOS or Android MCP for mobile, computer use for desktop, or running the service locally for backend work. It said nobody can read every change, so failures are used as one way to decide what needs a person.

The post said the team does not try to improve reviews by stacking on more reviewers, and that adding a second, more expensive, reviewer on top of the primary one is often a worse approach than tuning the primary. It said the team has a REVIEW.md that says what the reviewer should pay attention to for this code, and that review and verification rounds should build on each other, pointing each pass at context from earlier rounds and past failures rather than re-checking everything from scratch. It said the team also runs cheap checks first, and that on the team Claude runs the tests, build and linter before opening a pull request, which can be enforced with a hook that runs the tests when Claude finishes, or a /goal of a passing test suite. It said the team regularly reviews the reviewers, and that the Code Review team set up an evaluation based on previous incidents and reverts, recreating the repo to the state at the time of review for each example and providing a one-sentence answer key to what the bug was. It said only findings that correctly describe the bug in question get points, merged and stable changes are used as a control to prevent over-flagging, the tuning set is split out from the fixed test set, and recall was evaluated separately for raw findings, post-verification and final review.

stories.Headline: UH to predict invasive beetle spread with AI
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa’s College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resilience are developing an artificial intelligence tool to predict where the invasive coconut rhinoceros beetle is most likely to spread. The project covers Kauaʻi, Maui and Hawaiʻi Island and is dated November 17, 2026 in the university’s news release. Pascal Aigbedion-Atalor, an assistant professor in CTAHR’s Department of Plant and Environmental Protection Sciences, leads the project. The $300,000 project aims to help field crews decide where to place traps and look for new infestations. The university announced the work through its news service and Big Island Video News and Hawaii News Now reported it the same day.

The team will use machine learning to analyze local conditions that help the beetle survive and map areas where it is most likely to spread. Researchers plan to test the predictions against field observations to improve the tool’s accuracy. The maps could help crews decide where to place pheromone-baited traps and focus their efforts to contain the beetle. Researchers could also adapt the approach to help protect Hawaiʻi crops from other invasive pests. Funding comes from the Foundation for Food & Agriculture Research through its Rapid Outcomes from Agricultural Research program, with matching support from CTAHR.

Aigbedion-Atalor said knowing where the coconut rhinoceros beetle is likely to spread gives farmers and response teams a major advantage. He said the technology aims to help farmers and agriculture officials act early, target high-risk areas and protect valuable crops and landscapes. Kathy Munkvold, scientific program director at the Foundation for Food & Agriculture Research, said stopping invasive pests before they spread is one of the best ways to protect American agriculture. She said the research gives farmers a head start against a devastating introduced pest, helping to protect crops, livelihoods and the future of Hawaiʻi’s agriculture. CTAHR Dean Parwinder Grewal said mitigating the CRB crisis cannot be accomplished by a single organization.

Grewal said it takes a combined effort, from state agricultural inspectors and federal biosecurity officials to private funders and everyday community members checking their backyards. UH researchers are working with state agencies, federal partners, private organizations and residents to help limit the beetle’s spread. The maps would support those efforts by showing crews where to focus their fieldwork. Last week, it was reported for the first time that a coconut rhinoceros beetle was discovered in the Puna district on Hawaiʻi island. The Hawaiʻi Department of Agriculture and Biosecurity said the live, male CRB was found in a trap in the Kurtistown area.

The university’s news release describes the project as a two-minute read and lists it under agriculture, AI, entomology and invasive species tags. The release names the College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resilience and the Department of Plant and Environmental Protection Sciences as the units involved. Big Island Video News reported the story under a summary saying the tool will predict where the invasive CRB is most likely to spread in Hawaiʻi. Hawaii News Now reported that the project aims to help farmers and response teams identify high-risk areas on Kauai, Maui and Hawaii Island. Hawaii News Now also reported that UH officials said the technology could eventually be adapted to help protect Hawaii crops from other invasive pests.

Researchers plan to test their predictions against field observations, and the maps could help crews decide where to place traps and focus efforts to detect and contain new infestations. The articles do not say when the tool will be finished or when the maps will be available to field crews. The articles do not say how many traps would be placed or where on Kauaʻi, Maui and Hawaiʻi Island the mapping would begin. The articles do not say whether the Kurtistown beetle find is connected to the new prediction project. The articles do not give the outcome of any testing of the predictions against field observations.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave raises full-year revenue forecast as quarterly revenue jumps 168%
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave reported third-quarter results on Nov. 10, and its stock jumped about 14% in premarket trading the next morning, after the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5% on Nov. 5 and sat about 12% below its October record. CoreWeave, Nebius and Iren had each fallen at least 40% from the Nasdaq's Oct. 6 peak, and Nvidia lost more than $400 billion of market value in one two-day slide. That was before the scandal and departure of CEO Jensen Huang came to light. Nvidia, Nebius, Iren, Oracle and many other AI-related stocks rose with CoreWeave after the report. Nvidia was set to report earnings after the close on Tuesday, Nov. 17.

CoreWeave's revenue rose 168% year over year in the third quarter, and management raised its full-year revenue forecast to $13.0 billion to $13.3 billion from $12.4 billion to $13.2 billion in August. Its revenue backlog rose 138% from a year earlier to about $132.5 billion. CEO Michael Intrator told analysts the company is largely sold out through 2027, with roughly 10 times as much qualified demand as available capacity through the end of next year. OpenAI, Perplexity and Jane Street all expanded their relationships with CoreWeave during the quarter, and the company expects to collect about $9 billion of customer prepayments and deposits over the next three months. CoreWeave's debt more than doubled this year to about $47 billion at the end of September.

Management said CoreWeave doesn't plan to issue additional unsecured debt at the parent company level through 2027 and expects cash flow from existing contracts to cover its debt repayments. Intrator told analysts the company is largely sold out through 2027. CoreWeave's net interest expense was $846 million in the third quarter, more than twice its adjusted operating income, and management expects it to be $1.05 billion to $1.15 billion in the fourth quarter. The company still lost $709 million under generally accepted accounting principles. Amazon still expects about $220 billion of capital expenditures in 2026, and Alphabet expects its spending to increase significantly in 2027.

Analysts at Bernstein called it about the best quarter we could have asked for, but warned CoreWeave will be among the first and hardest hit when the shortage of AI computing capacity eases. The report eased fears about AI demand, but the cost of financing data centers is still the biggest risk for the most indebted companies. The 10-year Treasury yield topped 5.3% in October. Several candidates who won in last week's midterm elections campaigned for tighter regulation of data centers, including moratoriums on new construction in Texas. On Nov. 10, SoftBank took a $3.7 billion write-down on payments for equipment to power its U.S. data centers.

CoreWeave rents out Nvidia-powered computing capacity to AI developers and has borrowed heavily to build its data centers, which made its report one of the most closely watched tests of the AI build-out this earnings season. Most of the recent fear has centered on the cost of building AI infrastructure, especially for companies that need to borrow money to fund the build-out. CoreWeave sits at the center of those concerns. The report lines up with what the biggest AI spenders said a few weeks ago. One strong quarter doesn't end the debate about an AI bubble.

Nvidia reports after the close on Nov. 17, and investors will be watching the close, not just for the company's growth metrics, but for management's commentary in its first report since founder and CEO Jensen Huang stepped down. The articles leave open whether customers are still willing to pay for AI computing capacity beyond the strong yes seen for now. They leave open how heavily indebted companies like CoreWeave fare if that changes. They leave open whether the cost of financing the build-out remains the bigger risk for the sector than demand. They leave open what Nvidia's management will say in its first report since Huang stepped down.

stories.Headline: Max Roser finds every high-quality US survey shows more negative than positive views on AI
stories.Summary:
Max Roser of Our World in Data published an article on November 16, 2026, combining five recent high-quality surveys on American views of artificial intelligence. Every survey found that more Americans hold a negative view of AI than a positive one. In Pew's survey, 52% said they were more concerned than excited, and 9% said they were more excited than concerned. When Pew first asked the question in 2021, the ratio was about two to one. In the Ipsos survey, 17% said AI is an extremely bad thing for society, and just 2% said extremely good.

Pew's survey covered 3,488 US adults on the American Trends Panel, conducted June 22 to 28, 2026, with November 2021 data from the same panel collected November 1 to 7, 2021. Gallup and Bentley University surveyed 3,270 US adults on the Gallup Panel from May 4 to 11, 2026. Quinnipiac polled 1,397 US adults by telephone from March 19 to 23, 2026, and released results March 30, 2026. The Annenberg Public Policy Center surveyed 1,320 US adults from June 16 to July 19, 2026, and Ipsos surveyed 2,545 US adults on its KnowledgePanel from October 9 to 13, 2026.

When a middle answer was offered, 37% took it in Pew's recent survey, and only 9% chose a positive view in both Pew's and Gallup's surveys. In Pew's survey, 56% of Democrats and 49% of Republicans were more concerned than excited, and in both parties only around one in ten were more excited than concerned. In a Quinnipiac poll in September 2026, 35% said they were somewhat concerned and 38% very concerned that future AI systems could threaten human survival. Most Americans, 73%, believe there is a risk that AI could threaten the survival of humanity. Roser wrote that if the industry wants to earn the public's trust, it will have to take these widespread concerns much more seriously than it has so far.

In the same Ipsos survey, 50% said AI is a good thing for them personally and 49% a bad thing, though 15% said it is extremely bad for them personally against 3% who said extremely good. In Quinnipiac's March 2026 poll, 55% expected AI to do more harm than good in their day-to-day life, against 34% who expected more good. Quinnipiac's September survey of 1,202 US adults, conducted September 24 to 27, 2026 by random digit dialing with live interviewers, found 14% not so concerned, 11% not concerned at all, and 1% who did not know or did not answer. A September 30, 2026 Quinnipiac release reported that 86% support independent safety standards for AI companies. Roser included only surveys based on probability samples, excluding opt-in online panels, and noted an opt-in poll that found 20% of Americans under 30 agreed the Holocaust is a myth, against 3% when Pew asked on its probability-based panel.

Just Capital released the third edition of its monthly National AI Monitor on November 18, 2026 in New York, New York, through GlobeNewswire. The survey was conducted online by The Harris Poll for Just Capital from October 19 to 21, 2026 among 1,008 US adults ages 18 and older, accurate to within plus or minus 3.6 percentage points at a 95% confidence level. Respondents answered seven questions on a five-point scale from very negative to very positive, with I don't know as a non-forced option. Just Capital said Americans' experiences with AI have trended positive or remained steady across every measure since the research began in August 2026. Scores are the percentage of positive responses minus the percentage of negative responses, and month-to-month changes are not statistically significant.

The Monitor's overall score was +42 in October, +37 in September and +35 in August, with work at +47, +44 and +48, customer experience at +26, +25 and +21, community engagement at +15, +12 and +7, investments at +31, +24 and +21, environmental stewardship at -9, -12 and -17, and the next few years at +14, +12 and +15. Changes between August and October were statistically significant for community engagement, investments and environmental stewardship. Full-time workers, college graduates and adults ages 35 to 44 maintained a positive outlook, while retirees, people not employed, those with some college but no degree, and Americans 65 and over turned net negative. Just Capital CEO Martin Whittaker said Americans feel more positively about AI when they see tangible opportunities for themselves in the AI-powered economy, and that people can feel good about AI in their own lives while worrying about what it means for society at large.

A 58-year-old man in Florida with an associate's degree, self-employed part-time and lower income, said AI tools automate his routine administrative tasks and let him focus on high-level strategy, business growth and new niche markets. A 37-year-old woman in Texas who completed graduate school, employed full-time and upper income, said companies' use of AI makes her customer experience faster and more convenient through personalized recommendations and quicker customer support, though she worries about data privacy, inaccurate information and less human interaction. A 33-year-old man in California who completed graduate school, employed full-time and middle income, said AI optimizes local traffic management to cut city gridlock. A 73-year-old woman in Texas with some college but no degree, retired and lower income, questioned whether AI is needed in every application when it requires enormous facilities and land and water resources for data centers. A 32-year-old woman in Ohio, a college graduate, self-employed part-time and lower income, said she lost her job to AI while it makes her technology increasingly unusable.

Whittaker said whether America successfully embraces AI economically, socially and politically rests on how good the country is at closing the gap between what ordinary working Americans expect the technology to deliver and what they actually experience, and that decision makers in tech, business and government will ignore this at their peril. Roser's article noted that in 2021 Pew introduced its question with a short definition referring to artificial intelligence computer programs rather than artificial intelligence (AI), with the same answer options, and Pew reports the results as one trend. Roser's article was archived on November 16, 2026, and Just Capital said additional qualitative findings and drivers of experience are available in the National AI Monitor. The articles leave open what happens next, and the Monitor's month-to-month changes are not statistically significant.

stories.Headline: UN chief Guterres warns autonomous weapons cross a moral red line as Geneva talks open
stories.Summary:
United Nations negotiations are currently underway in Geneva to create rules for lethal autonomous weapons. These killer robots are the focus of a conference on Certain Conventional Weapons this week. Supporters believe this meeting is the last chance to agree on rules before it is too late. Experts warn that weapons capable of choosing targets autonomously could exist within months. AI-assisted weapons have already been used in Gaza and Ukraine to take out targets.

The conference meets once every five years to discuss these specific conventional weapons. At least 50 countries, including France, Germany, Italy, Ireland, Brazil, and Mexico, want a strict timetable. The United States, Russia, and Israel oppose legally binding rules for these autonomous systems. Washington proposes a five-year timetable to draft guidelines that are not legally binding. This process requires consensus, which was previously achieved in 1995 to ban blinding lasers.

Secretary-General Antonio Guterres stated that allowing autonomous weapons to kill crosses a moral red line. The International Committee of the Red Cross and the Pope also called for binding rules. Legal adviser Georgia Haines said autonomous weapons cannot understand contextual signals like humans do. She worries these machines cannot distinguish between fighting soldiers and those who are wounded. Humanitarian organizations argue that the responsibility for the decision to kill must remain human.

Human rights groups warn that AI weapons are becoming cheap and easy to use. They fear terrorist groups or repressive regimes could use drones to target specific languages. Civilians in Ukraine report being hunted by drones while they go to school or shop. Illinois Governor JB Pritzker compared the threat of artificial intelligence to that of nuclear weapons. AI leaders like Sam Altman suggest an international authority to inspect systems and require audits.

AI researcher Yoshua Bengio told the UN Security Council that frontier AI needs licensing. The US previously used coercion to stop nuclear programs in Libya, Syria, and Iraq. South Korea and Taiwan gave up weapons programs after intense pressure from the United States. The US traditionally avoids some treaties, such as the Ottawa Convention on landmines. Secretary of State Marco Rubio recently warned against quoting laws to men with swords.

Diplomats may compromise with an open-ended period for states to adopt their own rules. Some campaigners believe this approach is like kicking a dangerous can down the road. The US could lead by disclosing risks and limitations of its own AI systems. It could also require private companies to report serious safety failures and near misses. The articles leave open whether the world can reach a consensus on binding laws.

stories.Headline: InMobi launches AI platform to manage advertising campaigns for small businesses
stories.Summary:
On November 18, 2026, InMobi launched a platform called InMobi Accelerate to help small and medium businesses. This new tool uses seven AI agents to plan, build, launch and measure advertising campaigns for users. The company released the announcement from San Mateo, California, at 7:00 AM Eastern time on that day. It targets small firms and the agencies that serve them to manage ads from one single dashboard. The platform is available at accelerate.inmobi.com and InMobi states that it is free to start.

The tool manages ads on Google Ads, Meta Ads, Microsoft Advertising, TikTok Ads and ChatGPT Ads. Seven agents act as a business analyst, audience strategist, media planner, copywriter, creative designer, launch engineer and optimizer. It uses a first-party pixel and universal conversion tracking to report a single figure called True ROAS. This data feeds Mobius, a decisioning system unveiled on October 5 that processes 25 trillion daily predictions. The system evaluates over 200 billion advertising opportunities each day to forecast options against desired advertiser outcomes.

Rohit Dosi, the VP and GM of InMobi Accelerate, said that AI agents change the economics of expertise. He stated that growing businesses should run disciplined programs without hiring seven specialists and agencies should take more clients. InMobi claims that assembling reports from different platforms into one picture is slow work that is difficult to get right. The company says the platform allows businesses to grow without standing up a large in-house marketing function. They describe Accelerate as a self-serve agentic AI advertising platform for planning and measuring campaigns.

InMobi says that 70 percent or more of 800 US small advertisers run campaigns on two or more platforms. A survey by NewtonX in May 2026 found that only 4 percent can launch a campaign the same day. Another StackAdapt survey of 885 senior marketers found that only 7 percent run fully unified measurement across their brands. Many advertisers are affected by single-publisher attribution, where multiple platforms claim the same sale for one single conversion. This structure creates silos that 42 percent of senior marketers say waste over a fifth of programmatic budgets.

The platform was introduced at Glance Forward in New York to examine how AI changes how consumers buy products. OpenAI opened ChatGPT Ads Manager to all US businesses on May 5 and expanded to 89 countries by October 21. Over 100,000 advertisers have run campaigns on ChatGPT since its launch, which includes cost-per-click bidding for all users. InMobi's Mobius system previously reached 8.6 million Grocery Outlet shoppers over a 12-day campaign to prove its scale. The company also plans an integration with Glance, which it describes as an AI-powered personal shopping tool.

Users must approve every plan, creative asset and budget before any advertising goes live on the connected platforms. Continuous optimization only runs if the advertiser authorizes it and sets specific parameters for the AI to follow. The articles leave open which specific parameters can be set, if budget caps exist, or if changes are logged. It is unclear how sales are credited when multiple platforms touch them or which lookback windows the system applies. The announcement does not name an independent auditor or measurement partner to verify the reported True ROAS figures.

stories.Headline: Baidu CEO Robin Li urges companies to monetize AI and overhaul organizational structures to avoid a bubble
stories.Summary:
Baidu CEO Robin Li spoke about the urgent need for artificial intelligence adoption during the APEC CEO Summit in Shenzhen on November 17, 2026. He explained that the actual spread of AI applications is moving more slowly than people expected despite the intense competition in the technology sector. Li argued that companies must prioritize the monetization of these tools to prevent the risk of a market bubble. He believes that the industry cannot sustain its current growth without finding clear ways to generate revenue.

The process of reaping the benefits of AI requires a complete overhaul of traditional organizational structures within a company. Robin Li stated that he has made radical attempts to break down the boundaries of traditional jobs at Baidu to better integrate these new technologies. This shift involves reorganizing how teams operate to ensure that AI is not just a tool but a core part of the business model. Such changes are necessary to keep pace with the rapid evolution of the global tech map.

As the leader of Baidu, Robin Li is responsible for guiding his company through this transition while advising other executives on the necessity of structural change. He suggested that the current way of organizing work is an obstacle to the full potential of artificial intelligence. By removing rigid job descriptions, he believes companies can become more agile and responsive to technological breakthroughs. He emphasized that those who fail to reorganize their internal systems will likely struggle to compete in the future.

stories.Headline: FBI warns hackers use Artex AI tool to breach global networks in under three hours
stories.Summary:
The FBI warned that hackers are using an autonomous AI tool called Artex to launch cyberattacks globally and across the United States. These malicious actors have targeted various industries in recent months, including government, defense, tech, phone, internet companies, and law firms. The agency issued a flash cybersecurity advisory on November 13 to alert businesses and government organizations about these escalating AI-assisted threats. Cybercriminals and state-aligned groups have used this software to automate attacks and gain privileged network access in under three hours. The FBI says these intrusions have occurred since the tool first made its public debut in July of this year.

The framework requires connections to frontier large language models from OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as open-source or non-U.S. models. It targets security flaws like weak protections and stolen passwords to breach networks in South Korea and the United States. Hackers used Artex to access Microsoft 365 cloud environments of at least 2,250 customers of the IT company ConnectWise. In South Korea, the tool targeted financial institutions and stole the personal data of at least 68,000 people due to weak defenses. The tool also breached Barracuda by finding an exposed credential from a third-party vendor that the company had not revoked.

The FBI stated that AI makes sophisticated attacks faster and easier to automate, which makes them more difficult for organizations to detect. Federal investigators noted that Artex intrusions are noisy because they generate reams of traffic and data that trigger defensive alerts. The agency warned on X that the tool allows attackers with limited technical expertise to carry out complex, specialist operations. Barracuda's chief information security officer, Arve Kjoelen, said defenders relying on spotting activity often arrive after the attacker has finished. A spokesperson for ConnectWise did not respond to requests for comment regarding the claims made by the FBI.

Microsoft identified a China-aligned threat actor known as Storm-0940 as the group behind the Artex-assisted campaigns targeting hundreds of organizations. The breach at Barracuda affected stores of credentials used to collect data, though the company cannot rule out customer access. Victims include the financial industry in South Korea and customers of the IT management giant ConnectWise who suffered data theft. Other affected entities include the 178 organizations whose websites were hit by a separate supply-chain attack involving the platform Optimizely. This separate incident involved 188 compromised scripts that could potentially capture sensitive information entered by visitors to those various websites.

Artex was originally developed as an open-source penetration-testing platform designed to identify security weaknesses in applications and computer networks. The tool relies on rapidly scanning a victim's network for signs of weakness before exploiting simple bugs to gain a foothold. Recent reports of banking disruptions at Wells Fargo, Bank of America, and JPMorgan Chase were not linked to these cyberattacks. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin attributed those specific outages to ageing computer infrastructure rather than malicious activity from AI hacking tools. JPMorgan Chase blamed a software bug for its problems, while Microsoft attributed its own disruption to various server issues.

The developer of Artex made the software closed-source to prevent further attacks, but the FBI says the open-source version remains accessible. Researchers recently found hundreds of publicly exposed Artex systems online without passwords, including the system used to target South Korea. The FBI continues to warn that the tool's ability to automate reconnaissance presents a significant challenge for traditional cybersecurity defenses. It remains unclear how many customers were affected by the Barracuda breach because the company's logs were not detailed enough. The articles leave open whether other organizations have been compromised by the circulating open-source version of the Artex tool.

stories.Headline: Shenzhen plans a new center to promote APEC cross-border data cooperation
stories.Summary:
Shenzhen prepares to host the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting from November 18 to 19 under a theme of prospering together. EngineAI Robotics Technology Co., Ltd. organized a robot fighting competition to test movement capabilities for potential future agricultural applications. A Malaysian researcher suggested that humanoid robots could eventually guard orchards, harvest oil palm fruit, or pollinate durian trees. Yao Qiyuan, a co-founder of the firm, noted that expanding overseas involves developing new applications with local partners. These events highlight the potential for deeper artificial intelligence cooperation across the Asia-Pacific region during the upcoming leaders' meeting.

The city's core AI industry generated 220 billion yuan, or 33 billion U.S. dollars, in revenue during the year 2025. More than 2,600 AI enterprises above designated size operate in Shenzhen, and trade with APEC economies reached 1.98 trillion yuan. This trade figure for the first half of 2026 rose 33 percent and accounted for nearly 70 percent of foreign trade. Shenzhen exported 8.27 billion yuan of 3D-printing equipment in early 2026, which was an increase of 127.5 percent. The city released an AI action plan for 2026 to 2028 in September to strengthen cooperation with ASEAN countries.

Hu Zhenyu of the China Development Institute said the AI industry is now bringing entire industrial chains to overseas markets. Yao Qiyuan stated that robot fighting tests gait and balance before these capabilities are applied to various agricultural tasks. Bai Xue of the Shenzhen 3D Printing Association said integrated supply chains have boosted the competitiveness of Chinese printers. Shi Xiaoliang of SmartMore Corporation hopes APEC will allow for deeper technological innovation, industrial collaboration, and global talent exchanges. Yang Qian of X Square Robot said open-source technologies are lowering barriers to technology access for small and medium enterprises.

SmartMore Corporation has served over 730 enterprises and deepened cooperation with partners in Japan, the Republic of Korea, and Southeast Asia. These partners work in sectors including precision manufacturing, new energy, and consumer electronics to detect defects too small for eyes. Micro, small and medium-sized enterprises account for over 97 percent of businesses and provide most private sector jobs. These smaller businesses generate about half of the private sector output and are affected by new AI-powered digital transformations. Eduardo Pedrosa of the APEC Secretariat said Shenzhen's research and innovation can benefit the entire region and the world.

In 2025, APEC's 21 member economies housed 3 billion people and represented 61.6 percent of the global real GDP. The APEC Artificial Intelligence Initiative for 2026 to 2030 was adopted in 2025 to promote secure and reliable ecosystems. On July 23, ministers in Chengdu adopted the Chengdu Statement to promote AI transformation in agriculture, services, and manufacturing. China announced in July that it would provide 5,000 AI training opportunities and seminars for developing countries over five years. The Huaqiangbei electronics market now attracts enthusiasts interested in 3D printers, robots, and AI glasses instead of just components.

China plans to establish a center in Qianhai, Shenzhen, to promote APEC cooperation regarding the flow of cross-border data. This center will serve as an open platform for regulatory alignment, policy research, and various services for different businesses. The city seeks cooperation with countries in the Belt and Road Initiative regarding AI solutions and intelligent computing hardware ecosystems. The articles leave open how specific regulatory alignments will be reached through the new center in the Qianhai district. They also leave open the specific timeline for when humanoid robots will begin guarding orchards in the country of Malaysia.

stories.Headline: Chinese entities use output from US AI models to train domestic rivals amid chip curbs
stories.Summary:
Chinese entities are using output from leading American AI models to train domestic rivals, according to a review of over 300 documents. This practice, known as distillation, has moved from academic experiments into mainstream industrial use to offset tightening US chip curbs. The process involves a powerful teacher model generating answers that developers then use to train a smaller student system. Chinese researchers use these models to produce computer code, find solutions to difficult problems, and answer various questions. This trend continues as China aims to broaden its AI strategy and reduce its reliance on American technology.

Washington announced on November 16 that it would further restrict China's access to chips from companies like Nvidia. In November 2024, Shanghai Jiao Tong University researchers used 5,000 answers from OpenAI's o1 model to train Alibaba's Qwen2.5-72B model. Alibaba researchers used OpenAI's GPT-4 and GPT-4o in April 2025 to generate training material in languages other than Chinese. In February 2026, Meituan and Shanghai Jiao Tong University used GPT-4o to train a model to organize AI agents. Beijing is encouraging distillation to make AI cheaper and easier to deploy across the manufacturing sector in China.

US Commerce Department officials raised concerns in Chengdu in July that some distillation activities could amount to intellectual property theft. A US official stated that industrial-scale distillation is the main reason Chinese AI models have narrowed the gap with rivals. Chinese officials defended the practice as a standard development technique and said they were open to acting against theft. The US Commerce Department and China's Cyberspace Administration did not respond to requests for comment on these matters. Chinese officials made no concrete commitments to the US regarding the regulation of these specific AI training activities.

OpenAI and Anthropic have terms that restrict using their model output to develop competing systems without receiving prior permission. US authorities publicly accused Chinese companies in September of conducting aggressive, targeted distillation of American AI models on an industrial scale. Two people familiar with Chinese operations disputed US claims, citing advances in algorithms, data, and model design as factors. Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Alibaba, and Meituan did not respond to requests for comment regarding their specific research papers. Researchers cautioned that excessive reliance on distillation could stifle original innovation and leave developers dependent on more advanced providers.

Eight Chinese government agencies published a national AI+Manufacturing policy package in January supporting model training, fine-tuning, and distillation. The cities of Shanghai and Shenzhen have also encouraged techniques that reduce the computing requirements for artificial intelligence. Distillation is not illegal and is prevalent in other parts of the world, though it cannot reproduce full capabilities. The process helps developers preserve selected skills in smaller systems that cost less to operate than the original models. These policies reflect Beijing's ambition to deploy smaller and cheaper AI systems across the world's second-largest economy.

President Donald Trump and Xi Jinping are expected to meet at the APEC summit in Shenzhen on November 18 and 19. Chinese AI developers have recently asked Beijing's industry regulator for guidance on the boundaries of organized collection of output. China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology did not respond to requests for comment regarding this request for guidance. The articles leave open whether the US and China will reach an agreement on intellectual property during the summit. It remains unclear if Chinese regulators will implement concrete restrictions on the industrial use of American AI output.

stories.Headline: Fed governor Michael Barr warns AI poses risks to trading, cybersecurity and consumer protection
stories.Summary:
Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr on Monday laid out a range of perils that AI could bring to trading, cybersecurity and consumer and investor protection. He built on a central bank report issued the previous Friday that showed a surge in concern about the risks the new technology poses to financial stability. Barr spoke in prepared remarks for delivery in Milan, Italy. His remarks came hours before Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh was to open a conference at the San Francisco Fed. AI developers, business leaders and academics were expected at that conference to discuss the implications of the new technology for productivity, jobs and the economy more broadly.

Some 87% of contacts surveyed for the Fed's latest Financial Stability Report, issued on Friday, cited AI as a salient risk to the financial system. They pointed to worries about cyberattacks, complex AI-related financing, and the possibility of an AI earnings slowdown spurring broad stock market declines. Barr expanded on some of those concerns and added several more. He cited the potential that increased reliance on AI models in trading could lead to herd-like behavior that could disrupt markets. He cited the possibility that self-learning algorithms could manipulate and destabilize markets.

Barr said banks may be unable to confirm whether an AI agent attempting to take actions in retail customer accounts is actually authorized by the customer to do so. He said even legitimate AI agents acting at lightning speed on behalf of retail banking customers could accelerate bank runs and overwhelm traditional safeguards. He pointed to cyber risks from AI-enabled cyberattackers or even rogue AI agents exploiting vulnerabilities in the financial system. He said AI developers struggle with ensuring their models are well controlled, numerically and legally precise, explainable, and replicable. He said the risk needs to be reduced that AI reinforces biases in consumer lending.

Barr said there is also a need to guard against risks that could result from the use of AI in financial markets, including collusion, market manipulation, or trading strategies that result in significant market volatility or even systemic risk. He did not comment in his prepared remarks on the outlook for monetary policy or the economy. A new Federal Reserve review of the best available evidence suggests the emerging AI revolution is still in its early days when it comes to seeing a return on AI investment. The Fed economists find that the data show AI adoption is high and growing. AI-adopting firms tend to apply it in only a couple of business areas at a time, such as IT and HR, or marketing and strategy, rather than across the entire organization.

Research and development, a business area where AI might provide a particularly significant boost to more fundamental innovation and productivity gains, has relatively low uptake, according to the Fed economists. Business areas like IT, marketing, finance, and strategy seem to be the most common AI applications, with less use in HR and actual production. More dramatic changes, such as using AI as part of a firm's core production process, engaging in wholesale reorganization, or fully automating some tasks, might be necessary to sustain any productivity boost over the long term. The establishment of new AI-centered businesses could also be an important channel for longer-run productivity improvements. Demand for new AI products has resulted in AI adoption growing rapidly both among consumers and firms, though most firms are currently not using AI very intensively or at all.

A report from METR, an AI research nonprofit, finds that Anthropic's internal use of AI has helped the company roughly double the pace at which its models improve on tasks that can be clearly measured. AI pundit and podcaster Dwarkesh Patel said he has come to the view that the world is only a couple years away and possibly only a couple months away from AIs that are as good as the best humans at AI research. Anthropic's S-1 public offering document offers a bunch of underwhelming case studies of how customers are using its models. As the company puts it, it believes enterprises are still in early phases of deployment, and it believes most knowledge workers have yet to fully experience what frontier AI can help them accomplish. The Fed paper concludes that AI is not yet playing much of a role, if any, in the recent upturn in US productivity growth.

The Fed paper's conclusion leaves open when AI will play a role in US productivity growth. Barr's remarks leave open what the Fed will do about the risks he listed. The articles do not say what the Milan remarks or the San Francisco Fed conference will lead to. The articles do not say how the Fed's review or the Financial Stability Report will change policy. The articles do not say what Anthropic's public offering will result in.

stories.Headline: Calif uses OpenAI's Codex agent to find a critical Java flaw in three hours
stories.Summary:
The cybersecurity startup Calif discovered a critical Java vulnerability on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. An artificial intelligence agent found the flaw in just three hours of work. One hour was spent discovering the bug and two hours creating an exploit. This discovery happened only a few weeks after the discovery of PHP2Shell. The company revealed these findings in a recent blog post.

The flaw, called Java4Shell or CVE-2026-114938, is a memory-corruption bug in the OpenJDK Base64 decoder. It can be triggered by 64 A characters followed by one equals sign. Oracle released a patch for the vulnerability after Calif disclosed the memory-corruption issue. The flaw allows for remote code execution and can reveal sensitive memory. It affects a platform powering over 90 percent of the world's largest companies.

Researcher Quang Luoung audited the OpenJDK compiler, cryptography, and APIs to find the bug. He used OpenAI's Codex agent, which The New York Times reported was the GPT-6 Cyber model. Luoung said many of the AI responses were slops, but one found the corruption. Calif stated the bug sits in hand-rolled assembly code handling the final exploit characters. The company spent only 200 dollars in tokens during the discovery process.

British expert Kevin Beaumont told his social media followers to stay calm about the vulnerability. He wrote that the flaw is not world ending and is not very exciting. He advised users to patch the system as they normally do later that day. Many government systems and large companies are affected because they rely on the Java language. These organizations are urged by AI providers to use agents for their own defense.

Java is written using languages like C and C++, which allows memory corruption to persist. This is a problem because memory safety is one of the main selling points of Java. PHP2Shell was disclosed on October 21 and impacted the popular PHP language and hosting platforms. AI agents are increasingly revealing vulnerabilities and making it easier for hackers to attack systems. These tools can build exploitation chains almost autonomously after initial pipelines are established.

Organizations must now apply the Oracle patch to protect their systems from the Java4Shell vulnerability. There is no universal exploit because the impact depends on how an organization uses Base64. The articles do not state if other AI agents have found similar flaws in Java. They leave open whether more vulnerabilities exist in the hand-rolled assembly code of OpenJDK. It remains unclear which specific OpenAI models are most effective for this security research.

stories.Headline: Portland council president Jamie Dunphy proposes temporary moratorium on city AI procurement
stories.Summary:
On November 17, 2026, Council President Jamie Dunphy proposed a temporary moratorium on the City government's procurement and implementation of artificial intelligence. The proposal would pause new contracts and limit the expansion of AI use in City operations. Portland City Council will hear the proposal on December 2, according to Portland.gov. KOIN reported that Dunphy proposed the moratorium on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. The proposal asks for a pause on new contracts and AI expansion so the city can properly evaluate the technology.

The ordinance adds a new Chapter 34.20 to Portland City Code. The City may not procure or implement AI-enabled technologies by any means, including trades or giveaways. Existing software uses are limited to minimal-risk uses only, and AI contracts already in effect may continue through their current term but may not be renewed, extended, or amended to add AI functionality without a Council exemption by ordinance. New AI pilot projects must meet strict criteria for safety and public benefit, and the City must produce a citywide inventory of AI in use, approved or pending approval as a pilot, or under contract within 60 days of adoption, kept updated.

Dunphy said emergent AI technology carries substantial risks to both the public and the City, so the City cannot go full steam ahead without proper policy guardrails in City Code. He said his goal is to protect public privacy, security, and civil rights while the administration makes the City's Data and Privacy Office fully operable and adopts comprehensive legislative guidelines. He said government is not beholden to profit-driven shareholders and must move more intentionally to serve the public interest. He said considering impacts on real people is not being slow but taking time for critical thinking. He said his staff spent the last calendar year trying to get more information on the structural thinking behind the current internal process and found the guardrails and access to those guidelines unsatisfactory given the stakes and community members' vulnerability to data leaks.

Megan Notarte, co-founder of AI Portland, told KOIN 6 News that Seattle has a responsible AI use policy and that she would look at what Seattle is doing for a more educated view. She said there are probably ways of moving forward that maybe are not a moratorium for the year. The City's 7,500 employees include 800 represented by the City of Portland Professional Workers, who began a strike Nov. 9. Portland is a Sanctuary City. Cybersecurity and essential City functions are not impacted, and exceptions protect necessary software with embedded AI, like spellcheck and mail sorting, leaving staff free to defend City systems against cybersecurity threats.

The City established a Data and Privacy Office, led by a Citywide Data Officer, through Ordinance 192143 on March 7, 2026, and that office is not yet operable and cannot review technology contracts. Dunphy cited several cases where the City piloted risky AI models without first establishing rigorous safety testing or clear accuracy metrics. A recent WIRED article quotes Yoshua Bengio, a computer science professor at the Université de Montréal considered a godfather of modern AI, saying pauses are our best bets to avoid the most catastrophic things and that it takes time for democracy to adapt. Governor Kotek signed Executive Order 26-26, Establishing Responsible Artificial Intelligence Procurement Standards for State Government, and Dunphy said the City's pause aligns with the Governor's leadership. Dunphy said AI is increasingly embedded in software and services sold to the government, including tools that generate content, analyze personal data, and support or automate decisions affecting the public.

The ordinance will be heard at the City Council meeting on Thursday, December 3, 2026, and Dunphy encourages public feedback and engagement before the meeting. The full text of the ordinance is available on the Council website, where people can also sign up to submit written or verbal testimony. Portland residents can submit written or verbal testimony regarding the City's approach to AI on their website. Contact is Madeline West, Chief of Staff, Councilor Dunphy, at Madeline.West@portlandoregon.gov. The articles do not say what the Council will decide or when the moratorium would end.

stories.Headline: Fractal Analytics talks to 20 to 25 AI startups about acquisitions, CEO says
stories.Summary:
Fractal Analytics, an enterprise AI firm, is actively talking to 20 to 25 startups to potentially acquire them, its group CEO Srikanth Velamakanni told Reuters, as reported on November 16, 2026. The company is India's first publicly listed pure-play AI company and helps clients including Citibank and Nestle make business decisions using data analytics and AI. Fractal reported profit of 812 million rupees, or $8.63 million, and revenue of 9.57 billion rupees for the quarter ended September 30. Earlier in November, it acquired Geneva-based analytics firm PricingOne via a subsidiary, Asper, for 1.32 million Swiss francs, or $1.57 million. Velamakanni described that transaction as an acqui-hire, which would also give Asper.ai a foothold in Europe.

The company does not have a target but is open to acquisitions of up to 10 billion rupees, or up to ₹1,000 Cr, Velamakanni said. There is no lower floor for acquisitions, and Velamakanni said the sweet spot is between $50 million and $100 million for what the firm would spend. Fractal evaluated about 800 targets over the last 12 months and reported cash and cash equivalents of ₹1,728 Cr as of September 30, 2026. The firm is evaluating startups in healthcare, as well as agentic AI and AI engineering companies, to access good engineering talent and harness relationships that the target startups have with large cloud computing firms and frontier labs. Fractal is evaluating businesses with deep AI engineering talent, strong local presence across geographies and specialised expertise in industrial verticals.

Velamakanni said acquisitions and partnerships are a major vehicle of growth for Fractal. He said AI is getting better at doing longer-horizon tasks and solving more complex problems, and the cost of using it is continuously dropping, spurring greater demand for enterprise AI solutions. He said the cost of what he termed "fixed intelligence" has declined 48% quarter-on-quarter, and at that rate the cost of intelligence from a foundation model could fall 93% over a year. He said the upcoming IPO of frontier AI model company Anthropic will be a major tailwind for AI companies, including Fractal, if it succeeds, but warned that there were structural risks with the level of debt that US companies have taken on to build out AI infrastructure. He said the structural risk the US economy has is that it is very much driven by AI growth today, but that does not mean the need for AI will come down or that companies are not going to spend on AI.

Nearly half of all M&A deals in the last two fiscal years among Indian IT and tech companies involved AI and allied technologies, with most acquisitions being used to find specialised talent and access clients faster, according to research from Indian ratings agency Crisil Ratings. Velamakanni said acquisitions would not be treated merely as a growth lever and must improve Fractal's "right to win" by materially increasing its chances of securing future business. He said the company is looking for deals that can create a multiplier effect on its growth potential rather than simply adding the acquired business to its existing operations. He said Fractal has a healthy M&A pipeline and that its board is keen to explore the opportunity, and he added that the company has sufficient cash to pursue deals and expects to announce more transactions soon. He expects enterprise AI to scale significantly over the next year as foundation models become more capable and cheaper to run, with the impact becoming meaningful as early as FY28, and he added that this shift should also reflect in metrics such as Fractal's revenue per employee.

Founded in 2000, Fractal provides AI and advanced analytics solutions to enterprises including Google, Citibank, Nestlé and Wells Fargo, and it also earns revenue through licensing and subscriptions for its AI platforms including Cogentiq, Iqigai and Kalaido.ai. In April, the company reorganised its business around three pillars: AI-led Transformation, AI Foundations, and AI Work & Workforce, and its agentic AI platform Cogentiq is positioned as the common technology layer across the three divisions. As part of the restructuring, Fractal announced a leadership reshuffle in May, appointing Kunal Jain as head of AI workforce transformation and Suraj Amonkar as chief AI research officer, while Matthew Gennone was given additional responsibility as chief commercial officer and CEO of Cogentiq. Fractal reported record revenue from operations of ₹956.5 Cr in Q2 FY27, up nearly 20% from ₹798.5 Cr in the year-ago quarter, and revenue also grew 4.8% sequentially from ₹912.5 Cr in Q1 FY27. Its net profit more than doubled 139% YoY to ₹79.2 Cr, compared with ₹33.2 Cr in Q2 FY26, though profit declined sequentially from ₹115.8 Cr in Q1 FY27.

Adjusted EBITDA rose 30% YoY to ₹154.9 Cr during the quarter, while the adjusted EBITDA margin improved 123 basis points to 16.2%, which the company attributed to operating leverage while noting that investments in AI engineering talent had a short-term impact on gross margins. Among its business verticals, healthcare and life sciences recorded the highest revenue growth of 79% YoY in Q2 FY27, revenue from banking, financial services and insurance grew 30%, and consumer packaged goods and retail, its largest vertical, reported 19% growth, while revenue from telecom, media and technology clients declined 18% during the quarter. The company made its stock market debut earlier this year, listing at ₹876 on the NSE, a 2.7% discount to its IPO price of ₹900, and on the BSE its shares listed at the issue price of ₹900. Shares of Fractal ended today's trading session 3.41% lower at ₹802.80 apiece on the BSE. Inc42 said it has reached out to the company and that the story will be updated on receiving a response.

stories.Headline: Paris Hilton and lawmakers press House to pass deepfake victim lawsuit bill
stories.Summary:
Paris Hilton joined Democratic Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Republican Rep. Laurel Lee at the U.S. Capitol on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, to press House lawmakers to pass legislation letting people targeted by sexually explicit AI-generated deepfakes sue those responsible. The bill would allow victims to seek up to $250,000 in damages under certain circumstances. The bipartisan DEFIANCE Act passed the Senate unanimously in January but waited 10 months for House action. Hilton and the lawmakers renewed their appeal alongside survivors of digital sexual abuse. Supporters sought a vote before the current congressional term ends.

The legislation would let individuals bring federal lawsuits against people who knowingly distribute sexually explicit digital forgeries without consent, possess them with intent to disclose them, or knowingly solicit and receive them. Certain claims involving creation of a deepfake alone would qualify when the person knew or recklessly disregarded the lack of consent and the resulting harm or likelihood of harm. Successful claims could bring $150,000 in damages, rising to $250,000 when conduct involves actual or attempted sexual assault, stalking or harassment under conditions outlined in the bill. Individuals could alternatively seek compensation for actual losses, including profits earned by those responsible. Courts could order removal or destruction of the material, award attorney fees and permit lawsuits under pseudonyms, and the bill generally provides 10 years to bring a claim from discovery of the violation or the person's 18th birthday, whichever is later.

Ocasio-Cortez and Lee introduced the House version of the bill, which has attracted support from both parties. Republican Rep. Kat Cammack, who chairs the Republican Women's Caucus, helped organize Tuesday's gathering with members of the Democratic Women's Caucus. Hilton said she keeps her promises to survivors and will return to these halls as many times as it takes until the DEFIANCE Act is signed. Lee said in a statement that laws have lagged behind the technology, leaving victims without clear legal tools when their likeness is stolen and weaponized, and that the bill closes that gap. Ocasio-Cortez said every day the bill does not pass and is not signed into law is a day more children, women and people are victimized with no recourse and no accountability for abusers and predators.

Ocasio-Cortez also said thousands of people in this country, if not tens of thousands and eventually millions, could be subject to sexual abuse on our watch due to complacency. Hilton said that ten months ago she stood at the Capitol and told the world what it feels like to have your body exposed without your consent, and asked Congress to do something about it. Hilton said the laws aren't protecting us, and that if this can happen to someone with her resources and platform, imagine how powerless a young girl might feel facing this completely alone. Hilton joined the press conference along with survivors of tech-enabled sexual abuse and advocates Elliston Berry and Elizabeth Cline, and advocate and father Joseph Tucker Daniels, according to RAINN's press release. The bill has attracted 70 cosponsors, including 36 Democrats and 34 Republicans, according to RAINN.

Hilton has publicly discussed the unauthorized release of an intimate video involving her when she was 19 and has since become an advocate for people subjected to sexual exploitation and abuse. She previously helped secure passage of the Stop Institutional Child Abuse Act, signed into law in December 2024, which established new federal oversight and reporting requirements for youth residential programs. Her latest Capitol Hill appearance followed an earlier visit in January, when she joined Ocasio-Cortez and Lee to urge the House to advance the DEFIANCE Act after its Senate approval. President Donald Trump signed the TAKE IT DOWN Act into law in May 2025, making certain nonconsensual publications of intimate images, including AI-generated material, a federal crime, and covered online platforms must remove qualifying content within 48 hours of a valid request. The Federal Trade Commission began enforcing those platform removal requirements in May 2026, and existing federal law also allows civil lawsuits over certain disclosures of intimate images.

The Senate previously approved an earlier version of the DEFIANCE Act in 2024, but the House did not advance it before that congressional term ended, and lawmakers reintroduced the measure in 2025. The Senate approved it again on January 13, 2026, after it had passed the first time in July 2024, and since then the bill has stalled in the House. House leaders have yet to schedule a floor vote despite the legislation attracting 70 cosponsors. Congress has until January 3, 2027, to complete passage of the legislation and send it to the president for approval. If the deadline passes, supporters will have to reintroduce the bill when the next Congress convenes.
