stories.Headline: KAIST professor Jaeseung Jeong unveils his own AI-era assessment system on tvN show
stories.Summary:
The 369th episode of tvN’s You Quiz on the Block, airing on the 18th, features Remco Breuker, a Dutch scholar of Korean studies who completed an English translation of the Samguk Yusa, Professor Jaeseung Jeong, a neuroscientist who looks to the future of AI, and actor Kim Myung-min. The episode arrives as cases of cheating using artificial intelligence come to light, raising concerns about its misuse in the 2027 College Scholastic Ability Test, which is just a day away. Professor Jaeseung Jeong, a professor in KAIST’s Department of Brain and Cognitive Sciences, will share his views on assessment methods in the age of AI and the future of technology. Making his first appearance on You Quiz, Professor Jeong will have a warm meeting with Yoo Jae-suk, who reacts as though he looks familiar, asking whether he has been on before. It will turn out that Professor Jeong has made more indirect appearances on You Quiz than anyone else, adding to the interest.

On the show, Professor Jeong will share his experience of feeling a chill while talking with AI, as well as a scientist’s insights into the age of AI. As reports of exam cheating using high-tech devices such as AI glasses raise concerns about the misuse of AI, attention is turning to Professor Jeong’s views on the issue ahead of the CSAT. He is expected to unveil a novel assessment system for the AI era that he developed himself at KAIST and discuss the potential of new approaches to assessment. Viewers will also hear the life story of Professor Jeong, who once dreamed of becoming an astrophysicist before pursuing neuroscience. From how he asked Dr. Stephen Hawking a question in person at Hawking’s first lecture in Korea when Jeong was in high school to what sparked his interest in neuroscience, the program will look at the scientific life of a pioneer who has had a major influence on popularizing science.

Viewers will also hear the fascinating idea that the brains of people in love are on a different level, as well as a neuroscientist’s perspective on love. The story behind the creation of the emotion-tracking watch featured in Park Hae-young’s drama We Are All Trying Here will also be revealed for the first time on You Quiz. Marking the 10th anniversary of the historic match between AlphaGo and Lee Sedol, the program will also revisit behind-the-scenes stories from the match, which Professor Jeong watched as a commentator, and explore the future AI will transform. Viewers can hear the stories of Professor Jeong, who even captivated Yoo Jae-suk, on the show. Professor Jeong became a familiar face to the public through tvN’s variety show Encyclopedia of Useless Facts, and through books including Science Concert and Twelve Footsteps he has steadily engaged with the public, offering lively explanations of neuroscience, human behavior and social phenomena.

The top scorer on South Korea’s tax accountant certification exam, who admitted Sunday to using AI to cheat, reportedly turned over a miniature camera, a laptop and a phone to police, and no smart glasses were among the devices submitted. He first drew attention after boasting that he had scored 397.5 out of 400 on the first stage of the exam, well above the average. Affiliates of Samsung, SK, Hyundai Motor and LG, along with shipbuilders and defense contractors, said that as of Tuesday they restrict smart glasses or require prior approval to bring them onto their premises. Companies are stepping up employee training and asking workers to report unauthorized devices, and some facilities are adding visual inspections to existing entry checks. Smart glasses can conceal cameras, microphones and wireless transmitters in ordinary-looking frames, and the security risk extends to everyday objects such as shirt buttons and pens, which can also house miniature cameras.

The stakes are particularly high at semiconductor and defense facilities that handle technologies protected under South Korea’s industrial and defense security rules, because the same kind of device that can capture an exam question could also record a chipmaking process, a vehicle prototype or a confidential document. An industry official said companies were already struggling with AI-related hacking threats, that tiny wearables like smart glasses add to their security worries, that a leak can change a company’s fortunes, and that businesses need targeted government support and clearer rules. Samsung Electronics generally prohibits on-site photography with smart devices and requires camera-blocking stickers on smart glasses brought onto its premises. SK hynix bars smart glasses and reminded employees Monday to leave them in lockers before entering company buildings and to report anyone using similar devices inside. South Korea protects key semiconductor manufacturing processes under laws governing national core technologies and national advanced strategic technologies.

The National Police Agency’s National Office of Investigation recorded 179 technology leak cases last year and apprehended 378 people, with semiconductors accounting for five overseas leak cases, the most of any sector. Hyundai Motor has required visitors to its Seoul headquarters to declare smart glasses and other AI wearables and get approval before bringing them in since June, and has reportedly extended the policy to its domestic research centers and factories. It has added AI-based battery detection to its X-ray equipment and uses visual checks to spot wearables. LG Group bars unauthorized smart devices and requires cameras to be covered on smart glasses that cannot run its security software, while HD Hyundai has restricted some smart devices at major sites and updated its confidentiality agreements and employee training. Hanwha Aerospace has added visual inspections to existing security checks and metal detection at research facilities that handle sensitive technology.

As scrutiny grows, smart glasses makers are highlighting safeguards: Samsung Electronics said its upcoming glasses will feature an external LED that lights up when in photo or video mode and the camera will be disabled if the light is blocked or malfunctions, and Meta said its models sold in South Korea rely on spoken commands and audible replies, making them unlikely to be used for cheating. President Lee Jae Myung on Tuesday ordered additional measures to curb AI-assisted cheating during Thursday’s college entrance exam, a proposed reward of at least 100 million won, or $75,000, for tips. The Ministry of Education has detected 22 test takers with smartphones in nine cities and provinces. tvN’s You Quiz on the Block airs every Wednesday at 8:45 p.m. The Korea Herald article was published Nov. 17, 2026, at 12:11:00, and the Maeil Business article on Nov. 18, 2026, at 06:00:00.

stories.Headline: Former Wall Street enforcement chief warns AI bubble will burst and cause recession before 2028 election
stories.Summary:
A former top Wall Street regulator said in mid November 2026 that the artificial intelligence bubble will likely burst and cause a recession by the 2028 election, according to CNN. The warning came as a survey reported by the Chosun Ilbo on November 15, 2026 found that 87% of Wall Street experts cite AI as a major risk. The two reports together frame a market that has risen sharply on AI enthusiasm while professionals increasingly flag the danger. The CNN report identifies the speaker as Wall Street's former top cop, a reference to a senior enforcement official, though the supplied text does not name the person.

The CNN account says the expected burst would be severe enough to tip the economy into recession before voters go to the polls in 2028. The Chosun Ilbo figure of 87% is the share of Wall Street experts who named AI as a major risk in the survey it reported on November 15, 2026. Both dates fall in November 2026, which places the warnings roughly two years before the 2028 election. The articles give no further numbers, no specific forecast dates beyond the election, and no named companies or individuals beyond the former official described in the CNN headline.

Responsibility for the warning rests with the former enforcement chief, who according to CNN expects the bubble to pop and drag the broader economy down with it. The Chosun Ilbo survey places the concern among a large majority of Wall Street experts, who see AI as a major risk rather than a purely positive force. The former official's view, as CNN frames it, is that the run-up resembles a bubble that cannot hold. The experts surveyed by the Chosun Ilbo did not, in the supplied text, offer a single unified prediction beyond flagging the risk.

The context is a market that has climbed on AI optimism while a growing share of professionals warn of a correction, and the CNN report ties that correction to a possible recession before 2028. What happens next depends on whether the bubble deflates gradually or bursts suddenly, and the articles do not say which outcome they expect beyond the former official's warning. The Chosun Ilbo survey suggests the concern is widespread rather than isolated to one voice. Neither article, in the text provided, gives a timeline for the burst beyond the 2028 election horizon.

stories.Headline: OpenAI researchers report critical PHP flaws that attackers exploit before fixes
stories.Summary:
On August 11, 2026, researchers from OpenAI privately reported critical security vulnerabilities in PHP, a foundational technology powering millions of websites including those built on WordPress and Drupal. Attackers exploited these critical AI-identified PHP vulnerabilities before fixes were publicly released, targeting operational websites and critical systems supporting businesses, government agencies, and essential public services. Reported attacks included the theft of credentials and security keys, unauthorized access to vulnerable servers, and the installation of persistent malware. Attackers also conducted destructive file-wiping and caused permanent loss of critical data, and security researchers reported millions of malicious probes and attempted exploits worldwide. Research published on November 12, 2026, confirmed that attackers exploited the PHP vulnerabilities to compromise production security gateways, install persistent malware, move into internal infrastructure, and conduct destructive attacks against victims.

One principal set of related fixes to PHP to address these AI-discovered defects changed 423 files, adding 11,556 lines and removing 1,017. Developers spent more than two months developing and testing fixes for these vulnerabilities, and attackers began exploiting the weaknesses before the fixes were released, with attacks continuing afterward. Emergency patching creates multiple obligations including eliminating the vulnerability and confirming that the service still works, and questions arose about whether critical user functions were tested and whether the many PHP extensions were tested with the proposed changes. Soon after the fixes were released, a verified crash resulted in new corrections. The available evidence indicates that PHP's automated regression tests are primarily designed, developed, and maintained by members of the open-source development community rather than by a separate, independent professional software testing organization.

The Software Development Technologies Board (SDT Corp) has committed to raising awareness of the urgent need for independent professional software testing and providing financial support to establish the Professional Independent Testing (PIT) Initiative. The mission of PIT is to strengthen the quality of critical open-source technologies by establishing independent professional testing teams, led by experienced Test Managers and Test Architects, with dedicated professional Test Designers and Test Automation Engineers responsible for developing comprehensive, risk-based automated regression test libraries. Ed Kit, author of "Software Testing in the Real World" and CEO at Software Development Technologies, wrote that developers and professional testers bring distinct but complementary expertise, and that believing in your implementation influences what you think to test. He proposed that for significant changes to foundational open-source software, an independent professional testing capability be established, bringing experienced professional testers in early to challenge requirements and design assumptions. He suggested documenting and making public what was tested, what was not, and which risks remain before a release decision, and said one possible discussion point is investing $1 in independent testing for every $2, $3 spent on open-source development.

Kit wrote that he recognized the PHP developers who added automated checks, used continuous integration and sanitizer builds, and worked with outside security specialists, but that he had not found a comprehensive public, independently authored professional QA assessment of the broader release risks. He said there is no publicly established evidence of a dedicated, independent team of professional test engineers responsible for test design and challenging developers' assumptions. He asked who independently evaluates the quality of foundational open-source software supporting businesses, hospitals, banks, governments, airports, space, and much of the internet, naming Linux, OpenSSL, Apache, Python, and PostgreSQL among widely used projects. He said corporate beneficiaries of open source could support shared testing teams through foundations, grants, and sponsorships, and that AI companies should also contribute. The PHP Foundation describes its primary mission as funding PHP developers rather than maintaining a separate professional testing organization, which Kit called fine but said another capability is needed to become the independent professional testing organization.

Kit wrote that he began his career developing software at Bell Laboratories and later worked at Tandem Computers, where he knew extraordinary developers and also saw extraordinary defects created by extraordinary developers, and occasionally was the developer himself. He said he has long advocated Keyword Driven test automation because it separates the work of designing meaningful tests from implementing and executing them. He said AI can now generate code at extraordinary speed, which makes designing the right tests more important, not less, and that developers, test designers, and test automation professionals are not competitors because critical software needs all three. He said testing is risk management, that we can never test every combination of all possible feature variations, but that professional testers should intelligently select the best combinations most likely to reveal the most significant failures. He said that without an independent professional software testing organization there is no dedicated Test Manager to lead and coordinate the testing effort, no independent Test Architect responsible for designing and maintaining a comprehensive test automation framework, and no separate team of professional test designers systematically identifying what needs to be tested.

Kit wrote that we can debate the value of AI discoveries without a coordinated plan to fix vulnerabilities before attackers exploit them, but that the larger concern is dependence on foundational open-source software without sufficient assurance of comprehensive, independent professional testing. He said the PHP vulnerability is much bigger than PHP. The plan is to establish PIT as a private operating foundation and use Open Collective to help launch the initiative, and Kit said this would complement, not replace, the work of developers and security researchers, and that it needs funding. He wrote that AI finds vulnerabilities, developers fix them, and independent professional verification and validation deserve equal attention. The articles leave open whether PIT has been established, who will fund it beyond the stated commitments, and what the outcome of the new corrections after the verified crash will be.

stories.Headline: South Korea plans unannounced disaster alerts during exam to catch AI-assisted cheaters
stories.Summary:
The government is considering sending unannounced disaster alert messages during this week's annual college entrance exam to catch cheaters using their phones and prevent cheating assisted by artificial intelligence, an interior ministry official said Wednesday. Authorities have been mulling measures to root out cheating during the College Scholastic Ability Test on Thursday following a recent cheating scandal in the certified tax accountant exam using AI. As part of anti-cheating measures unveiled Tuesday, the government said it would send an emergency alert message, designed to reach most mobile phones and sound a loud alarm even when muted, before the start of the exam to detect any unsubmitted devices. The official said the government is considering sending alerts unannounced in addition to the planned alert scheduled to be sent between 8:25 and 8:30 a.m.

President Lee Jae Myung said Tuesday he had instructed authorities to review sending additional alerts, even during testing, to catch cheaters. The government will send another disaster alert at an unspecified time during this week's annual college entrance exam to catch cheaters using their phones and prevent cheating assisted by artificial intelligence, the interior ministry said Wednesday. While the first alert will be sent at 8:30 a.m., just before the start of the test, the ministry plans to send another message at an undisclosed time to find any test takers with unsubmitted phones, according to the ministry. The ministry said the alerts will ring for 10.5 seconds at full volume, urging the public not to be alarmed.

The education ministry notified schools nationwide Wednesday that it will allow test takers to only bring in pencils inside CSAT exam rooms, revising its list of permitted items, according to sources. Authorities earlier notified test takers that they were allowed to bring black marker pens, correction tape, erasers, pencils and mechanical pencil lead for the exam. Under the revised rules, stationery items, except for pencils, will be provided at the test sites. The move appears to reflect concerns of misconduct involving miniature cameras hidden inside personal items brought by test takers.

South Korea has recently been rocked by the recent confession of the top scorer on this year's certified tax accountant exam that he had cheated with the help of AI and digital devices. The incident has deepened worries of such cheating on the upcoming CSAT, widely seen as a major life event in South Korea, where the university one goes to can heavily influence career prospects. President Lee Jae Myung on Tuesday ordered additional measures to curb AI-assisted cheating during Thursday's college entrance exam, a proposed reward of at least 100 million won ($75,000) for tips. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Nigeria wins global privacy accountability award in Brussels after beating over 145 jurisdictions
stories.Summary:
Nigeria won the Excellence in Accountability Award at the 48th Annual Global Privacy Assembly held in Brussels, Belgium, on November 19, 2026. The Nigeria Data Protection Commission received this international honor for strengthening accountability in personal data processing and promoting regulatory transparency and governance. This achievement occurred after Nigeria beat out other jurisdictions from a total of more than 145 countries represented at the global forum. The award recognizes the country for its leadership commitment to privacy and its exemplary compliance frameworks and governance within the regulatory system. Nigeria also reached the finals in two other competitive categories, which were Innovation and Education and Public Awareness, during the assembly.

The regulatory framework requires a public-private partnership approach that has led to the licensing of 367 Data Protection Compliance Organisations across the country. This specific model aims to promote accountability among more than 500,000 data controllers and processors of major importance operating within Nigeria. The system is designed to extend the regulatory reach of the Commission and strengthen the monitoring of compliance for various institutions. These efforts follow the signing of the Nigeria Data Protection Act into law by President Bola Tinubu less than four years ago. The Global Privacy Assembly is a leading international forum that brings together privacy authorities from more than 145 jurisdictions worldwide.

Dr Vincent Olatunji, the National Commissioner and Chief Executive Officer of the NDPC, stated that accountability is fundamental to effective data protection. He explained that this principle is essential for building public confidence in the expanding digital economy and earning trust from citizens. Olatunji noted that the award reflects the commitment of the Federal Government to building a sustainable and trusted digital ecosystem. He believes that upholding these standards positions Nigeria as a destination of choice for investors seeking a secure digital environment. The commemorative citation praised the Commission for its leadership commitment to privacy and its transparency in managing personal data processing.

The award affects over 230 million data subjects in Nigeria who rely on the protection of their personal information from misuse. Financial institutions, technology firms, telecommunications companies, and public institutions are all affected as they handle increasing volumes of sensitive consumer data. Other foreign data protection authorities are now studying the Nigerian model to see if it can expand their own regulatory capacity. These authorities are interested in how private sector participation can be encouraged to improve the enforcement of data protection laws. The recognition comes as global concerns grow regarding identity theft, unauthorized access to information, and various large scale data breaches.

The articles state that the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence and digital financial services has increased concerns over the security of information. The 48th annual conference focused on emerging challenges like privacy enhancing technologies, digital governance, and the protection of data belonging to children. Nigeria's framework was developed to address the risks associated with the collection and processing of personal information by various entities. The broader discussions at the assembly aimed to strengthen cross border cooperation and develop common approaches to protecting personal information globally. This background highlights the critical need for effective enforcement of regulations to build confidence in the national digital economy.

The award is expected to boost the visibility of Nigeria within the field of international privacy governance and regulatory leadership. Future progress will be measured by sustained enforcement, public awareness, and the accountability of organisations that handle personal information. The articles leave open how the licensed compliance organisations will continue to monitor the thousands of data controllers in Nigeria. It remains unclear how the government will address the ongoing threats of identity theft and unauthorized access to sensitive consumer data. The text does not specify the exact timeline for implementing the innovative compliance mechanisms mentioned in the competition finals.

stories.Summary:
Kansas State University is proposing a new master’s degree in artificial intelligence systems and their applications, which the Kansas Board of Regents was considering this week, according to a report by Megan Moser published on November 18, 2026. The degree would be part of the Department of Computer Science in the College of Engineering at K-State, and K-Staters soon may be able to earn a master’s in AI if the proposal is approved. According to the proposal, demand for AI-related jobs is growing rapidly, and the new degree will help students compete in a changing job market. The proposal cites a market analysis by Veritone, itself an AI company, that showed an increase of 25.2% in AI jobs in the first quarter of 2025 compared to the first quarter of 2024. Another company reported that jobs such as AI engineer have shown growth of nearly 150%.

The proposal ties the degree to a job market that the articles describe as changing quickly, with demand for AI-related work growing rapidly and students needing new credentials to compete. The numbers given in the proposal are a 25.2% rise in AI jobs in the first quarter of 2025 over the first quarter of 2024, from the Veritone analysis, and growth of nearly 150% in jobs such as AI engineer reported by another company. The degree, as described in the proposal, would cover artificial intelligence systems and their applications and would sit in the Department of Computer Science within the College of Engineering. The Kansas Board of Regents was considering the master’s degree this week, and the articles do not say when the board would vote or when the degree would begin.

The proposal is attributed to K-State, which would offer the degree through its Department of Computer Science in the College of Engineering, and the Kansas Board of Regents is the body considering it this week. The articles do not name a specific person at K-State who wrote or presented the proposal, and they do not include direct statements from university officials or regents about the degree. The market figures in the proposal come from Veritone, described as an AI company, and from another company that the articles do not name. Megan Moser wrote the report, which appeared on News Radio KMAN and was also posted by B104.7, and the full article is available at theMercury.com.

The context given in the articles is a rapidly growing demand for AI-related jobs and a job market that the proposal says is changing, which the new degree is meant to help students compete in. What happens next depends on the Kansas Board of Regents, which was considering the master’s degree this week, and the articles do not say what the board decided or when a decision is expected. The articles also do not say when the degree would be offered or how many students it would enroll, and they direct readers to theMercury.com for the full article. stories.Headline: Microsoft unveils Windows Server 2028 with hardened security and local AI inference
stories.Summary:
Microsoft announced Windows Server 2028, the next major release of its server operating system, at the Ignite 2026 conference on Tuesday, according to TechGig. Network World reported the announcement was made this week at Microsoft Ignite and called it the largest platform update since Windows Server 2025. The new version introduces a hardened Server Core configuration by default, alongside new AI accelerators and streamlined administration capabilities. It also features simplified administration through Intune management and performance boosted by native NVMe storage and ReFS boot capability. The AI accelerators enable local inference deployment and custom model support.

The hardened Server Core configuration features a new security baseline that allows administrators to relax specific settings, reducing the effort to establish a secure environment from day one. Trusted Launch extends protection to virtual machines, ensuring boot integrity across the VM fleet, and Confidential VM support begins a journey to support integrity-protected runtimes on compatible CVM hardware. Security settings include Kerberos over NTLM, LSASS protection, and strong passwords for identity and authentication, while network exposure is reduced with SMB signing and encryption, a firewall active in every profile, and legacy name resolution turned off. Cryptography is limited to modern TLS cipher suites, with key exchange using hybrid post-quantum (ML-KEM) methods, and privilege and admin access require approval for elevation while the sign-in process runs only Microsoft-signed code. The paging file is also encrypted for platform and code integrity, and performance improvements include native NVMe storage enabled by default, NVMe over TCP, and RDMA transports.

Neil Hinnant, Director of Windows Server & I/O Fabrics PM, said the baseline allows administrators to relax specific settings, reducing the effort to establish a secure environment from day one. He added that the release begins long term investments extending Microsoft Foundry to bring AI inference to fleets of local token factories, offering customers more choices to place intelligence with the right cost structure. In a blog post, Hinnant explained that customers do not have to build and operate a separate AI stack for every location. He wrote that as AI-accelerated workloads diffuse across the enterprise, different workloads have different needs, and cost, latency, IP protection, data residency, and regulatory requirements all shape that decision. He also said administrators need to get close to the machine and understand what is happening when a workload needs attention or a virtualization host needs troubleshooting.

Infotech associate VP John Annand noted that this is the public preview phase, so a lot remains a promise on the roadmap. He said that if customers want to use Server 2028 for local AI on existing hardware, they would have to add Nvidia or AMD accelerators, with a lot of interest in AMD's ROCm open-source GPU, not to mention adding lots and lots of ever more expensive RAM. He added that the 10GbE network cards that were blazingly fast 3 years ago will likely be a bottleneck until customers upgrade to 50 or 100GbE+, and that if you want to use Server 2028 for AI, you will need to invest in a new kit. Annand said many enterprises are more interested in the quality-of-life improvements than the AI hype, and for these customers Server 2028 is a viable midpoint upgrade for existing hardware. He said running AI in the public cloud has proven to be expensive, and implied in the Windows 2028 feature set is a tacit acknowledgement that some Microsoft customers want to return to on-prem from the blue skies of their Azure environments.

Microsoft is introducing AI accelerators in its servers, and AMD's Instinct MI350P card is to be in preview in the first half of 2027 for supported Windows Server systems, including Server 2028. The company is also developing tools to manage that hardware, deploy and configure inference environments, and direct model requests to appropriate environments, and the offering supports open-weight and custom models across Foundry Local, Windows ML, vLLM, and Llama.cpp. Intune management for Windows Servers, now in preview, brings endpoint management workflows including configuration, compliance, and updates to eligible and always-on servers, while Windows Admin Center Virtualization Mode (WAC vMode), now in general availability on Windows Servers, gives admins further ability to work with specific servers and infrastructure as one fabric. The hybrid intelligence capabilities are available to a limited number of customers through an early-access program, which includes hardware requirements, and customers interested in early access can apply through the Windows Server Technology Adoption Program (TAP). NVMe and Intune management for servers are available for testing now.

Microsoft emphasized that while it is moving toward general availability, Windows Server 2028 is a prerelease product, and some elements may be substantially modified before its official release. Because security and memory defaults will be locked down, some things that worked on Windows Server 2025 may not work on Windows Server 2028 without configuration changes, and problematic features could include older protocols, legacy authentication, and some management tools and scripts. The company advised enterprises to test apps and operational tooling against these configurations before deployment, and to relax settings only when required. Windows Server 2025 will remain under extended support until 2034, and previous editions are also covered through Windows Long-Term Servicing Channel (LTSC): Windows Server 2022 until Oct 14, 2031; 2019 until Jan. 9, 2029; and Windows Server 2016 sunsets on January 12, 2027. Admins interested in testing Windows Server 2028 can register for the Windows Insider Program for Windows Server or apply to enrol in the Windows Server Technology Adoption Program (TAP) for earlier access.

stories.Headline: Investors shift funds to Chinese bank stocks amid volatility in the AI trade
stories.Summary:
Chinese bank stocks have gained significant momentum in November 2026 as investors flee a volatile artificial intelligence trade. This shift follows a scandal involving Nvidia Corp. that surfaced early last week, driving a rotation toward defensive assets. The CSI 300 Banks Index has risen more than 4 percent since the turmoil began, while the tech-heavy Star 50 Index fell about 3 percent. These lenders have climbed more than 20 percent from their late June lows due to improving margins and record profits. The rally is supported by strong financial results, including a 10 percent third-quarter net income increase for Industrial & Commercial Bank of China Ltd. Agricultural Bank of China Ltd. also reported double-digit growth, while China Construction Bank Corp. and Bank of China Ltd. saw gains of 9.8 percent and 6.4 percent.

Investors are attracted to expected yields of 4.6 percent over the next year, which exceed the 3.2 percent for the CSI 300 Index and 1.6 percent for 10-year government bonds. However, Citigroup Inc. warns that earnings growth could slow to 4.5 percent in 2027, and a proposed 25 percent tax on bond interest could hit earnings by 2 to 3 percent annually. Winnie Wu of BofA Global Research stated that banks have become the anti-AI trade because they are liquid and can absorb funds leaving the tech sector. Kenneth Goh from UOB Kay Hian noted that the appeal of these banks rests on their dependable dividends. Richard Tang of Julius Baer added that the sector remains attractive for the next six to twelve months due to stable earnings and dividend visibility.

These experts suggest that the rotation is fueled by wavering confidence in AI spending and new US restrictions on advanced chips. The current trend is reinforced by seasonal patterns, as the CSI 300 Banks Index has risen in the fourth quarter during seven of the last ten years. Analysts from UBS Group AG believe there is still room for growth because domestic mutual funds were underweight in banks during the second quarter. Future catalysts for the sector may include further weakness in tech stocks or new policies to support the property market. Despite a sluggish economic recovery, the sector remains a primary destination for investors seeking stability amid global tech uncertainty.

stories.Headline: Baltimore County students sue schools and police after AI flags chip bag as gun
stories.Summary:
A lawsuit filed Tuesday in Baltimore County Circuit Court says an artificial intelligence program mistook a student’s bag of chips for a gun at Kenwood High School, and that county police and school officials turned the mistake into a terrifying encounter for four teens. The 31-page complaint claims officers inflicted pain and suffering on Oct. 20, 2025, on Taki Allen, then 16, and his three friends, Yui-Osa Ogbeide, Devon Thompson Jr. and Keith Winfield III, all now 18. The incident began about 6:30 p.m. as the four talked and waited outside the school for a ride after football practice. Allen had a bag of Doritos his coach gave him after practice, and the school’s Omnilert Gun Detection identified the bag as a gun, alerting school officials.

The suit was filed a little more than a year after the confrontation. Three officials who received the alert recognized the mistake and canceled it within minutes, but principal Catherine Smith never acknowledged the cancellation or took steps to verify whether the alert remained active, the suit says. More than 10 minutes after the cancellation, she sent a screenshot of video footage of Allen holding the chip bag and a text message to the school resource officer, who forwarded the screenshot to the police department, prompting an armed police response. The alert went out about 7:05 p.m., and by 7:21 p.m. six police cruisers surrounded the teens and officers got out, many with guns drawn, according to the complaint.

Officers forced the teens to the ground, cuffed and searched them, according to the suit, which shows a picture of the boys with their arms raised outside the school. After officers determined there was no gun, one told the students that AI is not the best, and another muttered about stupid AI cameras and Omnilerts, according to the complaint. The complaint states that officers relied on the alert to initiate the painful encounter with the students. One officer, Corp. Michael Foehrkolb, allegedly told the teens, “Hey, thanks for not running away, that would have been a real problem,” the suit says. The suit shows a text message from the principal to school staff and administrators that made light of the incident, stating “No worries.

SRO (school resource officer) had patrol car roll through. It was a bag of chips,” with four emojis crying from laughter. Freya Jamison, an associate counsel with the Lawyers’ Committee’s Criminal Justice Program, said in an interview Tuesday there has been no public apology from the principal to the teenagers or their families. Jamison said Smith remains at the school. Jamison said the potential consequences of an armed police encounter cannot be ignored, especially with young Black men like Takei, Osa, Devon and Keith, who survived but whose safety never should have depended on luck.

She said that as AI rises around the country, it is critical that technology companies and public officials are held accountable when they use that technology to violate constitutional rights. She said human judgment simply cannot be outsourced to machines, and this case shows exactly why. Omnilert spokesperson Blake Mitchell said in an email Tuesday that the company, named as a defendant, cannot comment on lawsuits. Baltimore County police and county school officials also declined to comment on pending litigation. The complaint notes that Omnilert’s AI weapon detection system was patented in 2022, barely a year before it was deployed in Baltimore County Public Schools, which was among the first of its initial deployments.

Richard Henry, the Maryland Office of Inspector General of Education, said in December on the “C4 and Bryan Nehman” radio show on WBAL that Omnilert works in Baltimore County schools. Henry attributed the Kenwood High situation to human error when looking at video and still images on a cell phone. Henry said the case occurred in the evening hours, so it was low light, the student had the bag next to their hip, and a couple fingers were in and a couple out, and that movement was detected as a possible threat. The complaint notes that Omnilert’s AI software suffered false negatives before, including in January 2025 when it failed to detect a shooter’s gun at Antioch High School in Nashville, where two students died, including the shooter, and another was shot in the cafeteria.

All four teens in the Kenwood High incident remain friends, the complaint says. Allen is still at the school, while Ogbeide, Thompson and Winfield, who graduated earlier this year, plan to visit the school on breaks from college and attend basketball games and other activities. The complaint states that with the current AI system in place and without adequate training for police and school staff, concern remains for all four teenagers’ safety. The complaint states that the policies, customs and training failures that produced this incident also remain in place, putting all four plaintiffs at ongoing risk of being detained and searched without reasonable articulable suspicion.

stories.Headline: Stanford Medicine professor Rhiju Das says AI-designed RNAs fold into novel 3D shapes
stories.Summary:
In August, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved the first-ever mRNA flu vaccine for adults ages 50 and up, Stanford Medicine reported on November 17, 2026. The approval followed the COVID-19 vaccine, which for most people was an introduction to RNA therapeutics, medicines that use molecules to carry genetic instructions that treat or prevent disease. Rhiju Das, PhD, a professor of biochemistry at Stanford Medicine, discussed the state of RNA therapeutics and how artificial intelligence could accelerate the field. Das' latest research revealed that AI-designed RNAs can fold into novel 3D shapes, a development with promising implications for future RNA therapeutics. This could enable researchers to manipulate RNA to create medicines in ways that weren't thought possible before.

Das said that over the past 25 years there has been a renaissance in the development of RNA therapeutics that has been amazing to watch and, in some cases, take part in. He said it is likely that, within our lifetimes, RNA will become a dominant, or the dominant, kind of medicine. It may end up competing with or displacing medicines based on proteins or cells or small molecules, because RNA therapeutics are more sophisticated and adaptable. He started working on therapeutics by collaborating with pharmaceutical companies that were having trouble stabilizing the RNA vaccines, which had to be kept frozen, making them difficult to ship. He had the idea that if RNAs could fold up tightly they would become more stable, and he said folded RNA medicines have a longer shelf life.

Das said he has led a community science platform called Eterna for 15 years, crowdsourcing difficult problems in RNA design to humans on the internet and providing them feedback on their designs. The front end is a video game, and the participants are called players, who solve problems that his lab, experts and supercomputers haven't been able to solve, and not for lack of trying. Almost 40 peer-reviewed publications have come out of Eterna, he said. A few years ago the platform decided to tackle designing RNAs that would form complex three-dimensional shapes, and Eterna players got really good at it. Das said he then heard about research groups at Stanford University and elsewhere developing AI-designed approaches for 3D proteins and thinking about how to apply it to RNA.

Das said he reached out to those teams to test their AI algorithms head-to-head with Eterna players, and the first time the AI teams did very poorly. After a couple of rounds, these AI teams, when taken in aggregate, could do as well as the human participants, which he said was the first time, at least that he is aware of, that any computational method has been better than experienced humans designing RNA molecules. He said they weren't sure if the AI-generated designs from this Eterna challenge would form a sufficiently well-defined 3D structure. It turned out that all four AI designs could be visualized with a technique called cryo-electron microscopy, and some folded up into beautiful, atomically ordered shapes that were new to nature. They didn't match any fold that existed, but they were as ordered as the most well-defined structures ever seen in nature, and Das said these RNA folds were elaborate, intricate interactions he thought would take billions of years of evolution, and they came for free.

Das said this kind of sophistication could mean it is possible for future RNA therapeutics to sense what kind of cell they are in, compute molecular signals, and even control when a treatment turns on or off. He said there are a lot of AI-designed small molecule drugs and proteins going through clinical trials, and those fields benefited from incredible AI tools beginning around 2021 or 2022, and it has taken several years to build up momentum and investment. He said RNA therapeutics is probably at least another five years away, and there are several foundational design problems to solve. He said they can solve them on Eterna and with the rest of the RNA and AI community over the next year, and those will become seminal proofs of concept that can seed a new ecosystem of RNA design. Das said he is much more optimistic about RNA design now than he was a year ago.

Das said there is an exciting window in the next few years where folks who are interested in this problem can take part in the foundational technologies that will define all future RNA therapeutics. He said it is happening on platforms like Eterna, and he invited people to take part. He said you don't even have to be a scientist to get in at the beginning of RNA design for RNA therapeutics. He said it is not often you get in on the ground floor of something that will have such a huge impact. The article did not say when an AI-designed RNA drug might reach patients beyond Das' estimate of at least five years.

stories.Headline: Stanford awards $3.5 million to seven teams for human-centered AI research
stories.Summary:
Seven interdisciplinary research teams at Stanford University recently won a total of $3.5 million to pursue human-centered approaches to artificial intelligence across medicine, science, law and education. The Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI awards the Hoffman-Yee grants to groups of scholars who aim to solve the toughest scientific, technical and societal challenges in the field. Each winning team for 2026 received $500,000 in support of its proposed research, and every proposal had to show a commitment to the institute's three research priorities. Those priorities are understanding the human and societal impact of AI, augmenting human capabilities, and developing AI technologies inspired by human intelligence.

Philanthropists Reid Hoffman and Michelle Yee gifted funding for the program in 2018, and in 2026 Google.org also supported it. A new cohort of grant recipients has been named every two years, with additional funding available to select teams in the second year of their research. To date, the program has allocated a total of $31 million to 25 teams. One winning team of legal AI scholars at Stanford will develop technologies to augment the capabilities of human lawyers and policymakers in high-stakes legal settings such as housing policy, benefits adjudication and policy formulation. After initial development, the team plans to pilot its novel AI systems with several government agencies and public institutions.

James Landay, the Denning Director of Stanford HAI, said this year's grant winners are reimagining what AI can do for humans and society. He said that across medicine, science, law and education they are building novel systems to work alongside human expertise instead of replacing it. Daniel E. Ho, a professor of law, political science and computer science by courtesy and a senior fellow at Stanford HAI and the Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research, described his team's goal. He said the aim is to develop, assess and evaluate AI systems that are not only powerful but also legally rigorous, transparent and aligned with democratic values.

The legal team notes that the U.S. legal system is vast and complex, consisting of 50 million words in the U.S. Code and another 200 million words in the Code of Federal Regulations. The article says AI can help reform and simplify this legal and policy language, but only if it is deployed responsibly. It adds that legal AI must prove it can reason in environments of disagreement and uncertainty created by shifting human values and hierarchies of authority if it is to be trusted. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the planned pilots with government agencies and public institutions.

stories.Headline: Economists Dynan, Elmendorf and Sheiner assess how fiscal policy could respond to artificial intelligence
stories.Summary:
Karen Dynan, Douglas Elmendorf and Louise Sheiner published a Brookings paper on November 17, 2026 that asks how fiscal policy might respond to the rise of artificial intelligence. The paper says artificial intelligence will probably generate major changes in the United States economy, although the nature, timing and magnitude of those changes are highly uncertain. The authors analyze a set of long-term scenarios that combine faster productivity growth, greater income inequality, job displacement and a higher capital share of income. The research is part of a series prepared for a conference at the University of Utah in June 2026 called The Forces Shaping America's Fiscal Future.

For each scenario the authors assess the implications for federal debt and for potential policy responses related to faster economic growth, the distribution of income, support for workers who are laid off, and taxation and ownership of capital. The paper argues that policies which are robust to different scenarios would be especially valuable, given the uncertainty surrounding the economic effects of artificial intelligence. Dynan is a professor of the practice of economics at Harvard University and a nonresident senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics. Elmendorf is a nonresident senior fellow in Economic Studies and at The Hutchins Center on Fiscal and Monetary Policy. Sheiner is the Robert S. Kerr Senior Fellow in Economic Studies and policy director of The Hutchins Center on Fiscal and Monetary Policy.

The authors state in their acknowledgements that Dynan and Elmendorf are affiliated with Harvard University and NBER, and that Sheiner is affiliated with the Brookings Institution. They note that the paper was written for the Brookings Institution and University of Utah conference held in June 2026, and that they are grateful for valuable comments by participants at the conference. The Brookings Institution says it is committed to quality, independence and impact, and that it is supported by a diverse array of funders. It also says that, in line with its values and policies, each Brookings publication represents the sole views of its authors.

stories.Headline: Penn's John Lapinski leads a new Chief AI Officer Initiative to connect government AI leaders and students
stories.Summary:
The University of Pennsylvania's School of Arts & Sciences has launched a new Chief AI Officer Initiative, which was announced on November 17, 2026, as the newest facet of the AI & Data Across SAS Collaborative under the SAS Horizons strategic framework. The program aims to fill the current networking vacuum for Chief AI Officers, a leadership role that has emerged in government as artificial intelligence expands into new fields, and to partner with a few such professionals to create experiential learning opportunities for Penn students. Leading the initiative is John Lapinski, the Robert A. Fox Leadership Professor of Political Science, who is one of three SAS AI Advisory Group members and also serves as Faculty Director of the Robert A. Fox Leadership Program and Fels Institute of Government. Mark Trodden, Dean of the School of Arts & Sciences and Thomas S. Gates, Jr. Professor of Physics & Astronomy, said it is a vital moment for this kind of work and that some of the best and brightest minds in SAS are thinking critically about the new technology.

As a first step, Lapinski began working with key faculty at Penn to build out a team, and this academic year their focus is on starting discussions about AI's role in government through workshops and an inaugural conference. Lapinski also hopes to begin collaborating with AI leaders in governments from Philadelphia to Seattle and Washington, D.C., working closely with Penn San Francisco and Penn Washington to start building relationships. Down the line, the plan is to help public officials navigate AI use more broadly and to foster expanded curricular opportunities for students in data-related minors in the College of Arts & Sciences. Overall, Lapinski sees the initiative as a way to bring together theory and practice, to learn from and engage with colleagues about AI, and to foster dialogue about the right mix of how this technology gets used and taught.

Trodden noted that the Chief AI Officer Initiative will foster collaboration with AI leaders at many levels of government and drive important conversations in this space. Lapinski said the initiative will not solve all the challenges but that he would like the group to be convening the table, and that they are well-positioned to do so. The program is the newest facet of the AI & Data Across SAS Collaborative under the strategic framework SAS Horizons: Pathways for a Changing World. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the planned workshops, the inaugural conference and the hoped-for collaboration with government AI leaders.

stories.Headline: Margot Kaminski co-authors AI law casebook released on Nov 12 2026
stories.Summary:
Professor Margot Kaminski has co-authored a new casebook, Artificial Intelligence Law, with Paul Ohm of Georgetown Law and Andrew D. Selbst of the UCLA School of Law. The book was published as part of the Foundation Press University Casebook Series and was released on Nov. 12, 2026. The casebook surveys developments in AI law and policy through five lenses, which are automated decision-making, laws addressing physical harms, issues relating to generative AI, privacy laws, and approaches for designing AI law. It also covers dozens of substantive legal topics, including copyright, tort, product safety regulation, the First and Fourth Amendments, data protection, and consumer protection law.

The book devotes entire chapters to cross-cutting case studies, including one on facial recognition and one on recidivism-prediction algorithms. Kaminski said the authors had been working on the project for over three years and that it was a joy to have it finally coming out in print. She said it had been hard but necessary work to come up with a workable structure for teaching a field as fast-moving as AI Law. She also said she was grateful to her students at Colorado Law for their enthusiasm, patience and support as they had been taking the course.

Kaminski is the Moses Lasky Professor of Law and director of the privacy initiative at Silicon Flatirons, and she specializes in the law of new technologies. Her focus includes comparative AI law and information governance, privacy, and freedom of expression. Her academic work has been published in the Yale Law Journal, Columbia Law Review, UCLA Law Review, Minnesota Law Review, and Boston University Law Review, among others. She has received two Fulbright grants supporting her research and has served in multiple public service capacities, including on the Colorado AI Impact Task Force and the Legal Technology Advisory Committee to the Colorado Supreme Court.

stories.Headline: MIT scholars study how AI reshapes cognition, creativity and society through MITHIC projects
stories.Summary:
The MIT Human Insight Collaborative supported scholars exploring how AI affects the human experience and reshapes higher education, MIT News reported on November 18, 2026. Pawan Sinha, professor of brain and cognitive sciences, spoke at an “AI and the Brain” event at MIT in October, supported by MITHIC. Sinha co-leads a research project exploring how AI might reshape human intellect over time. Eric Klopfer, professor of comparative media studies/writing, presented at the October “AI and the Brain” event. Klopfer co-leads the MITHIC project exploring the impact of AI on human cognition.

MIT students are going to office hours less often and spending less time working through problem sets and with one another, findings of MIT’s recent report on artificial intelligence and education. MITHIC launched in 2024 as a strategic initiative bringing together scholars, artists, educators, and researchers to explore the human dimensions of defining challenges. Since its launch, MITHIC has supported 67 projects across 31 MIT units, offering a total of $5.5 million in funding. Roughly a third of those projects focus on AI, society, and humanity, a topic MITHIC faculty co-lead Heather Paxson says has become increasingly important. An AI and Society Forum took place on campus earlier this year, co-organized by MITHIC, SHASS, SERC, and the MIT Generative AI Impact Consortium (MGAIC), featuring presentations and panels on jobs, democracy, and AI.

Paxson, a professor of anthropology and associate dean of the School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences, said that when they refer to AI and society they are not only speaking about individual ethical decision-making or how to retrain workers. Paxson said they are looking at how AI is reshaping sociality and how people relate to one another. Seth Mnookin, MITHIC faculty co-lead, a science writing professor and head of Comparative Media Studies Program/Writing, said the report was not saying AI is here and everyone needs to adapt. Mnookin said the report was saying we need to be asking more fundamental questions. Mnookin said that when the United States entered World War II in 1941, the Institute’s newly minted scientists and engineers helped shape that era through science and technology.

Mnookin said we are at a similarly consequential moment with AI, and the difference is that this time the questions that matter most cannot be answered by technologists alone. Mnookin said that is where the humanities, arts, and social sciences come in. The report on AI and education warned that AI is eroding the “creative friction” that has long defined an MIT education, students debating ideas and challenging one another, their professors, and their teaching assistants, in class and out of it. In the context of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, political science professors Adam Berinsky and Charles Stewart III and MIT Sloan School of Management Assistant Professor Chara Podimata are studying how large language models have become intermediaries of democratic knowledge. The ongoing project demonstrated how voters in Alaska’s midterms who conducted their pre-election research using Anthropic’s AI model, Claude, may have received incomplete information about candidates and their views, and was recently featured in The New York Times.

Podimata told the Times that AI is becoming part of the way people encounter and make sense of political information, yet we know relatively little about what that information environment actually looks like. Podimata said we know relatively little about how it differs for different user demographics, political identities, and geographies. Klopfer and Sinha co-lead research measuring AI’s near- and long-term effects on cognition, meeting at the intersection of AI, education, and neuroscience. The professors are examining whether generative AI is increasing the human brain’s consumption of information but offloading cognitive function, or supporting an increase in cognitive function when used as part of the creative process. Anna Huang, a professor of music technology holding an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position with the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, and Joe Paradiso, a professor at the MIT Media Lab, are examining how incorporating AI impacts the creative process and live performance experience.

Huang and Paradiso’s project, “Live Musician-AI Improvisation, Tuning the Social Aesthetics in Human-AI Partnerships,” explores what happens when human composers and contemporary machine learning systems improvise to make music together. A collective of MIT musicians, ethnomusicologists, and engineers meets for regular sessions to experiment with improvisation frameworks like stopping to discuss how technology impacts authorship and musical direction, ensemble dynamics, and other cornerstones of improvisation. Faculty will ultimately incorporate their takeaways into a future course or practicum on AI-improvisation. Graham Jones, professor of anthropology, and Arvind Satyanarayan, associate professor of computer science, used MITHIC’s SHASS+ Connectivity funding to help launch a course, 6.S061/21A.S02 (Humane User Experience Design). In the course, students examine how AI systems are designed and grapple with the consequences of AI agents entering into socio-cultural relationships with people through their ability to mimic human thought and speech.

Jones said at the inaugural MITHIC Annual Event that the crux of their collaboration is the term “humane,” a bit of a double-entendre meaning both human-serving or benevolent, and humanlike. Jones said what is interesting is that their students are discovering a fundamental tension between building a system that is good for people and one that seems human, because real people can develop dangerous dependencies. Another project, “Rebuilding Computing and Society at MIT,” is supported by MITHIC’s Education Impact Fund and led by Dwai Banerjee, associate professor of science, technology, and society. The initiative revitalized the Computing and Society concentration launched in 2019, a HASS concentration that had gone dormant, listing classes no longer being offered and with minimal student interest. The concentration now features current classes across 11 SHASS units in which students can explore computing through different humanistic and social science angles.

Banerjee, who serves as the concentration’s advisor, is also working with lecturer and research affiliate Mariel Garcia-Montes PhD ’26 to find ways to connect the concentration instructors and campus initiatives on computing and society. MIT senior Daniel Gonzalez is also part of the project, developing a research and outreach program that centers undergraduate voices in computing and society efforts across the Institute. Another MITHIC project funded by the EIF, “Review of Generative AI Assistive and Resistant Communication Assignments and Supporting Workshops,” is led by Michael Trice, a lecturer in MIT’s Writing, Rhetoric, and Professional Communication program. The project is responding to a consistent SHASS faculty request for additional training and skills needed “to fully address generative AI concerns in their classes.” Trice is creating a bank of faculty resources and facilitating workshops and visiting lectures on generative AI and writing, including a talk given earlier this fall by John Gallagher from the University of Illinois, who presented findings from a large-scale survey on AI-usage and writing conducted with undergraduates at his institution in 2026.

MIT leaders agree that MITHIC, now in its third year, is playing a central role in the Institute meeting the moment, as AI presents both extraordinary potential and disturbing risks. MIT President Sally Kornbluth recently said there has never been a more important time for constructive collaboration between science and technology and the human-centered disciplines. Kornbluth said that through MITHIC, MIT is giving faculty the support to reach out across disciplines and pursue their dreams. Agustín Rayo, dean of SHASS and co-chair of MITHIC, said MIT is uniquely placed to help us understand this extraordinary moment and to generate the values, tools, and policies we will need to shape AI so that it becomes a force for good. Rayo said it is essential that we deploy AI technology in a way that elevates human existence, rather than diminishing it.

At the recent SHASS 75th Anniversary Symposium, Provost Anantha Chandrakasan said given the rapid development of AI, an understanding of the ethical implications and societal impact of implementing new technologies is especially urgent. Chandrakasan, who also serves as MITHIC co-chair, said SHASS provides an essential perspective on questions concerning how technology can be developed thoughtfully and deployed responsibly, with the aim of improving human well-being. Looking ahead, MITHIC and SERC are developing a series of events that pair humanists or social scientists with colleagues in a single field, starting with mathematics, to examine what AI is changing about how that field produces knowledge. The articles do not state what the events will conclude or when the series will begin. The articles do not state further outcomes of the projects described.

stories.Headline: Mary Nichols says California lacks data on AI data centers carbon emissions
stories.Summary:
California is trying to find out how much artificial intelligence is contributing to climate change, and UCLA School of Law's Mary Nichols spoke with Marketplace about the lack of data regarding carbon emissions from AI companies' data centers in the state. Nichols is the former chair of the California Air Resources Board, and she said that once regulators and the public gain a better understanding of what data centers are and their carbon footprint, pressure will build on companies to clean up. The discussion was highlighted by UCLA in its daily news archive on November 17, 2026, alongside other media coverage of university research. The article does not give specific figures for the emissions involved or name the companies whose data centers are concerned.

The account does not specify any new rule, reporting requirement or deadline that California has adopted, and it gives no numbers for energy use or emissions from the data centers. What it describes is a gap in information, since Nichols points to the absence of data on the carbon emissions of AI companies' data centers in California as the starting problem. The piece also does not say which state agency, if any, is conducting the inquiry or when any findings might be published. It frames better public and regulatory understanding as the step that would precede any pressure on companies.

Nichols, who formerly led the California Air Resources Board, is the person quoted on the issue, and her view as paraphrased is that clearer knowledge of what data centers are and what they emit will lead to demands that companies reduce their impact. The article does not attribute any statement to the companies involved or to current state officials. It also does not say what steps, if any, firms have taken in response to concerns about AI's energy use. No further comments from Nichols beyond that assessment appear in the piece.

The item appeared among UCLA's media highlights for November 17, 2026, which also covered a study in Psychoneuroendocrinology linking inflammation and anhedonia, a KTTV-TV interview with UCLA's Anne Rimoin on measles no longer being considered eliminated in the United States, and New York Times comments from David Jewitt on light photons pushing bodies in space. The articles do not say what happens next in California's effort beyond Nichols's expectation that pressure on companies will grow as understanding improves. They give no timeline for further action or additional data. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Model ML raises 250 million dollars to value its AI banking tools at 1.5 billion dollars
stories.Summary:
Model ML, a startup creating artificial intelligence tools for asset managers, consulting firms, and banks, raised 250 million dollars on Tuesday, November 17. This significant investment has increased the total valuation of the company to 1.5 billion dollars. The business was founded by serial entrepreneurs and brothers Arnie Englander and Chaz Englander. Their technology provides professional investors and bankers with personal AI agents that can anticipate important events and execute complex tasks.

The new funding will allow the company to expand its engineering and research teams located in New York and London. These resources are intended to deepen product innovation and support the deployment of tools for a broader range of customers. The AI agents are designed to filter out noise and prepare detailed analysis in specific firm formats within minutes. This process replaces traditional workflows that previously took several days to complete after news broke about a specific company.

Chief Executive Officer Chaz Englander stated that these tools are revenue generative rather than simple instruments for productivity or efficiency. He downplayed the idea that the primary purpose of the software is to reduce operational costs for firms. Englander noted that the average user of the technology is 33 years old, suggesting the tools appeal to experienced professionals. He explained that the models provide critical context and analysis regarding why specific news developments matter to a banker.

stories.Headline: Maxine Dexter introduces bill to ban AI data centers on federal public lands
stories.Summary:
On November 11, Oregon Representative Maxine Dexter introduced a bill to ban AI data centers on national forests and Interior-managed lands. This legislation, called the Protecting Our Public Lands from Data Centers Act, was backed by thirteen Democratic cosponsors in the House. On October 5, 2026, Assembly members Cody Miller, Marisa Sweeney, and Joe Danielsen introduced New Jersey Assembly Bill A5607. This New Jersey bill aims to classify AI chatbots as consumer products to make providers more liable for user harm. Both legislative efforts seek to regulate the rapid growth of artificial intelligence technology within their respective federal and state jurisdictions.

The federal bill prohibits data centers on national forests and lands managed by the U.S. Department of the Interior. It requires federal land sold or transferred to return to government ownership if used for data centers without congressional authorization. New Jersey Bill A5607 imposes a two-year limit on chat log retention and restricts their use for advertising or profiling. This state bill also establishes civil penalties of 5,000 dollars per violation and allows users to sue for actual damages. New Jersey Bill A5090, introduced in May 2026, would impose civil penalties of 20,000 dollars per violation for specific harmful conduct.

Representative Maxine Dexter stated that public lands belong in public hands and Oregonians must have a say in their management. She argued that her bill keeps treasured lands safe for hunting, fishing, hiking, grazing, and protecting critical watersheds for future generations. Kara Williams of EPIC testified that the New Jersey bill would limit the ability of providers to exploit users' personal data. The Consumer Federation of America stated that the model bill provides a straightforward approach to address harms caused by tech companies. Ross Barnes of Galahad said that treating chatbots as consumer products is the right instinct for determining who is responsible.

Randi Spivak of the Center for Biological Diversity called data centers water-guzzling, pollution-spewing facilities that turn wildlife lands into corporate industrial sites. EPIC warned that unregulated chatbots cause devastating harms, including suicide, self-harm, violence, sexual exploitation, financial scams, and various mental health injuries. The legislation affects chatbot users, including those using OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude, as well as businesses that distribute these tools. A Pew Research report found that 54 percent of Americans believe data centers are bad for the environment since January. A Rutgers study found that 74 percent of New Jersey residents used AI tools, while 59 percent favored strict regulation.

The Trump Administration sought to build data centers on public lands throughout 2026, with the BLM reviewing fifteen data center applications. The Interior Department published a strategic plan for fiscal years 2026 through 2030 to sell federal land to states and tribes. In July, the BLM approved an 86-acre AI data center near Lake Mead National Recreation Area, though an appeals board paused it. Meta built a 2.4-million-square-foot data center in Eagle Mountain, Utah, while 14 other proposed centers sit within ten miles of national parks. California's SB 243 and New York's AI Companion Models Law previously focused on chatbots designed for social or emotional relationships.

The federal bill was referred to the House Natural Resources and Agriculture committees, but it currently has no Republican cosponsors. Senator Ron Wyden introduced a similar measure in September, but Republican Senator Rand Paul blocked that specific legislative effort from moving forward. New Jersey Bill A5607 was referred to the Assembly Appropriations Committee on October 19 after a five to one and one vote. If passed by both chambers, Governor Mikie Sherrill will decide whether to sign or veto the New Jersey chatbot legislation. The articles leave open whether the House will pass the federal ban or if the New Jersey bill will be amended.

stories.Headline: Oakland City Council extends its AI data center moratorium for 10 months
stories.Summary:
The Oakland City Council voted unanimously this week to extend the city's moratorium on AI data centers for 10 months, giving the city time to produce a policy protecting residents from public health and safety dangers posed by data center proliferation. The extension passed at Tuesday's council meeting. It keeps the existing 45-day moratorium in place until Oct. 5, 2027. Councilmember Carroll Fife is leading the City Council's efforts to pass the moratorium. Protesters rallied against data centers outside Oakland city hall in September.

The original 45-day moratorium passed on Oct. 6 and was set to expire on Nov. 20. Mayor Barbara Lee backed the original moratorium in her recent State of the City address. Other California cities that already have passed data center moratoriums include San Francisco, Hayward, Oakley, Richmond, Monterey Park, Gilroy, South El Monte, Montebello, and Calexico. Thirty-five public speakers signed up to talk about the moratorium extension, and almost all of them supported it. A speaker for Care for Community Action said her organization surveyed more than 400 residents and found that 73% favor a permanent ban on all data centers being built in Oakland.

Fife said two of the giants in the tech industry have leased space in West Oakland, and another has shown interest in a downtown location. She said she felt it was imperative to take immediate action to protect Oakland residents from what has been seen in other parts of the country. She said the move is not a rejection of technology or economic growth but guardrails against an industry that has steamrolled individuals throughout the entire globe. She said it is important that staff have the ability to do the appropriate study and outreach so the community has a voice in anything that will impact their lives. Lee said residents need to weigh in on any industry that is trying to come to Oakland.

Bill Gilchrist, director of the city's Planning and Building Department, said the city is committed to looking at areas that might be most severely impacted by land use and residential proximity. He said the city will make sure to engage members of the community who may historically have not been able to participate or be invited to participate in this kind of discussion. He said the idea is to do no harm. Laney College professor Peter Brown said not to cast votes based on the illusion of the old economy, where corporate investment in Oakland meant thousands of lasting, good-paying jobs and property, business, and income taxes flowing into city coffers.

Nyah Tisdell, an East Oakland community organizer with Communities for a Better Environment, said community members say no to data centers that will go straight to East Oakland, which already has so much industry and pollution. Rev. Leslie Bowling-Dyer said data centers are part of the necessary infrastructure for the rise of an economically and politically untouchable class. He said people are not being lunatics displaying an irrational fear of technology.

He said technological innovation is not equivalent to social progress. He said technological advance is not the problem in itself, but the people who control it are. Some of the speakers urged the council to consider a permanent ban on data center development in the city. The articles do not state what specific policy the city will produce during the 10 months.

The articles do not state when the council will take up the matter again. The articles do not state the names of the tech companies that leased space in West Oakland or showed interest downtown. The articles do not state what action, if any, the council took on the calls for a permanent ban. The articles do not state whether the mayor signed the extension.
