stories.Headline: Sarasota school board adopts AI policy as students warn it lacks clear standards
stories.Summary:
Sarasota schools adopted a seven-page artificial intelligence policy on Tuesday, November 18, 2026, by a 3-1 vote at the first meeting of the newly elected board, after Tom Edwards was named chair and Liz Barker vice chair. The policy said the district will integrate AI into learning while emphasizing critical thinking and creativity. Several high school students voiced concerns about AI in the educational setting during the public comment portion of the meeting. Kennedy Cole, a senior at Booker High and its student body president, said the new AI guidelines do nothing to set adequate standards for AI use. Edwards was absent from Tuesday's meeting.

The policy requires that by July 1 the district must do training on AI, maintain a publicly accessible list of all approved AI instructional tools, report all tools to the Florida Department of Education, and review the effectiveness of the AI tools and student interactions. It also requires vendors to disclose known instructional limitations during the approval process. Superintendent Terry Connor said the policy has been in the works for a year and a half. The new Sarasota school board was sworn in on November 17, 2026, and this year's election saw three new members elected, ousting the former 3-2 conservative majority. The board members sworn in were Heidi Brandt, Liz Barker, Megan Tennimon and Beth Mayberry, alongside superintendent Terry Connor.

Connor urged the board to pass the policy and said he hears what constituents have to say and agrees on a lot of it, adding that the district needs a better grasp of how it expects students to use artificial intelligence. He said the reason it was brought to this particular update is that a Florida state rule requires the district to put some language into the existing policy, as inadequate as it may be at that time. Connor promised to keep revisiting the policy and to include the community in the process of updating it. He said he appreciates suggestions to get more student input, teacher input and community input, and that the district will have that availability moving forward with upcoming town halls and other availability. Beth Mayberry, the only board member who voted against adopting the policy, said that if the district has until July and has already selected the tools it will use to implement the policy and is already taking steps, there is no rush to approve this particular policy as is without getting more input from students, families and the community.

Barker, who voted for the policy, said it gives the district a little bit of structure, some guardrails and a place to start, and that it is absolutely not the end of the discussion but the beginning, and she is not comfortable not having any guardrails at all. Sandra Otis, a student at Sarasota High, said that in addition to her personal opinion that AI usage can stunt educational development, she has noticed that the AI usage policy at discussion is rife with contradictions and includes concerns of student discrimination along with unstandardized and ambiguous enforcement standards. Andrew Light, a senior at Sarasota High, pointed to a clause saying district employees are responsible for the accuracy of AI content, and said that as a student, as the son of a teacher and as a student in classes with very hardworking teachers, he does not really see it as fair to force teachers to take the blame for a model the district approves and regulates. Cole said teachers are not told what tasks AI should be used for, and that today it may be a simple email, but before long study guides, lesson plans and entire units of curriculum are made with AI, which he said is happening in schools right now. Cole added that students do not have firm guidelines either, asking how come in one class they can use AI for citations but in the next they get in trouble for using it for research, and said a campus run by AI quickly gets demotivated, frustrated and apathetic, which he said is happening to his school right now.

Since generative AI went mainstream in late 2022, there have been plenty of important and sometimes difficult discussions about it, especially in education, with questions coming from educators, policymakers and parents. A 2025 Project Tomorrow survey found that 63% of students in grades six through 12 worry about being wrongly accused of cheating with AI. In the last year alone, more than 400 CEOs from various industries, including those from Adobe, IBM and Microsoft, have signed an open letter advocating for mandatory computer science and AI education in schools, seeing AI education as a way to maintain the US competitive edge. In Utah, the Utah State Board of Education's Artificial Intelligence Student Taskforce was formally established just a few weeks ago and now exists under the current Student Advisory Council, meeting roughly four times during the school year to advise the board, alternating between in-person and virtual meetings. The AI Student Taskforce was approved during the October USBE Board Meeting.

Matt Winters, Utah's State Board of Education's former AI Specialist, said the board regularly hears from parents, superintendents and advocacy groups but does not hear from students and teachers as consistently. LeAnn Wood, vice chair of the Utah State Board of Education, said she hopes the task force will give some real boots-on-the-ground perspective of how students feel AI is impacting their education, for better or for worse, because they are the ones who actually have to see it in action. Winters credited students for driving the work forward, saying the story is 100% about the kids, that they figured out how to do this, and that the work is flowing through him, not because of him. Although students have not yet been assigned to the task force, several have helped set the effort in motion, including one student from one of Utah's largest districts who contacted the technology director about a year ago and asked how to get started, a high school senior who recently interned at an AI law office and hopes to continue learning about AI policy, a charter school student who wants to bring his own experience with learning disabilities to the conversation, and another student running projects with the STEM Action Center. Wood said one challenge might be getting more students beyond the 15 who currently serve on the council, and Winters has prompted students on how they can bring in more of their peers, with ideas such as a hackathon or another collaborative, judged experience already taking shape.

stories.Headline: California enacts four AI employment laws requiring disclosure and human review
stories.Summary:
The California legislature recently enacted several laws relating to the use of Artificial Intelligence in employment, according to articles published on November 17, 2026 by employmentlawworldview.com and natlawreview.com. The articles describe Senate Bill 951, Assembly Bill 1331, Assembly Bill 1883 and Senate Bill 947, known as the “No Robo Bosses Act.” The articles state that employers with employees in California should take note of the requirements imposed by these new laws and modify practices if necessary. The articles were written by Eric W. Witt of Squire Patton Boggs (US) LLP and appeared in Employment Law Worldview and the National Law Review. The articles state that the California legislature recently enacted the laws and that the pieces were published on Tuesday, November 17, 2026.

Senate Bill 951, effective January 1, 2027, requires additional disclosures in California Worker Adjustment and Retraining Act notices when a mass layoff, relocation or termination is caused wholly or substantially by AI or other automated technology replacing employment positions. The notice must identify the number, classifications or occupations, and work locations of affected employees, the job functions being automated, and the category or type of technology responsible. It must also state at the top of the notice: “This notice is for a technology displacement.” The Employment Development Department will publish summaries of these notices and statewide reports on technology displacement on a quarterly basis. Assembly Bill 1331, effective January 1, 2027, will prohibit employers from using workplace surveillance tools in employee bathrooms and allow employees to discard workplace surveillance tools when entering a bathroom.

As a result of Assembly Bill 1883, effective January 1, 2027, California law will restrict the use of AI tools designed to analyze employees’ emotions or collect neural data, and the law includes limited exceptions for safety, security and certain federally regulated activities. Effective July 1, 2027, Senate Bill 947 will prohibit employers from relying solely on automated decision systems to discipline or terminate employees. When an employer primarily relies on ADS, a human must corroborate the decision using underlying data or other relevant information, and employers may not use ADS results that cannot be corroborated or are found to be inaccurate, incomplete or misleading. Employers must also provide affected employees with separate written notices explaining the ADS reliance, confirming human review, and describing employees’ rights to request information about the data used. The law also prohibits using ADS to infer protected status or predict and take adverse action against workers for exercising legal rights.

The articles state that Senate Bill 947 may prove to be the most impactful of the recently enacted laws concerning the use of AI in employment. As AI tools become more widely used to assess employee performance and to discipline or terminate underperforming employees, employers will need to review underlying data to corroborate the accuracy of the AI-based decision making and prepare notices to affected employees containing the legally required information. Senate Bill 947 states that it may be enforced by the Labor Commissioner or a public prosecutor, and therefore, arguably, it may be enforced through a private right of action. Given that the use of sophisticated AI tools capable of analyzing employees’ emotions or collecting neural data may be nascent, impact of this law on present employer practices is likely to be limited. Conceivably, however, as AI tools become more sophisticated and incorporated into more workplaces, this law may become relevant to more employers.

The articles state that the California legislature recently enacted several laws relating to the use of Artificial Intelligence in employment. The articles state that employers with employees in California should take note of the requirements imposed by these new laws and modify practices if necessary. The articles state that the laws concern AI-related disclosures in CalWARN notices, restrictions on AI workplace surveillance, and limits on automated discipline and termination decisions. The articles state that Senate Bill 951, Assembly Bill 1331, Assembly Bill 1883 and Senate Bill 947 are the laws at issue. The articles state that the laws take effect on January 1, 2027 and July 1, 2027.

The articles state that the Employment Development Department will publish summaries of the notices and statewide reports on technology displacement on a quarterly basis. The articles state that Senate Bill 947 may be enforced by the Labor Commissioner or a public prosecutor. The articles state that employers will need to review underlying data to corroborate the accuracy of AI-based decision making and prepare notices to affected employees containing the legally required information. The articles state that the impact of Assembly Bill 1883 on present employer practices is likely to be limited. The articles do not state what penalties apply under Senate Bill 951, Assembly Bill 1331 or Assembly Bill 1883, and they do not state whether any of the laws have been challenged in court.

stories.Headline: European Commission proposes MDR 2.0 package to ease AI medical device rules
stories.Summary:
In December 2025 the European Commission published a proposal to amend the Medical Device Regulation, the In Vitro Diagnostic Medical Devices Regulation and the AI Act in a single legislative package, called the MDR 2.0 proposal in the Comment. The Comment, published in npj Digital Medicine on 18 November 2026, reflects the situation of 26 August 2026 and includes the most recent Draft Report of the European Parliament's Committee on Public Health. The authors offer a multidisciplinary expert interpretation drawing on their experience in regulatory science, law, health policy and industry. They ask whether the reforms, if implemented, would materially improve the regulatory environment for AI-enabled medical devices in the EU. A provision-level comparison is provided in Supplementary Table 1.

The proposal aims to eliminate double regulation, reduce documentation requirements and introduce new regulatory tools. It would move the MDR and IVDR from Section A to Section B of Annex I of the AI Act, so that the AI Act's Chapter III obligations would not directly apply to medical devices. The Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, was adopted in July 2026 and permits the Commission to limit AI Act requirements where sectoral legislation provides an equivalent level of protection. It delays the applicability of high-risk requirements to August 2028, and the Commission must adopt the corresponding delegated acts by 2 August 2027. The proposal revises classification rule 11 to make medical device software Class I by default, with up-classification when output informs or drives clinical management in increasingly serious situations, while rule 3.5, which assigns the highest applicable sub-rule, is left unchanged.

It codifies the Helsinki procedure through changes in MDR Article 4 and new Articles 4a, 51a and 51b, and it broadens clinical data to include studies in scientific literature that may not be peer-reviewed, while whether this includes preprints remains unclear. It further broadens the possibility to demonstrate safety and performance solely through non-clinical data, explicitly encouraging New Approach Methodologies such as in-silico testing, and it outlines a new pathway for highly innovative devices with priority and rolling reviews by Notified Bodies after review by a designated expert panel. The European Commission concluded in its evaluation of the current MDR that the challenges limit patient access to innovative medical technologies within the EU and reduce competitiveness. The authors argue that the changes are generally well-targeted but leave specific challenges for innovative AI-enabled medical devices unresolved. In their interpretation, the revision does not remove rule 11's central difficulty but relocates the distinction between informing and driving clinical management to the Class I boundary, where misclassification carries greater risk.

They say the fault lines remain vague, inviting divergent interpretation and inconsistent decisions, and that the rule stays anchored in a comparatively narrow and now dated conception of software risk. They think the current wording and its interaction with rule 3.5 would have the opposite effect to the intended substantial improvement. The authors say relaxing clinical evidence requirements could create space for innovation but raises legitimate questions about whether the resulting evidence base will be robust enough to protect patients, particularly for higher-risk AI-enabled devices. They critique the new pathway as possibly uncoordinated, because scientific advice from the panel and conformity assessment are structured as largely separate steps rather than an integrated dialog among manufacturer, panel and Notified Body. The EP draft report addresses this partially by stating that the notified body shall be able to participate in the expert panel's discussions.

The pathway is confined to conformity assessment and is not linked to health technology assessment or reimbursement, though selected Class IIb and III devices meeting the criteria in Article 7 of Regulation (EU) 2021/2282 may undergo EU joint clinical assessment, while Member States retain responsibility for conclusions on added clinical value, coverage and reimbursement. The authors think success depends on practical implementation of the somewhat vague proposal text, on how broadly or cautiously expert panels interpret the designation criteria, and on whether Notified Bodies can deliver faster reviews. In 2025 the EU's Artificial Intelligence Board and the Medical Device Coordination Group issued non-binding guidance, AIB 2025-1/MDCG 2025-6, on the interplay between the AI Act and the MDR/IVDR, describing how AI Act requirements for high-risk AI-enabled devices can be incorporated into the medical device conformity assessment process. The guidance does not eliminate the existing overlap, since meeting the integrated conformity assessment does not remove the need to fulfill the requirements of both frameworks.

Currently the MDR and IVDR are listed in Section A of Annex I, so for AI-enabled devices classified as high-risk under the AI Act the full set of AI Act requirements, including data governance, transparency, human oversight, accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, applies alongside the MDR's general safety and performance requirements. This affects all medical devices that must involve a Notified Body in their conformity assessment, usually Class IIa or higher, where the AI system itself is a medical device or meets the AI Act definition of a safety component. The move of the MDR from Section A to Section B remains an option for targeted revisions. The articles leave open whether the proposal will be adopted, delayed or substantially revised in the ongoing negotiation processes.

They leave open whether preprints count as scientific literature under the broadened clinical data definition. They leave open how broadly or cautiously expert panels will interpret the designation criteria for the new innovative-product pathway. They leave open whether Notified Bodies can deliver faster reviews. The Comment reflects the situation of 26 August 2026 and includes the most recent Draft Report of the European Parliament's Committee on Public Health.

stories.Headline: Ackman says Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta can better handle data center constraints than neoclouds
stories.Summary:
Bill Ackman said in his third-quarter letter to Pershing Square shareholders that Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta are better positioned than smaller AI infrastructure providers to handle data center constraints. The letter followed Democratic victories in several key gubernatorial elections, including Gina Hinojosa’s defeat of Republican incumbent Greg Abbott in Texas on November 3. Hinojosa, the governor-elect, has pledged to suspend approvals for new data centers until lawmakers introduce stronger protections for communities, electricity consumers and water supplies. The US midterm elections brought renewed attention to political opposition against AI data center construction, with voters supporting candidates who called for tighter regulation and restrictions on new developments. Local ballot measures aimed at limiting or blocking data center projects added to the uncertainty surrounding the industry’s expansion plans.

Ackman identified capital availability, regulatory approvals, electricity supply, semiconductor access and political considerations as major constraints on data center development. He wrote that standing up new data center capacity requires permitting, power, chip supply and the navigation of political considerations in addition to capital. He said the neoclouds and other secondary participants face meaningful challenges with each of these requirements. Amazon trades as NASDAQ: AMZN, Microsoft as NASDAQ: MSFT, Alphabet as NASDAQ: GOOGL and Meta Platforms as NASDAQ: META. McKinsey estimates that global investment in the data center sector could reach $6.7 tn by 2030, with approximately $5.2 tn allocated to infrastructure supporting AI workloads.

Ackman argued that smaller infrastructure providers face greater difficulties meeting these requirements than the largest technology companies. He said the neoclouds and other secondary participants face meaningful challenges with each of these requirements. He identified capital availability, regulatory approvals, electricity supply, semiconductor access and political considerations as the major constraints. He wrote that standing up new data center capacity requires permitting, power, chip supply and the navigation of political considerations in addition to capital.

Neocloud companies, which specialize in supplying cloud computing infrastructure for AI workloads, have benefited from shortages of available computing capacity. Major hyperscalers are among their customers, outsourcing certain workloads to third-party providers while reserving internal resources for operations requiring their own infrastructure. This demand supports the neocloud business model, but continued revenue expansion depends heavily on bringing additional capacity online. Unlike established hyperscalers, smaller providers generally have fewer financial resources to absorb construction delays, secure electricity supplies or manage prolonged permitting processes. Their growth depends more on increasing available computing capacity than on raising prices for existing services.

Texas, the country’s largest market for planned data center development, is expected to adopt a tougher approach under Hinojosa. Projects already under construction or holding the necessary permits are generally better positioned to proceed than developments still seeking regulatory approvals. Some developers could shift planned investments to states with more favorable conditions, including Louisiana and Oklahoma. Others may delay projects while awaiting clarity on electricity pricing, water requirements and tax treatment. The decisions taken by incoming governors and state legislatures in 2027 will determine how much planned infrastructure proceeds on schedule and whether developers must revise their investment strategies.

For the AI industry, the central risk is a slowdown in the deployment of computing capacity rather than an immediate halt to all construction. Potential moratoriums on construction and permitting could delay infrastructure investments, particularly for companies dependent on rapidly increasing computing capacity. The consequences of the November elections will depend on the scope and duration of new restrictions. The articles do not say what Ackman’s letter concluded about the neoclouds’ prospects beyond the challenges he named. The articles do not give the date of Ackman’s third-quarter letter or the size of Pershing Square’s holdings.

stories.Headline: Marcos signs Executive Order 131 adopting a national AI governance framework
stories.Summary:
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. signed Executive Order 131 on Nov. 12, creating an inter-agency council chaired by Executive Secretary Ralph Recto to oversee the rollout of the country's first national artificial intelligence governance framework. The directive establishes the National Artificial Intelligence Council (NAIC), which reports directly to the president and assumes central authority over coordinating, facilitating and monitoring government AI programs. Under the order, the council will align state initiatives, eliminate overlapping projects across agencies and resolve regulatory or resource bottlenecks. Executive Order No. 131, signed by President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. on November 12, 2026, adopts the Philippines' National AI Governance Framework and establishes the National Artificial Intelligence Council. Palace Press Officer Claire Castro explained that the initiative aims to establish a unified direction for AI development while ensuring that technological progress delivers meaningful benefits to Filipinos.

Recto will lead the 12-member council in his capacity as executive secretary, while the secretary of the Department of Economy, Planning and Development (DEPDev) serves as vice chairperson. DEPDev also acts as the council's secretariat and must form an interim secretariat within 30 days of the order taking effect while submitting a permanent staffing plan to the Department of Budget and Management. Nine other cabinet-level officials sit on the council: the secretaries of information and communications technology, science and technology, trade and industry, finance, education, labor and employment, and budget and management, alongside the chairperson of the Commission on Higher Education and the director general of the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority. The president will also appoint one private-sector representative from nominees submitted by recognized business groups to serve a three-year term, with eligibility for one reappointment. Council members may designate permanent alternates holding a rank no lower than assistant secretary, and the body may invite local government units, state universities, government corporations, academe and civil society groups as resource persons.

Executive Order 131 tasks the council with recommending policy, fiscal, regulatory and legislative measures to accelerate AI adoption while protecting workers and learners affected by automation. The body will also pursue international partnerships and private-sector collaboration to strengthen domestic AI infrastructure and supply chains. To execute its mandate, the council will organize five technical working groups to draft action plans with specific deliverables, timelines and key performance indicators. Section 3 authorizes the council to recommend measures that "safeguard the rights and welfare of workers and learners affected by AI-driven transitions." Section 4 directs the relevant technical working group to "promote AI and digital education and literacy across sectors, and institutionalize scholarship programs supporting AI research, development, and use."

The order directs the Department of Information and Communications Technology to build a digital platform to track agency deliverables and milestones. Concerned agencies must submit quarterly updates through the system, and the council must submit a consolidated progress report to the president within 30 days after each quarter ends. Initial funding for the council will come from existing appropriations of member agencies and sources identified by the budget department, with future allocations integrated into regular agency budget proposals. The council must review the governance framework at least once every two years, or earlier if technological or market shifts require adjustments. Alongside creating the council, Executive Order 131 formally adopts the AI Governance Framework for the Philippines.

The framework rests on four interconnected elements: ethics and principles covering safety, fairness and accountability; technical standards and conformity assessments; a risk-based policy toolkit utilizing regulatory sandboxes, impact assessments and grievance mechanisms while preserving existing sector regulators' mandates; and enabling resources. Section 1 specifically identifies "transparency and explainability, security and safety, accountability and integrity, human centricity, fairness and equity, and sustainable development." Section 1 explains that "AI governance measures shall be proportionate to the nature, context, and level of risk." The framework builds upon the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy for the Philippines, approved in May 2025. Executive Order 131 operationalizes the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy for the Philippines, which the government approved in May 2025, as well as the AI Governance Framework subsequently endorsed by the National Innovation Council.

The issuance also aligns with Chapter 8 of the Philippine Development Plan 2023, 2028 on advancing research, development, technology and innovation. The order takes effect immediately upon publication in the Official Gazette or a newspaper of general circulation. Section 1 describes the framework as the "national strategic guide for policy formulation, regulatory coordination, institutional development, capacity-building, and other governance measures necessary to support and strengthen the country's AI ecosystem." Section 2 states that the council shall "serve as the inter-agency body responsible for coordinating, facilitating, and monitoring the implementation of the AI Governance Framework and related initiatives." The executive order does not immediately introduce mandatory AI subjects or specific classroom regulations.

stories.Headline: Bill Gross launches AI platform to help 30 million Americans start one person companies
stories.Summary:
Serial entrepreneur Bill Gross launched an AI powered platform called Idealab.ai on November 17, 2026, to help people start new businesses. The founder of the technology incubator Idealab created this tool to provide free startup ideas and potential investment to users. Gross believes that artificial intelligence can lower the barriers to entrepreneurship and help offset job losses caused by automation. He hopes this new platform will eventually create 100 million jobs and 30 million one person companies in America. This initiative aims to spread wealth more broadly and reduce economic inequality by democratizing the process of starting a company.

The Pasadena, California based Idealab Studio offers a database of 1.2 million AI generated business ideas for free to the public. This platform analyzes thousands of news articles about consumer problems and unmet needs, such as potholes, to generate these concepts. Gross wants to mirror China, which he says has 30 million one person companies, to improve taxation and income equality. Census Bureau data shows more than 500,000 new businesses launched in October, following a peak of 550,000 monthly starts earlier. The platform recently attracted 130,000 visitors, with 28 percent from the U.S., followed by Saudi Arabia, India, and Russia.

Bill Gross, the Co-founder and Chairman of Idealab, spoke about his vision at the Web Summit 2026 in Lisbon, Portugal. He told Fortune that he dreamed of making a million companies to help people who do not know where to start. Gross stated that using AI as a leveling tool could distribute wealth to many more people than the biggest companies. He encourages multiple entrepreneurs to pursue the same concept in different markets, such as Egypt or Venezuela, and eventually collaborate. Gross believes this project is where he can have the most leverage and will likely do this for his life.

The platform attracts a specific demographic, as 80 percent of recent visitors were men and 8 to 15 percent were students. Between 50 and 60 percent of these visitors are currently employed by someone else, showing interest in independent work. Many Americans are affected by wealth inequality, as the top 1 percent of households own over 50 percent of stocks. Federal data shows the top 0.01 percent of households alone own over 16 trillion dollars of corporate assets and mutual funds. These figures highlight the macroeconomic headwinds and the growing national debt that Gross hopes his AI platform can help balance.

Bill Gross founded the original Idealab incubator in 1996, which has since been credited with 45 initial public offerings and acquisitions. He also founded the education software provider Knowledge Adventure and made his personal fortune by building various types of software. The articles note that more than six in 10 Americans express a desire to run their own private companies. Current U.S. business formation remains strong, but Gross sees additional opportunity for growth through the use of artificial intelligence. This background establishes his history as a serial entrepreneur before launching the new AI powered studio for the general public.

Gross intends to focus on this platform as his final company to make the most positive impact on the world. Users can continue to take the free ideas and only contact the company if they want funding or tools. The articles leave open whether the goal of 30 million one person companies in the United States is actually achievable. It remains unclear how many of the 1.2 million generated ideas will successfully turn into profitable, long term business ventures. The text does not specify the exact criteria Idealab uses to provide investment to the entrepreneurs who use the platform.

stories.Headline: Cato Networks launches AgentSense to block harmful AI agent actions in real time
stories.Summary:
Cato Networks launched AgentSense this week to block harmful AI agent actions in real time. The company announced this patented breakthrough from Cato AI Labs on November 17, 2026. This new security capability is built into the cloud-based secure access service edge platform. It stops AI agents from carrying out harmful actions prompted by untrusted content. The tool protects the integrity of decisions, actions, and outputs as agents operate autonomously.

The tool targets indirect prompt injection found in emails, documents, webpages, or tool responses. Administrators enable it via a toggle in the Cato SASE platform in Tel Aviv-Yafo, Israel. It includes three rules covering high-risk operations, external sensitive information exposure, and critical resource changes. AgentSense is included at no additional charge for customers with Cato AI Usage licenses. It reduced attack success from 19 percent to 0.05 percent on the Agent Dojo benchmark.

CEO and co-founder Shlomo Kramer said security must intervene before autonomous agent actions cause harm. He believes enterprises need confidence to put agents in charge of critical business processes. Itay Ravia, head of Cato AI Labs, noted that AgentSense helps preserve trust against attackers. He mentioned prompt injection vulnerabilities like DuneSlide, EchoLeak, and CurXecute as reasons for this tool. The company says Untrusted Influence Detection distinguishes trusted instructions from untrusted content within sessions.

Nithin Reddy of Dayforce said scaling AI safely requires detecting actions that risk customers or data. Grace Trinidad from IDC stated that security must connect agent permissions to their business purpose. Gartner reports that 71 percent of organizations expect to deploy agentic AI within twelve months. However, only 21 percent of these organizations currently have agentic AI governance capabilities in place. These gaps leave enterprises vulnerable to data exposure, system compromise, and business process manipulation.

Agents cannot reliably distinguish between trusted instructions and untrusted data they pick up while working. This architectural weakness allows attackers to hide malicious instructions in various digital materials. Gartner forecasts that ungoverned AI agent abuse will drive 25 percent of enterprise breaches by 2028. Cato describes a lethal trifecta where prompt injection becomes a significant business risk. One example involved Claude Code attempting to modify a sensitive local file after reading a webpage.

Cato opened a public challenge where the first three eligible winners receive 10,000 dollars each. The company will use findings from this adversarial testing to evaluate and improve the guardrail. Future plans include Drift Detection to check if actions still serve the user's original task. Cato also plans to implement controls for which specific resources and data an agent can reach. The articles leave open how these future capabilities will be integrated into the existing platform.

stories.Headline: Lansing residents oppose a data center ban vote as TeraWulf subsidiary sues the town
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday night, Nov. 17, 2026, residents of Lansing, a town in Tompkins County, packed the Lansing Central School District Middle School Auditorium to oppose a proposed data center. They spoke at a special Lansing Town Board meeting held for public comment on a proposed local law. The law would amend the town code to define “cryptocurrency,” “cryptocurrency data mine,” “data center” and “general processing.” The meeting came as officials weigh a possible outright ban on data centers. The company behind the project, TeraWulf, argues in a lawsuit that lawmakers are working behind-the-scenes to stop the potential undertaking.

The law, if approved, would include “cryptocurrency data mine” or “data center” as uses within the Schedule of Land Uses or Activities. That would establish that cryptocurrency data mines and data centers are disallowed uses for the town’s zoning code, according to the local law proposal. This would essentially ban data centers within the town. TeraWulf, a company that started in bitcoin mining and is expanding into data centers, previously proposed a facility at the former Cayuga Generating Station along Cayuga Lake’s eastern shore. The town board is set to vote on the proposed ban during a regular meeting starting at 6:30 p.m.

Wednesday at the middle school auditorium. Pace Ralli, vice president of product development for TeraWulf, took to the podium to defend the proposal. He said it was an opportunity to put an unused industrial property back into productive use, create jobs and rethink what exists on the lakeside waterfront when the coal power plant is taken down. He also asserted the undertaking could bring significant private investment and new tax revenue to the community, helping support schools, public services and local infrastructure. Lake Hawkeye, a limited liability company and subsidiary of TeraWulf, filed a suit against the Town of Lansing, the Lansing Town Clerk’s Office and town supervisor Ruth Groff.

Town supervisor Ruth Groff, who is named in the suit, declined to comment. One member of the public said loons are often heard in the distance because sound really travels over the water, and contrasted that with a data center emitting over 50 decibels of noise 24/7 at the lake’s edge. Another speaker argued that going against the ban “doesn’t mean automatic support of a data center,” and said it means individual projects should be thoughtfully reviewed as they come along. Many attendees showed their support for the ban by wearing red, and a person in red said that with the same supply of electricity and more demand from data centers, everyone’s costs go up.

Lake Hawkeye, which operates at the site of the former Cayuga power plant, is seeking an order directing the Town of Lansing “to conduct a legally sufficient search and produce responsive documents in response” to the LLC’s two state Freedom of Information Law requests. The suit said the Town has not complied with FOIL and appears to have concealed documents responsive to the requests. It said Lake Hawkeye filed the FOIL requests to obtain information about back-channel discussions among Lansing Town officials seeking to thwart the construction of a data center on the site. The document claimed that to avoid detection or produce communications under FOIL, town board members took to a private Google Group managed by Ms. Karen Edelstein, the spouse of Town Board member Joe Wetmore, to discuss strategies to block the Data Center.

It said access to the group was strictly limited by Ms. Karen Edelstein, ensuring that town residents who supported the data center and the jobs it would bring could not join. It said the petitioner sought admission to the private group and was explicitly denied, so it was not able to participate in these discussions of public concern to the Town. The suit contends that the alleged use of a private, exclusionary forum by a quorum of Board members to discuss and formulate official policy on the Data Center Project violates the New York Open Meetings Law, which states all of a public body’s meetings must be open to the general public. The town board is set to vote on the proposed data center ban during a regular meeting, which starts at 6:30 p.m.

Wednesday at the middle school auditorium. People argued for and against the data center ban at the meeting. The articles do not say what the board decided at that Wednesday vote. The articles also do not say how the town will respond to the lawsuit.

stories.Headline: Ashish Mishra urges governance for AI agents that act without human oversight
stories.Summary:
Ashish Mishra, Lead Solutions Architect for Agentic AI Services at NTT DATA, published an article on 16 November 2026 about governing AI that acts rather than only answers. He described a voice bot his colleague had asked to suggest an itinerary for a trip to France, which instead supplied one for India. Mishra called it an obvious hallucination that could be verified easily. He wrote that the consequences can be far more serious when an autonomous AI agent makes the wrong decision and runs with it. He said organizations are moving away from “vanilla” AI, which simply answers questions, toward AI that can make decisions, act and carry out entire business processes.

Mishra wrote that existing governance will remain relevant, covering the quality and accuracy of AI, data protection, privacy, security and bias. He said agentic AI does not change any of that and simply gives organizations more to govern. Traditional AI produces an output and a person decides what to do with it, while agentic AI can use other tools and systems, communicate with people or initiate the next step in a process without any human intervention. He said this means questioning the output as well as the activity throughout the workflow. He wrote that every agent should have a clear business purpose and a named owner, its own identity and access only to the information and tools required for its job.

Mishra said the excitement around new technology is understandable but that letting it get ahead of the controls is a mistake he sees far too often. He wrote that by the time you discover a problem, the agent may already have acted on it. He said organizations without effective AI governance can face compliance failures and operational problems, and that when AI acts without guardrails those consequences are amplified. He said an action that is difficult or impossible to reverse needs a different level of control than a simple day-to-day task. He wrote that if something goes wrong, you should be able to see what information the agent was working with, which tools it used and what approvals it received.

Mishra wrote that AI risk is no longer confined to the information an agent produces and now extends to the running of the business. He said AI agents can take information from emails, documents and websites and interact with different tools, systems and even other agents. He said testing an agent before it starts working is essential but you cannot stop there, because the information it receives and the environment it operates in will continue to change. He said you need to know what an agent can retain, how long it keeps that information and whether anything sensitive could be exposed. He compared an agent carrying out one small, contained task to hiring a freelancer for a specific piece of work.

Mishra cited NTT DATA’s 2026 Global AI Report: A Playbook for AI Leaders, which found that 55.9% of AI leaders use a centralized governance model, compared with 37.6% of other organizations and 33.3% of AI laggards. He wrote that NTT DATA has learned many of these lessons by being its own client zero, experimenting with AI internally and encountering security and compliance issues before taking that experience to clients. He said one of the most important lessons is to start with the end in mind, being clear about what an agent should achieve, how its value will be measured and what it is prepared to let the agent do. He wrote that trying to add the right controls once an agent is already operating across your business is far more difficult. He said applying governance to AI agents does not limit their freedom but puts the right rules in place for them to operate as intended.

Mishra wrote that before you build, you should be clear on the agent’s purpose, who owns it, the data it will use and how much freedom it should have. He said that before an agent goes live you should check its permissions, testing and approvals and make sure you can reverse or stop an action if something goes wrong. He said that once it is working you should monitor how well it performs, the decisions and actions it takes, how much it costs to run and whether it delivers the results you expect. He wrote that if you cannot see every agent operating in your business, trace what happened or step in quickly, you should start with visibility. He directed readers to learn more about NTT DATA’s Agentic AI Studio and how it can help build, govern and manage AI agents across their lifecycle.

stories.Headline: Democratic Party leader Kim Min-seok pushes for 10-year exam ban for AI cheating
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday, November 17, 2026, the leader of the ruling Democratic Party announced a plan to target artificial intelligence cheating. Rep. Kim Min-seok said the party will push for legislation to bar cheaters from retaking national exams for ten years. This proposal includes the annual college entrance exam and follows a cheating scandal involving the national tax accountant exam. The top scorer of that exam admitted to using a microcamera and AI devices to cheat on the test. These events raised significant concerns just before the nationwide college entrance exam scheduled for the following Thursday.

The proposed law would extend the ban to ten years, while national exam cheaters currently face a five year ban. Those caught cheating on the College Scholastic Ability Test are currently barred from retaking the exam the following year. The government previously stated it would push to extend the ban for CSAT cheaters to a period of three years. Rep. Kim Moon-soo and twelve other lawmakers proposed a Higher Education Act revision to extend the CSAT ban to five years. This specific proposal also requires universities to share records of such misconduct with other colleges in the country.

Rep. Kim Min-seok spoke on the official YouTube channel of the Democratic Party about preparing this new legislation. He stated that a ten year ban would effectively deprive cheaters permanently of their opportunity to ever take the exam. Kim added that such a strict penalty would deter students from attempting to cheat on these important national tests. Prime Minister Han Seong-sook vowed on Tuesday to root out AI cheating by activating an interagency emergency response team. President Lee also called for a thorough crackdown against AI assisted cheating during the upcoming college entrance exam.

The People Power Party criticized the government for failing to effectively address these incidents of cheating using artificial intelligence. PPP leader Jang Dong-hyeok wrote on Facebook that the education ministry's announced measures could hardly be considered actual measures. He described the ministry as incompetent, irresponsible, indiscriminate, and reckless in its handling of the current cheating situation. PPP chief spokesperson Park Choong-kwon criticized Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin for blaming his age for not detecting AI cheating. This criticism came just three days before the CSAT after the minister spoke during a recent parliamentary session.

South Korea has seen a series of AI assisted cheating incidents involving university entrance exams and other school tests. Test takers have recently been caught using AI glasses on middle school and high school tests across the country. The case involving the tax accountant exam is the latest example of this trend of using technology to cheat. The military has also toughened its screening of smart wearables amid the scrutiny over these AI cheating incidents. Police have secured a miniature camera as part of their ongoing probe into the tax accountant exam cheating.

The Democratic Party called for thorough preparations and clear guidelines for handling suspected AI cheating ahead of this week's CSAT. The top scorer of the tax accountant exam apologized for cheating before being questioned by the police. Authorities are now working to ensure the integrity of the nationwide college entrance exam taking place this Thursday. The articles do not state if the proposed ten year ban has been officially introduced as a bill. It remains open whether the Higher Education Act revision will be passed or if the government will adopt it.

stories.Headline: California regulator Rohit Chopra warns AI companies face court action over state rule violations
stories.Summary:
Rohit Chopra, secretary of the California Business and Consumer Services Agency, said on Monday that greater accountability is needed from technology companies rolling out artificial intelligence into the broader economy. He told a Reuters Momentum AI Finance conference in New York that his agency is already eyeing the possibility of taking companies that fail to observe state rules to court. Chopra, the former head of the US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, said there is no AI exception to state legislation that mandates licensing rules governing everyone from doctors to bankers. The remarks came during a Reuters NEXT Newsmakers interview with Reuters US Financial Regulation Correspondent Pete Schroeder at the event in New York City.

Chopra said he is concerned that artificial intelligence companies may be acquiring and weaponizing consumer data, and that he has little confidence federal regulators will be willing or able to step in through enforcement action. He voiced unease about whether the Federal Reserve is assessing AI-related vulnerabilities, asking whether it is simply rooting the industry on as a cheerleader because the economy has too many eggs in that basket. He said he has real worry that any pullback or correction would end up jeopardizing the health of the overall economy. He also said self-regulation without enforcement makes it difficult to determine whether technology companies' idea of self-regulation is adequate to address the potential risks of a new technology such as AI.

Chopra said state regulators are examining ways to collaborate around developing new rules and regulations governing the use of AI as it becomes increasingly ubiquitous. He said states cannot just sit and watch, and cannot simply rely on federal regulators to shoulder the task or leave it up to companies to self-regulate. He said the situation amounts to breaking the social contract with American citizens. The articles do not say what specific enforcement actions or court cases, if any, have been filed or when they might come.

stories.Headline: Greg Abel holds 30.2% of Berkshire’s $367 billion portfolio in Apple and Alphabet
stories.Summary:
Adam Spatacco wrote an article on November 17, 2026, regarding the investment holdings of Berkshire Hathaway. He analyzed how the company manages its large portfolio under the leadership of CEO Greg Abel. The report focuses on the firm's significant exposure to the artificial intelligence sector through specific stocks. It examines the current distribution of assets within a total portfolio valued at 367 billion dollars. The author evaluates which technology investments align best with the long term philosophy of Warren Buffett.

The portfolio holds 30.2 percent of its value in Apple and Alphabet, which are both artificial intelligence stocks. Apple represents 21.9 percent of the holdings, consisting of 228 million shares worth about 80.5 billion dollars. Alphabet makes up 8.3 percent of the portfolio, with a stake worth roughly 30.4 billion dollars. Berkshire bought 17.8 million Alphabet shares in the third quarter of 2025 and increased this to 106 million. A 10 billion dollar investment was made through a private placement in June to fund AI infrastructure.

Warren Buffett personally initiated the investment in Alphabet, while Greg Abel has overseen the expansion of that specific position. Spatacco stated that Apple is the more defensive long term investment because of its sticky ecosystem and brand. He noted that Apple does not need to dominate infrastructure spending to benefit from the adoption of AI technology. Alphabet provides direct exposure to AI through Gemini models, cloud infrastructure, and the development of custom semiconductor hardware. However, the author warned that Alphabet's aggressive capital expenditures introduce uncertainty regarding the company's future financial returns.

Large language models like ChatGPT present challenges to the business model of Alphabet by competing with Google Search services. Investors prioritizing business durability over speculative upside may find Apple more aligned with the preference for established, enduring franchises. Other market participants are watching Nvidia, where founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO following a probe into alleged spying. Interim CEO Colette Kress will lead the fiscal 2027 third quarter earnings report after the market closes November 17. This report could affect AI power stocks like Constellation Energy, Bloom Energy, and the pipeline network Energy Transfer.

Berkshire first started building its position in Apple a decade ago, and it became the portfolio's largest holding. By mid 2023, Apple accounted for more than 50 percent of holdings, but Berkshire trimmed this stake in 2024. The company continued reducing its exposure throughout 2025, though it did not sell any Apple shares in early 2026. Nvidia reported second quarter revenue of 96.2 billion dollars, with its data center segment bringing in 89 billion dollars. Constellation Energy has power agreements with Amazon for 690 megawatts and with Alphabet for about 890 megawatts.

Nvidia has projected third quarter revenue of 108 billion dollars, which would be an 89 percent gain over last year. Investors will wait to see if demand for the next generation Vera Rubin platform is progressing as expected. The outlook for the fourth quarter will determine if AI infrastructure demand is accelerating or beginning to moderate. The articles leave open whether Alphabet can maintain its search dominance against new AI competitors and large language models. It remains unclear if Nvidia's leadership crisis will impact the broader spending trends of its global AI customers.

stories.Headline: Mark Ruffalo urges followers to oppose S.5653 over AI data centers and ICE camps
stories.Summary:
Marvel star Mark Ruffalo criticized Senate Democrats on November 18, 2026, for supporting a new legislative package. The actor used his Instagram account to post a video and text attacking the political leadership. He claimed that Democrats are bending to Republicans and giving President Trump more power over specific issues. Ruffalo expressed anger that this is happening while many Democrats celebrate their recent midterm election wins. He urged his followers to contact their legislators to stop the progress of the bill.

The 494 page Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, known as S.5653, fast tracks AI data centers and ICE camps. It would allow President Trump to build more pipelines, mines, and power plants faster than ever before. The bill guts Tribal sovereignty, Native American rights, the Endangered Species Act, and the Clean Water Act. A manager amendment was released on November 7, 2026, and an explainer was updated on November 8, 2026. The Senate took a cloture vote on the motion to proceed on Monday, November 9, 2026.

Mark Ruffalo stated that the bill is a horrific legislative win for the fossil fuel industry and Republicans. He asked why Senate Democrats are ignoring their election mandate to topple the agenda of President Trump. Senate leader Chuck Schumer of New York voted in favor of the legislation despite the actor's public protests. Ruffalo called the title of the bill cynical and warned of a devastating rollback of environmental laws. He believes the bill gives the president more power than he already possesses under current law.

Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon told the New York Times that he cannot support the current bill. He argued that the administration has spent two years waging a war on new clean energy projects. The Bipartisan Policy Center stated that federal reviews of business applications now take years or even decades. They noted that delays on polluting projects also block conservation projects and clean energy technologies. The bill affects public lands, endangered species, and the permitting process for various national business applications.

The Bipartisan Policy Center noted that previous reform attempts were introduced in both the House and the Senate. Senators worked for over a year to negotiate a compromise that addresses the nation's permitting process. The bill earned a 65 to 31 vote in the Senate on November 18, 2026. Twenty one members of the Democrat caucus voted for it, including John Fetterman, Jon Ossoff, and Raphael Warnock. Other supporters included Martin Heinrich, Sheldon Whitehouse, Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia, and Mike Lee of Utah.

The legislation now moves forward after receiving wide bipartisan support from members of both political parties in the Senate. The Bipartisan Policy Center intends to continue updating its explainer as the legislation advances through the Congress. The articles do not state if the bill has been signed into law by the president. It remains unclear how the administration will handle the handshake promises mentioned by Senator Ron Wyden. The text does not specify the exact date for the final vote or the next step.

Commission I of the House of Representatives proposed adding a Draft Law on Artificial Intelligence to the National Legislative Program. This proposal occurred during a coordination meeting held on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, at the Senayan Parliament Complex in Jakarta. The meeting focused on preparing the priority legislative program for the year 2027. This move aims to address the rapid development of the digital world through formal legal frameworks. The proposed legislation would enter the medium term plan if the necessary academic text is completed.

Commission I is currently managing other priorities, including the Draft Law on Broadcasting and the Draft Law on Cybersecurity and Resilience. They are also finalizing a single article amendment to Law Number 23 of 2019 regarding the Management of National Resources for State Defense. This specific amendment is required to align the law with a decision made by the Constitutional Court. Dave Laksono, the Deputy Chairman of Commission I, stated that the draft law is a necessity due to digital growth.

He noted that several other regions have already established significant regulations for this technology. He specifically mentioned that Malaysia, Singapore, China, Europe, and the United States have advanced their legal frameworks. stories.Headline: Rio Grande Valley coalition adopts term sheet setting community benefits for AI data center deals
stories.Summary:
In 2026 the Rio Grande Valley Broadband Coalition brought residents, community organizations and local governments together to explore how communities can negotiate with AI data center developers, according to an op-ed by Jordana Barton-Garcia published by the Benton Institute for Broadband & Society on November 18, 2026. The result was the RGV AI Data Center Community Benefit Agreement Term Sheet, which sets out what the region expects in return from developers. Those expectations include protections for water, air and wildlife, local jobs and support for workforce programs, affordable broadband and adoption, and public accountability. The Lower Rio Grande Valley Development Council board, the local Council of Governments, adopted the term sheet on October 28, 2026, for cities and counties in the region to use in negotiations with developers. The coalition translated its priorities into five broad areas, which are environment and resources, workforce and jobs, closing the digital divide, healthcare and telehealth, and governance and accountability.

It also set principles for any agreement, including no NDAs so that all terms are public, and English and Spanish throughout. The principles call for an advisory board with resident-majority representation, and for binding commitments rather than aspirations. Any commitments should be specific, long-term and regional in scope, according to the term sheet. Barton-Garcia is identified in the article as director of the Texas Rio Grande Valley Broadband Coalition. The article says that when an AI data center developer comes to a city or county in the Rio Grande Valley, local leaders are now prepared for the conversation.

The term sheet is described as setting out what the region expects in return from developers. The article does not name any developer, city or county that has used the term sheet in negotiations. The op-ed was published on November 18, 2026, by the Benton Institute for Broadband & Society, which describes the piece as an op-ed. The article does not say what happens next beyond the term sheet being available for cities and counties to use in negotiations with developers. It also does not report any response from developers or from the council board.

He delivered these insights during his appearance at the APEC CEO Summit to discuss how financial institutions can best capitalize on new technology. The Chairman emphasized that banks must focus on specific strategic goals to successfully integrate these advanced digital tools into their operations. He believes that the current era is being defined by these major transformative technologies.

The strategy requires banks to align their technological advancements with their existing organizational structures to ensure efficiency. Financial institutions must also coordinate their investment cycles to keep pace with the rapid speed of technological change. Furthermore, the Chairman stated that banks must find a careful balance between pursuing innovation and managing potential risks. These three pillars are intended to guide banks as they move from pilot programs into full production.

Liao Lin explained that the Asia-Pacific region offers unique opportunities for AI due to its diverse financial services and vast markets. He also pointed to the highly interconnected industrial and supply chains within the region as a primary driver for growth. The Chairman described artificial intelligence as one of the most significant transformative technologies of the modern time. stories.Headline: US restricts advanced AI chip exports to Southeast Asia and Brazil to prevent diversion to China
stories.Summary:
The United States Department of Commerce announced tighter controls on the export of advanced artificial intelligence chips on Monday, November 16, 2026. These new restrictions target Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, and Brazil because Washington believes there is a higher than normal risk of these chips being illegally diverted to China. The move follows a scandal involving the Singapore-based cloud computing firm Megaspeed, which was accused of funneling Nvidia chips to China. This regulatory shift comes as President Donald Trump travels to China to meet with President Xi Jinping.

Under these rules, companies must obtain a US license to export, re-export, or transfer advanced semiconductors to the four listed Southeast Asian nations. Overseas data centers providing significant computing power to companies headquartered in China must secure US export licenses by mid-February 2027 to maintain their services. While US-headquartered companies are exempt if they report shipments, non-American regional AI cloud companies and data center operators will need licenses for new advanced chips. Operators serving Chinese customers at scale will face the hardest challenges, as they require separate licenses for those specific clients.

Josh Gilbert, a lead analyst for Asia Pacific at eToro, stated that these restrictions act as a speed bump for the AI ambitions of Singapore. He noted that investors will now seek more clarity because the Nvidia-Megaspeed situation increased political pressure on Washington to limit China's access to computing capacity rented overseas. Matthias Hendrichs, an advisor to AI companies, explained that the rules highlight gaps in current checks since most chips reaching China recently passed through Southeast Asia. He warned that uncertainty regarding chip delivery could cause financing delays of several months for new projects.

Dr. Maria Monica Wihardja from the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute observed that Southeast Asian governments have tried to remain neutral during the rivalry between the US and China. She pointed out that while Singapore and Malaysia have export control laws, Thailand has not fully implemented its framework and Indonesia lacks a dedicated regime. This lack of oversight in some countries may increase the perception that the region is helping enemies of the United States. Experts suggest that these curbs could eventually push the region to toughen its own regulatory oversight to attract more stable AI investments.

Standing vice chairman Ha Jung-woo of the National AI Strategy Committee visited several research sites in Daejeon on November 17, 2026. He toured the National AI Science Research Center, Daejeon Tipstown, and the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology to discuss industrialization. This trip followed previous regional visits to Daegu-North Gyeongsang and Gangwon that took place during October. Ha met with various officials from academia, industry, and research to review ways to apply artificial intelligence in the field.

The committee is focusing on the K-Moonshot project, which uses AI across twelve mission areas including nuclear fusion, semiconductors, and new drugs. This effort is supported by the National AI Science Research Center, which was established in May to integrate AI into the entire research process. Additionally, the government is promoting K-Factory, an intelligent unmanned factory system that utilizes digital twin technology and robots. Ha reviewed the KAIROS platform at KAIST, which is an unmanned operating system built with domestic technology to control logistics and humanoid robots.

Ha Jung-woo and other officials discussed the necessity of strengthening industrial competitiveness to help South Korea become one of the top three AI powers. During a talk concert at Innovate Korea 2026, Ha exchanged views with Yoon Kuk-jin, Jin Yohan, and Hong Won-hwa regarding corporate survival and future talent. He also spoke with investors and startups at Daejeon Tipstown, a facility established in 2021 that currently hosts thirty companies. The participants focused on the tasks required for entering global markets and exporting the K-Factory system overseas.

stories.Headline: NTT Data launches generative AI service to rebuild COBOL systems in Java and targets ¥50 billion in revenue
stories.Summary:
NTT Data said on November 17 that it has begun offering a service called Clean Modernization, which uses generative AI to analyze core systems built in COBOL and other legacy languages and redesign them into highly maintainable Java systems. The company applies generative AI across processes that run from recovering business specifications to testing, and it expects to cut project timelines by about 40% compared with manual work. It will target financial institutions and government agencies, aiming for cumulative revenue of ¥50 billion, or approximately $313.9 million, over the three years starting in fiscal 2027. The service migrates existing core systems in stages to a state that is easier to maintain and modify over the long term. The service covers four domains, which are applications, infrastructure, operations and organization, and it reviews existing systems from two angles.

The first is visualization, which documents the current state to make it easier to understand, and the second is change enablement, which restructures systems to make it easier to limit the scope of change impacts. In the core application overhaul, generative AI recovers business specifications from COBOL and other programs and design documents, organizes intricately intertwined processing into functional units, and then redesigns the system into highly maintainable Java. The AI models used can be selected from multiple frontier AI options depending on the customer's environment and policies. At companies and local governments across Japan, core systems written in COBOL remain in operation, and the aging and retirement of engineers who understand the specifications has become a serious problem.

Against this obsolescence risk, known as the 2025 cliff, the approach of recovering specifications with generative AI could help compress modernization costs and timelines. At the same time, how to verify the accuracy of specifications recovered by generative AI is an important consideration for adopting companies. NTT Data has indicated a policy of advancing visualization and change enablement in stages, aiming to reduce migration risk by avoiding wholesale replacement. Demand for core system modernization is expected to remain at a high level, and the company's order trends are likely to affect the competitive environment in Japan's IT services market.

stories.Headline: Dell adds Nvidia and AMD systems to its AI Factory to move agentic AI into production
stories.Summary:
Dell announced new additions to its Dell AI Factory with NVIDIA on 16 November 2026, according to IT Brief Australia, extending a portfolio it says now includes more than 420 offerings and serves more than 6,500 customers. Dell Technologies also expanded its Dell AI Factory with new AMD-based infrastructure products spanning servers, modular platforms and rack-scale systems, IT Brief Asia reported on 17 November 2026. The Nvidia announcements focus on four areas: data preparation for AI, management software for AI infrastructure, partner-built validated solutions, and new storage options for large AI workloads. The AMD update includes the Dell PowerEdge M8825 server, new configurations for the Dell AI Platform with AMD, and the AMD Helios Rack-scale Solution from Dell. Dell says the changes are intended to help companies move agentic AI projects from pilot stages into production.

The PowerEdge M8825 is an air-cooled server based on AMD EPYC processors, offering up to 512 cores and 1,024 threads per node for agentic AI and other compute-intensive workloads. Dell expanded its Dell AI Platform with AMD by adding modular configurations built on the PowerEdge XE7745 and R7725 servers, which use AMD Instinct MI350P PCIe GPUs. The AMD Helios Rack-scale Solution can deliver up to 2.9 exaflops of performance with 72 AMD Instinct MI455X GPUs, paired with Dell PowerRack for networking and storage. Dell added Agentic Data Gateway, which in internal testing reduced token consumption by as much as 76% and increased answer accuracy from 60% to 94%. Dell introduced Dell OpenManage Rack Scale, which can manage up to 100,000 devices, up from 8,000 in the previous generation.

Arthur Lewis, President, Infrastructure Solutions Group, Dell Technologies, said AI outcomes do not come from models alone and take data with the right context, infrastructure that scales and solutions validated to work together. Lewis said the Dell AI Factory with NVIDIA is that full-stack foundation, one you own and control, with 6,500 customers already proving it works. Dell said Dell and AMD are giving customers more ways to deploy AI with confidence, whether they are starting small, scaling fast, or going all-in on frontier infrastructure. Dell describes the liquid-cooled storage platform as a 2OU platform supporting up to 32 NVMe drives and designed for file, block, object or parallel file storage. Dell says the 1U platform offers 67% higher drive density per rack unit than the previous generation.

Ashish Nadkarni, Group Vice President and General Manager, Global Domain Lead, Enterprise Infrastructure, IDC, said success increasingly depends on combining trusted data, scalable infrastructure, operational simplicity and ecosystem integration into a repeatable model for AI deployment. Nadkarni said vendors like Dell that help reduce complexity and accelerate time to value will be well positioned to support enterprise AI adoption. Dell says software-defined PowerScale on Dell Exascale has achieved NVIDIA-Certified Storage validation at the Foundation level. Dell says Dell Fabric Manager, in internal lab analysis, could cut Day-2 operational effort by up to 80% while maintaining a fully accurate device inventory. Partners in the latest wave include F5, JFrog, DataRobot, Dynatrace, Ipsotek, Iternal Technologies, Teradata, Aible, Atolio, Maven AGI, OpenAI and ClearML.

Dell is also adding hybrid data pipeline orchestration so pipelines can run where data already sits, including on-premises private clouds, Dell AI Factory with NVIDIA environments, non-Dell systems and public clouds. Other changes include Storage Intelligence and Data Intelligence tools to show data provenance, quality and usage across large file environments, along with a unified data access layer for tables, images, video and documents. Dell says the system can route vectors to existing databases without requiring migration, and cited indexing speeds of up to 12 times faster based on external benchmark data. The platform is also being linked with tools from LangChain, OpenAI, Codex and Unstructured.io. The Enterprise SONiC Distribution by Dell Technologies is being extended to support additional platforms, including the Z9964F-ON and NVIDIA Spectrum SN4700 switches.

The broader architecture also includes modular infrastructure built around Dell PowerStore, Dell PowerEdge XE9785 systems with NVIDIA HGX B300 GPUs, and Dell-supported NVIDIA AI Enterprise software. The expanded AMD platform will include validated support for AMD Enterprise AI Suite, Red Hat OpenShift Container Platform and Red Hat AI Enterprise. Dell says its AI Factory Engineers model brings together teams across platform design, workload delivery, data, governance and security, while its data centre services focus on power, cooling and space planning for AI deployments. Dell says the modular approach lets customers start with a single compute node and add GPUs, nodes, storage or networking as demand grows. Dell said the AMD package is backed by deployment and lifecycle services, giving customers a single supplier for integrated AI infrastructure.
