stories.Headline: South Korea activates emergency response team to stop AI cheating in national exams
stories.Summary:
An anonymous user on the online community DC Inside claimed to have used artificial intelligence to cheat on the 2024 Suneung exam. This individual allegedly used a miniature camera disguised as a shirt button and a smartphone to obtain an average percentile score of 98.6. These claims surfaced shortly after Han Won-seok, the top scorer on this year's tax accountant qualification exam, confessed to using similar AI tools. Han admitted to using a miniature camera and generative AI during both rounds of the national exam in April and July. He scored 397.5 out of 400 points and achieved perfect scores in three of the four subjects.

The current situation requires the Education Ministry to implement strict measures to prevent the use of hidden cameras and smart glasses. YouTuber Kim Min-woo, known as Mimiminu, has urged the government to postpone the upcoming Suneung to ensure proper security. He noted that the exam was previously delayed in 2017 due to the Pohang earthquake and in 2020 because of the COVID-19 pandemic. To combat these threats, Prime Minister Han Seong-sook vowed on Tuesday to root out AI cheating by activating an interagency emergency response team. The government plans to ban smart devices and deploy additional staff at testing sites to maintain the integrity of the process.

Several education experts have expressed deep concern regarding the ability of authorities to detect modern cheating devices. Kim Min-woo explained that tiny devices hidden in bracelets or buttons can solve complex questions very quickly. Kang Sung-tae, the founder of Gongsin.com, argued that checking for thick-framed glasses is insufficient because many smart glasses from China have discreet designs. He stated that he has warned for years that AI-assisted cheating was inevitable and hoped his warnings would raise awareness. These experts believe that the current screening methods are outdated and cannot stop sophisticated technology.

The South Korean government is now racing to curb these technological breaches before the college entrance exam takes place this Thursday. Authorities are focusing on identifying a wide variety of smart glasses and other wearable electronics that students might smuggle into the rooms. The Education Ministry must now decide if the existing laws allow for a schedule change to better prepare for these threats. If the government cannot guarantee a fair environment, the pressure to delay the exam may increase. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Micron President says China lags behind in high bandwidth memory development
stories.Summary:
Scott J. DeBoer, the President and Chief Technology and Products Officer of Micron, spoke about the global artificial intelligence chip race on November 18, 2026. During an interview with Deirdre Bosa on Yahoo Finance, he addressed the current competitive landscape regarding high bandwidth memory. He stated that China is currently far behind other nations in the development of this specific memory technology. This discussion highlighted the ongoing struggle for technological dominance in the semiconductor industry during a period of rapid growth.

Maintaining a lead in this sector requires a constant focus on outperforming all global competitors through superior core technology. DeBoer emphasized that Micron must partner with key customers to build products that are better than any others available in the world. This strategy involves staying significantly ahead of rivals from China, Korea, and other regions to ensure market leadership. The company believes that the only way to win is to create products that no other entity can build.

DeBoer explained that the memory business has been intensely competitive for the past 30 years without any periods of respite. He noted that there is always someone attempting to beat them, which is why the company takes this competition very seriously. When asked about political restrictions versus innovation, he replied that he can only control the ability to out innovate and compete. He mentioned that political aspects are not in his personal picture because his primary job is to deliver the products.

The context of these remarks reflects a broader international effort to secure the most advanced hardware for artificial intelligence applications. Micron intends to maintain its advantage by focusing on technical excellence rather than relying on external restrictions to hobble competitors. The company will continue to prioritize the development of high bandwidth memory to support the evolving needs of the AI chip market. Future success depends on the ability to sustain this technological gap through continuous research and strategic partnerships.

stories.Headline: Jason Wei leaves Meta to become chief scientist at AI startup Mercor
stories.Summary:
Jason Wei, known as the father of Chain-of-Thought, left Meta to join the AI startup Mercor on November 18, 2026. Brendan Foody, the CEO and co-founder of Mercor, announced the hire on the X platform. Wei has officially taken the role of Chief Scientist at the company. This move follows his time at Meta's Superintelligence Lab. He previously worked at Google Brain and OpenAI.

Mercor is an AI unicorn valued at 200 billion US dollars that recently completed a 750 million dollar Series D financing. The funding involved NVIDIA, Salesforce, Benchmark, and General Catalyst. The company was founded in 2023 by Brendan Foody, Surya Midha, and Adarsh Hiremath. It provides expert data services and talent recruitment using a network of over 5 million people. The new funds will support post-training infrastructure, model evaluation, and AI agent workflows.

Brendan Foody stated that Jason Wei will help build a research team focused on data and evaluation. He noted that Wei had been a customer and a communication partner for the company for several years. Jason Wei expressed happiness about joining Mercor after spending over a year at Meta TBD Lab. He believes that data will shape the next frontier of AI development as more companies train models. His work will intersect with his previous experience in creating evaluation benchmarks.

The transition affects AI labs and enterprise customers who need specialized data for financial, legal, or software engineering tasks. Mercor's research team already includes Edward J. Hu, the first author of the LoRA paper. Other team members include Victor Barres and Minyang Tian, with researchers from Ai2 and Anthropic. The company uses the APEX benchmarks to test if AI can complete actual work requirements. They recently improved a Qwen3.5-397B model score from 16 percent to 27 percent on APEX-Agents.

Wei became famous for a 2022 paper on Chain-of-Thought Prompting that improved multi-step reasoning in large language models. While at OpenAI in 2023, he worked on Deep Research and OpenAI o1. He developed SimpleQA in 2024 to measure factual accuracy using 4326 questions. In 2025, he released BrowseComp for web search and HealthBench for medical conversations. He then joined Meta's Superintelligence Lab in July 2025.

Wei will now focus on promoting research in data and evaluation for real work scenarios. Mercor is expanding its services from providing expert data to helping customers adapt AI models. The company aims to discover tasks models cannot complete and use experts to build training data. The articles do not state the specific projects Wei will lead first. They leave open the long-term impact of his move to a data-focused startup.

stories.Headline: Port Washington mayor Ted Neitzke leads tours of a $15M AI data center site as residents raise concerns
stories.Summary:
A $15 million artificial intelligence data center is under construction in Port Washington, Wisconsin, developed by Vantage in partnership with Oracle and OpenAI, and it is drawing both community curiosity and criticism. The 672-acre site, with an additional 1,000 acres reserved for expansion, is larger than the entire Village of Whitefish Bay, and the construction site sees 3,500 workers daily. Port Washington Mayor Ted Neitzke has been leading van tours of the site to engage locals and address their concerns about the project. The first phase includes four data center buildings, each with a footprint of 800,000 square feet, large enough to hold two Lambeau Fields.

Vantage says the center will be operational by early 2028, providing internet and cloud services while storing, processing, and distributing data. The project is expected to bring significant tax benefits by transforming agriculturally zoned land assessed at a few million dollars into a site valued at $120 million, which is anticipated to support the majority of city services. Construction on the data center began in December 2022 and is scheduled to be completed by 2028. Neitzke said almost everything visible at the site is manufactured, made or fabricated in Wisconsin, so it is not just a Port Washington thing but a statewide one.

Neitzke said he was surprised and caught off guard by the unexpected backlash, saying he did not see that coming. He has emphasized transparency during the tours, addressing concerns about water usage, power supply and electricity rates, and he said the center does not use a lot of water and that power is protected and rates do not go up. He believes data centers are the newest of all the utilities, something everyone needs alongside clean water, clean sidewalks and electricity, and now information. He has also been advising elected officials across the country on how to navigate similar projects, saying local communities are in an amazing position to negotiate.

Clean Wisconsin and other groups have raised concerns about the environmental impact of AI data centers and the power plants required to support them. A Clean Wisconsin representative said Wisconsin is incredibly vulnerable right now to AI data centers, and that a project as large as the one in Port Washington will be vastly bigger in terms of energy needs than anything the state has ever seen. The representative said those are resources everyone relies on and that the conversation needed to happen well before now, when construction is going on and almost done. One contentious meeting resulted in the arrest of three women, and Al Poull, whose family has lived on a nearby farm for 126 years, acknowledged the changes, saying things change and it is just the way it is.

stories.Headline: Asia-Pacific university leaders urge redefining core missions as AI reshapes knowledge delivery
stories.Summary:
University leaders from the Asia-Pacific region met during the APEC meetings week in November 2026 to discuss how artificial intelligence is challenging traditional knowledge delivery. These educators believe that institutions must redefine their core missions to foster humanistic judgment and bridge the digital divide to ensure education equity. They argue that universities should transition from being the sole providers of teaching to becoming hubs for the co-creation of validated knowledge. This shift requires universities to reform teaching methods by using AI for content delivery while reserving class time for critical discussions and case studies. Angelo Jimenez of the University of the Philippines suggests establishing jointly recognized doctoral programs in bioscience and engineering to retain highly skilled talent.

Tatacipta Dirgantara from the Bandung Institute of Technology emphasizes the need for professor-to-professor partnerships and shared resources to foster intercultural understanding. These changes aim to strengthen foundational literacy and numeracy so that humans maintain control over advanced technology. Angelo Jimenez stated that humans must control legitimacy and validity because AI cannot replace the responsibility of human judgment. Tatacipta Dirgantara noted that while AI is an enabler like the calculator, it cannot replace empathy or the responsibility educators have toward the people. Yang Bin of Tsinghua University observed that some faculty are moving to industry for better computing resources and real-world data.

He believes that sustained dialogue during events like the APEC University Leaders Forum will help build consensus on academic credits and quality assurance. The academic community expects the center of gravity for global higher education to shift toward the Asia-Pacific region as it grows as an innovation hub. Many institutions used the recent APEC gatherings to sign new partnership programs or expand existing collaborations to address the revolutionary impact of AI. These leaders believe that mutual benefit and shared research interests will make these cross-border connections sustainable for the future. Future efforts will focus on mutual recognition of degrees to support the region's expanding role in global economic development.

stories.Headline: Dharma-AI researchers predict fine-tuning job duration from pre-dispatch configuration with a CatBoost model
stories.Summary:
The articles report a preview of an upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models, by Bruno Duarte, Gabriel Pimenta de Freitas Cardoso, Isis F Carvalho, Breno de Almeida Beleza and Felipe Lima of Dharma-AI, posted on Hugging Face on November 18, 2026. The authors took 272 real supervised fine-tuning jobs from their production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors. The usual FLOP-based estimate explained little of what they observed, with R² = 0.31 and MAE 12.41 h. A CatBoost regressor seeing only information available before dispatch reached R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The full version of the paper will be on arXiv soon.

The FLOP baseline counts scheduled evaluation tokens as well as training tokens, and the authors swept MFU from 0.25 to 0.65, with the best setting, 30%, still leaving a mean error above 12 hours on jobs that last 23 hours on average. The final CatBoost model uses 24 features, with the FLOP estimate itself, MFU fixed at 0.45, included as a feature called baseline_time. The 272 SFT runs covered several model families up to 15 billion parameters, both LoRA and full fine-tuning, and jobs ran on 1, 2 or 4 GPUs drawn from a pool of 8 to 32 H200s across 1 to 4 nodes. Durations ranged from 1.6 to 172.4 hours, with a mean of 23.43 h and a median of 15.29 h. The stack was Hugging Face Transformers and Unsloth, modelled as a categorical feature with no assumption of a fixed speedup between the two.

The authors say the gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do: the regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs. They note that real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance. They say a job is more than its optimization loop, since before the first step there is environment setup, model download and loading, and tokenization, during training there are periodic evaluations and checkpoint uploads, and at the end the final model goes to object storage. They write that on a multi-tenant cluster all of it competes with other jobs for network and storage I/O, and that two jobs with the same nominal compute can finish hours apart. They state that everything is known before dispatch, with every input coming from the submitted configuration, and that this is what makes the prediction usable for scheduling.

As a second baseline the authors took Calculon (Isaev et al., SC '23), an analytical performance model for LLM training from prior work, and extended the public implementation to cover LoRA, grouped-query attention, fused attention, bfloat16 and SwiGLU. Its estimates still corresponded to a median of only 11% of the observed wall-clock time, which the authors say says nothing against Calculon as a step-level tool, which is what it was designed for. Ridge brought MAE down to 7.23 h, and CatBoost and XGBoost landed within one standard deviation of each other on every metric, with CatBoost carried forward because it had the lowest mean error across the board. In CatBoost's feature importance, num_eval_data ranked first, followed by num_trainable_params, batch_eval_size_percent, num_all_params and num_gpus*batch_train_percent, with num_params_saved close behind, and SHAP values told the same story. The authors caution that feature importance is not a causal claim, and that larger GPU allocations show positive contributions to predicted time because in their data bigger allocations go with bigger jobs, so num_gpus acts partly as a proxy for job scale.

The authors compared Linear Regression, Ridge, XGBoost and CatBoost, with feature selection combining correlation filtering, mutual information and permutation importance across 18 candidate feature sets, followed by a grid search with MAE as the criterion. They treat end-to-end duration as a supervised regression problem, predicting the wall-clock time between the moment the job gets its GPUs and the moment it is done, with queue time excluded. On top of the raw configuration they derive quantities such as num_eval_data, num_saves and num_params_saved, and per-GPU token volumes. Across all 272 out-of-fold predictions, 80% are within 2.20 h and 90% are within 4.31 h, and up to 60 hours the median error stays at about one hour or less, with the long tail where the model struggles read as a data limitation given only 13 runs above 60 hours. On a fixed 20% holdout, MAE dropped from 1.63 h to 1.50 h when going from 85% to 100% of the training partition, with no clear plateau.

The authors list limitations: SFT only, with other training and alignment strategies such as RLHF, DPO or RLVR not included; one GPU type, since every run used H200s and the fitted model is calibrated to that infrastructure and should not be expected to transfer numerically to other GPU generations without retraining; and few very long runs, with errors widening above 60 hours. They say a predictor for mixed pools would also need hardware descriptors such as compute throughput, memory capacity and bandwidth, and interconnect topology. They say what does transfer is the method: overhead-aware features, multicollinearity-aware selection and the comparison protocol. They add that the full paper will report the feature formulas, the selection procedure, the search spaces and the final hyperparameters in full, so the pipeline can be rebuilt on any execution-log dataset with a similar structure. They note that in practice the predictor gives a scheduler a duration it can plan around before a job starts: which jobs to run together, when GPUs will free up, and whether a run will finish in time for its deadline.

Next on the authors' list are hardware-specific descriptors and validation on other GPU types, transfer learning for configurations with few observations, other training objectives, and more data on long runs. They invite readers to follow the Dharma-AI organization on Hugging Face to be notified when the full paper is out and to leave questions in the comments. They say they would like to hear how readers estimate job duration on their own clusters. The articles leave open the contents of the full paper, including the feature formulas, the selection procedure, the search spaces and the final hyperparameters, which they say will be reported there. They also leave open how the method performs on other GPU types and on configurations with few observations.

Nvidia and Siliconware Precision Industries signed a multibillion-dollar agreement on November 18, 2026, to increase chip production. This multi-year deal focuses on expanding advanced packaging capabilities within the borders of Taiwan. The two companies intend to triple the existing capacity for chip-on-wafer-on-substrate packaging by the year 2029. This strategic partnership aims to support the growing demand for high-performance artificial intelligence hardware.

The agreement requires a multibillion-dollar investment to scale the specific CoWoS packaging processes used for AI chips. Siliconware Precision Industries, which operates as a subsidiary of ASE Technology Holding, will manage the expansion. This growth is necessary to prevent bottlenecks in the supply chain for advanced semiconductor components. The project will specifically target the infrastructure needed to meet the goals set for 2029.

The leadership at Siliconware Precision Industries announced the deal to ensure they can meet the needs of Nvidia. They stated that the expansion is a significant step toward increasing their advanced packaging output in Taiwan. The company believes this partnership will strengthen its position as a key supplier for the AI industry. These officials emphasized the importance of scaling their technical capacity to handle complex chip designs.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: AI tools drive school book removals as states expand restrictions
stories.Summary:
As a growing number of states pass or propose restrictions on what books children can access in school libraries, authors and advocates are concerned about the role artificial intelligence is increasingly playing in books being removed from shelves. The free speech advocacy group PEN America said in a report published during Banned Books Week in early October that the phenomenon of using AI to guide removals will worsen the snowball effect of book bans that has already gone much too far. Some districts have had AI review their collections to flag certain types of content and make recommendations on what to remove. The first known example of AI being used for such purposes was in 2023, when an Iowa school district used it in response to legislation prohibiting books depicting sex acts in school libraries. Several Texas districts followed in 2025, according to the Houston Chronicle.

The Florida Freedom to Read Project reported in October that a local school district's use of AI to scan library collections led to more than 1,800 titles being removed from shelves to undergo further review. A Utah law requires that if three public school districts, or two school districts and five charter schools, take a title off library shelves, all public and charter schools must follow suit. There are 44 books currently banned statewide under the law, according to PEN America. The organization's October report found that Texas and Florida's bans made up more than 11,400 of the nearly 12,000 total book bans recorded during the 2025-2026 school year. Texas enacted a law in 2025 that prohibits schools from having library materials with indecent or profane content, and Florida has sought to impose similar restrictions for several years.

The Florida Department of Education sent a memo in September to the state's 67 public school districts, as well as charter schools, that directed them to review their library collections and compare them to the department's list of books that have been removed from schools around the state. Florida Education Commissioner Henry Mack wrote that the Department will hold districts, and the superintendents who lead them, accountable for failing to protect students from inappropriate content and material. Maggie Tokuda-Hall, an author and co-creator of Authors Against Book Bans, told USA TODAY that we've crossed the Rubicon and are in a really different place. A spokesperson for Moms for Liberty told USA TODAY the group believes AI recommendations should always be followed by human review. The spokesperson said anyone who blindly trusts AI to make decisions for them is using it in an irresponsible manner.

A Knight Foundation report in 2024 found that more than three-fourths of all adults felt very or somewhat confident that local public schools select appropriate books, including nearly 90% of public school parents, more than 60% of conservatives and 69% of Republicans. Stephana Ferrell, a public school parent who is also the director of research and insight at the Florida Freedom to Read Project, said these are not things public school parents want prioritized right now, and yet it's being amplified at the state level. Moms for Liberty, which describes itself as the nation's largest grassroots organization fighting for parental rights, has chapters that have called for scores of titles to be removed from school library shelves, including Colleen Hoover's "It Ends With Us," "The Kite Runner" by Khaled Hosseini and John Steinbeck's "Of Mice and Men." In October, the group announced a new AI tool to scan school board meeting agendas and identify topics related to parental rights, free speech, the curriculum and diversity, equity and inclusion efforts. A spokesperson for the organization told USA TODAY it may also be used on school library collections.

James Joyce's 1922 work "Ulysses" was deemed legally obscene and faced a nationwide ban until a court reversed it in 1933. J.D. Salinger's 1951 classic, "The Catcher in the Rye," has stirred controversy for decades and was the 10th-most challenged book of the 1990s, according to the American Library Association. A book that was even more widely challenged in that decade was "Heather Has Two Mommies," a 1989 children's book about a young girl raised by lesbian parents. The book's author, Lesléa Newman, told USA TODAY that while there have been longtime battles over her work, as well as other books with LGBTQ+ themes or written by non-White authors, she's noticed a change in recent years.

Newman said things have really escalated in a way that's very disturbing and frightening, and noted that statewide bans now affect dozens of titles. According to the American Library Association, pressure groups, government officials and other decision-makers were behind more than 90% of all book challenges in 2025. Author Lee Wind, whose 2021 book, "No Way, They Were Gay? Hidden Lives and Secret Loves," has faced several bans, criticized what he called very calculated attacks on books and said book bans further marginalize certain groups, such as the LGBTQ+ community.

Wind said he thinks all it's doing is empowering people that want there to be fewer books about diverse people in public spaces to do it more thoroughly. Sarah Lamdan, executive director of the American Library Association's Office for Intellectual Freedom, told USA TODAY she has some optimism that the trend will taper off. Lamdan said one thing that gives her hope is people are becoming fatigued by AI, and the overuse of AI, and the use of AI in contexts where maybe it shouldn't be used. Kris Austin, CEO of Draft2Digital, a self-publishing and distribution platform for independent authors, pointed to the negative feedback loop created by having more state restrictions alongside more advanced AI.

Austin said the next time we see this data, it's going to be worse, and it's going to be shockingly worse. The article carried an editor's note stating the story was updated to add additional information. BrieAnna Frank's role covering First Amendment issues at USA TODAY is made possible by a collaboration among Freedom Forum, Journalism Funding Partners and the USA TODAY Network, and Freedom Forum does not provide editorial input. The article originally appeared on USA TODAY and was reported by BrieAnna J. Frank, USA TODAY, via USA TODAY Network and Reuters Connect.

stories.Headline: Portland council president Jamie Dunphy introduces a proposed city AI moratorium for a December hearing
stories.Summary:
Portland City Council President Jamie Dunphy introduced Ordinance 2026-423 this week, a proposed moratorium on new artificial intelligence in city government, and the full council will hear it on December 3, 2026. The measure would add a new Chapter 34.20 to the Portland City Code, establishing a temporary moratorium on the City's procurement and implementation of artificial intelligence. Nothing has passed yet, and the Portland AI moratorium is a proposal, not a law. The draft carries a $250,000 ceiling on exempted pilots, a ban on no-cost deals, and an expiry date of December 31, 2027. The city's own announcement of Ordinance 2026-423 states the details.

Under the draft, the City could not sign new AI contracts or roll out AI, including upgrades that add or expand AI functionality in software the City already owns. Pilots, trials, trades, giveaways, purchase orders and no-cost agreements are covered. Existing contracts and pilots could continue through their current terms but could not be renewed, extended or amended to add AI functionality unless the council grants an exemption by ordinance. A pilot can proceed if the council approves it with a cost of no more than $250,000, a duration of no longer than 12 months, and a ban on using City data to train vendor models. Basic AI in existing software such as spell-check and spam filtering, and cybersecurity uses, are exempt, and a citywide AI inventory is due within 60 days of adoption, updated on an ongoing basis.

Dunphy said the aim is to protect public privacy, security and civil rights while the administration gets the Data and Privacy Office running and writes legislative guidelines. He said, "Emergent AI technology carries substantial risks to both the public and the City, meaning we cannot simply go full steam ahead without establishing proper policy guardrails in City Code." He told reporters, "I'm not saying we shouldn't have AI." He said, "We have to have thoughtful, smart AI, and we shouldn't run full speed into whatever the latest technology is just because it's there." At a Tuesday press conference he said of the police pilot, "That pilot is already up and going and, as of now, they have a set scope."

OregonLive reported that the proposal could affect a Portland Police Bureau program using AI to screen suspects' data files, such as those on mobile phones or in online profiles, for child sexual-abuse material, as described by reporter Isabel Funk. Dunphy said that if the bureau wanted to connect it to the internet, expand its uses beyond internet sex crimes, or use it for retail theft, "that would not be allowed." Chief Bob Day said in a statement that the bureau is always looking for smarter, more efficient ways to work, particularly given staffing challenges, and wants to balance innovation with accountability, transparency and public trust. OpenAI has been offering a free CSAM classifier to vetted groups. Chicago has been eyeing an AI gun-detection pilot that would run six months across six districts.

KOIN reported that the Data and Privacy Office was established in March and is not yet operational. According to the ordinance summary on Portland.gov, the moratorium could end ahead of schedule if the Data and Privacy Office is certified as operational and the council adopts AI legislation. KOIN reported that Dunphy cited the growing volume of software and services with embedded AI being sold to the City as a reason for concern about how fast governments are being pushed to adopt it. The FBI has warned about the ARTEX AI hacking tool, which reportedly breaches networks in under three hours. A $250,000 budget over 12 months works out to roughly $20,800 a month.

The moratorium would expire on December 31, 2027, unless the council extends it by ordinance. If the council adopted the ordinance on December 3, which is not guaranteed, 60 days would land on February 1, 2027. The articles lay out five predictions for the December hearing without stating them here. The record is silent on whether the ordinance will pass.

stories.Headline: DDN offers software-defined EXAScaler deployment for enterprise AI infrastructure
stories.Summary:
DDN announced a new software-defined deployment option for EXAScaler on November 17, 2026, in Santa Clara, California. This new option is enabled by the upcoming EXAScaler 7 release for enterprise AI infrastructure. The company allows customers to run high-performance data infrastructure software on qualified industry-standard servers. This change provides an alternative to using purpose-built systems or cloud partners for deployment. A limited beta for this software-defined deployment is planned for early 2027.

The software will start on DDN AI2200 servers, with qualified third-party appliances following later. This makes both EXAScaler and DDN Infinia available in software-defined formats for various customers. Hyperscalers and NCPs with established storage infrastructure can now deploy EXAScaler on industry-standard hardware. This model allows AI platform teams to select hardware suited to their specific requirements. DDN will continue developing purpose-built systems for those preferring integrated performance and reliability.

Omer Asad, the Chief Product Officer at DDN, is responsible for this product direction. He stated that AI infrastructure is becoming more diverse and customers want more freedom. Asad explained that making EXAScaler available as software extends flexibility across the company portfolio. He noted that customers can choose integrated systems or deploy software on third-party hardware. This approach maintains the core capabilities that customers depend on from the EXAScaler platform.

The new model affects organizations that bring AI and HPC workflows together in one environment. In life sciences, researchers use AI surrogate models on molecular dynamics simulation outputs to predict protein behavior. Software-defined EXAScaler on qualified hardware allows simulation and training to run on the same data. This removes the need for copying data between different environments during the research process. These capabilities help researchers avoid repeating every computationally intensive simulation during their work.

DDN has provided AI data storage and management platforms for over 20 years of innovation. The company serves national labs, research institutions, financial firms, and autonomous vehicle innovators. Its platforms support next-generation AI factories, hyperscale clouds, and Sovereign AI initiatives. DDN is recognized as a leading provider for the largest AI deployments on Earth. The company offers EXA, Infinia, and various intelligent data management platforms to its customers.

DDN is developing enhancements for multi-tenancy, performance, and data protection for the EXAScaler platform. These specific enhancements are targeted for general availability in the first half of 2027. The company will share validated performance data as it becomes available to the public. The articles leave open the specific dates for general availability, as they may change. It remains unclear which third-party appliances will be qualified for the software-defined deployment.

stories.Headline: Lawmakers move to preserve 2026 CSAT exam papers as police investigate Lee Jin-woo for AI cheating
stories.Summary:
Lawmakers sought to preserve exam papers on November 19, 2026, to investigate AI cheating. Lee Jin-woo, 32, faces allegations of using artificial intelligence on several high stakes tests. He scored a perfect mark on the Legal Education Eligibility Test. He also took the College Scholastic Ability Test for the 2026 academic year. Police are now investigating him for fraud and obstruction of official duties.

The request covers original question booklets, OMR answer sheets, and scoring records from the 2026 CSAT. Rep. Jung Sung-kook sent letters to the Ministry of Education and provincial education offices. Rep. Park Jung-hun noted Lee's papers were kept at Younghoon High School in Seoul. The 2026 CSAT was administered on November 13 of the previous year. These materials include handover documents for each test district and site.

Rep. Jung Sung-kook said authorities should check for AI cheating on past exams. He argued that a lack of handwritten calculations might suggest AI use. He proposed reviewing score distributions and work traces for medical and dental admissions. Jung stated that these traces are circumstantial evidence to be weighed with other material. He suggested expanding the review if multiple suspicious cases are confirmed.

Lee Jin-woo is affected by these allegations and a police investigation. Some people allege he cheated on the 2024 and 2026 CSAT exams. Reporters and instructors waited for him at the IDA Admissions Research Institute. About 2,000 people joined a YouTube live stream to watch his verification. Lee failed to appear for the session and could not be reached.

Lee previously scored in the sixth to eighth grade bands on earlier CSAT exams. He entered Korea University in 2024 and Seoul National University dental school in 2026. Doubts arose after a top certified tax accountant was caught cheating with AI. The Korea Institute for Curriculum and Evaluation usually destroys booklets after one year. The retention period for the 2026 CSAT papers has already lapsed.

Police are searching for Lee after he disappeared from his Gwanak District home. He was last seen leaving lodgings in Gwangjin District on the morning of November 19. He had agreed to metal detectors and endoscopic checks for the verification session. The police investigation will now determine the facts behind the cheating allegations. It remains open whether Lee actually used AI to improve his scores.

stories.Headline: KB Securities invests 2 billion won in UNIST Holdings regional tourism AI fund
stories.Summary:
KB Securities announced on November 19 that it invested 2 billion won into a specialized venture investment association. This specific fund focuses on deep tech and artificial intelligence for regional tourism and is managed by UNIST Holdings. The investment was made through Npay Startup, which is a venture capital platform that connects various investors with emerging companies. This transaction represents the first time a financial firm has committed capital using this particular digital investment platform.

The total value of the fund is 15.4 billion won, which includes 10 billion won from the Korea Venture Investment Corp. fund of funds. UNIST Holdings will use these resources to identify regional startups that utilize AI technology in the tourism sector to provide them with growth capital. The Npay Startup platform was launched in July with official support from the Ministry of SMEs and Startups and the Financial Supervisory Service. This initiative aims to shift the flow of venture capital away from the greater Seoul area toward promising local companies.

A representative from KB Securities stated that this move is meaningful because it expands the supply of venture capital to regional areas. The official added that the firm intends to continue contributing to balanced growth and the revitalization of regional economies through productive finance. This action follows a meeting on the 12th of this month where the Financial Supervisory Service urged financial firms to diversify their channels for supplying capital. The regulator specifically cited the review of this funding proposal as a positive example for other comprehensive financial investment business operators.

The Australian Prudential Regulation Authority is examining the third parties that banks, super funds and insurers rely on as it deals with the risks of artificial intelligence, according to Law360 Australia. APRA Chair John Lonsdale said those third parties are a focus for the regulator, the report said. The report was published on November 18, 2026, and was written by Antony Scholefield. stories.Headline: Calif uses OpenAI's GPT-6 Cyber AI model to uncover Java4Shell flaw in Java
stories.Summary:
Security researchers have identified a critical vulnerability in Java, the widely used open-source programming language, which is listed as CVE-2026-114938 and known as Java4Shell. The flaw allows hackers to gain remote access to sensitive internal systems and affects Java 17.0.6 on systems running x86-64 Intel and AMD chips with AVX-512 VBMI support. The cybersecurity startup Calif brought Java4Shell to light using OpenAI's GPT-6 Cyber AI model. Oracle, the owner of the Java trademark, and the OpenJDK project have released software patches, while Amazon has issued fixes for its Corretto Java builds and Red Hat is rolling out patches for its Java distributions. Other at-risk Java distributions include Eclipse Temurin, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, BellSoft Liberica, and SAP SapMachine.

The flaw resides in a performance shortcut Java uses to decode Base64 data faster, and when this shortcut receives a specially crafted Base64 string, it writes data beyond its allocated memory and corrupts other information. Attackers could exploit this to access application memory containing credentials or to run malicious code on the server. Calif researchers demonstrated this by exploiting Java4Shell to breach Keycloak, an authentication system. Other applications potentially compromised include Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, PingFederate, Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker.

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has urged organisations to immediately patch the Oracle Java vulnerability, and the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team issued an advisory warning that Java4Shell could allow remote attackers to execute arbitrary code. CERT-In advised users of affected Oracle Java SE and Oracle GraalVM products to implement available patches immediately. Google has rolled out mitigations and patches across its services and developed detection to ensure no exploitation, according to The New York Times. The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security also issued an alert advising organisations to identify affected systems and apply vendor updates as they become available, and it stated that no active exploitation of Java4Shell has been observed yet.

The use of AI tools to uncover critical security vulnerabilities, as seen with Java4Shell, highlights underlying infrastructure flaws. Fouad Matin, who leads cyber preparedness and safety at OpenAI, noted that this research shows how AI can assist expert security researchers in finding serious software flaws.

stories.Headline: AI code generation erodes developer understanding of software systems, Storey warns
stories.Summary:
The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence for code generation is quietly undermining human comprehension of software systems, according to a TechGig article published on August 11, 2026. The article says this erosion of understanding is described as cognitive debt and intent debt, and it poses significant risks to a system's ability to evolve safely. Human comprehension, unlike performance or availability, decays silently over time, and a system that is not understood cannot evolve safely. The article draws on Margaret-Anne Storey's expansion of Peter Naur's idea of programming as theory building, which holds that a system includes not just the code but also the mental model held by its developers.

Three primary forces accelerate this decay, the article says. Decentralised architectural decision-making can fragment global understanding of a system's why, and team churn compounds this as departing engineers take their mental models with them. The most recent and rapid force is generative AI, which commoditises code generation and removes the comprehension naturally formed during design, implementation and verification. Architects can watch for large pull request sizes, reliance on agentic code reviewers as sole approvers, superficial human review feedback, and missing design reviews for critical changes. Other signals include knowledge concentration around a few individuals, shown by a high degree of authorship or a low truck factor, and rising onboarding friction measured by the time new hires take to contribute to design and architecture.

The article says human code reviews in an AI-assisted workflow must shift from mere quality gates to comprehension checkpoints. The goal is to validate, strengthen and disseminate the understanding reached before code generation, not just verify the output. Pre-hoc comprehension, formed during active problem-solving and design, keeps humans in control of the system's evolution and prevents reliance on statistically default designs from large language models. Shared mental models across teams are vital, especially at bounded context seams, and this requires deliberate team topologies and rotating engineers across modules to prevent knowledge silos. The friction of manually writing commit messages and pull request descriptions can serve as a probe for authors to confirm their own understanding.

Treating comprehension as an architectural characteristic demands leading indicators, fitness functions and continuous practices, the article says. Monitoring pull requests that touch core modules without adding Architecture Decision Records can help, and domain leakage, where changes degrade architectural boundaries, signals a breakdown in shared understanding. If comprehension gaps are found only after AI-generated code is in production, the opportunity for cheap intervention is lost. The article says deliberate and continuous engineering of comprehension, particularly at core domains and system seams, is essential for building truly evolvable software systems.

stories.Headline: Researchers in Mexico use a five-stage human-AI workflow to make shifts in violence representation visible
stories.Summary:
Researchers across institutions in Mexico, including the Metropolitan Autonomous University, Universidad de las Americas, and Tecnologico de Estudios Superiores de Ecatepec, published an exploratory study in Frontiers in Computer Science on how recursive human-AI interaction can make changes in the representation of violence visible. The authors developed a five-stage exploratory workflow grounded in mixed-initiative design, in which computational tools handle structured comparison and generative variation while human contributors supply critical judgment. The first stage involved an exploratory computational evaluation of a non-probability corpus containing 105 news items addressing violence in Mexico, applying techniques to identify recurring terms, prominent actors, geographic locations, and underlying semantic relationships. The team then organized and visualized these computational findings to prepare structured materials for subsequent participatory evaluation.

The second and third phases brought these computational visualizations into an interactive participatory workshop conducted with 15 participants. In the fourth stage of the workflow, the authors analyzed changes across textual and visual iterations. The fifth stage integrated the project findings through expert-supported synthesis, producing both an infographic and a video that summarized the workshop results. The results suggest that recursive human-AI interaction can make changes in the representation of violence visible by combining semantic analysis, participant interpretation, and visual synthesis.

The authors noted significant methodological boundaries, stating clearly that the study employs an exploratory design that does not attempt to estimate population parameters or establish causal relationships. They explained that the reported findings and observed narrative shifts remain specific to the non-probability corpus of 105 news articles and the 15 workshop participants. Despite these constraints, the study authors concluded that the collaborative, mixed-initiative framework effectively demonstrates how computational methods can support generative exploration and comparison while keeping human interpretation central to the analysis of complex media narratives. The article was published in Frontiers in Computer Science, volume 8, as Article 1877314, with a DOI of 10.3389/fcomp.2026.1877314, and was reported by Denise Maddox for Scienmag on November 18, 2026.

Articles.Title: Recursive Human-AI Interaction Can Make Changes in Violence Representation Visible

stories.Headline: Anthropic floats on the US stock exchange, making its seven founders multi-billionaires
stories.Summary:
Seven founders of the AI firm Anthropic will become multi-billionaires on paper very soon. These individuals left the rival company OpenAI in 2021 to start their own venture. The company announced on Wednesday that it is floating the business on the US stock exchange. This move follows five years of growth from an unknown start-up to a tech giant. The firm is now worth more than a trillion dollars.

Anthropic will sell its shares at $83 each on the US stock exchange. This price makes the founders' shareholdings worth at least $19.3bn each. Dario Amodei will have $19.7bn, while Daniela Amodei and Jack Clark will have $19.8bn. Jared Kaplan also has $19.8bn, while Chris Olah and Sam McCandlish will each have $19.9bn. Tom Brown will hold the highest amount at $20bn.

Chief executive Dario Amodei left OpenAI because he worried some people put profit before safety. President Daniela Amodei says her brother is the person who makes the company ambitious. Chief compute officer Tom Brown argued that datacentres are an enormous source of prosperity. Jack Clark serves as head of public benefit and leads the Anthropic Institute think tank. Chief science officer Jared Kaplan heads technical research and teaches at Johns Hopkins University.

Chris Olah is the interpretability research lead and is reportedly exploring morality and AI. The New York Times describes Olah as boyish with the zeal of an evangelist. Sam McCandlish is the chief architect who helps implement policy to mitigate AI risks. These seven founders will each own around 1.6 percent of the company. Their stakes will crystallise into hugely valuable assets after the shares go on sale.

Dario Amodei studied physics at Princeton and Stanford before switching to biology and biomedical sciences. Daniela Amodei studied English Literature at the University of California Santa Cruz and worked for Matt Cartwright. Tom Brown led GPT-3 engineering at OpenAI and previously worked on the Google DeepMind project. Jack Clark is a former technology journalist from Brighton who studied at the University of East Anglia. Chris Olah received a $100,000 Thiel Fellowship after leaving the University of Toronto early.

The company will now move from being a private start-up to a public entity. The founders will transition from being tech entrepreneurs to some of the world's wealthiest people. The articles do not state when the shares will officially begin trading. They do not mention the specific reactions of rival firms to this valuation. The text leaves open how the founders will use their new wealth.

stories.Headline: Boston Dynamics and GlobalFoundries plan Atlas humanoid robot testing at chip plants from early 2027
stories.Summary:
Boston Dynamics, a subsidiary of Hyundai Motor Group, announced on November 17, 2026, that it is expanding its strategic collaboration with GlobalFoundries. This partnership will involve on-site testing of the Atlas humanoid robot at advanced semiconductor manufacturing facilities starting in early 2027. GlobalFoundries will be the first semiconductor maker and the first customer outside the automotive industry to test this specific robot. The companies intend to identify suitable tasks for humanoid robots in precision manufacturing and conduct AI training to explore physical AI applications.

The initiative requires the deployment of additional Spot quadruped robots across major sites in Singapore, Dresden, Germany, Burlington, Vermont, and Malta, New York. GlobalFoundries has already operated Spot in Burlington for over four years and used two units in Singapore since April. Those Singapore robots traveled about 900 kilometers through sub-fab areas and completed over 90,000 inspections with a 99 percent success rate. The company now plans to use these visual inspection capabilities to more than double the number of routine checks performed.

Pradip Singh, the chief manufacturing officer at GlobalFoundries, stated that Spot improved facility efficiency and helped the company move toward predictive maintenance. He described the upcoming Atlas testing as a necessary step toward achieving AI-enabled manufacturing. Zack Jackowski, the chief product and technology officer at Boston Dynamics, noted that innovative companies are already gaining tangible operational value from robotics. He added that the data being collected will be extremely useful for future innovations in the manufacturing sector.

Boston Dynamics is currently validating Atlas for automotive tasks at the Robotics Metaplant Application Center in Georgia. This center began pilot operations in June 2026 and officially opened in September 2026 to teach the robot tasks like parts sequencing. Hyundai Motor Group intends to begin deploying the Atlas robot at the HMGMA vehicle manufacturing plant in 2028. This broader strategy aims to bring automotive production expertise into the precision semiconductor industry to test the robot's versatility.

stories.Headline: Jassy says Amazon is talking to outside AI agent companies about shopping access
stories.Summary:
Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said on Tuesday at Semafor's Silicon Valley & The World conference that Amazon has not permanently closed the door on outside AI shopping agents making purchases on its platform. He said the company has not said it will never open things up, but that any arrangement has to offer a good customer experience and a fair exchange of value. In September, Amazon publicly blocked Meta's Muse agent from making purchases on its platform, saying the block helps ensure a safe, secure, and reliable customer experience. Amazon has said it applies its policies evenly, and users have also reported that Instinct AI and OpenAI's Dots struggled to buy items on their behalf on Amazon.

Jassy said Amazon is talking to every one of those companies, and he added that every retailer should have the right to decide how it interacts with agents. He said he believes the primary way people will use agentic shopping is in concert with the retailer they like to use, telling an app to buy the deodorant they normally buy using past orders, shipping information, and payment information. Amazon is also betting heavily on its own AI shopping tools, including Alexa for Shopping and Buy for Me, which are guided by Amazon's About You customer dossiers. The outside agents, which include Meta's Muse, Instinct AI, and OpenAI's Dots, are advertised as capable of taking action on a customer's behalf, including making online purchases.

That capability could cut retailers out of the browsing experience they have long controlled, and it raises thorny questions about ad sales, account security, identity verification, and who is on the hook when an order goes wrong. Other companies have taken a different tack, with Shopify openly embracing outside AI shopping agents. Home Depot's chief information officer recently told Business Insider that the home improvement store's online marketplace wants agents to identify themselves first. The article does not say what happens next beyond Jassy's comments that Amazon is talking to the agent companies.

Articles.Title: Andy Jassy isn't ruling out opening Amazon's doors to outside AI agents

stories.headline_source: Andy Jassy isn't ruling out opening Amazon's doors to outside AI agents

stories.Headline: Chinese bottle-cap manufacturer challenges AI automation hype at Shanghai conference
stories.Summary:
Zhu Shihui, a manufacturer of bottle caps, presented a critical perspective on artificial intelligence during an AI Engineer conference in Shanghai in early November. The speaker challenged the prevailing hype by arguing that the final stage of implementation represents half of the total journey. Zhu criticized consultants who believe every industrial process can be easily automated regardless of the existing infrastructure. This presentation highlighted the practical difficulties of integrating advanced technology into traditional manufacturing environments. The speaker explained that many factories rely on pre-digital equipment and employ workers, averaging in their late 40s, who lack deep digital skills.

Furthermore, these companies often operate on margins so thin that they cannot afford a complete digital transformation. Instead of using an aggressive approach, Zhu suggested that the best method is to exercise humility. This requires seeking out the tacit knowledge of an organization to serve as the foundation for any technological change. Zhu argued that the current trend of ignoring human expertise in favor of automation is a mistake. The presentation served as a reminder that technical capabilities must be balanced with the reality of the workplace.

Other attendees, such as Ryo Lu, also questioned how self-worth is measured when code can be written by machines. Lu expressed a desire to build tools that increase human involvement rather than proving that people are needed less. The conference showcased a relaxed attitude toward artificial intelligence in China, where practitioners view it as a marketing tool rather than a global threat. Demos included a 35 billion-parameter model from AutoArk running on an iPhone 16 Pro and robot hardware from DYNA. The event also featured a significant number of women engineers, contrasting with the gender dynamics often seen at similar events in America or Australia.

stories.Headline: 16 Questions Law Firms Should Be Asking About SEO, AI Search and Online Visibility
stories.Summary:
The article, published on 17 November 2026 on the Social Media Butterfly blog, sets out 16 questions law firms should ask about SEO, AI search and online visibility. It was written by an author who says she has worked with law firms of all sizes. She says she has worked with firms whose attorneys have decades of experience, impressive client relationships and extensive publication histories. She says very little of that information appears on their websites. She calls that a missed opportunity as more people turn to AI tools to research legal issues and find lawyers.

The article says a smaller firm with 30 substantive, well-organized pages may perform better for its target searches than a firm with hundreds of generic articles. It names Chambers and Best Lawyers as organizations whose recognition firms should record. It cites New York Labor Law Sections 200, 240 and 241(6), contractual indemnification and risk transfer as topics a construction litigation firm may address on dedicated pages. It says a smaller firm may benefit from concentrating on three to five areas where it has a meaningful track record. It names Google Search Console and website analytics as tools for monitoring organic search impressions, keyword performance, traffic and inquiries.

The author says larger firms have extensive marketing resources and thousands of pages of content, while smaller firms may have only a handful of articles and relatively basic practice descriptions. She says the amount of content a firm publishes is only part of the equation. She says how well that content demonstrates expertise, answers relevant questions and connects to other credible information also matters. She says one of the biggest opportunities she sees is making better use of the experience and content firms already have. She says improving online visibility often starts with documenting accomplishments, strengthening existing pages and creating a more comprehensive picture of what the firm and its attorneys actually do.

The article says attorneys can often reference and link to articles they wrote at previous firms, but republishing the full content may require permission from the copyright owner. It says any description of prior work should accurately identify the attorney's experience and avoid suggesting that matters handled at another firm were handled by the current firm. It says recognition does not automatically improve search rankings or guarantee AI citations. It says different AI search tools use different methods for retrieving and citing information.

It says adding external links simply to increase their number is not an effective SEO strategy. The article says firms should review attorneys' historical articles, client alerts, CLE materials and conference presentations to identify content worth updating, summarizing or linking to. It says a CLE presentation can become an article, a series of FAQs and several LinkedIn posts. It says a webinar can generate a written recap, shorter practice-specific articles and updated content for attorney biographies.

It says an initial project might involve collecting attorneys' publications and credentials, expanding three priority practice pages, updating biographies and creating a centralized archive of news and recognition. It says outside marketing support can help coordinate the work without requiring a large internal team. The article says firms should monitor organic search impressions, relevant keyword performance, website traffic, engagement with priority practice pages and inquiries from prospective clients. It says firms can periodically test how AI-powered search tools describe their capabilities, whether they reference accurate information and which sources they cite.

The text of the article ends mid-sentence in the fifteenth question. The article does not give the sixteenth question. The article gives no figures on results achieved for any firm. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Democrats prepare to take Congress and press Trump on AI rules and data center costs
stories.Summary:
Democrats are preparing to take control of Congress in January, setting up a possible confrontation with President Donald Trump over artificial intelligence, data centers and how much responsibility technology companies should bear when AI causes harm, according to azfamily.com. Polling showed AI was a significant issue for many voters in the midterms. An NBC News exit poll found that 56% of voters considered AI and data centers a crucial or major factor in their congressional vote, while 76% of respondents opposed construction of a new data center in their community. In both cases, those respondents favored Democrats by about 30 percentage points. Caroline Lynch, a former congressional committee counsel and founder of the lobbying firm Copper Hill Strategies, said the election could mark a turning point.

Lynch said one of the most promising areas for compromise is who should pay for the enormous electricity demands of AI data centers. She pointed to the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a Senate proposal that would require data centers to pay for the additional electricity infrastructure needed to serve them rather than passing those costs to other customers. That proposal goes further than the Ratepayer Protection Act, which passed the Republican-controlled House 417-3 in September and required states to consider adopting protections for electricity customers but did not require them to implement those protections. Lynch said there is currently no comprehensive federal requirement governing how much of those costs data center operators must absorb. Democrats are also exploring ways to hold AI developers responsible when their technology causes harm, including situations in which autonomous AI systems commit fraud, breach computer networks or expose sensitive information.

Lynch, a former prosecutor, said existing criminal laws generally require prosecutors to identify a responsible person or corporation, and applying those laws when an AI system acts beyond its instructions presents unresolved legal questions. She said Congress may eventually have to address whether AI developers should receive protections similar to Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, which shields online platforms for content created by third parties. Rep. Yassamin Ansari has called for a pause on advanced AI development and a ban on superintelligence, while Sen. Mark Kelly has proposed taxing certain AI-related windfall profits to help fund worker retraining. Lynch believes narrower regulations have a better chance of attracting support than sweeping restrictions on advanced AI.

Lynch predicted Democrats may advance AI bills in a bid to call the president's bluff, forcing Trump to decide whether to block measures addressing concerns about the technology. Lawmakers could also try attaching AI provisions to larger spending bills, making a veto politically more complicated, she said. Democrats will gain control of congressional committees and the ability to summon technology executives for oversight hearings, and Texas Rep. Greg Casar has discussed calling AI executives to testify under oath. Lynch cautioned that such hearings can produce more political theater than substantive results, but she noted that several leading AI companies have publicly supported some form of federal regulation, which could make the hearings less confrontational than previous congressional investigations of social media companies.

Articles.Title: What’s next for AI regulation once Democrats control Congress?

stories.Headline: Hong Kong Monetary Authority explores agentic AI to detect crypto financial crime
stories.Summary:
The Hong Kong Monetary Authority began exploring the use of agentic AI to monitor crypto asset transactions on Tuesday, November 18, 2026. Executive Director Raymond Chan announced this initiative during a speech at a workshop hosted by the central bank to combat money laundering. This new technology aims to analyze both onchain transfers and offchain customer transactions to identify anomalies. The system would specifically flag rapid fund layering that occurs when users switch between cryptocurrency and fiat money.

This approach requires integrating blockchain analytics, scam intelligence, and customer due diligence into a single on-chain AI agent. Such a system would allow for the monitoring of suspicious wallets and the rapid freezing of illicit funds. Raymond Chan noted that illicit addresses received over 150 billion dollars in 2025, with stablecoins making up 84 percent of those transactions. He also highlighted the Virtual Asset Intelligence Taskforce, which was established in November 2025 to strengthen these efforts.

Raymond Chan stated that the central bank wants to make financial crime monitoring more effective and efficient through AI. He explained that criminal networks use digital assets for human trafficking and fraud because of their global reach and pseudonymity. Chan admitted that no single tool provides complete protection, so the city must rely on multi-layered safeguards. He noted that the primary challenge is quickly linking digital wallet activities to real-world identities to stop funds from disappearing.

The Virtual Asset Intelligence Taskforce treats crypto crime as an ecosystem issue involving regulators, law enforcement, and trading platforms. This public-private group includes the Hong Kong police, the Customs and Excise Department, and the Securities and Futures Commission. By collaborating with licensed crypto trading platforms, the task force has already improved the quality of intelligence. These agencies continue to work together to strengthen the prevention and detection of crimes across the entire digital asset landscape.

Articles.Title: Hong Kong central bank explores agentic AI to detect crypto-related financial crime

stories.Headline: Florida House speaker urges quick action on AI as Senate president prioritizes affordability
stories.Summary:
Florida’s Legislature opened its new term with the House speaker urging lawmakers to move quickly on artificial intelligence, while the Senate president put affordability at the top of his agenda. Both leaders took office with a $12 billion question hanging over local budgets after voters approved a sweeping property tax cut. The Jacksonville Business Journal reported the opening on November 18, 2026, and noted that a new Florida House panel will focus on AI and digital security. The same report pointed to related action on Amendment 3, which state leaders had delayed in special session.

The property tax cut approved by voters leaves local governments facing a $12 billion gap, and the article ties that figure directly to the budgets the new term must address. The House speaker wants fast movement on AI, and a new House panel will focus on AI and digital security. The Senate president’s priority is affordability, which the article places at the top of his agenda. The report also lists related coverage on flying cars taking another step forward in Florida, without giving further detail.

Responsibility sits with the new House speaker and the Senate president, who each set a priority as the term began. The speaker urged lawmakers to move quickly on AI, and the Senate president put affordability first. The article does not name either leader or give direct quotations beyond those paraphrased positions. It also does not say what specific AI legislation the speaker wants or what affordability measures the Senate president supports.

The context is a term opening under the weight of the voter-approved property tax cut and its $12 billion effect on local budgets. The article notes that Florida leaders had delayed a special session on Amendment 3, and that Governor DeSantis had called a special session on the property tax cut. What happens next is not detailed beyond the speaker’s call for speed on AI and the Senate president’s affordability focus. The article gives no timeline for legislation, no vote counts and no further statements from either leader.

stories.Headline: Imagen Technologies raises $100M to expand radiologist recruitment and train AI models
stories.Summary:
Imagen Technologies, a New York-based radiology practice that describes itself as artificial intelligence-enabled, has raised $100 million in growth capital as it seeks to boost physician recruitment, the company announced on November 19, 2026. The funds come from both new and existing investors, though the company did not name the specific contributors behind the raise. Founded in 2015, Imagen currently provides radiology services across 28 states and handles more than 2 million imaging studies every year. Imagen estimated that its physician head count has grown 100% year over year, with the company now employing a team of more than 230 radiologists and cardiologists. Leaders said they will use the funds to further build out what they believe is the best place for radiologists to practice their craft.

As part of the capital raise, Imagen also secured the rights to up to 150 million additional imaging studies, which it will use to train its AI models. Those scans include X-rays, CTs, MRIs and ultrasounds, and the company plans to build and validate models against the diverse, real-world caseloads that its radiologists handle every day. Imagen's AI strategy centers on improving the experience of practicing radiologists while boosting clinical quality and efficiency, and as its technologies advance it plans to reinvest the resulting benefits into its radiologists and the resources that support them. Laurence Eckel, an associate chief medical officer who joined the company in April after spending 26 years with the Mayo Clinic, said in a November 18 statement that Imagen is building the entire practice around the radiologist, from the technology they use to the clinical teams supporting them. He said the goal is to create a place where physicians can do the best work of their careers and feel proud of the practice they are helping build.

Serge Sicular, the chief medical information officer who also leads emergency imaging at the Mount Sinai Health System, said the greatest opportunity for AI in radiology is not simply to make physicians faster but to give them better tools to deliver exceptional patient care. Imagen said the growth capital will also help further accelerate radiologist recruitment and retention, and it plans to invest in other clinical resources, operational infrastructure and technology to support physicians. Previous contributors have included venture capitalists, hospitals and health systems, and technology entrepreneurs, with institutional investors including Google Ventures and DFJ. The company also previously touted new leadership appointments in August amid rapid growth and recently published new research in Population Health Management.

Articles.Title: ‘AI-enabled’ radiology practice raises $100M in growth capital

stories.Headline: House lawmakers introduce bipartisan bill to create federal cyber and AI review board
stories.Summary:
House lawmakers introduced a bipartisan bill on Wednesday to create a federal board. This board would investigate major cyberattacks, artificial intelligence incidents, and technology failures. Rep. Morgan Luttrell of Texas introduced the ROOT CAUSE Act with Rep. Ritchie Torres. The proposal follows outages that disrupted air travel, workplace software, and National Security Agency operations. These disruptive events occurred over the last week before the bill was introduced.

The ROOT CAUSE Act creates a National Cyber and AI Investigations Board in CISA. This board would examine serious disruptions from faulty updates, configuration errors, or AI failures. The AI INSIGHT Act by Rep. Matt Van Epps addresses AI agents on civilian networks. Rep. Andy Ogles of Tennessee introduced the SECURE IT Act on Wednesday for IT security. These measures exclude national security systems, defense systems, and intelligence community systems from their authority.

Rep. Luttrell stated that action is critical because adversaries are becoming increasingly sophisticated in this space. Rep. Van Epps said every agent on a federal network is a potential target for adversaries. Rep. Ogles noted that recent outages exposed American dependence on shared IT infrastructure. He stated that stronger coordination between government and industry is needed as cyber threats grow. The bills aim to prevent the executive branch from abolishing the board without Congressional acts.

Sens. Maria Cantwell and Mike Rounds urged Jay Clayton to coordinate a national response to AI threats. They wrote that the digital economy cannot rely on individual companies to solve these problems. The senators cited AI's role in uncovering flaws in PHP software used to run websites.

They noted that banks cannot always distinguish authorized AI agents from rogue actors accessing customer accounts. The proposed SECURE IT Act would keep company participation in its coordination efforts entirely voluntary. The board proposal comes nearly two years after the Trump administration emptied the Cyber Safety Review Board. That previous board had faulted Microsoft for security failures that allowed Chinese hackers to access emails.

Recent disruptions include a Friday FAA ground stop that delayed more than 10,000 flights. A Microsoft outage disrupted workplace tools, and maintenance caused a Tuesday outage of the classified NSANet. The Trump administration emptied the previous board during an investigation of China's Salt Typhoon telecom intrusions. Democrats will take control of Congress in January with Rep. Bennie Thompson chairing the homeland panel.

CISA would establish supporting capabilities for AI agent tracking within one year of the act's enactment. The legislation would prevent outside officials from altering or suppressing the findings of the new board. The articles leave open whether the proposed bills will pass under the new Congressional leadership. They do not state if the current administration supports these three specific legislative proposals.

Articles.Title: Bipartisan bill would create cyber and AI review board amid series of tech outages

stories.Headline: FPT Software chair Chu Thi Thanh Ha says AI shifts firm from hourly billing to outcomes
stories.Summary:
FPT Software, which serves as the IT services arm for a major Vietnamese technology firm, is changing its business strategy. The company is moving away from a traditional offshore outsourcing model that focused on providing engineering manpower to international clients. This shift is happening because artificial intelligence is altering how the industry operates and how services are delivered. The announcement was made public on November 17, 2026, following discussions about the evolving global tech landscape. The transition requires the company to stop relying on a billing model based on the number of engineering hours worked.

Instead, the firm must now focus on delivering specific outcomes to satisfy the changing demands of its American customers. This change marks a significant departure from the previous approach of simply offshoring labor to reduce costs for clients. The company is transforming its entire operational framework to remain competitive in an era dominated by automated intelligence. Chairperson Chu Thi Thanh Ha explained these changes during an interview with Nikkei Asia on November 10 in Tokyo.

She spoke while attending the Nikkei Forum Global Management Dialogue 2026 to describe why the company had to transform. According to the chairperson, the shift is necessary because U.S. customers no longer want to pay for hours of labor. She emphasized that the business must move beyond being an offshoring provider to survive the current technological shift. More to follow.
