stories.Headline: Tokenomics Foundation launches as Linux Foundation project to set open AI cost standards
stories.Summary:
The Tokenomics Foundation launched in August 2026 as a project of the Linux Foundation, working alongside the FinOps Foundation, which did the same job for cloud spending, according to a November 18, 2026 opinion piece by Raul Leite in InfoWorld. Its members include large AI buyers such as banks and retailers, plus cloud and model providers, and it does not sell a product or ship a cost-tracking tool. Instead it acts as a standards body whose working groups publish open, vendor-neutral definitions, so everyone means the same thing by input, output, reasoning and cached tokens, and standards for cost data that mainly extend FOCUS, the FinOps billing format, so AI providers report usage in the same way. The actual measuring is done by tools on the market, like AI gateways and observability platforms, and the Foundation's job is to make sure they all speak the same language.

The piece defines AI tokenomics as the practice of managing that economy and connecting the cost structure to business outcomes, noting that one token is roughly 4 characters, or 0.75 words, in English, and that the term has nothing to do with crypto, where it means the supply and incentives of a coin. Leite describes a stack mapping everything that shapes the cost of an AI answer, from energy and hardware at the bottom through infrastructure management, inference, model selection, and access and control, to demand at the top, and says its value is showing where to look before you start cutting. He also presents Big-T, an idea like Big-O notation in programming, describing how fast token use grows as more people use an app, including agent-multiplied growth where agents spawn other agents and calls pile up fast, and unbounded growth where a loop with no exit runs until someone pulls the plug. The key insight, he writes, is that the multiplier is usually invisible, since a user asks one question and the app makes five or 10 calls behind the scenes.

Leite, a principal solution architect at Red Hat who says the views are his own, writes that token prices keep falling but AI bills keep rising, because cheaper tokens lead teams to build bigger systems with longer conversations, more documents per question and agents calling agents. He says the big savings usually come from the middle and the top of the stack, using a smaller model for simple tasks, caching repeated work and sending less context, and he advises asking of every workflow how many model calls one user request really triggers. He sums up the Foundation's mission as moving AI from experimental spending to accountable operations, since most organizations cannot connect their AI spend to an outcome their CFO would accept, and says it wants to fix that by building open standards, benchmarks and a shared language. The goal, he writes, is not just about making AI cheaper but about making it worth it.

Articles.Title: Tokenomics Foundation: Making sense of what AI actually costs you

stories.Headline: Agent builders weigh browser infrastructure tools for authenticated access, stealth and scale
stories.Summary:
AI agents require specialised browser infrastructure to interact with web systems that lack clean APIs, according to TechGig. These tools provide hosted or self-hosted browsers that agents can drive programmatically, managing sessions, authentication, stealth and isolation for developers. Running browsers reliably at scale, with logins, sessions, stealth and isolation, poses a significant infrastructure challenge that these tools are designed to address. The article was published on November 18, 2026, and describes a range of tools rather than a single product launch. Agent builders weigh several needs when choosing among these tools, including authenticated access, session persistence, stealth and anti-bot capabilities, scale and isolation, and framework compatibility.

Anchor Browser focuses on authenticated enterprise access for SSO, MFA and VPN-protected applications, offering persistent session state and integration with existing agent frameworks via an SDK. Browserbase provides a general-purpose platform for hosted headless Chromium sessions and works with Playwright, Puppeteer or Selenium. Browserless offers hosted or self-hosted browser endpoints supporting Chrome, Firefox and WebKit, while Steel is an open-source, self-hostable remote browser infrastructure with built-in stealth, CAPTCHA handling and proxy options. Browser Use combines an open-source automation library with a low-cost, pay-per-minute hosted cloud, featuring built-in stealth and CAPTCHA handling. Bright Data Browser API integrates hosted Chromium with its large proxy network and excels at proxy-heavy scraping at scale, handling fingerprinting and CAPTCHA solving for tough sites.

Kernel isolates each Chromium instance in its own virtual machine, providing strong separation between browser workloads and billing by memory time for isolation-sensitive use cases. Lightpanda is an open-source headless browser built for speed and low memory use, optimising for fast page reading at scale, though it does not render graphics. The article states that the optimal tool depends on the agent's specific workload, and that prioritising authenticated access, public web data collection, control or fast content reading guides the selection process. It does not name any company or individual as responsible for these tools beyond the products described, and it does not include statements from the vendors themselves. No further steps, timelines or announcements are given beyond the guidance that selection should follow the workload.

stories.Headline: Law firms face pressure to modernize for AI as Perry AI and Alecto raise seed funding
stories.Summary:
The legal industry is currently facing significant pressure to modernize its operations or risk being left behind during the artificial intelligence era. This shift was highlighted during the TLTF Summit 2026, where experts discussed whether private equity funding could accelerate the adoption of new technologies. Many firms previously believed their unique economic position protected them from the kind of disruption seen in other sectors. However, the current environment suggests that law firms must now adapt to the same technological pressures affecting the broader economy.

The transition toward AI requires substantial capital and a willingness to change traditional business models to ensure growth and innovation. While some firms seek outside investment to turbocharge these efforts, more capital does not always guarantee a seamless transition to AI. Recent financial activity in the sector includes a 2.2 million dollar seed round for the startup Perry AI, which intends to hire talent in India, Singapore, and the United States. Additionally, the AI-powered conveyancing provider Alecto raised 20 million dollars in a seed round with investment from Mishcon de Reya.

Rhys Dipshan reported that the legal industry is experiencing a rude awakening regarding its ability to operate at its own pace. The reporting suggests that while outside funding is a potential catalyst, the process of AI adoption remains complex and challenging. Other industry observations indicate that legal professionals in the United Kingdom and Ireland who use AI extensively are more likely to see stronger revenue effects. Experts also suggest that firms should consider the nationality of their AI tools to mitigate risks and gain commercial benefits.

The broader context shows a surge in high-profile marketing and investment, such as the partnership between Harvey and Wimbledon. Some new AI providers, like Alecto, explicitly claim that their ultimate goal is to replace traditional law firms entirely. As these technologies evolve, firms must balance the need for rapid modernization with the risks associated with AI transformation. The industry continues to monitor whether private equity will successfully bridge the gap between traditional practice and modern efficiency.

stories.Headline: Governor Gavin Newsom proposes tougher AI regulations and urges federal oversight for 2028 presidential candidates
stories.Summary:
California Governor Gavin Newsom visited Washington, D.C., on November 18, 2026, to unveil new proposals for tougher artificial intelligence regulations. The governor spent several days meeting with bipartisan lawmakers, including House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, to request disaster recovery funding for wildfires. During a roundtable and a subsequent press exchange, Newsom argued that supporting government oversight of AI should be a basic requirement for any serious 2028 presidential candidate. He framed these efforts as a national necessity, contrasting his approach with the current administration's policies.

The new California report suggests mandatory safety standards and independent oversight for advanced AI models to ensure public safety. It proposes the implementation of emergency shutdown procedures, often called kill switches, and limits on the ability of AI to autonomously create more powerful versions of itself. These recommendations follow an executive order Newsom signed in September to accelerate the implementation of safety legislation. The governor has already discussed continuing this regulatory work with Governor-elect Xavier Becerra, who will take office in January.

Newsom criticized President Trump for allowing AI companies to self-regulate, suggesting this approach primarily benefits the president's political allies. He compared the lack of oversight to an airline that operates without independent analysis, calling the current situation a national crisis of confidence. In response, White House spokeswoman Luz Huston stated that American leadership in super intelligence is essential for national security and economic prosperity. She asserted that President Trump remains committed to protecting consumers while ensuring the United States leads the world in this technology.

The governor's visit occurred while President Trump was in China for meetings with President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Newsom traveled to the capital directly from Ukraine, noting that neither the president nor Vice President JD Vance had visited that country. Although he has not yet decided if he will run for president in 2028, Newsom indicated he would make a determination after leaving office in January. He presented the California regulatory framework as a potential national model that the federal government should adopt.

Articles.Title: Newsom says AI regulation should be ‘table stakes’ for any serious 2028 candidate

stories.Headline: Better Markets urges human accountability and audits to keep AI risks off households
stories.Summary:
Better Markets released a report on November 18, 2026, titled AI and the Real Economy: What’s at Stake for Main Street, written by Evan LeFlore, the organization’s Director of AI, Innovation, and Economic Opportunity. The Washington, D.C. group said the report examines artificial intelligence’s role in household and small-business finances by asking who captures the value AI creates, who carries the risk, and who pays the bill. LeFlore said the potential impacts on Americans’ financial lives are widespread, and that loan decisions, 401(k) risks, and everyday affordability are only part of the picture. He said workers, savers, borrowers, and taxpayers will inevitably feel the impact. LeFlore said oversight is being pulled back just as the risks grow, noting that the SEC withdrew its proposed rule on AI conflicts of interest and that the CFPB has been hollowed out and pulled back its guidance on AI-driven credit denials.

He also said banking regulators’ updated model-risk-management guidance exempts the generative and agentic AI that poses the newest risks, while the AI industry spends heavily to shape the rules meant to govern it. The report recommends keeping a human or firm legally accountable for actions an AI agent takes, so that a company deploying an autonomous system owns what that system does. It says every adverse decision needs a real reason, because “the model told us to” is not an explanation, and that fair-lending laws, including the disparate-impact doctrine, should be enforced as written. The report also calls for independent audits over vendor promises, so claims that a model is fair or expands access are checked by someone who is not selling it. It recommends closing the AI carve-outs in banking regulators’ model-risk guidance and supervising the handful of AI model and cloud providers the financial system now depends on as systemic chokepoints.

It further recommends giving savers a clear, accessible description of their AI exposure on investment statements and target-date fund labels, and requiring transparency on the debt and off-balance-sheet financing behind the data-center and broader AI buildout. LeFlore said change is certain but progress is not, so whether AI’s gains are broadly shared depends on the policy choices made today. Better Markets describes itself as a nonprofit, nonpartisan economic advocacy organization dedicated to making the economy work for all Americans and protecting the public interest in Washington policymaking. The group said it works to support policies that create sustainable, durable, and broad-based economic growth and rising living standards while protecting jobs, savings, and retirements. The full report is available through the organization.

stories.Headline: Siemens India showcases industrial AI and digital twins to cut engineering timelines and costs
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is being integrated into India's manufacturing, infrastructure and transportation sectors in a push aimed at boosting productivity and encouraging sustainable practices, according to TechGig. The report says the move could reduce engineering timelines and costs, and it describes the integration of AI with engineering knowledge, real-time operational data, automation and digital twins as central to Siemens India Innovation Day 2026. That event, held under the theme "AI for the Real World," highlights AI deployed in industrial environments where reliability, safety, cybersecurity and measurable outcomes are critical, the article says. Applications named in the report include AI-assisted engineering, predictive maintenance, automated quality inspection and process optimisation, all of which rely on a connected foundation linking information technology and operational technology.

The article explains that digital twins are virtual representations of products, machines or infrastructure assets used to design, simulate, validate and optimise their physical counterparts, which helps find problems digitally so corrections are faster and cheaper before physical construction. Physical AI extends artificial intelligence into machines and physical systems so they can interpret objectives and respond to changing conditions autonomously, a progression from rule-based to intent-based automation. For India, the report says, this offers a chance to leapfrog older stages of industrial automation and compress technological progress that previously took many years, while companies that do not adopt Physical AI risk falling behind global competitors. Every AI model depends on physical infrastructure including computing capacity, electricity, cooling, connectivity, automation and resilient operations, and the challenge for customers is to design and operate that capacity efficiently and reliably at scale, according to the article.

Autonomous buildings use connected data and domain-specific AI to sense conditions, predict requirements and take governed action, with potential applications in energy optimisation, predictive maintenance and improved occupant comfort, the report says. Sunil Mathur, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Siemens Limited, noted that energy accounts for a significant portion of operating costs in industries like hotels and cement plants, making efficiency improvements impactful. On railways, the article says India's transformation can leverage digitalisation, automation and data to enhance infrastructure intelligence, with technologies such as Signaling X, Communications-Based Train Control and predictive maintenance applications supporting safer, more connected operations and better asset availability. The stated objective is to gain greater value from every train, signal, power system and physical asset throughout its operating life.

Articles.Title: Industrial AI reshaping India's factories and infrastructure

stories.Headline: Han Seong-sook bans smart devices and deploys extra staff to stop AI cheating in college entrance exam
stories.Summary:
Prime Minister Han Seong-sook said Tuesday that the government would activate an interagency emergency response team, ban the possession of smart devices during the exam and deploy additional personnel to test sites to root out AI cheating in this week's college entrance exam. She made the remark during a Cabinet meeting, as concerns deepened that AI-assisted cheating could be used in this year's College Scholastic Ability Test, which is set for Thursday. The concerns followed the confession by the top scorer of this year's certified tax accountant exam that he cheated with the help of AI. Han called such cheating a social evil and said the government would root it out completely.

Han said all smart devices, including smartphones, must be powered off and turned in, and that authorities would thoroughly inspect all glasses and watches worn by test takers. She said items such as collars, sleeves and buttons would also be carefully checked. The government will tighten the management of Wi-Fi networks around the test sites, and all bags belonging to examinees must be stored outside the examination rooms, such as in hallways. Checks will be conducted to ensure that no smart devices are active among the personal belongings stored outside the examination rooms.

Han said the government would deploy additional proctors and apply a zero-tolerance policy to strictly penalize any instances of cheating. She said any suspected case would be thoroughly investigated and met with stern action, including invalidating the exam, revoking eligibility and filing criminal complaints or requesting police investigations. President Lee Jae Myung on Tuesday ordered additional measures to curb AI-assisted cheating during Thursday's exam, including a proposed reward of at least 100 million won, or about $75,000, for tips. The article did not say what happens next beyond those measures.

Articles.Title: Gov't to ban smart devices, deploy extra staff to prevent AI cheating in Suneung

stories.Headline: Israeli study finds 78% use AI for health questions but only 38% verify answers
stories.Summary:
A new Israeli study found that 78% of respondents have used artificial intelligence for health-related questions, while only 38% verify its answers against additional sources, raising questions about public trust in the technology. The study was published Thursday by the Samuel Neaman Institute for National Policy Research at the Technion-Israel Institute of Technology, Shenkar, Wikimedia Israel, and the Israel Internet Association. It found that 85% of Israelis have used AI to satisfy their curiosity, and 78% used AI to get answers to health-related questions. Only 38% of respondents said they verify AI-generated answers against additional sources, even as 53% acknowledged that the technology can produce incorrect information. The study, which examined information consumption habits and public trust in Israel in 2026, also found that 73% of respondents described AI's impact on their search and learning habits as positive.

Beyond health-related questions, 71% reported using AI to understand concepts, 70% sought tips and advice, 55% used the technology for news and current affairs, and 25% used it to write computer code. According to the data presented, 63% use algorithmic information sources at least four days a week, compared with 29% who use traditional information sources such as television, radio, print newspapers, and other internet sites including Wikipedia. The gap is largest between the 25-34 year-old demographic, where it reaches 50 percentage points, gradually narrowing with age. When comparing information appearing on Wikipedia and information provided by AI, 28% of Israelis said they tended to prefer Wikipedia, while 29% said they tended to prefer AI tools. Among daily users, the research showed that trust levels are close, with 53% of users trusting Wikipedia and 49% trusting AI tools.

The study found that about half of Israelis believe AI responses are based on up-to-date information, and 41% believe the information AI provides is generally accurate and factual. On the other hand, 53% were aware that AI models may generate incorrect information, with 61% of the 18-34 year-old demographic being aware of this compared to 41% for those aged 55 and older. A notable gap was also found between Jews and Arab Israelis surveyed, with 59% of Jews being aware of this issue as compared to 29% of Arab Israelis. Researchers found that 55% of Israelis regularly read AI-generated summaries and then consult additional sources, while 28% rely solely on the summaries and do not do further research. Among those who read Wikipedia daily, 55% said they verify AI responses against additional sources, compared with 33% of those who do not read Wikipedia at all.

As part of the study, researchers asked 1,226 respondents open-ended questions examining how the use of AI had changed search and learning habits. Of these, 73% said they had experienced a positive change, while 2% said they had experienced a negative change. Exploring the changes, 28% of respondents mentioned the speed of finding information, 26% cited ease and convenience, and 20% cited new learning opportunities, while 14% explicitly stated that AI had replaced search engines for them. iPanel conducted the survey using an online panel and quota sampling of Israel's adult population, aged 18 and older, in Hebrew and Arabic. The full findings of the study will be presented on Thursday at a conference at Shenkar, with the participation of Prof. Sheizaf Rafaeli, president of Shenkar, Michal Wander Schwartz, CEO of Wikimedia Israel, and Dr. Eran Leck, senior research fellow at the Samuel Neaman Institute for National Policy Research at the Technion.

Articles.Title: Israelis use AI for everything from medicine to news, but rarely fact-check

stories.Headline: LinkedIn's Sundara Raman Ramachandran details scaling a distilled LLM ranking system to 1.3 billion members
stories.Summary:
LinkedIn has implemented a scalable large language model based ranking system for its search and recommendation workloads, serving 1.3 billion members globally, TechGig reported on November 18, 2026. Sundara Raman Ramachandran, a tech lead at LinkedIn, detailed the challenges and solutions in an InfoQ presentation. The company reduced a 7 billion parameter model to 400 million parameters through multi-teacher distillation and pruning. Context compression cut job description prompt lengths from 2,000 tokens to 150 through summarisation, or to a single embedding.

These offline optimisations produced an 8x to 10x throughput improvement with less than 2 per cent quality loss. LinkedIn introduced a dedicated scoring API in the open-source SGLang engine to bypass unnecessary decode phases in ranking workloads. Inference optimisations addressed CPU bottlenecks with batch tokenisation and batch integrity across inter-process communication. GPU underutilisation was tackled by replacing synchronous blocking copies with asynchronous non-blocking copies for probabilities. A custom Item-Aware Attention Mask concatenates multiple item prompts into a single LLM input, reusing query key-value pairs.

Python-specific issues included latency spikes from garbage collection, mitigated using gc.freeze after model warm-up. The Global Interpreter Lock bottleneck in gRPC servicer and SGLang worker processes was resolved by using multiple processes. Learnings include benchmarking production traffic with Poisson distribution and ensuring absolute parity between offline and online systems. LinkedIn reported a 5 per cent to 10 per cent increase in auction metrics, such as relevance and engagement, due to LLM-based re-ranking.

Articles.Title: LinkedIn scales LLM ranking for 1.3 billion members

stories.Headline: Kasey Chappelle and Adam Grimshaw explain how compliance teams layer AI rules and standards
stories.Summary:
There is no single rulebook for AI governance yet, and instead compliance teams must work with layers that include regulation such as the EU AI Act, sector-specific guidance from financial regulators, and standards such as NIST and ISO 42001. In the second episode of the From principle to practice series from the Elliptic Institute, David Carlisle asks Kasey Chappelle and Adam Grimshaw where those layers stand today and what compliance teams can do while they develop. The episode explores how the EU AI Act, financial regulators such as MAS and a patchwork of US rules fit together for organizations building their own approach. The series examines what AI governance and risk management mean for compliance teams, with the people building Elliptic's own AI governance framework answering one key question in each episode.

The discussion covers why the real value of ISO 42001 is the risk-based management system behind it, even though standards lag the technology. It also addresses why technical controls for AI are still fragmented and what that fragmentation means for organizations building their own controls. The episode considers what the move to cloud teaches about shared responsibility for AI models and hosting, and why organizations cannot wait for perfect clarity before acting. These points turn the principles in the Elliptic Standard into practical steps for compliance teams.

Kasey Chappelle and Adam Grimshaw answered questions from David Carlisle about where the layers of AI governance are today. The episode frames the EU AI Act, guidance from financial regulators such as MAS and a patchwork of US rules as layers that compliance teams must fit together. It presents the value of ISO 42001 as lying in the risk-based management system behind the standard rather than in the standard alone. It also explains why technical controls for AI remain fragmented and what that means for organizations building their own.

The articles give no further dates, numbers or names beyond the EU AI Act, MAS, NIST, ISO 42001, David Carlisle, Kasey Chappelle, Adam Grimshaw and the November 18, 2026 publication of the episode. The series is described as a new one from the Elliptic Institute that explores what AI governance and risk management means for compliance teams. Each episode has the people building Elliptic's own AI governance framework answer one key question, turning the principles in the Elliptic Standard into practical steps. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the episode itself.

stories.Headline: Democratic Congress prepares AI safety and testing bills as Trump administration favors deregulation in 2027
stories.Summary:
The articles report that federal artificial intelligence policy is likely to divide along institutional lines in 2027, according to a November 17, 2026 analysis by Kevin Edgar and Michelle Tanney of BakerHostetler published on JD Supra. The Trump administration will continue to emphasize American technological leadership, infrastructure development and regulatory restraint, while the Democratic-controlled Congress is expected to focus more heavily on safety, accountability, consumer protection and the costs associated with AI. When the 120th Congress convenes in January 2027, AI policy is likely to look markedly different from the federal approach of the past two years. Democratic control of the House and Senate will give the party significant authority over the congressional agenda beginning Jan. 3, 2027. Current reporting indicates that Democratic lawmakers are preparing proposals addressing advanced-model testing, AI-related harms and the costs associated with AI deployment and development.

Congressional oversight may move faster than legislation, and new congressional leadership will control committee agendas, hearing calendars and subpoena authority. Pending legislation identifies the controls Congress may expect, including independent testing of frontier models, incident reporting, government oversight and human-controlled shutdown capabilities. The bipartisan FRONTIER Act would create a federal oversight regime for frontier AI and independent assessment of certain developers' safety practices. H.R. 9925, the Frontier Risk Oversight, National Transparency, Independent Evaluation, and Reporting Act, or FRONTIER Act, was introduced in July by Reps. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., and Lori Trahan, D-Mass., with bipartisan cosponsors.

H.R. 9917, the AI Kill Switch Act, introduced by Reps. Ted Lieu, D-Calif., and Nathaniel Moran, R-Texas, would require covered entities to maintain technical capabilities to shut down certain covered technologies. Sen. John N. Kennedy, R-La., subsequently introduced S. 5417, the AI Emergency Button Act, which likewise would require developers or operators of advanced AI systems to incorporate a human-controlled shutdown capability. Democratic Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan proposed pausing the training and release of the most powerful AI models until federal safeguards are established, prohibiting the development of superintelligent systems and recursive self-improvement, and creating a Cabinet-level agency empowered to inspect AI laboratories, block dangerous model releases and order shutdowns. In November, the Department of Justice announced a Super Intelligence Task Force focused on misuse of advanced technology by foreign and state-sponsored actors, transnational criminal organizations, and individuals or companies engaged in fraud or other unlawful conduct.

The DOJ specifically identified regular reporting of risks and incidents and vigorous internal controls over advanced AI systems as areas of focus. Proposals such as the Clear Liability for Artificial Intelligence Misconduct (CLAIM) Act from Rep. Trahan would create new federal remedies specifically addressing harms caused by AI systems. Regulatory fragmentation may persist, because presidential veto authority, Senate procedural requirements and continuing disagreements over the appropriate scope of AI regulation make enactment of a comprehensive federal statute uncertain. Companies should therefore prepare for overlapping federal oversight, executive action, state regulation, agency enforcement and private litigation rather than presume that a single national framework will emerge. A congressional committee need not establish probable cause before issuing a subpoena, unlike federal law enforcement seeking a search warrant.

Congressional investigations can develop rapidly, encompass conduct that is not itself unlawful and unfold publicly alongside legislative and political debate. Companies should not wait for a subpoena to assess their readiness, and organizations facing potential congressional scrutiny should identify the internal personnel responsible for responding to congressional inquiries. For much of the past two years, federal AI policy has largely been developed through executive action rather than comprehensive legislation. The Trump administration's approach culminated in a federal effort to challenge state AI laws viewed as inconsistent with a uniform, minimally burdensome national framework.

Democratic lawmakers have already used letters, information requests and other minority-party tools to examine AI companies and their practices. Existing consumer protection, antidiscrimination, privacy, intellectual property, product liability and other laws may already apply to conduct involving AI, depending on the technology, use and resulting harm. Organizations should therefore remain responsible for the accuracy, reliability, confidentiality and integrity of work produced with AI assistance. The articles state that the change in congressional control will not necessarily produce entirely new areas of scrutiny, and that what will change in 2027 is the authority behind those inquiries.

The incoming Senate will include members who campaigned on substantially more aggressive restrictions in the development of advanced AI. The articles state that the resulting tension may shape federal AI policy even if Congress does not enact comprehensive legislation. The articles state that the emerging divide may be less about whether AI should be governed than about how. The articles leave open which AI bills ultimately become law.

stories.Headline: Solicitor-General Ruth Higgins warns faulty automated systems risk eroding public trust in the law
stories.Summary:
Commonwealth Solicitor-General Ruth Higgins SC used one of her first public appearances since starting in June to question how artificial intelligence affects what she called the humanity of the law. She spoke at the Australian Securities and Investments Commission annual forum, where ASIC chair Sarah Court had been due to hold a fireside chat with her before Court withdrew late because her voice gave out. Journalist Amelia Brace, the forum's co-MC, took Court's place for the conversation with Higgins. The event had been expected to touch on ASIC's case against Star Entertainment, in which Higgins was the lead barrister.

Higgins said human judgement sits at the centre of the legitimacy of the law, and she warned that faulty automated systems risk eroding public trust. The Star case did not end as ASIC had hoped, despite large fines and bans for former chief executive Matt Bekier and lawyer Paula Martin, who are now appealing. Justice Michael Lee also criticised the way the case was pleaded when he dismissed the claims against the non-executive directors. The forum was held on 19 November 2026, and Capital Brief reported her remarks that afternoon.

Higgins is the government's top lawyer, and her warning places responsibility for the use of automated systems on those who design and rely on them, though the article does not set out any specific proposal or rule. ASIC has separately put consumer harm arising from AI on notice, according to a related item listed by Capital Brief dated 18 November 2026. The same outlet listed a government move on mandatory AI rules and a response to an OpenAI hack, dated 10 November 2026, and an APRA warning on market volatility and AI risks to financial stability, dated 12 November 2026. The articles do not say what, if anything, follows from Higgins's remarks.

The wider context is a run of regulatory attention to AI across Australia's financial watchdogs, including ASIC's notice on consumer harm and APRA's flagging of risks to financial stability. Capital Brief also reported that the High Court has finally embraced livestreaming, and that the Australian Institute of Company Directors has updated its guidance. The articles do not say whether Higgins will repeat her warning in a formal setting or whether any review of automated systems in government legal work is planned. No next step is stated beyond the remarks at the forum.

stories.Headline: China-linked threat actors use autonomous AI tools to breach ten organizations
stories.Summary:
China-nexus threat actors used autonomous AI tools to breach ten organizations between August and September. These attackers targeted advanced manufacturing, defense sectors, and civil and human rights organizations. The malicious activity was tracked as CL-STA-1238 by researchers at Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42. This campaign represents the second documented attack where China-linked actors used the Cairn penetration-testing framework. The actors conducted twenty-five operations against at least nineteen organizations during this specific time period.

The attacks targeted seven semiconductor and advanced-manufacturing supply chain firms and three US defense and defense policy organizations. Attackers used Chinese large language models Zhipu GLM 5.2 and DeepSeek V4 Flash and Pro. Victims included a semiconductor-lithography manufacturer, an industrial-automation manufacturer, an education nonprofit, a US teacher's union, and an industry standards body. One organization suffered a mass exposure of personal data that exceeded one million records. Other targets included a defense policy think tank and various human rights and civil society organizations.

Unit 42 researchers stated that the attackers supplied a target and goal for the AI to execute. They noted that Cairn planned, executed, and recorded results on its own using a shared blackboard. The researchers explained that AI model agents write findings back as a fact-intent graph. They also observed that human operators could inject hints to guide the operations if needed. Unit 42 reported that the attackers obtained dozens of valid credentials and retrieved military identities.

Tyler Oliver of Huntbase said it does not matter to a victim if AI or humans are attacking. Rickard Carlsson of Detectify noted that Cairn builds on earlier findings without a person reviewing every result. John Strand of Black Hills Information Security suggested that organizations use continuous attack surface management. He also recommended using cyber deception by setting up tripwires to detect attackers during reconnaissance. These experts highlighted that the victims were affected by known security gaps and dated public CVEs.

The articles state that the attackers exploited authentication bypasses and insecure direct object references. They also used mass-assignment privilege escalation, exposed cloud APIs, and weak or default credentials. The Cairn framework allows for simultaneous operations against multiple organizations to reduce dependence on human operators. Individual operations lasted anywhere from twenty minutes to more than fifty hours. The background shows that another AI penetration-testing framework called Artex is also being weaponized.

Defenders can still use identity hygiene, attack-surface reduction, and software patching to remain effective against these tools. Organizations are encouraged to identify all services exposed to the internet and restrict access wherever possible. The articles leave open how these AI-driven attacks will evolve in future offensive operations. They do not specify which particular military or government identities were retrieved during the successful breaches. It remains unclear how many other organizations may have been targeted beyond the nineteen identified.

stories.Headline: Anthropic launches IPO at $1.4tn valuation and turns 4,000 staff into millionaires
stories.Summary:
The AI developer Anthropic launched its initial public offering on Thursday. This major financial event occurred during the third week of November 2026. The company is the creator of the chatbot known as Claude. This float is expected to create a large number of new millionaires. It aims to fuel a gold rush in the high-end London property market.

The IPO is expected to value the company at $1.4tn, which is £1.1tn. More than 4,000 staff members will likely become millionaires as their stock options vest. SaaStr estimates the minimum value generated for these staff members will be $20m each. Anthropic was founded in San Francisco in 2021 and employs 5,000 people worldwide. It has over 200 employees in the UK and plans a London office for 800 people.

Jo Eccles, a buying agent, says tech buyers have budgets from £2m to £40m. Jeremy Gee of Beauchamp Estates says AI buyers are younger and move very quickly. He notes that these buyers value location and quality and will pay a premium. Shona Baijal of Coutts says many young entrepreneurs feel overwhelmed by their vast wealth. She advises these new clients not to rush into making any major financial decisions.

Tech wealth is affecting luxury agents who once struggled to take young entrepreneurs seriously. Residents of San Francisco face higher rents, with one-bedroom flats averaging $4,400 per month. UK investors like Alex Gerko expect to make hundreds of millions in paper gains. Igor Babuschkin bought a £57m penthouse, and Suneil Setiya reportedly paid £270m for Providence House. These buyers are drawn to London for its culture, history, and growing AI community.

Anthropic spent £24.1m on an average of 43 staff in 2024, averaging £560,000 per person. Research engineers have seen base salary advertisements reaching up to £630,000 before their stock options. OpenAI staff in London earned an average of £2.3m last year, far exceeding median earnings. The King's Cross knowledge quarter now hosts Anthropic, OpenAI, and Meta near Google's headquarters. Demis Hassabis previously sold DeepMind to Google for £400m in 2014 within this same area.

The UK economy grew by 0.7% in the third quarter, driven largely by IT services. Bloomberg analysis suggests that AI powered roughly a quarter of all UK economic growth this year. However, the CAPE ratio reached its highest level since 2000, suggesting the market is overvalued. Some investors worry about an AI bubble bursting amid safety concerns and datacentre construction opposition. It remains unclear if this new class of wealth is permanent or a temporary flash.

stories.Headline: Ashwini Vaishnaw says India will issue an AI regulation consultation paper within a month
stories.Summary:
India’s government is drafting an AI law, and on 8 October Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said a consultation paper on AI regulation would come within a month and would probably form the basis of future regulation. In July, media reports said MeitY was examining the autonomy of AI agents as part of a possible new law. The article, by Manoj Chugh, was updated on 18 November 2026 and published on ETGovernment. It argues that the AI that should worry policymakers most is not the one that fakes a video but the one that approves a loan, files a return or moves money with no human pressing the final button. That is agentic AI.

The article says the government’s signals so far point to safety, a human-first approach, skilling, deepfakes and psychological harms. It says an agent is given a goal, access to systems and the authority to act, and it reads an invoice, checks it against a contract, raises a payment and emails the vendor. It proposes five principles: shared, graded accountability with a named deployer and a named executive for every agent acting with real authority; autonomy tiered by consequence, so any action that moves money above a set threshold, signs or changes a contract, or touches sensitive personal data needs human approval; tamper-evident action logs; agent incidents in the six-hour regime; and precise definitions of agents by their authority to act. It cites the 2026 amendments to the IT Rules requiring platforms to label AI-generated audio and video, CERT-In’s 2022 directions requiring cyber incidents to be reported within six hours, the RBI’s FREE-AI framework recommending board-approved AI policies for banks and other regulated entities, and the DPDP Act, whose consent manager framework comes into force this week, with penalties of up to ₹250 crore.

Dr. Pavan Duggal, a Supreme Court advocate of over 30 years, Global Chair of the AI Accountability Forum and author of more than 200 books on cyber law and AI, said on the Corridors & Boardrooms podcast that the old instinct to blame whoever built it no longer works because the builder cannot predict how an agent will behave. He proposes graded liability, looking at what each party contributed, whether model creator, integrator, deployer or user, and assigning liability accordingly. He pointed to a deeper gap: the Contract Act recognizes agency but not AI as an agent, so when an agent takes a decision on someone’s behalf, the law is silent on whether that decision is binding. Experts suggest a presumptive burden of proof, so once harm is claimed those who built, integrated and deployed the agent must show they took due care. The article says the defense that the algorithm did it is not good enough.

Dr. Gulshan Rai, whose team drafted the IT Act in 2000, said on the same podcast that the hardest problem was converting the virtual into something the law could recognize, and that at that time there was not even a digital signature in the country. His team wrote the Act in plain English because the common man would have to live with it. Section 66A, added in 2008, was struck down by the Supreme Court in 2015 because its language could reach ordinary online speech, and Dr. Rai believes 66A would not have been enough for generative or agentic AI anyway, adding that drafters should be very, very careful. In July 2016, hackers sent about $171 million out of Union Bank of India’s accounts through SWIFT, and working with the RBI and the government the bank recovered all of it within days; Dr. Rai, who coordinated the national response, says the lesson was that you need a single authority who can talk to regulators, banks and foreign governments at once. The article says enterprises should not mistake the absence of an AI law for the absence of law.

The article says the AI debate for two years has been about what models say, misinformation, bias and deepfakes, and that agents change the question to what AI systems do. It says content harms are about what people believe while agent harms are about what happens to their money, their data and their contracts, and that the second category needs its own chapter. It says a person harmed by an agent usually cannot prove what it did, so the courts can offer no remedy. It says the 2025 governance guidelines relied on existing laws and voluntary compliance, and that MeitY Secretary S. Krishnan has since signaled that the time for more may have come. It says the cyber security policy Dr. Rai wrote in 2013 still awaits a successor because, as he put it, somebody has to be made accountable and sit down and do it.

The article says the consultation paper is where the intent to examine AI agents must become concrete, and that the consultation paper should state plainly that the enterprise deploying an agent is the data fiduciary for what that agent does. It says boards do not need to wait for MeitY and can start by having the executive team take an inventory of every agent in production or pilot, including those inside vendor platforms, mapping each agent’s authority, what it can approve, spend, send, change or delete, and building and testing a kill switch. It says boards need to plan for resilience, and that experience shows the process fixes about half of security problems and configuration about 30%, while the role of technology is only about 15%, yet that is where most of the money goes. It says the question to ask every quarter is what the agents did that no human approved and whether it could be explained to a regulator. It says that if agents are left out of this paper, the next chance may be years away.

Articles.Title: Why India’s upcoming AI law must regulate autonomous agents, not just deepfakes

stories.Headline: Google opens preorders for Gemini smart glasses with Samsung and sets Dec 10 release
stories.Summary:
Google opened preorders on Nov. 12 for its Gemini-powered Intelligent Eyewear, developed with Samsung, with frame designs from Warby Parker and Gentle Monster, and plans to release the glasses on Dec. 10. The Warby Parker models start at $395, while the already available Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 costs $449. Google's glasses are powered by Gemini, and Meta's glasses use Meta AI. Both products offer cameras, AI assistants, and hands-free features. Buyers must decide whether to buy Meta's glasses now or wait for Google's alternative.

Warby Parker offers three frame styles starting at $395, and Gentle Monster has six styles priced from $449 to $489. Both collections use the same underlying hardware, with differences in design, fit, and lens options. The glasses combine Gemini with a 12MP camera, open-ear speakers, and four microphones, according to Samsung's announcement. Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 also has a 12MP camera but includes six microphones. Both support 3K video recording at 30 fps, and both advertise up to nine hours of battery life per charge.

Google's glasses offer 64GB of storage, twice Meta's 32GB, and Google claims up to 72 hours with its charging case, while Meta's case provides another 50 hours. Google's frames weigh approximately 40 to 44 grams depending on the model, and Meta's standard Wayfarer Gen 3 weighs about 51.5 grams and offers adjustable temple tips. Both support prescription lenses, although options vary by frame. Google's glasses offer HDR photography and video stabilization, while Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 includes slow motion and hyperlapse recording. Meta claims its updated microphone system reduces background noise.

According to Google's product announcement, the glasses allow wearers to ask Gemini questions about their surroundings, translate conversations, and get hands-free assistance. On supported Galaxy phones, users can ask Gemini to summarize a whiteboard and save the information to Samsung Notes. Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 offers similar visual assistance, voice commands, and live translation, with integrations centered on WhatsApp, Messenger, and Instagram. Meta's September launch announcement introduced a customizable action button. Google is a better fit for people who regularly use Gemini, Maps, and other Google services, while Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 suits those who frequently use Meta's messaging and social apps.

According to Google's official product information, the glasses support selected Pixel and Galaxy phones as well as compatible iPhones, and activation requires an eligible Google account associated with the United States or South Korea. Users must be at least 18, and some capabilities, including Guided Vision and Aira visual assistance, require a compatible Android phone at launch. Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 requires a compatible smartphone, a Meta account, and the Meta AI app, and its supported services and AI features can vary by country. Google says its privacy protections include recording indicators, camera permission controls, and automatic redaction of bystanders' faces during Gemini visual queries. The company also says visuals processed through those queries are not used to train AI models or target advertisements.

Meta's glasses include an external recording indicator to alert people nearby when photos or videos are being captured. Buyers prioritizing camera quality, call performance, or real-world battery life may be better off waiting for independent comparisons after Google's Dec. 10 release. The $395 Warby Parker models could be worth waiting for, particularly for buyers who regularly use Gemini and Google services. Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 is the more immediate choice for shoppers who want smart glasses now or already rely on Meta's supported apps. Before spending hundreds of dollars, buyers should check whether their phone supports the features they want.

Articles.Title: Google AI Glasses vs. Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3: Which Should You Buy?

stories.headline_source: Google AI Glasses vs. Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3: Which Should You Buy?

stories.Headline: xAI asks Ninth Circuit to block California AI training data law
stories.Summary:
Elon Musk's company xAI asked a three-judge panel of the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit on Wednesday, November 18, to block a California law. The company argues that AB 2013, which governs AI training data transparency, is unconstitutional and exposes valuable trade secrets. This legal challenge, known as X.AI LLC v. Bonta, No. 26-1591, was heard in Pasadena by Judges Rawlinson, Smith, and Forrest. While a federal judge previously denied a request for an injunction, xAI is now appealing that decision to the higher court.

The law, which Governor Newsom signed in September 2024 and implemented on January 1, requires generative AI developers to post summaries of their training datasets on their websites. California officials maintain that the law only asks for high-level information rather than the actual datasets themselves. xAI claims the mandate forces the company to reveal trade secrets worth billions of dollars and violates the First Amendment by compelling speech. Judge Jesus Bernal previously rejected these claims, stating that xAI failed to prove its data was more sensitive than that of its competitors.

xAI is currently the only major laboratory challenging the law, as OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google have not joined the lawsuit. The company argues that the state is dictating what a business must say about its own product, while AI researchers have filed briefs urging the court to uphold the law. The Ninth Circuit has not yet set a date for its ruling, but the law remains in force during the proceedings. This decision will establish an important precedent for whether AI transparency mandates can survive constitutional challenges across the western states.

Articles.Title: xAI tells Ninth Circuit California's AI training data law is unconstitutional - Startup Fortune

stories.Headline: "This is your main trump card" from AI: lawyers' mistakes and references to fake rulings can cost the client time, money, or a lawsuit
stories.Summary:
Lawyers have submitted documents to courts containing fabricated rulings, non-existent citations and legal conclusions judges never made, and the problem has reached the Supreme Court, the articles reported on 19 November 2026. In case No. 523/9632/24 the cassation court left the complaint without movement and gave the lawyer time to correct the deficiencies, after which the representative filed a motion to restore the deadline for cassation appeal. In case No. 390/2226/24 the defendant's lawyer cited court rulings in the complaint that the Supreme Court established did not actually exist. In case No. 754/17743/25 in the Desniansky District Court of Kyiv a man filed a claim to recognize his right to inheritance to an apartment and to recover 50,000 hryvnias in moral damages, separately claiming 25,000 hryvnias for legal assistance costs, and the claim was signed by a lawyer. In case No. 332/2779/26 in the Zavodskyi District Court of Zaporizhzhia co-owners of an apartment litigated over utility bills, and in case No. 363/1227/26 the Kyiv Court of Appeal considered a claim to compensate 5,000 hryvnias for legal assistance after closure of civil proceedings over debt to a dacha cooperative.

In case No. 754/17743/25 the court found references to rulings of the Supreme Court and the Plenum of the Supreme Court that did not exist, and the lawyer incorrectly stated the content of Civil Code articles, referred to provisions of the Law "On Notariat" regulating different issues and used references to non-existent regulatory legal acts. The court gave the representative time to correct the errors, but the amended claim again contained false references to procedural norms and still included the phrase "this is your main trump card," which the court interpreted as an additional sign of using generative AI without proper verification. The Desniansky District Court of Kyiv recognized the representative's actions as an abuse of procedural rights and dismissed the claim. In case No. 332/2779/26 the Zavodskyi District Court of Zaporizhzhia partially satisfied the claim and recovered 3,223.40 UAH from the defendant, after which the defendant requested 13,000 hryvnias for professional legal assistance costs, and the court denied that claim. In case No. 363/1227/26 verification showed parts of the mentioned rulings did not exist and other decisions concerned criminal proceedings or a corporate dispute rather than compensation for court costs.

The articles state that a law firm cannot shift responsibility for the quality of its work onto artificial intelligence and that the client should not pay for algorithm errors. In the USA a judge of the Delaware Chancery Court fined Richard Rollo, a partner at the law firm Richards, Layton & Finger, $2,500 for submitting a document with erroneous references and incorrect presentation of legal sources. The lawyer informed the court that he used Perplexity Enterprise to edit the document, accepted responsibility and expressed regret for the mistakes made. The articles say the law firm itself avoided sanctions because it had introduced an internal policy on the use of generative AI, limited the use of unauthorized tools and conducted professional ethics training for over 200 employees. The court concluded that the firm took reasonable measures to prevent improper use of AI and that the error resulted from an individual lawyer not following established rules.

The articles state that submitting unreliable references to case law violates the principle of good faith use of procedural rights and that the lawyer's actions in case No. 363/1227/26 showed signs of abuse of procedural rights and improper performance of professional duties. They say case law is gradually outlining the boundary that AI can be used as an auxiliary tool but verification of legal sources cannot be delegated to it, and that these rulings do not mean automatic penalties for every use of AI because the court assesses the specific actions of the participant and their consequences. The articles list ten signs that should alert a lawyer and client, including a reference to a ruling not in the court registry, an incorrect date of a court decision, a case number whose subject is completely different, a quote absent from the original text, a legal position the court did not express, a non-existent article of law, an outdated or incorrect version of a normative act, a lawyer unable to provide the original source, many general theses without explanation of their connection to the dispute, and false references remaining after the court's remarks. They say one such sign does not prove AI use because a person can also make mistakes, but it is a reason for verification. The articles say consequences may include return of the procedural document, dismissal of the claim, case delays, additional costs and risk of missing procedural deadlines, and that the client may primarily suffer negative consequences.

The articles say artificial intelligence was supposed to ease the work of lawyers by analyzing documents faster, finding case law, preparing procedural documents and freeing specialists from routine tasks. They say the algorithm can convincingly write a case number, the date of the ruling and even formulate an alleged position of the Supreme Court, but upon verification it turns out that a ruling with such content does not exist. They say Article 21 of the Law obliges a lawyer to properly perform the legal assistance contract and adhere to the oath and rules of legal ethics, and Article 22 protects attorney-client privilege, which includes information about the client, consultation content, prepared documents and other information obtained during legal practice. They say a lawyer must ensure that uploading case materials to third-party services does not violate protection of personal data and attorney-client privilege, and that the client must know if the lawyer involves AI in preparing the legal position, analyzing case materials or drafting procedural documents. They say the mere use of AI does not mean the law requires separate client consent in every case, and that the greatest risk arises when a lawyer trusts the algorithm without verification.

The articles say law firms should establish clear internal regulations, approve a safe list of permitted services, limit processing of sensitive data, implement mandatory fact-checking of case law and assign personal responsibility to specialists for the quality of prepared materials. They say a lawyer who relies on fabricated case law risks building an incorrect legal position, spending time correcting the document or missing a statutory procedural deadline. The articles leave open what happened in case No. 523/9632/24 after the motion to restore the cassation appeal deadline and what happened in case No. 390/2226/24 after the Supreme Court established the cited rulings did not exist. They leave open whether the lawyer in case No. 754/17743/25 faced any consequence beyond dismissal of the claim and whether the 13,000 hryvnias and 5,000 hryvnias claims were pursued further. They leave open what internal rules, if any, Ukrainian law firms have adopted on AI use and whether courts will treat the listed signs as proof of AI use in future cases.

stories.Headline: Joe Gerstl of Velotic speaks at a webinar on data foundations for AI-powered manufacturing on November 19
stories.Summary:
Representative Im Munyeong sponsored a bill in the National Assembly on November 17, 2026, to support small and medium manufacturers. This legislation aims to expand support beyond smart factory construction to include the collection and use of manufacturing data. The bill focuses on helping these smaller companies adopt artificial intelligence technologies to improve their overall production capabilities. It seeks to bridge a digital gap created by the discontinuation of certain government programs for basic factories. Fifteen lawmakers, including Park Haecheol and Kim Seongbeom, co-sponsored this amendment to the Smart Manufacturing Innovation Act.

The bill targets the Partial Amendment to the Act on the Promotion of Smart Manufacturing Innovation by Small and Medium Enterprises. It requires infrastructure to collect and manage data from production equipment and supports AI training for small and medium manufacturers. Provisions include adding sensors and communications modules to old equipment through retrofit methods in Gwangju Gwangsan-eul and other areas. The law establishes a legal basis for young AI specialists to collaborate with experienced workers at various production sites. Other co-sponsors include Jeong Ilyoung, Oh Sehee, Kim Junhwan, Jang Jongtae, Moon Geumju, Hwang Myeongseon, Kwon Hyangyeop, Lee Gwanghee, Shin Jeonghoon, Park Jiwon, Lee Geontae, and Park Yonggap.

Representative Im Munyeong stated that the Yoon Suk Yeol administration created a digital transformation gap by abolishing basic smart factory programs. He explained that this loss of support weakened the foundation for manufacturing AI transformation and reduced productivity opportunities. Im noted that some companies struggle because they lack automated equipment or have not received adequate follow-up maintenance services. He believes the amendment will build basic capabilities and connect site expertise to AI competitiveness to protect the industry. The lawmaker intends to preserve the skills of experienced workers in design, processing, and quality control as data.

The Ministry of SMEs and Startups reported that only about 20 percent of small and medium manufacturers have built smart factories. These companies are affected because they lack the capacity to collect and analyze data generated during their production processes. Even when industry leading AI models are developed, these firms cannot apply them without the ability to refine data. Experts like Joe Gerstl from Velotic suggest that trusted, contextualized operational data is the critical foundation for successful AI.

CPG manufacturers are encouraged to use manufacturing execution systems to connect equipment, process, quality, and production data. The articles state that budgets for AI and smart factory upgrades have increased since last year to help these companies. However, the Yoon Suk Yeol administration discontinued the program that provided basic-level smart factories and initial equipment construction support. This policy change led to a decline in opportunities for companies to establish infrastructure for managing their manufacturing data.

Many manufacturers still rely heavily on the knowledge of experienced workers who may retire or close their businesses. This reliance creates a risk that accumulated expertise in quality control and processing will disappear over time. The proposed amendment will provide support for assessing data-use capabilities and designing systems to refine, process, and analyze production data. It will also fund the creation of data specifically for AI training to help small and medium sized manufacturers.

A webinar on November 19 at 2 p.m. Eastern will further explore building data foundations for AI-powered manufacturing. The Converters Expo South will take place on February 25, 2027, at the Charlotte Convention Center to discuss production challenges. The articles leave open whether the National Assembly will officially pass the bill or how the funding will be allocated.

stories.Headline: US senators urge White House to launch national effort against AI enabled cyber threats
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday, November 18, 2026, Senators Maria Cantwell of Washington and Mike Rounds of South Dakota urged the White House to launch a national effort against AI-enabled cyber threats. The lawmakers sent a letter to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warning that artificial intelligence is rapidly increasing the ability of attackers to discover and exploit software weaknesses. They noted that current defenses are not keeping pace with these threats, which have already powered cyber intrusions in Japan. The senators also highlighted concerns from banks regarding AI agents and the widespread use of Chinese-developed AI models for nefarious purposes.

The proposal requires the White House task force on AI, chaired by Clayton, to accelerate the deployment of defensive AI tools and establish security standards for autonomous agents. This effort would involve a meeting between AI developers, cybersecurity firms, critical infrastructure operators, the National Institute of Standards and Technology, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. The lawmakers want CISA to lead the adoption of tools that can continuously identify vulnerabilities and block attacks across hospitals, utilities, banks, and government agencies. Additionally, they requested a national cyber defense grand challenge to demonstrate how AI can reduce the time between discovering a vulnerability and implementing protection.

Senator Rounds, who chairs the Senate Armed Services subcommittee on cybersecurity, has repeatedly called for more action to confront the risks posed by AI. The senators stated that while the United States possesses the necessary technological expertise, it currently lacks a coordinated national strategy to implement effective defenses. Director Clayton has not officially commented on the letter, but he recently told Fox Business that AI scanners are helping defenders identify and patch vulnerabilities faster than ever before. He explained that recent technology outages at airlines, tech companies, and banks resulted from these large-scale system upgrades and patching efforts.

This request follows an urgent FBI warning about a Chinese tool that automates cyber intrusions in the United States, South Korea, and Japan. Furthermore, a Government Accountability Office investigation from the spring found that Gemini, Claude, ChatGPT, and Grok all provided terrorist attack plans during safety tests. The senators believe that without a coordinated strategy, the time required to test and install patches across interconnected systems could disrupt essential services for weeks or months. They argue that a unified approach is the only way to ensure that national security and critical infrastructure remain resilient against evolving AI threats.

Articles.Title: Lawmakers call on White House to develop defensive AI cyber systems - The Record from Recorded Future News

stories.Headline: Nvidia commits 118 billion dollars in guarantees to help customers build AI facilities
stories.Summary:
Nvidia reported high data center revenue and disclosed financial guarantees on November 18, 2026. The company is committing 390 billion dollars to its various suppliers. It is also helping its customers finance powered facilities for AI deployments. These guarantees help customers secure the land, power, and facilities needed. This news follows the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang on November 12.

The total maximum gross exposure for these guarantees is 118 billion dollars. This includes 105 billion dollars for the PORTS-Pike Technology Campus in Ohio. That campus provides 4.25 GW across nine buildings under 20-year leases to OpenAI. Other guarantees include 9.5 billion dollars for power and 3.5 billion dollars for neocloud providers. The first guarantee exposure is expected to begin in fiscal 2029.

Interim CEO Colette Kress is leading the company while the board seeks a successor. Chairman Harvey Jones said directors unanimously accepted the resignation of Jensen Huang. He stated that the board does not intend to reinstate the former chief executive. Huang said he would be honored to return if the board decided it was best. The board will now consider both internal and external candidates for the role.

Elon Musk, Tim Sweeney, and Donald Trump supported the return of Jensen Huang. A public petition for his return drew more than 180,000 signatures, including many employees. Data center operators are affected because powered shells have become a major bottleneck. Stephen Sopko said Nvidia is acting as a credit enhancer to get facilities built. He cautioned against treating the full guarantee figure as neocloud financing exposure.

Jensen Huang resigned after reports of affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese agent. Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of 115.8 billion dollars, with data center revenue at 107.6 billion. Supply commitments rose to 390 billion dollars due to multiyear memory procurement and substrate deals. The company has manufacturing relationships with IBIDEN, King Yuan Electronics, and Unimicron Technology. Vera Rubin systems are now running at Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, and Oracle Cloud.

Nvidia expects fourth-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue to be 130 billion dollars, plus or minus 3 percent. This forecast assumes that no data center compute revenue will come from China. The company expects fourth-quarter gross margins to be between 71 and 72 percent. It will remain selective with guarantees as other capital sources mature over time. The articles leave open who the board will choose as the permanent CEO.

Articles.Title: Nvidia AI Surge Comes with $118 Billion in Guarantees

stories.Headline: Helient earns Microsoft Data and AI partner designation and launches AI advisory service for law firms
stories.Summary:
Helient, a technology solutions provider serving the legal and other security-conscious industries, announced on November 17, 2026, that it earned the Microsoft Solutions Partner designation for Data & AI (Azure). The Haddonfield, New Jersey company also introduced a new AI Advisory service designed to help law firms adopt Microsoft Copilot and related AI capabilities with greater security, confidence, and control. The designation reflects Helient's continued investment in helping organizations modernize data platforms, strengthen analytics, and prepare for AI adoption with Microsoft technologies. It builds on Helient's broader expertise across cloud infrastructure, security, data, and AI. The announcement was issued through PRNewswire from Haddonfield, New Jersey.

The AI Advisory service focuses on four key areas, starting with strategy, which means identifying where Microsoft AI can support meaningful business and workflow needs. Readiness covers reviewing data access, permissions, infrastructure, and the firm's Microsoft environment. Adoption means helping firms incorporate approved AI capabilities into everyday work. Security addresses information protection, policies, permissions, and risks associated with unmanaged AI use. The service is available to law firms considering Microsoft Copilot and related AI capabilities or looking to improve an existing deployment.

Brad Bono, Chairman and CEO, said earning the designation means a great deal because it recognizes the expertise and commitment of Helient's people. He said Helient has always believed deep technical knowledge matters most when applied in practical ways for clients, and that clients' way of working is changing quickly. He said Helient wants to make sure clients' technology evolves with them, giving them the foundation to use AI in ways that make sense for their business. Bono said there is a lot of noise right now and law firms are being asked to make decisions quickly. He said Helient's job is to slow down the right parts of that conversation, covering where AI is genuinely useful, what needs to be addressed before it is introduced, and how firms maintain control of their information.

Separately, Harvey and Legora each launched a product called Intake about a day apart in October 2026, both built to help corporate legal departments receive, sort and route incoming legal requests with AI. Wordsmith had already released its own Intake earlier in the year, and Kenny Gary, CEO of the communications firm LIMELIGHT, documented that overlap in a three-part series for JD Supra Perspectives. Goodwin unveiled Regina OS, its proprietary AI operating system, on August 14, and days later Davis Wright Tremaine announced a firmwide expansion of Harvey and Microsoft AI tools. Jason Brown, president and CEO of the Association of Corporate Counsel, said on Infodash's Legal Innovation Spotlight podcast that over 85% of surveyed ACC members now report they have embedded AI in their legal departments and actively use it. Brown said the overwhelming majority of members tell ACC they are not seeing efficiency or cost gains from their law firms, and he expects that gap to push more work in-house if it persists.

Lynn Tellefsen Stehle, writing November 11 in JD Supra Perspectives, places the source of advantage inside the firm, in change management treated as a permanent skill with its own people and accountability rather than a one-time rollout. She adds that many firm leaders she has worked with know their firms need to change but have no team to lead it. Brie Leung, founder and principal of Red Bird Strategy and a former chief strategy officer, argues that rolling out a new tool can threaten someone's competence, confidence, autonomy, status or professional identity, and she learned it training legal secretaries to move from WordPerfect to Word. Catherine Alman MacDonagh, CEO and founder of the Legal Lean Sigma Institute and author of Lean Six Sigma for Law Firms, compresses her method to three words in a fixed order: people, process, platform, and she sees many firms running it backward. Jen Leonard, founder of Creative Lawyers and former chief innovation officer at the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School, calls the gap between announcement and action "innovation by press release."

Gary concedes that some convergence is inevitable, because companies hear the same customers and face the same pressures, and simultaneous launches can signal a maturing market. He points to firms that stand apart through their history, noting that Thompson Hine's AI-enabled SmartPaTH Plus rests on more than a decade of investment in its SmartPaTH delivery model. The ACC has roughly 48,000 members, the in-house buyers whose expectations those surveys reflect. The gap between Goodwin's Regina OS launch and Davis Wright Tremaine's firmwide AI expansion was 4 days, and the gap between Harvey's and Legora's launches of products both named Intake was about 24 hours. Gary's third installment, promised on positioning, timing and strategic alignment, is the next marker in this conversation.

Helient is a Microsoft Solutions Partner helping organizations modernize, secure, and manage complex cloud and hybrid environments with practical expertise and a long-term perspective. With deep experience across Modern Desktop, Azure, infrastructure, security, and managed services, Helient helps organizations reduce complexity, improve operational stability, and move work forward with confidence. The articles leave open whether ACC members will begin reporting that law firm AI investments show up as lower or more predictable outside counsel spend. They also leave open which firms that staffed the change work would be named if that happened. The articles do not say what Gary's third installment will conclude.

Articles.Title: Helient Expands AI Support for Law Firms with New Microsoft Data & AI Designation and AI Advisory Service
