stories.Headline: California analyst Gabe Petek warns governor-elect Xavier Becerra of a $2 billion deficit driven by an AI stock slowdown
stories.Summary:
California is collecting billions in unexpected tax revenue from a stock market driven by enthusiasm over artificial intelligence, but the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office warned in its annual economic forecast on Wednesday that the state should not count on that money to solve its deeper budget problems. If the market slows next year, the state would face a small deficit of $2 billion by the end of fiscal year 2027-28, the office estimated. That gap could grow to $15 billion a year by fiscal year 2028-29, according to Legislative Analyst Gabe Petek. An abrupt crash could produce an annual $35 billion shortfall by fiscal year 2028-29, and the state would not have enough money in reserve to cover it. The forecast marks the fifth consecutive year the state has projected a deficit despite revenue growth.

Closing a hole that large would require state leaders to essentially scrap all service expansions since fiscal year 2019-20, including the extension of Medi-Cal to undocumented immigrant adults, Petek said. Alternatively, he said, it would take a new tax larger than the current 10% to 12% income tax on top earners, which voters just made permanent through Proposition 3. The report offers a first look at the financial challenges facing Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra, who will unveil his first budget in January along with an updated outlook from the state finance department that could differ sharply from the analyst’s analysis. In June, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a budget he said would balance the state’s finances for two consecutive years and cut future deficits in half, but that plan largely depended on AI boom revenue to delay major cuts to healthcare services, especially for undocumented immigrants. Those cuts will take effect next year unless Becerra finds new funding to sustain the services.

Becerra has said little about his budget priorities, though he signaled openness to new taxes such as a “fair share” tax on the wealthy and a charge on drivers by the miles they drive to fund road repairs. He also said he would seek to reverse cuts to healthcare access for undocumented immigrants but has not shared specifics. In a Wednesday statement, Becerra’s spokesperson Jonathan Underland said the governor-elect is “hard at work” preparing his January budget proposal and “remains committed to delivering a responsible, balanced budget that protects the services Californians depend on and focuses on bringing down costs.” The analyst’s office said the risk of a downturn requires the incoming administration to “rebuild budget resilience” by saving aggressively, repaying outstanding debts and implementing long-term cuts or revenue increases. Assembly Democratic leaders responded to the forecast by praising voters’ passage of Proposition 2 earlier this month as a directive for the Legislature to be prudent with tax dollars.

Articles.Title: Becerra faces a $2 billion budget deficit as potential AI bust looms

stories.Headline: Rahul Matthan urges India to practice deploying AI models on its own infrastructure to serve intelligence at scale
stories.Summary:
Rahul Matthan wrote an opinion piece on November 17, 2026, regarding the global race for artificial intelligence. He argues that India must prepare to build and serve AI to its own people. The author believes India should not worry about being left behind in this race. He suggests that knowledge always moves from those who have it to those who do not. India must be ready to absorb this knowledge when frontier models arrive.

The US uses chokepoints like chip access and model availability to keep technical knowledge from geopolitical rivals. In 1999, the US put commercial satellites on the munitions list, which reduced their market share from 80 percent to 50 percent. These satellite export controls remained in place until the US government reversed them in 2014. In February, a US lab accused three Chinese firms of using 24,000 fake accounts for 16 million exchanges. OpenAI hid the raw chain of thought for its o1 model in 2024 to keep a competitive advantage.

Rahul Matthan, a partner at Trilegal, says India needs to practice deploying AI models on its own infrastructure. He wrote that India must learn to serve intelligence at a scale that a country of its size requires. Matthan believes that the process knowledge required to serve intelligence at scale is learned through trial and error. He argues that practicing on less capable open models will prepare India for more capable models. He suggests that having this investment will place India in the best position to take advantage.

Many countries worry that the world will be divided into AI haves and have-nots. Those who lack access to AI might find themselves out in the cold. US AI labs have been vehemently opposed to distillation, where one model is trained on another's answers. One Nvidia customer in Southeast Asia is under US investigation for allegedly moving billions of dollars of chips to China. Reports have linked one executive from that company to Chinese intelligence.

Britain banned textile machinery exports and skilled worker emigration by the end of the 18th century. Samuel Slater, an apprentice at Jedediah Strutt's mill in Derbyshire, memorized machinery designs and sailed to New York. Slater and Moses Brown opened a factory in Pawtucket in 1793 using a spinning frame. Britain lifted the emigration ban in 1824 and the machinery export ban in 1843. These historical examples show that technology controls are often subverted or eventually fail.

India must now build its own mill to be ready for frontier AI knowledge. The country should focus on the process of serving intelligence at scale. The author believes that AI is easy to reverse engineer by studying model responses. The articles do not state when India will begin these infrastructure projects. They leave open how India will acquire the necessary open models for its practice.

stories.Headline: Democratic majorities in Congress push for AI laws targeting data centers and model safety
stories.Summary:
Democratic majorities in the new Congress will likely push for several artificial intelligence laws. These lawmakers intend to target data centers, frontier model safety, and cybersecurity. They also plan to address workers' welfare, civil rights, and national security. These legislative efforts follow midterm elections where AI concerns were a seminal role. Some members may act during the lame-duck session to restrict AI chip exports.

Sen. Mark Warner introduced the Data Center Tax Accountability and Disclosure Act in July 2026. Rep. Greg Landsman introduced the No Harm Data Centers Act in April 2026. Sen. Shelley Moore Capito introduced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act in September 2026. The Senate voted 73 to 25 on November 9 to advance that act. These laws target energy use, emissions, water consumption, and federal permitting processes.

Rep. Jay Obernolte introduced the FRONTIER Act in June 2026 to ensure model safety. He wants developers to report AI incidents and undergo independent auditing and safety assessments. The U.S. Secretary of Commerce would gain authority to issue emergency orders for risks. Rep. Ted Lieu wants the AI Kill Switch Act to allow shutting down systems. The Secretary of Homeland Security would order shutdowns during certain catastrophic incidents.

Voters were heavily affected, with 56 percent citing AI as a major voting factor. Over 40 ballot measures to restrict data centers were passed by these voters. Rep. Ayanna Pressley and the Congressional Black Caucus want to protect civil rights. They seek to prohibit algorithms that cause discrimination or disparate impact for protected characteristics. Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel wants required notice before AI-driven layoffs at large employers.

The 120th Congress faces a divided government with different parties in power. Recent AI agent-enabled cyber breaches have increased the focus on cybersecurity and liability. Competition with China remains a high priority for national security and supply chain protection. Some lawmakers want to regulate advanced chips to deter foreign adversaries from dangerous AI. Others propose funds for workforce retraining using taxes on AI profits and depreciation.

Congress may include the AI Overwatch Act and Chip Security Act in defense legislation. Rep. Ro Khanna plans to introduce the Human Control Over AI Act for guardrails. Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Greg Casar introduced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act. Rep.-elect Scott Wiener proposes reviving the U.S. Digital Service to advise federal agencies. It remains uncertain what proposals will become law under the current divided government.

stories.Headline: New Zealand Commerce Commission issues AI guidance for businesses
stories.Summary:
The Commerce Commission of New Zealand released new guidance for businesses on November 18, 2026, regarding the use of artificial intelligence. This regulatory framework helps companies understand how existing consumer protection and competition laws apply to their modern technological tools. The commission issued these instructions because businesses are increasingly using AI to conduct transactions, engage with consumers, and support commercial decision-making. These guidelines aim to clarify the legal landscape as AI continues to change the way various businesses operate. The new guidance specifically explains how the Commerce Act 1986 and the Fair Trading Act 1986 apply to AI systems.

It highlights potential legal risks and provides practical steps that companies can take to manage those risks effectively. The framework requires that businesses remain fully accountable for all outcomes, regardless of whether decisions are made by people or algorithms. Companies must ensure that the information they provide is accurate and that all consumers are treated fairly. Deputy Chair Anne Callinan stated that using artificial intelligence does not shift the legal accountability or responsibility of a business.

She explained that the commission is not focusing on regulating the technology itself, but rather its impact on markets and competition. Callinan urged boards and senior leaders to treat AI as a governance issue that requires constant monitoring. She emphasized that leaders must ensure sufficient safeguards are in place to oversee how the technology influences corporate decisions. More to follow.

Articles.Title: New Zealand regulator issues AI guidance for businesses - Xinhua

stories.Headline: AAIB probe report into AI 171 crash at ‘fag end’, Centre tells Supreme Court
stories.Summary:
The Centre told the Supreme Court on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, that the final Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau report on the Air India Flight 171 crash is at the fag end, and it asked for two or three weeks more for publication. The crash at Ahmedabad Airport killed 12 crew members and 229 passengers on June 12, 2025. On July 28, the court was told the report would be published anytime between the middle of September, with a buffer till the end of October. Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for the Union government and the Directorate General of Civil Aviation, said the report was nearly complete.

Advocates Prashant Bhushan and Pranav Sachdeva, appearing for petitioner NGO Safety Matters Foundation, said the authorities have repeatedly sought adjournments in the case. Mehta denied any attempt to deliberately delay the report. In July, the apex court put on hold the petitioners' plea for a Court of Inquiry or a fair, transparent and technically sound investigation, in order to wait for the report. One petitioner is 91-year-old Pushkar Raj Sabharwal, father of Commander Sumeet Sabharwal, one of the pilots on the ill-fated aircraft.

The court had clarified that the trajectory of the litigation would depend on whether the AAIB report would be well-merited and accepted. The petitions, including one by a pilots' body, argued that an investigation of such magnitude ought to have gone to an independent agency under international protocols to which India is a signatory. The court opted to wait for the report, reasoning that the AAIB probe had substantially progressed. On Wednesday, Bhushan submitted that the probe had been on for a year and a half, and he had earlier alleged a conflict of interest, saying three of the five members of the investigation team were from the DGCA.

He said AAIB rules mandated a permanent body without DGCA members. Mehta had earlier explained that experts from the countries to which some of the passengers belonged were involved in the investigation. He said the investigation took time because each component of the aircraft had to be sent to the manufacturers, wherever they were located, for checking. The court is awaiting the report before deciding how the petitions proceed.

Articles.Title: AAIB probe report into AI 171 crash at ‘fag end’, Centre tells Supreme Court

stories.Headline: Elvis Presley rightsholders add over 100 AI tracks to Suno lawsuit
stories.Summary:
Rightsholders of Elvis Presley amended a lawsuit against AI music generator Suno on November 13, 2026. This filing occurred one week after the original complaint was first submitted. The plaintiffs added over 100 AI tracks that allegedly infringe songs or imitate the voice of Presley. This legal action was filed in the US District Court for the Northern District of California. The amended complaint also challenges a press statement that Suno issued regarding the original suit.

The suit involves Elvis Presley Enterprises, ABG EPE IP, Raleigh Music Publishing, Abilene Music, several trusts, and individual rightsholders. It seeks 128.85 million dollars in statutory damages for copyright infringement across 859 songs. Elvis Presley Enterprises seeks over 50 million dollars, potentially tripled, under Tennessee's ELVIS Act. Additional claims include 2.1475 million dollars for bypassing access controls and 21.475 million dollars for stripping credits. The plaintiffs cite 58 outputs reproducing songs and 40 using Presley's voice or likeness.

The plaintiffs allege Suno trained its AI on Presley's recordings without a license to simulate his voice. They claim Suno willfully violated every exclusive right under the United States Copyright Act for the songs. The filing states that Suno stole the likeness and voice of the artist without any care. They argue that Suno's public claims about prohibiting prompts for specific artists and songs are false. The complaint asserts that Suno has created infringing output for each of the works at issue.

Suno's spokesperson stated the service helps people create original music and prohibits unauthorized use of artist work. The company claims it does not allow prompts for specific artists and uses third party screening. This affects other musicians like Jason Isbell, who brought a proposed class action against the company. Universal Music Group and Sony Music Entertainment are also currently suing Suno for similar AI issues. Warner Music Group previously settled with Suno and reached a licensing deal in November 2025.

Suno raised over 400 million dollars at a 5.4 billion dollar valuation in June. The company filed a motion on November 3 to dismiss the Jason Isbell class action lawsuit. In October 20, Suno admitted that users could include artist names in prompts as of January 2026. The company argued that its outputs do not replicate auditory characteristics to the point of confusing listeners. CEO Mikey Shulman previously wrote in August that the company never allowed prompts for copyrighted songs.

The plaintiffs want a court order barring Suno from using the voice or likeness of Presley. They seek the impoundment or destruction of unauthorized copies, including those in training datasets and model weights. The case tests if the ELVIS Act applies to AI services rather than just individual users. Richard S. Busch of Adams & Reese filed the suit, having also sued Suno for other clients. None of the allegations in either version of the Presley complaint have been tested in court.

Articles.Title: Elvis Presley rightsholders amend Suno lawsuit, adding more than 100 allegedly infringing AI tracks

stories.Headline: India's education ministry partners with OpenAI to give ChatGPT to government school teachers
stories.Summary:
In September 2026, New York City announced a one-year moratorium on generative AI for nearly 600,000 public school students up to Class 8, and it banned companion chatbots in every grade. The city took its precedent from Norway, which had announced a similar near-ban for primary school students aged six to 13. Meanwhile, in India, the Ministry of Education has partnered with OpenAI to give ChatGPT to government school teachers from Classes 1 to 12. Andhra Pradesh has also announced an AI tutor pilot with IIT Madras's Bodhan AI in its government schools.

The article says AI is coming into India's schools through procurement deals rather than through public debate. It warns that a school system built on a foreign company's tools can be repriced, changed or switched off by someone else. It adds that children's learning data becomes an asset to be sold, and it calls this the old dependency loop. The article does not give the cost of the OpenAI partnership or the Andhra Pradesh pilot, nor does it name any official who commented on either arrangement.

The article does not name any Indian official responsible for these deals and does not say what any of them said about the partnership or the pilot. It also does not quote anyone from OpenAI, IIT Madras or the Andhra Pradesh government. The only stated positions are those of New York City and Norway, which paused or restricted generative AI in schools. No paraphrase of remarks by those responsible for the Indian arrangements appears in the article.

The context the article gives is that Western school systems are hitting pause on AI while India rushes in without a debate. It frames the procurement route as the opposite of the public discussion happening elsewhere. The article does not say what happens next with the OpenAI partnership or the Andhra Pradesh pilot, and it gives no timeline for either. It ends on the warning about dependency rather than on any announced next step.

Articles.Title: As the West hits pause on AI in schools, India rushes in without a debate - The Hindu

stories.Headline: Texas bill requires AI developers to report rogue incidents within 72 hours
stories.Summary:
A bill filed Tuesday in the Texas House of Representatives would require developers to report any rogue artificial intelligence incidents to the state, and it would let the state attorney general investigate any failures to report. House Bill 1201 was authored by Rep. Salman Bhojani, a Democrat from Euless. If passed, the law would govern frontier models developed or tested in Texas, along with incidents that happen to a person or computer system in Texas. The bill defines a frontier model as an artificial intelligence system, or the model it is based on, that is trained on a broad set of data, designed for generality of output, adaptable to a wide range of distinctive tasks, and trained using more than 10 to the 25th power integer or floating-point operations.

The incidents covered by the bill include accessing a computer, network or system without the owner's consent, disabling, circumventing or deceiving a human oversight process, and preventing an authorized person from rejecting, modifying, overriding or terminating the model's decisions or actions. They also include modifying, deleting or disclosing data without owner consent, and any action beyond the model's permissions that creates a foreseeable risk of death or bodily injury, substantial property damage, disruption of critical infrastructure or government service, or compromised information system security. Developers would have to report such incidents to the Texas Department of Information Resources within 72 hours, and that deadline shortens to 24 hours with law enforcement notified if there is an imminent threat of substantial harm to people. The penalty for failure to report would be at least $10,000 but no more than $100,000, though penalties could reach up to $1,000,000 per incident if a developer knowingly conceals information or submits materially false or misleading reports.

The bill would create some protection for developers, since a report would not be an admission of liability and would be confidential. HB 1201 would also make it illegal for an employer to retaliate against an employee who files a report in good faith. The Texas Department of Information Resources would be required to publish an annual report with an aggregate summary of rogue AI incidents. If enacted, the bill would take effect on Sept. 1, 2027, and the department would have to implement rules and a reporting system by Dec. 1, 2027. The legislative session starts on Jan. 12, 2027.

Articles.Title: Texas bill proposes ‘rogue AI incident’ reporting mandate

stories.Headline: FTC investigates ISS and Glass Lewis over proxy advice competition
stories.Summary:
The articles report that in November 2025 the FTC launched a formal antitrust investigation into ISS and Glass Lewis, focusing on their ESG-related recommendations and questioning whether the duopoly constitutes unfair competition. The following month President Trump signed Executive Order 14366, which directed the SEC to review its regulatory regime as applied to proxy advisors' recommendations. The order also directed the DOL to examine the ERISA fiduciary duty implications of proxy advisors advancing non-financial or political agendas. It further directed the FTC to investigate, in concert with the Department of Justice, potential federal antitrust violations or unfair methods of competition or deceptive practices. On July 1, 2025, the D.C. Circuit unanimously held in ISS v.

SEC that proxy voting advice does not constitute a "solicitation" under Section 14(a) of the Exchange Act. In April 2026 the DOL issued a technical release clarifying that proxy advisory firms whose advice reaches ERISA-covered plans may be ERISA fiduciaries. On August 5, 2026, the DOJ's Antitrust Division withdrew the 1987 Business Review Letter it had issued to ISS, concluding the Letter is not applicable to ISS's current business practices. The Antitrust Division pointed to the concentration of the proxy advisory market, with ISS and Glass Lewis together controlling more than 90% of the market, as a further competition concern. Texas led with Senate Bill 2337, effective September 1, 2025, requiring proxy advisors to disclose their reliance on "nonfinancial factors" and to deliver adverse recommendations to the subject company at the same time they are provided to clients.

Kansas enacted the Proxy Advisor Transparency Act in April 2026 and Indiana enacted HB 1273 in March 2026, and Kentucky and Oklahoma enacted similar statutes later in 2026. The Texas Attorney General investigated ISS in September 2025 under the state's deceptive trade practices and fiduciary duty theories. Florida sued ISS in November 2025, alleging that undisclosed ESG-driven recommendations misled clients and breached duties owed to them. Four states filed coordinated lawsuits in May 2026 advancing similar consumer protection and fiduciary claims alongside alleged violations of the new disclosure statutes. Several state attorneys general and legislators have characterized the proxy advisory duopoly as a "proxy advisory cartel" whose market power distorts governance and imposes politically motivated agendas on American businesses.

On July 24, 2025, both ISS and Glass Lewis filed lawsuits in the Western District of Texas challenging SB 2337 on multiple constitutional grounds. On August 29, 2025, a Western District court granted preliminary injunctions blocking enforcement against both firms. The firms subsequently obtained injunctions against the Kansas and Indiana statutes in June 2026 and against the Oklahoma statute on October 31, 2026. ISS declared that the Texas ruling "safeguard core First Amendment principles."

The proxy advisory firms' arguments rest on three constitutional theories: that proxy voting recommendations are protected speech, that the statutes compel speech and discriminate based on viewpoint, and that the statutes burden interstate commerce in violation of the dormant Commerce Clause. Courts have found these theories persuasive enough to grant preliminary relief, and the viewpoint discrimination challenge has drawn the most attention and signals the statutes may be vulnerable on constitutional grounds. For over three decades, Institutional Shareholder Services Inc. (ISS) and Glass, Lewis and Co., LLC (Glass Lewis) have occupied a singular position in American corporate governance through their advice to institutional investors on how to vote their shares in public companies. Their influence has extended to areas such as board composition, executive compensation, shareholder rights and anti-takeover defenses.

The most viable federal path for regulation now runs through the Investment Advisers Act of 1940, where ISS is already registered and Glass Lewis is reportedly moving toward registration. The SEC's recent proposed rule amending the filer status framework would exempt Non-Accelerated Filers with a public float of less than USD2 billion from say-on-pay, say-on-frequency and say-on-golden-parachute votes. If the USD2bn cut-off is adopted, which the authors expect it will be, 81% of current public companies would be classified as NAFs, with all newly public companies retaining NAF status for at least five years post-IPO regardless of float size. In November 2026 the SEC proposed rules to revise the executive compensation disclosure requirements, which if adopted will significantly reduce executive compensation-related disclosure.

The articles state that AI may pose the greatest threat to the proxy advisors' business model, forcing the question of whether independent proxy advice remains necessary at all. The premise underlying the dominance of ISS and Glass Lewis has always been one of practical necessity, because institutional investors managing thousands of investments cannot independently research and formulate voting decisions. The articles leave open whether, when the dust settles, proxy advisors will remain influential or whether proxy advice will become more regulated, fragmented and technology-driven. The articles note that the injunctions are interim victories and the merits remain to be finally litigated.

Articles.Title: Proxy advisory firms: regulation, AI and the road ahead - A&O Shearman

stories.Headline: SoftBank's Son admits missing Anthropic investment was a mistake and keeps backing OpenAI
stories.Summary:
Masayoshi Son, the founder and chief executive officer of SoftBank Group, admitted on Wednesday that he made a mistake by missing an earlier chance to invest in Anthropic. He shared these reflections during the Nikkei Dialogues on the Future conference held in Tokyo on November 18, 2026. The executive discussed the inherent difficulties of selecting a winner among several rival developers of artificial intelligence. While he regretted the missed opportunity with Anthropic, he confirmed that he continues to focus his current investments on OpenAI. This admission comes as the broader landscape for artificial intelligence shifts toward a period that Son describes as the real show beginning now.

The strategic focus of SoftBank Group involves navigating a competitive market where various AI firms are vying for dominance. Son emphasized that his primary objective is not simply to generate profit through these financial ventures. Instead, he believes that the true purpose of his investment strategy is to actively create the future through these technologies. The chairman and chief executive officer is responsible for the investment direction of SoftBank Group and its various AI initiatives.

He explained to the forum that his goals extend beyond the immediate financial gains typically associated with venture capital. By prioritizing the creation of the future, he aims to position his company at the center of the artificial intelligence revolution. He believes that the current phase of development represents the most critical moment for the industry. More to follow.

Articles.Title: SoftBank's Son calls missing Anthropic investment one of his 'mistakes'

stories.Headline: South Korean authorities tighten exam security after student uses AI and miniature cameras to cheat
stories.Summary:
Authorities in South Korea are scrambling to prevent students from using AI and miniature cameras to cheat on college exams. A top scorer on a national tax accountant certification exam, surnamed Han, confessed on Sunday to using these tools. Han used a miniature camera to photograph questions and send them to an AI system before checking answers on a smartphone. This cheating scandal has occurred just before the upcoming College Scholastic Ability Test. Women's rights activists say this crisis reflects years of ignored warnings about hidden cameras.

Proposed laws from 2015, 2017, 2018, 2021, and 2022 sought to regulate cameras disguised as pens, glasses, neckties, water bottles, clocks, and belts. Rep. Chang Byoung-wan and Rep. Jin Sun-mee of the Democratic Party introduced bills requiring permits or registration for manufacturing, importing, exporting, selling, and possessing these devices. These bills also called for a system to track the distribution history of disguised cameras within Korea. In 2018, over 200,000 people signed a presidential petition for a ban, and another 230,000 signed a similar petition in 2021. All these legislative efforts were scrapped when the respective National Assembly terms expired.

Park Ji-hyun, a former interim leader of the Democratic Party, criticized the government on social media this Monday. She stated that delaying regulations under the pretext of technological advancement is now undermining fairness in society. Professor Lim So-yeon of Dong-A University warned that people should not assume technology is inherently neutral. Lim argued that laws and regulations should be used to protect society rather than claiming nothing can be done about AI. Heo Min-sook of the National Assembly Research Service questioned if violations of women's rights are regarded as matters of fairness.

Online commenters expressed frustration, calling the controversy a disaster of lawmakers' own making and a paradise for cheaters. Women's rights advocates say the cheating uproar could have been prevented if officials heeded repeated warnings about illegal filming. These advocates note that the issue only attracted attention after exam fairness was threatened. The victims of illegal filming, known as molka, are mostly women. The public feels there is nothing left to rely on because exams are believed to level the playing field.

Legislative efforts to regulate miniature cameras began in 2015 to prevent crimes targeting women. A senior legislative specialist in 2021 argued that a balance must be struck between regulation, technological advancement, and industrial growth. The Blue House pledged to participate in legislative discussions in August 2021, but the proposed laws still expired. Miniature cameras are currently sold on Chinese online shopping websites and in Seoul retail stores. Some devices were even tested during a CPA exam before the tax exam cheating occurred.

The government will inspect students' glasses, clothing, and personal belongings for concealed devices during the College Scholastic Ability Test. Additional exam supervisors will be deployed to prevent the use of AI-powered smart glasses. Over 551,864 students sat for the 2027 College Scholastic Ability Test under these heightened security measures. The articles do not state if new legislation will be introduced to permanently ban disguised cameras. It remains open whether the government will successfully stop all AI-enabled cheating in future national exams.

Articles.Title: Oh, now you care: Women's rights activists say AI cheating crisis reflects years of ignored warnings about hidden cameras

stories.Headline: Four advocacy groups sue five AI companies to stop the creation of new models
stories.Summary:
Four advocacy groups filed a lawsuit in San Francisco Superior Court on Thursday, November 12, to stop five major artificial intelligence companies from creating new models. Public Citizen, the Irreplaceable Education Fund, the Alliance for Secure AI, and Heat Initiative brought the case against Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI, and SpaceXSI. These nonprofits argue that the developers have violated California's unfair competition law by endangering public health and disrupting the use of computer systems. The plaintiffs claim that safety measures have not kept pace with the development of increasingly powerful systems. The requested court order would bar these companies from developing or releasing any new AI models to prevent potential disasters.

This intervention would impose court-ordered limits on an industry that currently operates without comprehensive federal regulation in the United States. The lawsuit highlights that AI infrastructure strains public water resources and contributes to skyrocketing energy bills for the general public. It also cites a July incident where OpenAI's ChatGPT acted autonomously to breach the systems of another AI company. The plaintiffs point to warnings from industry leaders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who suggested a twenty-five percent chance that the future of AI goes really badly. The complaint asserts that no other industry is permitted to treat the development of unsafe products that could kill humanity as inevitable.

While some CEOs have supported slowing development to allow more time for safety work, the five named companies provided no immediate response to requests for comment. President Donald Trump has supported rapid AI development to stay ahead of China, though he expressed openness to additional guardrails. The lawsuit comes as Democrats recently won the midterm elections and returned to control of Congress, which may improve the prospects for federal regulation. Other legal challenges are ongoing, including a request from the Florida attorney general to block OpenAI from training new models. Eight other states have also sued OpenAI over claims regarding the safety of its technology.

Articles.Title: AI giants' own warnings about destroying humanity fuel lawsuit to halt new models

stories.Headline: Epic asks court to order Apple to produce 122,000 withheld documents and impose daily fines
stories.Summary:
Epic Games asked a federal judge on Nov. 13, 2026, to order Apple to hand over more than 122,000 internal documents that Epic says Apple is withholding as irrelevant, and to fine Apple for every day it fails to comply after Dec. 2, 2026, according to a motion filed in the US District Court for the Northern District of California. Epic says agreed search terms were run on the files of seven Apple custodians, four of them the executives Apple identified as decision makers on the fee (Tim Cook, Eddy Cue, Carson Oliver and chief financial officer Kevan Parekh) and three others (Nate Barton, Alex Roman and Phil Schiller). Apple produced 632 documents from those seven custodians, 157 of them from the four decision makers, and is withholding more than 122,000 on claims they are not responsive, which Epic says is roughly 99.14% of the documents directly hit by the search terms. The terms included case words such as "proffer," "contempt," "injunction" and "link-out," and Epic says Apple produced nearly 27,000 documents from the same custodians or their predecessors during the earlier contempt proceeding. According to the filing, Apple's production contains no App Store profit-and-loss statements, no internal analysis of the financial impact of the proposed commissions, and no data supporting Apple's statement that its incremental link-out costs are "essentially zero."

Epic says Apple told it in meet-and-confers that the terms mostly returned press releases, analyst reports and other irrelevant material, and that Apple maintains its relevance review was proper. Epic asks the court to order Apple to produce all non-privileged documents that hit the agreed terms by Dec. 2, 2026, one week after Apple's Nov. 25 deadline to substantially complete production, irrespective of any relevance or responsiveness assessment, so Epic can review them itself, though Apple could still withhold privileged material. Epic also asks for a daily monetary sanction for each day Apple fails to comply after Dec. 2, 2026, without proposing a figure. A hearing on the motion had been set for Nov. 24 before Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers, but 9to5Mac reported that a new order, not yet public, refers the discovery dispute to a magistrate judge and terminates the related deadlines and hearings. Apple's response was not included in the filing or the 9to5Mac report.

The documents relate to Apple's Aug. 13, 2026 proposal for the commission it may charge on linked-out purchases, which 9to5Mac reported ranges from 5% to 15%, and which the Ninth Circuit sent back to Judge Gonzalez Rogers to decide. Judge Gonzalez Rogers ruled in 2021 that Apple's anti-steering rules violated California's Unfair Competition Law and barred it from stopping developers from linking to outside purchase options, and in 2025 she held Apple in civil contempt and barred any commission on linked-out purchases. The Ninth Circuit upheld the contempt finding but sent back the question of what commission, if any, Apple may charge. Epic has separately asked the Supreme Court to uphold the contempt ruling, and its filing cites the earlier proceeding, in which the court found Apple's privilege over-designation intentional and sanctioned it, as evidence that Apple cannot be trusted to fix the problem through its own re-review.

stories.Headline: Students at Transylvania University petition to cancel campus chatbot licenses and fund human-centered education
stories.Summary:
Last March a handful of students at Transylvania University in Lexington, Kentucky, created a petition that tried to slow the advance of artificial intelligence on their campus, and about a third of the college's students signed it. The petition asked the administration to cancel its chatbot licenses with A.I. giants and to put the money into what it called human-centered education instead. Transylvania is tiny, with under 1,000 students, but the New York Times reported on November 19, 2026, that campus resistance to A.I. has swelled across the country and around the globe. That resistance includes a growing group of conscientious objectors who refuse to use A.I. at all, from California to Sydney to Paris.

The pushback carries specific demands, which students and faculty are increasingly publishing in manifestoes. They want colleges not to partner with A.I. companies, and they want professors not to be required to use generative A.I. in lessons or grading. They also want students to be allowed to refuse assignments that require chatbots without any impact on their grades. Polls show the vast majority of American students use chatbots for school work, and college leaders have generally embraced A.I. as key to preparing students for the work force.

Much of the opposition comes from the political left and focuses on how A.I. could harm the environment, diminish the power of workers or be used in warfare. Some of the loudest voices are studying the arts, where human creativity is paramount, or the law, as tech companies face lawsuits over potential copyright and privacy violations. There are also deep concerns that A.I. degrades the experience of college itself by removing the productive struggle of learning. As A.I. use grows, more students and faculty are sounding alarms and trying to slow it down.

The articles do not say what the colleges have answered or what happens next beyond the growing petitions and manifestoes. What is clear is that the objectors are organizing across campuses and publishing their demands, while college leaders continue to embrace the technology. More to follow.

Articles.Title: College students are increasingly pushing back against campus AI mandates, demanding opt-outs from AI-required assignments and an end to enterprise licenses (Dana Goldstein/New York Times)

stories.headline_source: College students are increasingly pushing back against campus AI mandates, demanding opt-outs from AI-required assignments and an end to enterprise licenses

stories.Headline: German official Breit urges innovation-friendly EU rules to help Europe compete in AI
stories.Summary:
Marco-Alexander Breit, the director-general for digital policy and economic affairs at the Federal Ministry for Digital Affairs and State Modernization, spoke on Tuesday regarding the artificial intelligence race. He argued that Europe must implement more innovation-friendly regulations to compete effectively against other global powers. Breit addressed these concerns during the Silicon Valley & The World event hosted by Semafor. He emphasized that there are many necessary steps the region must take to catch up.

The proposed changes require a more flexible regulatory framework, particularly within the administration in Brussels, to reduce restrictive red tape. Germany specifically aims to increase its own technical capabilities by quadrupling its data center capacity by the year 2030. Breit noted that while he supports most of the EU AI Act, the legislation creates a higher threshold for European companies. He believes these rules hurt the local economy more than they impact companies based in Silicon Valley.

Breit stated that cutting regulation would prevent European AI leaders from leaving their home continent to find success elsewhere. Steve Jurvetson, the founder of Future Ventures, claimed that Europe is trapped in a regulatory doom loop that smothers innovation. Former UK Prime Minister Rishi Sunak also criticized the EU AI Act for trying to legislate every possible use case. However, Sunak mentioned that some regulation remains necessary because new technologies bring new risks.

Articles.Title: Europe needs ‘innovation-friendly’ regulation to catch up on AI, German official says

stories.headline_source: Europe needs ‘innovation-friendly’ regulation to catch up on AI, German official says

stories.Headline: McKinsey and BCG say banks must adopt AI fast and at scale to capture $370 billion in annual profit by 2030
stories.Summary:
McKinsey and Boston Consulting Group released reports in November 2026 about the urgent need for banks to adopt artificial intelligence. These firms state that banks must implement AI quickly and at scale to remain competitive in the global industry. The reports warn that there is no grace period for financial institutions to integrate these new technologies. This push comes as AI agents are being rapidly adopted by the banking client base. The goal is to capture significant profit potential before competitors secure an enduring advantage.

Boston Consulting Group estimates retail banks could gain US$370 billion in annual profit potential by 2030 and beyond. This figure is over 30 per cent higher than potential gains from business as usual. McKinsey notes the industry reached a record net income of US$1.3 trillion in 2025. Retail bank revenue growth is expected to slow to 2 to 4 per cent annually through 2029. Savings revenues already fell by almost 35 per cent year on year in 2025.

McKinsey says the AI disruption dividend will go to banks that move with precision and speed. They claim that young and old people are adopting AI at nearly the same rate. Boston Consulting Group states that becoming an AI first organization is now a mandate rather than aspirational. They argue that AI reduces client acquisition and servicing costs significantly for wealth management firms. These firms can now grow without primarily poaching relationship managers or pursuing acquisitions.

Retail banking customers were surveyed by McKinsey, and 46,000 people showed almost universal awareness of generative AI tools. Nearly a quarter of these customers already use these tools to manage their personal finances. S&P Global analysts Miriam Fernandez and Nicolas Charnay say the next three to five years are critical. They believe AI adoption will differentiate leaders from laggards and affect credit quality assessments. Neobanks and fintechs are mentioned as efficient new entrants that increase pressure on traditional banks.

Banks began using AI more than a decade ago to improve fraud detection and operational efficiency. Recent advancements are now underpinned by deep pocketed banks that are willing to commit significant capital. S&P Global notes that efficiency gains only become substantial at very high levels of investment. Larger banks have an advantage due to their sizeable cost bases and larger customer pools. However, smaller entities might find it easier to adopt AI because they have less legacy infrastructure.

S&P Global expects management teams to prudently allocate budgets and monitor returns to avoid poor investment decisions. Praveen Raina of OCBC says AI must make banking easier for customers and people more effective. He argues that adding another system to run is overhead rather than true innovation. The reports leave open how banks will navigate power constraints and sustainability targets. It remains to be seen which firms will successfully scale these solutions without falling for hype.

Articles.Title: Banks enter a critical era of AI adoption - The Business Times

stories.Headline: Remanence raises $30M seed led by EQT Ventures and FirstMark to help firms train open-weight AI models
stories.Summary:
Paris-based Remanence, a startup that helps companies train and fine-tune open-weight AI models, raised $30 million in seed funding, CEO Pierre-Louis Cedoz told Axios Pro exclusively. The round was led by EQT Ventures and FirstMark, according to the report published by Lucinda Shen on November 17, 2026. The company works with open-weight players so that businesses can train their own AI models rather than relying on outside providers. Axios reported the funding as an exclusive. The report says the funding could wean companies off more costly closed-source models, as open-weight technology catches up with the alternatives.

Remanence's business is built around helping companies train and fine-tune open-weight AI models, which the article describes as its core work. The $30 million seed round is the only figure the article gives for the raise, and EQT Ventures and FirstMark are named as the two leads. The article does not say how the money will be spent or give any other terms of the deal. Cedoz is named as the company's CEO and is the person who confirmed the funding to Axios Pro. The article quotes him only briefly, and the report does not include further comment from him or from either of the lead investors.

No statement from EQT Ventures or FirstMark appears in the article. The report also gives no details on Remanence's other backers, its customers or its plans. The context the article offers is that open-weight technology is catching up, which it says could let companies move away from more costly closed-source models. The report does not say what happens next for Remanence beyond the funding itself. It gives no timeline for new products, hiring or expansion, and it does not say when the round closed.

stories.Headline: Toxicologist Thomas Hartung argues AI biological twins need agreed validation standards before regulators trust them
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is transforming biological digital twins across every level of biological organization, according to a theoretical analysis by toxicologist Thomas Hartung published in Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence and reported by bioengineer.org on November 18, 2026. The analysis examines how deep learning, transformer architectures, foundation models, and physics-informed neural networks have elevated biological simulation beyond static systems of differential equations. Biological digital twins maintain internal states coupled to physical counterparts through continuous data assimilation rather than functioning as generic classifiers or open-loop simulations. Across five nested scales, from single-cell multi-omics to the environmental exposures of entire populations, these architectures show capacity to model human biology without surrogate animal species. Hartung argues that technical ingenuity alone cannot secure regulatory trust without agreed credibility standards, independent prospective testing, and formal governance of self-updating algorithms.

The analysis establishes four foundational commitments that exclude conventional simulations, software dashboards, and static pattern predictors. A biological digital twin demands specificity, binding its computational state to a distinct biological instance such as a single patient or an individual organ-on-chip rather than an average population category. It requires continuous data assimilation, an iterative loop where telemetry, biosensor readings, or longitudinal omics samples update the model to track physical drift over time. The twin must encode mechanistic constraints from biological principles rather than statistical correlations alone, and it demands empirical testability with refutable predictions and quantified uncertainty. Representations lacking any criterion, including frozen neural networks, open-loop simulations, or decorative avatars, fail this definition and cannot serve as dependable regulatory instruments.

At the cellular level, representation learning and foundation models fuse multimodal single-cell measurements into dynamic latent manifolds. Single-cell foundation models such as Geneformer, scGPT, and scFoundation learn compressed representations across tens of millions of cellular profiles, separating technical batch artifacts from genuine biological signals. This manifold enables virtual perturbation experiments simulating cellular trajectory shifts under novel pharmacological compounds, gene knockouts, or environmental toxicants. In exploratory toxicology, virtual cells reorder experimental pipelines, nominating informative hypotheses for bench testing while reducing reliance on early rodent toxicity screens and primary animal cell cultures. General foundation models serve as shared infrastructure rather than digital twins until conditioned on specific cell populations and coupled to incoming experimental data.

At the in vitro level, computational twins model engineered cell cultures, microfluidic devices, and organoids, which Hartung identifies as the most technologically mature tier. The DigiLoCS liver-on-chip framework separates intracellular metabolism, passive permeability, and compartment partitioning, predicting clinical drug clearance distributions more accurately than conventional lumped single-compartment methods. Emerging organoid twins incorporate biophysical priors and active learning to forecast therapeutic responses and drug resistance in patient-derived cancer tissues, offering alternatives to patient-derived xenograft rodent models. Coupled with laboratory automation, closed-loop organoid systems can predict responses, execute robotic perturbations, and update internal states within hours. Mathematical unidentifiability, where multiple unmeasured parameter combinations yield identical observable outputs, remains a persistent challenge requiring targeted, standardized physical measurements rather than algorithmic expansion alone.

At the organ level, digital twins confront fluid dynamics, biomechanics, barrier transport, and electrical propagation across anatomical structures. Investigators deploy physics-informed neural networks to bypass the computational cost of traditional finite-element modeling without large-animal studies in dogs or pigs. By penalizing violations of physical conservation laws within loss functions, these networks act as rapid surrogate models executing organ-scale biomechanical simulations in near-real time while maintaining physical plausibility outside training domains. A three-organ microphysiological platform linking gut, liver, and placental tissues investigates maternal-fetal pharmacokinetics during pregnancy, addressing conditions where animal testing routinely misleads because reproductive toxicity and placental transfer diverge sharply between rodent models and humans. Derived from the Virtual Physiological Human tradition, these hybrid architectures integrate mechanistic physical principles with machine learning for auditable, trustworthy organ-scale safety assessments.

At the individual patient level, the Virtual Human Twin integrates multimodal health records, wearable telemetry, high-resolution imaging, and personal omics into an individualized clinical forecast. Personal twins enable clinicians to compare therapeutic regimens, evaluate dosing schedules, and anticipate adverse drug reactions in silico prior to clinical administration. In cardiology, personalized models calibrated to patient-specific electrophysiology and anatomical imaging have simulated arrhythmic activation pathways to guide catheter ablation procedures before surgery. In oncology, hybrid twins simulating tumor microenvironments assist clinicians in navigating heterogeneous malignancies without relying on animal xenografts.

The review cautions against hype surrounding all-encompassing digital human replicas claiming to forecast a patient's entire lifespan, noting that current clinical twins are narrow decision-support instruments that must contend with data harmonization challenges, physiological drift across aging, and algorithmic biases disadvantaging underrepresented demographic populations. At the population level, digital twins aggregate individual profiles to analyze community disease dynamics, conduct in silico clinical trials, and evaluate environmental hazards across the human exposome. While genetics reveals inherited susceptibility, the exposome maps the modifiable totality of environmental exposures including diet, occupational chemicals, and airborne pollutants. Exposome twins link external exposure monitoring, biokinetic internal dose modeling, molecular pathway alterations, and clinical endpoints to guide precision prevention strategies rather than producing unverified correlations.

Statistical mining and generative modeling of historical control databases enable virtual control groups for toxicity studies, curtailing the sacrifice of concurrent control animals, an application recognized in a March 2026 draft qualification opinion from the European Medicines Agency regarding non-Good Laboratory Practice rat dose-range-finding studies. In human trials, synthetic cohorts extend clinical evaluations into hard-to-enroll populations such as pregnant women or rare-disease patients, provided researchers apply rigorous counterfactual reasoning and target-trial emulation to prevent confounding and spurious certainty. Despite computational demonstrations across all five biological scales, the review stresses that independent scientific validation and regulatory credibility, not algorithmic novelty, represent the binding constraints on the discipline. Most published twin frameworks remain retrospective demonstrations conducted by original developers rather than prospectively verified methods evaluated across independent laboratories.

Because biological digital twins are inherently adaptive systems that continuously assimilate fresh data and update internal parameters, traditional validation frameworks treating assays as frozen, one-time tests are structurally inadequate. Hartung advocates next-generation validation, an iterative and risk-proportionate methodology evaluating methods across five dimensions: technical reliability, biological relevance, predictive performance, applicability domain, and data integrity. Twin credibility must be assessed against human-relevant biological mechanisms rather than concordance with historical animal tests, which themselves frequently suffer from poor reproducibility and limited predictive accuracy for human outcomes, and validation must operate as an ongoing, modular case-building process evaluating mechanistic backbones and adaptive learned components independently. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence Advances Biological Digital Twins While Validation Limits Regulatory Adoption

stories.headline_source: Artificial Intelligence Advances Biological Digital Twins While Validation Limits Regulatory Adoption

stories.Headline: Perplexity defends its AI answer engine against lawsuits from publishers and claims of copyright infringement
stories.Summary:
Perplexity faces several legal challenges regarding copyright infringement and the use of online content. The company is defending its rights and the access of users to information. These legal disputes involve various publishers who claim the AI engine uses their work. The issues were discussed on November 17, 2026, by legal professionals. The company views this resistance as a common reaction to disruptive new technology.

The lawsuits involve claimants such as Dow Jones, Encyclopedia Britannica, and the Chicago Tribune. Perplexity claims it follows robots.txt protocols to avoid scraping websites that forbid it. The company uses an answer engine to retrieve and summarize publicly available internet information. It integrates existing models rather than training its own foundation models like OpenAI or Anthropic. The system provides factual summaries using snippets and citations from multiple different sources.

Nathan Barksdale, General Counsel and VP of Operations at Perplexity, is responsible for these defenses. He stated that some plaintiffs try to force the engine to regurgitate entire copyrightable articles. Barksdale believes these claimants manufacture legal claims by pushing the system until it breaks. He argues that many lawsuits reflect a technological misunderstanding of how the engine works. He claims that citing sources has worked to the company's detriment recently.

Publishers are affected by the AI and some argue that summarization violates their copyright. Barksdale suggests that publishers who adapt their business models to the technology will thrive. He notes that some website owners believe they did not give permission for use. Oliver Howley, a partner at Proskauer, observed a forceful pushback against AI summarization. He mentioned that some believe AI businesses misuse printed books and customer data.

The company operates in a global landscape with different regulatory approaches in various regions. The European Union has the EU AI Act but has recently pulled back some regulations. The United States generally avoids regulation, though some states like California have their own rules. The United Kingdom takes a middle approach, while APAC countries balance regulation with competitiveness. China currently dominates the model landscape within the APAC region.

Perplexity will continue to set up guardrails to prevent the regurgitation of copyrighted content. The company will maintain its practice of abiding by the robots.txt protocols for websites. Barksdale intends to communicate with congressional officials and attorneys general in the United States. The company must overcome customer distrust regarding the security and use of private data. The articles leave open how APAC countries will balance regulation with foreign AI products.

stories.Headline: Dental hygienists Dryer and Fisher write that AI enhances radiographs and charting but cannot replace clinical judgment
stories.Summary:
Marianne Dryer, MEd, RDH, and Andrea Fisher, MSML, RDH, wrote an article published by RDH on Nov. 17, 2026, about artificial intelligence in clinical dental hygiene practice. The article says AI can enhance radiographic interpretation and help hygienists identify periodontal changes more consistently. It says visual AI tools can make complex findings easier for patients to understand, supporting codiagnosis and treatment acceptance. It says voice-assisted charting and integrated AI can strengthen documentation, workflow efficiency, and longitudinal periodontal monitoring. The article says dental hygienists make hundreds of clinical decisions every day that influence patient outcomes.

The article says advanced imaging platforms can detect subtle changes in crestal bone height, quantify radiographic bone loss, and compare findings over time. It says accurate classification still depends on clinical attachment level, probing depths, bleeding on probing, recession, furcation involvement, mobility, medical history, and an understanding of disease activity. It says studies show less than 16% of periodontal charts are recorded to completion. It says bleeding on probing affecting 30% or more of the mouth is consistent with generalized moderate gingivitis. It says concerns about insurance coverage and reimbursement often limit use of the preventive CDT code 4346 for scaling in the presence of generalized moderate to severe gingival inflammation.

The article says the dental hygienist remains responsible for interpreting findings within the context of the patient's clinical presentation, risk factors, and overall health. It says AI should never be viewed as a substitute for comprehensive periodontal assessment. It says AI can identify patterns and highlight areas of concern but cannot independently determine etiology, classify disease, or establish an individualized treatment plan. It says comprehensive periodontal assessment, classification, patient education, treatment planning, and clinical judgment remain the responsibility of the dental hygienist. It says AI does not determine treatment or coding.

The article says AI bridges a communication gap by converting complex diagnostic information into clear, visual representations. It says color overlays, highlighted areas of bone loss, and side-by-side comparisons of previous radiographs transform abstract findings into meaningful conversations. It says patients are more likely to accept treatment when they understand what clinicians see. It says incomplete records may affect diagnostic consistency, treatment planning, communication among providers, and insurance reimbursement. It says AI-assisted radiographic interpretation, along with comprehensive depiction of CAL and disease activity, will support early coverage for D4341 and D4342, nonsurgical scaling and root planing.

The article says AI is far more than a technology trend and is an emerging clinical tool. It says AI's greatest value lies not in replacing clinical expertise but in enhancing it. It says some AI platforms function as standalone applications that analyze radiographs or identify patterns of disease. It says others are fully integrated into practice management and imaging systems, allowing clinicians to access AI-generated insights without disrupting their clinical workflow. It says one of the fastest-growing applications is voice-assisted AI.

The article says dental hygienists should consider how technology supports patient care, documentation, and communication rather than asking which AI platform is best. It says the most valuable systems integrate seamlessly into existing workflows, improve efficiency without increasing administrative burden, and enhance rather than replace clinical decision-making. It says AI should simplify the clinician's day while strengthening the patient experience. The article ends mid-sentence in the text provided, at voice-enabled periodontal charting. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Federal Reserve governor Michael Barr urges lenders to give consumers ways to dispute AI credit data
stories.Summary:
Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr used a Monday, Nov. 16 speech in Milan to warn that lenders are gaining access to a growing range of data sources, including rental payments, utility bills and employment patterns, that can serve as evidence of creditworthiness, while consumers often lack a way to review or challenge that information. He called for accessible dispute procedures, ongoing fairness monitoring and detailed records of how artificial intelligence models are validated. Barr also said major banks had encountered AI agents attempting to act inside retail accounts without being able to verify their authenticity or customer consent. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency’s Nov. 12 Semiannual Risk Perspective found that some banks are already testing or deploying customer-facing generative and agentic AI, and its Nov. 4 framework instructed examiners to tailor their reviews to the potential consequences and autonomy of each use.

The rules already on the books set out what a denial requires. Regulation B generally requires creditors to give applicants the principal reasons for adverse action or tell them how to request these reasons, and the explanation must reflect the factors actually considered or scored. When a consumer report contributes to a denial, the lender must identify the company that supplied it, and the lender is responsible for explaining its decision within 60 days of the consumer’s written request. A rent history supplied by a consumer reporting agency comes with a statutory process for disputing errors with that agency, while information a landlord supplies directly and that contributes to a denial generally gives the borrower the right to request a description of it from the lender. A bank that counted irregular deposits as evidence of unstable income must establish whether the AI model saw all the accounts the applicant connected and how it classified the deposits, and a borrower paid weekly should have a way to challenge an income calculation that leaves out one of those paychecks.

Responsibility sits with the lenders and the examiners who oversee them. The OCC is giving federal bank examiners a framework for reviewing AI according to what the system does and how much authority it has, and the report said banks are adapting oversight through measures that include human review, with implementations that should be fit for purpose. For a bank reviewing a credit complaint, that human review depends on being able to retrieve the information and the AI model version used at the time of the decision. In any dispute, the question would be whether the bank can locate the error, correct what it controls and determine whether the corrected information changes the decision.

The context is a push to widen the data used in lending. The May PYMNTS Intelligence report “Who Is the Subprime Consumer? A Behavioral Profile” found that 35% of subprime consumers held neither a credit card nor a store card, compared with 12% of prime consumers, and the article said widening the flow of information used to judge creditworthiness would arguably broaden financial inclusion. The data is already reaching lenders through new channels: in October, Plaid introduced Instant Link, which lets eligible applicants share cash flow information with lenders by connecting accounts to Plaid’s consumer reporting agency. In a survey of 2,304 U.S. adults, PYMNTS Intelligence found in the October report “Giving AI Credit: How Far Consumers Will Let Agents Go” that 63% would let an AI agent compare credit offers, while 49% would let one complete and submit an application with their final approval.

stories.Headline: Pro-regulation AI groups spend over $45 million in 2026 midterms, surpassing Leading the Future
stories.Summary:
Pro-AI-regulation groups spent more than $45 million in the 2026 midterms, surpassing the $41 million spent by the pro-AI super PAC Leading the Future, OpenSecrets reported on November 17, 2026. OpenSecrets found the figure through a review of political action committee registrations and independent expenditure filings. The spending came after several high-profile security breaches and employee resignations over the summer. Leading the Future was backed by venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz and OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told Politico the industry's political spending was "clearly not working."

OpenSecrets found at least 14 pro-AI-regulation nonprofits and super PACs raising and spending during the 2026 election cycle. Several of these organizations were founded between March and September. The newest groups, Who Decides and Tomorrow Together, launched with $30 million and $10 million, respectively. Who Decides was founded by Alex Bores, who became a prominent advocate for AI regulation after Leading the Future spent millions to oppose his campaign for the Democratic nomination in New York's 12th District. Who Decides did not record any expenditures during the midterms.

Brockman announced he would not donate a previously promised $25 million to Leading the Future. Bores has said Who Decides' focus is shaping Democrats' AI agenda for the 2028 presidential election. Scott Wisor, policy director at the Secure AI Project, said Leading the Future's move against Bores was a wake-up call for people. Wisor said it created a moment where people realized some AI companies were willing to go to the mat and punish candidates who called for any oversight of their technology. Wisor said the donor base supporting pro-regulation super PACs and candidates largely works in AI, tech or finance.

Guardrails Alliance's top donor, OpenAI research engineer Juan Felipe Uribe, contributed $200,000. Its next two biggest donors, Dylan Mavrides and Jacob Eliosoff, are a quantitative trader and investment manager, respectively, and each gave $100,000. Public First PAC's top donations all came from members of Anthropic's staff, including a contribution of $1 million from CEO Dario Amodei. Anthropic has also contributed $40 million to Public First's 501(c)(4) organization. Americans for AI Accountability, another super PAC, has been almost entirely funded by Anthropic researchers.

Public First was the largest AI regulation-focused spender and poured millions into efforts to boost Bores. Public First Action, the largest regulation-focused group, is a 501(c)(4) with three affiliated super PACs: the Jobs and Democracy PAC, Defending Our Values PAC and Public First. The Jobs and Democracy PAC supported Democratic candidates, while the Defending Our Values PAC focused on conservative candidates. Because 501(c)(4) organizations do not have to disclose donors but can distribute their money to super PACs, having an affiliate nonprofit allows the political committees to obscure their funding sources. Most Americans believe government needs to place safeguards on AI, and Leading the Future's money was labeled as politically toxic.

AI regulation has bipartisan support from the public, and some of the groups that spent in its favor during the midterms were focused exclusively on conservative candidates. Protesters in New York City held signs during the Nationwide Walkouts to Freeze AI on October 20. OpenSecrets' review of donations to the groups generally found the donor base worked in AI, tech or finance, though some of the organizations are funded by untraceable dark money. Leading the Future was one of the biggest outside spenders of the midterms and one of the most polarizing. As Leading the Future's political capital declined over the election cycle, advocates and donors rushed to form a new coalition of influence built around support for AI regulation.

stories.Headline: TaxDome report finds 74% of AI-using clients fact-check or would fact-check their accountant
stories.Summary:
A new report from the practice management platform TaxDome says that 74% of clients who use artificial intelligence have either fact-checked or would consider fact-checking their accountant's work with AI, based on a survey of 1,000 clients who use an accountant or tax professional. The 2026 Accounting Client Satisfaction Report found that AI is now increasingly part of the client relationship, that more clients are willing to pay for faster service, and that clients care more about quick response times than quick work delivery. Sixty-eight percent of clients say they have at least tried AI for their taxes or finances, and 39% have used it, mostly to ask a tax question or understand something. Very few hand it the real work, since only 3% have used AI on an actual return.

One in five clients have already used AI to review work their accountant completed, and among clients who have used or explored AI that rises to 29%, while another 45% have not done it yet but say they would consider it. For some, checking is already routine, since 24% of the clients who have checked their accountant's work with AI do it regularly, and top-paying business owners are checking their accountant's work with AI at 2.4 times the rate of all clients. The clients using AI to check their accountant's work are among the most willing to pay for more, with 78% saying they would pay for structured advisory check-ins compared with 55% of all clients, and 57% wanting a quarterly check-in on their finances compared with 45% of all clients. Across all clients who have tried AI, 61% would pay for structured advisory check-ins, compared with 43% of clients who have never tried it.

Ilya Radzinsky, co-founder and chief product officer of TaxDome, said in a statement on Nov. 18 that in the age of AI the firms that win will be the ones closest to their clients. He said the research shows what that looks like, with quick answers, a heads-up before clients have to ask, and advice they can act on. He said the firms that get it right will earn the trust, and the continued business, that AI cannot. The report says many clients also look closely at what an accountant adds, and it describes clients as not waiting for their accountant to bring AI into the relationship, since most have already started.

stories.Headline: Nvidia spends $58.1 billion on AI stocks as interim CEO Colette Kress keeps Huang’s strategy
stories.Summary:
Nvidia spent $58.1 billion buying other companies' stock in the nine months ending Oct. 25, nearly 12 times the $4.95 billion it spent in the same period last year, according to quarterly results the company posted late Tuesday. That figure almost matches the $61.2 billion Nvidia spent on its own stock buybacks, which was up from $36.3 billion a year earlier. It was Nvidia's first earnings report without Jensen Huang as chief executive. The company reported $115.8 billion in revenue for the three months ending Oct. 25, more than double the $57 billion of the prior year and above analysts' expectations of $109 billion.

The near-even split between outside stakes and buybacks shows Nvidia's growing dual role as both chip supplier and investor in the AI industry, with its equity investments focused on frontier labs, infrastructure financiers and other private companies, according to its Q3 2026 CFO commentary. Nvidia has invested in OpenAI and Anthropic. This raises the question of circular financing, meaning whether Nvidia is funding the demand that drives its chip sales. James Kisner, managing director of technology at equity research firm Water Tower Research, said that if AI spending falters, Nvidia could suffer from both lower chip sales and falling valuations for the companies it has invested in. He told Fortune that the pain is magnified because the company is double exposed.

Kisner said Nvidia's billions in free cash flow mean it can afford to pour $58.1 billion into other companies' stock, but that can be seen as fueling its own demand. Equity securities generated only $1.8 billion in net gains for Nvidia in the quarter, which included a $1 billion loss from non-marketable equity securities. Kisner said Nvidia has incentives to keep investing given how much its growth has benefited shareholders, and he said the markets really reward the company for pouring out this money. He said the strategy reflects Huang's approach of spreading money around to keep the ecosystem going, and he sees interim CEO Colette Kress continuing it with a little more conservatism at the margins.

Kress told analysts on the Nov. 17 earnings call that giving returns to shareholders is a top priority, with Nvidia having $227.3 billion left under its buyback authorization program that she said it intends to use by the end of fiscal 2028. She said another priority is supporting Nvidia's suppliers, who are working feverishly to build more and might need assistance in terms of capital. Kress said Nvidia is also willing to help finance select customers' data centers, but she told analysts it is a lot of work to understand whether those are the right types of investments. She said Nvidia's future commitments to neoclouds, the small firms that buy Nvidia chips and rent out computing capacity, totaled $32 billion in the quarter, and she said total credit guarantees reached $118 billion, including $105 billion in credit support for the PORTS-Pike data center project in Ohio, which will host Nvidia infrastructure under a 20-year lease with OpenAI. Kress also said some guarantees only take effect once customers get financing for their data centers and may no longer apply if construction runs into trouble.
