stories.Headline: Google backs about $19 billion of Anthropic leases for TeraWulf
stories.Summary:
TeraWulf has obtained Google credit support for approximately $19 billion of Anthropic lease commitments, the company announced on Nov. 4, giving lenders another contractual source of protection as the former Bitcoin-focused operator builds facilities scheduled to begin entering service in late 2027. The Anthropic lease is a 20-year arrangement, and TeraWulf’s Nov. 4 announcement says the arrangements support anticipated project financing at its Justified campus in Kentucky, where Fluor is handling engineering and construction for three buildings. Google’s Nov. 4 agreements cover specified Anthropic obligations, with support beginning after the corresponding building’s last data hall starts operating. TeraWulf’s September-quarter filing, filed Nov. 6, says the relevant backstop takes effect when the last data hall under the corresponding Anthropic lease begins operating. IREN closed $3.65 billion of GPU financing in June, combining borrowing with customer prepayments to fund most of a $5.81 billion equipment bill.

Dividing the approximately $19 billion headline value by the 20-year term produces a simple annual average of $950 million, before considering the actual payment schedule or the stages at which buildings enter service. IREN reported a 6% blended debt cost for that financing, while its lower 3.31% funding calculation included customer advances. A one-percentage-point change in annual interest on a hypothetical $3.5 billion balance changes the yearly bill by $35 million. Using a hypothetical $3.5 billion average debt balance, a reduction from 9% to 8% would save $35 million annually before fees or changes in principal, and over five years a constant $35 million annual saving totals $175 million without discounting. IREN’s original Microsoft agreement, announced Nov. 3, 2025, was valued at $9.7 billion over five years and included a 20% customer prepayment, and 20% of $9.7 billion is $1.94 billion.

TeraWulf Chief Financial Officer Patrick Fleury called the “cost of capital” fundamental to infrastructure development in the company’s announcement, and his argument is that stronger customer credit support can help the company obtain more competitive borrowing terms. The company said the facility, combined with customer prepayments, covered $5.59 billion of a $5.81 billion GPU capital requirement. Subtracting the two published totals leaves approximately $220 million, or 3.8% of that equipment bill, outside the described combination. The rounded 96% coverage figure concerns the stated GPU spending, not every expense across IREN’s development pipeline. Following specified payment defaults or insolvency events, Google can assume a lease or, in certain circumstances, permit termination and pay a fee.

The fee declines over time, has limits linked in part to project financing and can be accompanied by an interest in the landlord subsidiary. The disclosed protection concerns a customer failing to meet covered lease obligations, and it does not promise reimbursement of every cost the developer incurs before completing the buildings. TeraWulf’s planned Kentucky financing package was reported in July as potentially combining leveraged loans and high-yield bonds, and the reporting described a financing proposal, not evidence that the entire package had already been borrowed. Mining firms led declines, with $HUT down over 6%, while $RIOT and $MARA each lost over 3%, $HOOD fell 4%, $MSTR dropped 3.3% and $COIN slipped over 1.5%. The contracts can make construction easier to finance, and their value to shareholders still depends on the cost of borrowing, the equipment the operator must buy and how soon a customer begins paying for an operational facility.

The commercial agreement determines who supplies the computing hardware, and a facility owner leasing equipped space has a different purchasing obligation from a cloud provider that must acquire the GPUs, servers and networking equipment used by its customer. An operator cannot use the full lifetime value to pay today’s contractor unless a customer advances money or a lender agrees to finance against future payments, and borrowing converts part of the expected cash flow into construction funding, with interest and repayment obligations attached. A hypothetical $950 million annual receipt would have to cover whatever expenses the contract assigns to the operator before it became a return on invested capital, and maintenance, employees, insurance and debt service can sit between a customer payment and money available for another project. A loan announcement needs the same distinction, because the maximum amount a bank makes available can exceed the amount drawn, while borrowing may depend on construction milestones, documentation and specified uses of proceeds. Suppose an operator obtains a $1 billion facility but draws $200 million in its first construction stage, and interest on the borrowed balance and fees on unused availability can have different bases, so applying one interest rate to the entire advertised facility may overstate the immediate cost.

Conversely, counting only interest on the first draw can understate the eventual financing burden if the project requires the rest of the facility, and a fair comparison follows the draw schedule through construction and the repayment schedule after operations begin. The date a lease begins earning revenue matters just as much as its length, and a signed agreement can remain economically valuable while producing little current revenue during procurement and construction. Shareholders therefore need the lifetime commitment, the expected service dates and the remaining spending requirement together, and comparing only the contract value with a company’s market capitalization leaves out the capital that must be supplied to earn those payments. A lender examining a hypothetical construction loan would ask which event activates the support, and if a contractor needs payment before the guaranteed rent obligation becomes effective, the financing arrangement must address that intervening period. The distinction has consequences for the price of debt, and protection against a tenant’s eventual failure can improve a lender’s expected recovery without removing concerns about procurement, delays or whether the borrower can complete the asset.

The strongest case for these agreements is therefore concrete, and a credible guarantor can improve financing terms and make an otherwise difficult capital requirement more manageable. The contractual limits remain important even when that case holds, and a guarantor’s option to make a termination payment produces a different outcome from collecting every rent payment over the original lease term. Project lenders may accept that alternative if it covers their exposure, and equity investors have a different concern because their expected return can include profits beyond the repayment of secured debt. IREN’s Microsoft arrangement offers a separate example because the company is purchasing the computing equipment, and the combination answers the construction question in a way a headline contract value cannot. Some cash comes from the customer before service, some from institutions lending against equipment and contracted cash flow, and the residual has to be met through other available resources.

stories.Headline: Florida House Speaker Sam Garrison prioritizes property taxes and AI regulation
stories.Summary:
Florida’s new legislature took over on Tuesday, when Republican Sam Garrison became the new Florida House Speaker and Jim Boyd became the State Senate President. Garrison, who was originally from Illinois and moved to Florida in 2001, is a lawyer and former prosecutor who said he will focus on property taxes, artificial intelligence and public trust. He said his plan is not a quick five-point plan that will not be thought about again, and that the House will work on it very diligently this year. Governor Ron DeSantis was absent on Tuesday, but Governor-elect Donalds was there, and new faces could mean new relations at the capitol.

Democrats gained more than a dozen seats in the Florida House and one in the Senate after the mid-terms, even though they did not win any statewide seats. State Rep. Amy Trask, a Democrat from Gainesville, said part of what she called this blue wave is that Democrats got loud and said the status quo is not working anymore. She said the issues everyone faces are not red or blue but red, white and blue, and that affordability is hitting all of us. Tuesday’s organizational session had little to no mention of culture war type issues, and legislative leadership said voters sent a clear message to be focused on the future, not the past.

Boyd said he and Garrison work well together and that there is nothing they will not be able to accomplish together. Normally the legislature as a whole would not be back until next March, but questions about yet another special session are looming, with DeSantis saying new laws around Amendment 3 are needed before the new year. Both the speaker and the senate president poured water on that idea, arguing there is plenty of time to hash out the details of Amendment 3 during the regular session. Garrison said the rubber really hits the road at budget season this summer, and that they certainly have time, while he and Boyd have stated their opinions on when and where special sessions might happen.

Articles.Title: ‘Culture war’ issues out, AI regulation in on first legislative day

stories.headline_source: ‘Culture war’ issues out, AI regulation in on first legislative day

stories.Headline: Researchers describe technique to hide malicious payloads in open-weight AI models
stories.Summary:
Researchers described a technique called Lazarus last week to hide malicious payloads in open-weight AI models. This method allows an attacker to poison a model using a few near-imperceptible neurons. Microsoft described this specific process as turning an AI model into a sleeper agent. These poisoned models can grant an attacker access to the environment of the user. The attack targets models downloaded from the open Internet that users often trust.

The technique requires targeting fewer than 10 dormant neurons late in a model's processing cycle. These neurons are arranged to fire sequentially and stay inactive until they receive a specific trigger. Triggers can be user inputs, tool outputs, or a date read in a user's terminal. The payload can be any small, correctly formatted command that does not impact normal functioning. This differs from MaleficNet, a 2022 technique using code division multiple access to spread binaries.

Briland Hitaj of Confidencial said that people download models from strangers and give them system access. He explained that neural networks have more parameters than needed, allowing weights to be nudged unnoticed. Hitaj noted that while malicious models appear on Hugging Face, they usually abuse Python's Pickle format. He stated that no scan proves a model is clean because testing rarely finds triggers. He advised limiting agent access and requiring human approval for all consequential actions.

Luigi Vincenzo Mancini of Sapienza University of Rome advised organizations to take a defense-in-depth security approach. He suggested that users download models from official sources and compare them against a trusted baseline. Mancini noted that detecting these modifications requires diffing deployed weights against the original, unmodified weights. He said that monitoring for unusual shell commands or network connections is a more actionable technique. Users and organizations using open-weight AI models are the primary parties affected by these risks.

Open-weight models are popular because they are cheap, auditable, and liked by developers. McKinsey found that 63 percent of organizations used them early last year. Additionally, 76 percent of those survey respondents expected to use these models more in coming years. Qwen 3.8-Max is an example of an open-weight model with 2.4 trillion parameters. This model likely contains around 100 million neurons, providing ample cover for secret payloads.

Users should treat model weights like source code or binaries rather than ordinary data files. Organizations must monitor system boundaries for unexpected agent behavior to detect potential malicious intent. They should also keep production systems and credentials out of reach from AI agents. The articles leave open whether anyone has hidden payloads in weights outside of research. They do not specify if any real-world attacks using the Lazarus technique have occurred.

stories.Headline: Bank chiefs and NSA tell Congress that AI-found patches cause outages
stories.Summary:
Wall Street executives and the National Security Agency told members of Congress that this week's widespread technology outages were caused by attempts to fix vulnerabilities that artificial intelligence had identified, according to three sources familiar with the private conversations. Over the last few days the country faced a series of startling tech failures, including a pause in all flights nationwide, customers being unable to access their bank accounts, and a highly classified communications network at the National Security Agency going down. While the disruptions do not appear to have been caused by a cyberattack, government and banking officials told lawmakers that they stem from efforts to fix cyber defense gaps found by AI models, and those fixes temporarily overwhelmed the systems. On Monday banks such as JP Morgan Chase blamed software-related bugs for the service issues, and on Tuesday the NSA said scheduled routine maintenance was responsible for the temporary degradation of some of its networks. The outages carried costs and raised questions the articles leave partly open.

The Federal Aviation Administration canceled more than 20,000 flights as a result of the nationwide ground stop, according to The Wall Street Journal, and Microsoft experienced a major outage of Outlook, which Microsoft blamed on a technical defect. It is also unclear what caused the FAA systems to go down. One congressional official briefed on the matter said the models are identifying massive vulnerabilities, which increases the urgency to patch right away, and that agencies are trying to push through a lot of patches all at once, more than the system was designed for. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin told CNBC on Tuesday that new technology is being pushed on top of really old computer systems and it just seems to overwhelm the system, and he predicted the country will see more of this as new technology rolls out. Nathan Calvin, the chief strategy officer at Encode, said there is some sense in which this is reassuring because it means there is not an attack, but it shows the extent to which safety critical infrastructure relies on software with large vulnerabilities on legacy systems.

He said updating those will be a rocky process and, as more advanced models arrive, this will not be a one and done thing because more vulnerabilities will continue to be found. The NSA did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Powerful companies and government agencies have increasingly trained the most powerful AI models on themselves to identify vulnerabilities that others may weaponize against them, and once gaps are found they face immense pressure to patch them quickly, knowing malicious actors have access to comparable AI tools or will soon. That urgency has driven a wide range of public and private actors to rush fixes faster than they normally would, the sources said, but even entities with large resources, such as the nation's top banks and the intelligence community, are finding it difficult to do so without accidentally causing outages. The sources spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe private conversations.

stories.Headline: AI-driven security updates overwhelm legacy systems and cause widespread outages, officials tell Congress
stories.Summary:
Over the past month, a series of major outages took down a wide range of services, including a nationwide ground halt that stopped all US airfare for hours, days without access to core Microsoft services such as Outlook and Teams, disruptions at Apple's App Store and Apple Pay, major problems at US banks, and delays and cancellations at United Airlines after a system outage. The National Security Agency's in-house communications network for classified information also went down earlier this week. According to the Washington Sun, Wall Street and NSA sources have told Congress that the outages are being triggered by system updates designed to thwart future attacks by AI. Lawmakers have been flummoxed by the outages and a spate of wide-ranging hacks, and early indications suggest that suspicions AI played a role appear to be warranted, though there is nuance in exactly how.

The updates are meant to bolster defenses as AI continues to identify glaring cybersecurity vulnerabilities that could be exploited by bad actors, and load-bearing organizations appear to have inadvertently overwhelmed their systems while pushing them through. A congressional official told the Washington Sun that the models are identifying massive vulnerabilities, which increases the urgency to patch right away, and that organizations are trying to push through a lot of patches all at once, more than the system was designed for. Department of Homeland Security secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters on Tuesday that new technology is being pushed on top of really old computer systems, which overwhelmed them, and he said he could say with 98 percent certainty that this is not a cyberattack. Officials have continued to reassure the public that the outages are not related to any cybersecurity threats.

Experts have warned for years that AI is a dangerous double-edged sword, since it can give cybersecurity researchers a major leg up in identifying possible new attacks, and earlier this year Anthropic claimed in a report that its Claude Mythos model had found more than ten thousand vulnerabilities in existing software. Hackers can use the same tools to exploit these vulnerabilities, setting the stage for an arms race as companies rush to patch the defects. Encode chief strategy officer Nathan Calvin told the Washington Sun that there is some sense in which this is reassuring, in that it means there is not an attack, but that it shows the extent to which safety critical infrastructure we rely on is based on software with large vulnerabilities on legacy systems. To Calvin, it is an arms race that will more than likely drag on as we get more advanced models.

stories.Headline: GALEX AI expands forensic clinical auditing to four countries and offers free pilots to Colombian public hospitals
stories.Summary:
GALEX AI, an artificial intelligence platform specializing in forensic clinical auditing and medical record analysis, announced on November 17, 2026, that it is expanding its international operations across the United States, Colombia, Mexico, and Spain. The company also announced an initiative to offer free pilot programs to public hospitals of lower complexity in Colombia. The announcement was made from Bogotá, D.C., Colombia, through EINPresswire.com. GALEX AI was founded by Maikel Nisimblat, an attorney and entrepreneur. The initiative aims to make advanced artificial intelligence technology accessible to public healthcare institutions.

GALEX AI combines Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Big Data, and Machine Learning technologies to analyze extensive medical records and compare documented clinical care against clinical practice guidelines, medical protocols, healthcare regulations, and specialized reference sources. Its analysis may include medical history and previous clinical records, diagnosis and treatment decisions, medication orders and administration records, laboratory results and diagnostic imaging, surgical procedures and postoperative care, patient monitoring and follow-up, and informed consent and relevant medical records. The platform is designed to help identify potential deviations, omissions, inconsistencies, and documentation gaps throughout the patient care process. The free pilots will test the technology in practical institutional settings, including medical board meetings, clinical case reviews, and healthcare quality assessment processes. The company has filed a patent application in the United States, which is currently pending.

Nisimblat said that AI should not only transform healthcare technology but should help save lives and make better medical care accessible to everyone. The company said the platform is designed as a decision-support and auditing tool that does not independently establish medical negligence, replace professional medical judgment, or determine legal liability. GALEX AI said its findings require appropriate review and interpretation by qualified professionals. The company said any implementation will be subject to institutional agreements, appropriate authorizations, confidentiality safeguards, and applicable personal data protection and healthcare requirements. Nisimblat holds a law degree from Universidad de los Andes in Colombia and a specialization in Mining and Energy Law from Universidad Externado de Colombia.

GALEX AI said public hospitals frequently operate under significant resource constraints and face demanding patient volumes, and that reviewing extensive medical histories can be challenging when consultation times are limited. The initiative seeks to contribute to stronger clinical quality review processes, improved patient safety assessment, more structured medical record analysis, earlier identification of potential documentation gaps, better-informed discussions during medical board meetings, and greater access to advanced healthcare technology. GALEX AI is designed to serve hospitals, clinics, physicians, patients and families, medical malpractice attorneys, and medical expert witnesses. In Colombia, Nisimblat Law Offices serves as the legal representation associated with GALEX AI, providing legal evaluation of potential claims and constitutional actions involving urgent healthcare protection. The company also seeks to develop professional networks connecting medical malpractice attorneys, medical auditors, and expert witnesses in its target markets.

Nisimblat has more than 29 years of professional experience. His professional education also includes negotiation training through the Program on Negotiation, associated with Harvard, MIT, and Tufts, a specialization in Business Development from the George Washington University School of Business, IBM certifications in AI Prompt Engineering and Generative AI Foundations, and training at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania in AI for Finance and Marketing. He is currently pursuing a Tech MBA through ADEN International Business School and Euncet Business School, affiliated with the Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya in Spain. GALEX AI incorporates security measures intended to protect sensitive clinical information, with attention to encryption, confidentiality, and applicable healthcare data protection requirements. Institutional implementations must comply with the legal and regulatory obligations applicable to the relevant jurisdiction.

GALEX AI invites interested public hospitals, healthcare institutions, and medical professionals in Colombia to explore pilot collaborations. The company's media contact is GALEX AI ,  International Expansion, with Colombian representation through Nisimblat Law Offices. The articles do not state how many hospitals will receive free pilots, when the pilots will begin, or how long they will run. The articles do not state the status of operations in the United States, Mexico, and Spain beyond the announcement of international operations. The articles do not state the outcome of the pending patent application.

stories.Headline: Researchers study AI literacy and educommunication for Afro-Ecuadorian youth leadership in Esmeraldas
stories.Summary:
The study was an exploratory study with an explanatory-sequential mixed-methods design on artificial intelligence literacy and educommunication in educational processes related to Afro-descendant youth leadership in Ecuador. It was conducted by N J Narcisa Jessenia Medranda Morales and R G Robert Germán García Iturralde of Universidad Politécnica Salesiana, Quito, Ecuador. It was published in Frontiers in Education, Sec. Digital Education, Volume 11, 2026, on 17 November 2026. In the quantitative phase, an online survey was administered to 90 participants involved in educational, youth, and community processes.

The qualitative phase consisted of a virtual focus group with three young Afro-Ecuadorian participants selected to deepen specific survey findings. The sample was predominantly from the province of Esmeraldas, at 94.4%, with a small number of participants from Santo Domingo de los Tsáchilas. Descriptive statistics, internal-consistency estimates, and exploratory Spearman rank-order correlations between dimension scores were calculated. The survey showed high agreement across six dimensions, with Afro-descendant identity receiving the highest mean and critical AI literacy the lowest relative mean. Reliability varied substantially across dimensions, and exploratory bivariate results showed positive moderate-to-strong associations among the six dimension scores, interpreted as associations rather than causal effects.

The qualitative findings showed selective and cautious AI use and documented experiences of racialized digital representation, identity reaffirmation, and demand for ethical, community-based AI training. The authors wrote that the qualitative phase elaborated and qualified the quantitative patterns rather than merely reproducing them. They wrote that the findings support a culturally situated approach to AI literacy that combines technical understanding, ethical judgment, cultural recognition, and educommunicative production. They wrote that the findings are exploratory and non-generalizable but provide an empirically grounded framework for future educational interventions and measurement research in Afro-descendant and intercultural contexts. They framed the study around the research question of how educommunicative practices supported by artificial intelligence can strengthen Afro-descendant youth leadership in intercultural educational contexts in Ecuador.

They described the study's contribution as lying at the intersection of communication, education, and applied technologies through the proposal of a culturally situated model of AI literacy aimed at strengthening Afro-descendant youth leadership. The article cites UNESCO (2023) arguing that the integration of GenAI into education should be guided by human-centered approaches to ensure ethical, inclusive, and privacy-respecting practices that strengthen the agency of teachers and students. It cites UNESCO (2024) on international AI competency frameworks emphasizing simultaneous development of technical, ethical, and pedagogical competencies. It cites ECLAC (2020) arguing that recognizing the rights of Afro-descendant populations is essential to building more just, equal, and democratic societies. It states that in Ecuador the provinces of Esmeraldas, Imbabura, Guayas, Pichincha, Carchi, and El Oro have the largest Afro-descendant populations in the country.

It cites Noble (2018) warning that AI may pose risks through the reproduction of biases, stereotypes, and forms of algorithmic exclusion. The article states that educational, communicative, and cultural practices are being reshaped by the expansion of generative artificial intelligence. It states that in educational settings its use has extended to writing support, information retrieval, content production, feedback, assessment, and personalized learning. It states that in Latin America digital transformations are unfolding in contexts marked by social inequalities, educational gaps, and uneven access to technology.

It states that for Afro-descendant peoples and communities this scenario becomes more complex because of historical exclusion, structural racism, statistical invisibility, stereotyped representation, and limited access to public decision-making spaces. It cites Long and Magerko (2020) defining AI literacy as a set of competencies enabling individuals to evaluate AI technologies, communicate effectively about them, and use them as tools for technical, administrative, educational, and communicative support in everyday life. The article states that AI literacy involves critical competence, ethical competence, narrative competence, and participatory competence. It cites DigComp 2.2, which defines digital competence as a combination of knowledge, skills, and attitudes enabling safe and responsible participation in digital environments.

It cites Freire (1970), Kaplún (1998), and Soares (2009) as important reference points in Latin American educommunication because they place dialogue, voice, and collective meaning-making at the center of learning. It cites Santos Albardía, Peña-Fernández, and Agirreazkuenaga (2025) finding that introducing technology does not by itself produce critical media literacy, its educational value depending on teacher preparation, critical reflection, and purposeful pedagogical use. The article states that AI literacy does not replace media literacy but complements and expands it by introducing new questions about data, algorithms, automation, bias, and authorship. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Meta staff flag Muse AI privacy risks as researchers find exposed chats before US launch
stories.Summary:
Meta employees raised massive security concerns about the Muse AI agent before and after its release. These workers flagged serious doubts regarding privacy promises through internal channels during the launch week. Meta proceeded with the scheduled United States launch in September 2026 despite these warnings. Internal communications reviewed by Reuters showed employees feared the product was unreliable in real world conditions. The company launched the agent with claims that it was built for privacy and security.

The agent manages emails, calendars, and financial tasks through connected accounts and broad Android notification permissions. Meta began testing a human concierge phone feature with employees in August 2026 before public release. A vulnerability identified by Patrick Wardle put account tokens and dictated audio at risk for individual users. Claroc found that shared conversations were exposed through publicly searchable DNS records without requiring any login. These exposed records included financial reviews, business documents, and holiday schedules from entire companies and marketing firms.

Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts stated that the company prioritizes safety and follows strict internal rules. He described the examples provided by Reuters as isolated incidents and noted that Meta conducts extensive testing. Meta did not dispute that the internal posts from employees existed. The company temporarily disabled the sharing feature after being alerted to the DNS flaw. Meta subsequently restored the feature once a fix was in place to block the links.

Internal employees were described by Ars Technica as freaking out about the privacy implications of Muse. These workers observed behaviors that conflicted directly with how Meta marketed the product to the public. Users who shared conversations using the built in function were affected by the DNS discovery. Security researchers and IT experts now recommend that users treat broad device permissions with caution. Organizations are advised to establish clear policies about what information employees submit to AI assistants.

Meta is an American technology company headquartered in Menlo Park, California, founded by Mark Zuckerberg in 2004. The company rebranded from Facebook in 2021 to focus on the metaverse and Quest VR hardware. Muse operates in cloud virtual machines gated by a security process called Sentinel. Reuters tests showed Muse accessing private Signal messages and sending unsolicited bank balance figures to employees. The human concierge feature uses human contractors to handle calls when the AI cannot complete tasks.

Claroc confirmed that there was no evidence that anyone misused the exposed chats before the fix. Meta maintains that the AI agent is built with strong security foundations despite the reported failures. The articles leave open whether the pattern of issues suggests a systemic architectural failure. Experts suggest users monitor app permission settings to understand what data the agent can access. The reports do not state if Meta will change the broad permissions required by the app.

stories.Headline: Clemson University launches three AI degree programs in fall 2027
stories.Summary:
Clemson University announced on November 16, 2026 that three new degree programs in artificial intelligence will launch in fall 2027, according to a Clemson News article by Paul Alongi. Students will be able to pursue bachelor's, master's and doctoral degrees through Clemson's School of Computing. The programs are aimed at preparing the future workforce for careers in industries ranging from cybersecurity and advanced manufacturing to health care and finance. The South Carolina Commission on Higher Education has approved all three degree programs. All three programs will be based on Clemson's main campus and taught in person.

The interdisciplinary bachelor's program will require 123 credit hours and combine programming, mathematics and statistics with courses in artificial intelligence, business, ethics and human-centered design. The 30-credit-hour master's program will include six core courses and four electives covering advanced AI topics, with no thesis required. The doctoral program will require at least 70 credit hours for students entering with a bachelor's degree or 40 credit hours for those entering with a master's degree in a related field. The doctoral program combines advanced coursework with original research leading to a dissertation. Interested students can contact Brian Dean at bcdean@clemson.edu for information.

J. Cole Smith, executive vice president for academic affairs and provost, said the programs will strengthen Clemson's commitment to delivering the nation's No. 1 student experience while supporting its continued rise as a leading research university. Smith said artificial intelligence is transforming industries, creating new opportunities and changing the skills employers need. O. Thompson Mefford, associate dean for undergraduate studies in the College of Engineering, Computing and Applied Sciences, said graduates will gain technical knowledge, hands-on experience and an understanding of how AI affects people. Brian Dean, C. Tycho Howle Director of Clemson's School of Computing, said AI is opening doors to careers and research opportunities that would have been difficult to imagine just a few years ago. Melissa Smith, the college's associate dean of graduate studies, said the programs will help build a strong pipeline of talent and expand research capabilities.

Anand Gramopadhye, the college's dean, said the new programs will expand opportunities for students, strengthen Clemson's AI research capabilities and help meet growing workforce demands. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics projects employment growth of 15.8% for software developers, 19.7% for computer and information research scientists and 33.5% for data scientists. Altogether, those occupations are projected to generate about 141,800 job openings annually, with employment growth of 18.1%, well above the national average. The bachelor's program is intended for students with a wide range of interests who want careers in computing, AI and related fields or who plan to pursue graduate study. The master's program is aimed at students who want to build on their undergraduate education in computing, engineering, science or other fields with a strong mathematical foundation.

A Hindu article by P. John J. Kennedy, published November 18, 2026, said artificial intelligence is forcing India's universities to confront what it means to know something. The article cited experiments at IISER Pune, IIM Ahmedabad, IIM Bangalore and the Indian School of Business. IISER Pune allows AI use by default, IIM Ahmedabad encourages AI-assisted preparation for classroom discussions, and IIM Bangalore has experimented with an exam in which students build chatbots to answer questions. ISB is exploring personalised AI tutors and simulations. A 2024 study by Bastani and colleagues involving high-school students in Turkey found that those using a standard chatbot performed better during practice but worse in a subsequent exam without AI assistance.

The Hindu article said a version of the chatbot designed to provide hints rather than direct answers largely avoided this decline. It said banning AI is no longer a realistic option because it would leave students unprepared for workplaces where these tools are increasingly used. It said oral exams are difficult to conduct on a large scale in Indian universities, examiners may apply inconsistent standards, and students can misrepresent their use of AI. It said UNESCO's guidance on generative AI in education emphasises human agency and educational and ethical scrutiny. The article said the doctoral program is designed for students seeking research careers in academia or industry who want to develop new AI technologies and applications.

stories.Headline: Baidu head Robin Li warns that artificial intelligence could be a bubble
stories.Summary:
Robin Li, the chief executive of Baidu, warned that artificial intelligence could be a bubble on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. He spoke during a panel discussion with business leaders in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen. This event took place ahead of talks between the world's top two economies regarding the sensitive technology sector. The warning came while Shenzhen hosted the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting during that same week. Li expressed concern that the current global landscape for this technology has become an urgent situation.

Chinese President Xi Jinping is due to hold talks with U.S. counterpart Donald Trump on Thursday, November 19. These leaders are expected to discuss the risks posed by AI during the APEC meeting in Shenzhen. The situation involves Nvidia, a U.S. chip titan reporting quarterly results after former CEO Jensen Huang quit. Huang resigned last week following an affair scandal involving a suspected Chinese spy, which increased scrutiny of export rules. Nvidia has since rejected an offer from Jensen Huang to return as the chief executive of the company.

Robin Li stated that AI adoption is not boosting profits for most companies and has fallen short of expectations. He questioned if companies are seeing higher revenues or increased profits after adopting the technology at the foundational level. Li warned that the concern about an AI bubble could become a reality if these issues are not addressed. He acknowledged that Baidu faces headwinds in online marketing despite seeing tangible results in the company's AI strategy. The Beijing-based search engine provider posted a sixth straight drop in quarterly revenue on Monday, November 16, 2026.

IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva told AFP in October that losing confidence in AI returns could lead to worldwide financial stability risks. She noted that tanking stock market valuations could occur if investors lose faith in the future of these investments. The scandal involving Jensen Huang has heightened market jitters over the boom and how Chinese companies access powerful chips. These chips are used to train and run AI systems despite the existing export rules set by the U.S. government. Many business leaders are affected by the intense competition and the lack of profit growth in the application layer.

Baidu, which is sometimes called China's Google, has made an aggressive push into artificial intelligence in recent years. However, the company's challenges have grown as a domestic consumer slump drags on cash flows generated by advertising. The U.S. and China are currently pushing for AI safety steps despite their fierce rivalry in the field. There are growing calls for cooperation between the two tech powerhouses to manage the risks of the technology. The global investment boom is now under question as companies struggle to turn AI adoption into actual profit.

President Xi Jinping and Donald Trump will meet on Thursday to discuss the risks and cooperation regarding artificial intelligence. The world awaits the quarterly results from Nvidia to see the health of the global AI investment boom. The articles leave open whether the two leaders will reach an agreement on AI safety and cooperation. It remains unclear if other companies will find ways to increase revenues through the application of AI technology. The reports do not state if the domestic consumer slump in China will continue to affect Baidu's cash flows.

stories.Headline: Anthropic sells shares to the public for the first time as Samsung and SK hynix cash holdings surge
stories.Summary:
Anthropic is selling its shares to the public for the first time according to a report from November 17, 2026. This company was founded in 2021 by seven former employees of OpenAI to create the Claude models. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix also saw their cash holdings surge during the same period of the AI boom. These two South Korean chip giants reported their financial results in corporate filings released on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. The surge in wealth for these firms is driven by strong global demand for artificial intelligence memory chips.

Combined liquid holdings for the chipmakers reached 329.23 trillion won, or 246.33 billion dollars, by the end of September. This total rose from 136.3 trillion won a year earlier and from 277.91 trillion won at the end of June. Samsung Electronics held 214.77 trillion won in cash and short term instruments, up from 108.44 trillion won last year. SK hynix reported 114.46 trillion won in liquid assets, which is more than quadruple its previous 27.85 trillion won. The combined holdings increased by 51.32 trillion won in the three months between June and September of 2026.

Corporate filings from the two chipmakers show they benefited from high bandwidth memory used in AI data centers. Samsung Electronics posted cumulative operating profits of approximately 254 trillion won during the first three quarters of this year. SK hynix reported cumulative operating profits of approximately 181 trillion won for the same period of the current year. Katie Prescott, the technology business editor at The Times, explained who will make a fortune from the Anthropic float. She noted that the company is now selling shares to the public for the first time since its founding.

The investors in Anthropic are set to win big from the mega float of the AI powerhouse, Katie Prescott wrote. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix account for more than one fourth of the stock market credit loans in Korea. Some Seoul stocks fell sharply on Tuesday morning because of lingering worries regarding the artificial intelligence industry. Authorities are investigating potential AI assisted cheating across 528 national exams before the 2027 College Scholastic Ability Test. The prime minister vowed to root out this cheating during the college entrance exams taking place this week.

The AI boom has increased demand for advanced memory chips and high bandwidth memory used in large AI data centers. Anthropic was started by seven people who previously worked at OpenAI before they founded their own company in 2021. Korean startup Upstage is now teaming up with Canada's Cohere to provide sovereign AI solutions for enterprise clients. These security focused solutions are being developed for clients located across the Asia Pacific region of the global market. The chipmakers have seen their combined cash holdings more than double over the past year due to this demand.

The company Anthropic will now move forward with its initial public offering to sell shares to the general public. Authorities will tighten checks on smart glasses to prevent cheating before the 2027 College Scholastic Ability Test begins. The articles do not state the specific price of the shares being sold during the Anthropic mega float. It remains unclear how the Seoul stock market will react to the lingering woes of the AI industry. The reports leave open whether the AI chip demand will continue to drive cash holdings for Korean chipmakers.

stories.Headline: AMD completes World Labs and Taalas acquisitions to expand its AI hardware and model research
stories.Summary:
AMD completed the acquisitions of World Labs and Taalas in November 2026 to boost its AI strategy. The company bought these firms to add AI model research and inference chip design to its operations. These deals expand the reach of AMD across AI hardware, software, and model development. The company seeks to secure more of the technology stack behind training and inference. This move allows AMD to compete more directly across a wider range of workloads.

AMD paid 8.2 billion dollars for World Labs on Monday, November 16, 2026, to access its research. Dr Fei-Fei Li joined the company as executive vice president and chief scientist reporting to Lisa Su. Taalas provides specialized silicon for AI inference to be integrated with Instinct GPUs and EPYC CPUs. The company will use ROCm software and its Helios rackscale offering alongside the new Taalas technology. This acquisition also expands the engineering presence of AMD by adding technical staff in Canada.

Chair and Chief Executive Officer Dr Lisa Su said that compute platforms and models must be optimized together. She stated that the pioneering research from World Labs will help shape future hardware, software, and systems. Su believes these teams will enable developers across the ecosystem to push the boundaries of AI. Vamsi Boppana, Senior Vice President of the Artificial Intelligence Group, said customers need broad compute solutions. He noted that Taalas expands the ability of AMD to deliver differentiated inference performance and efficiency.

The World Labs team will continue foundational model research while collaborating with engineers at AMD. This research focuses on AI models that simulate interactive 3D environments for robotic learning and simulation. These models train robots to maneuver in both virtual and real worlds to compete with Nvidia. Nvidia has already grabbed a strong foothold in this space through its collection of open-weights models. Researchers and developers across the open AI ecosystem are the primary people affected by these changes.

Chipmakers and cloud providers are looking for ways to reduce the cost and power of serving models. Training large models remains a major spending category, but workloads are becoming more specialized over time. Semiconductor groups are tightening links between silicon, systems software, and the behavior of AI models. AMD has been building its AI line-up around EPYC server processors and Instinct accelerators. Companies increasingly use acquisitions to secure scarce expertise in model architecture and specialized silicon design.

AMD intends to use insights from emerging model behavior to inform the design of future infrastructure. The company will integrate Taalas technology into its accelerator strategy to strengthen its long-term inference roadmap. The World Labs team will work with AMD engineers on future systems for the open AI ecosystem. Yahoo Finance named Lisa Su its CEO of the Year for 2026 during its Invest conference. The articles do not outline the financial terms for the acquisition of the company called Taalas.

stories.Headline: HPE and AMD debut Lux AI cluster at No 14 on TOP500 with 220.79 petaflops
stories.Summary:
At SC26 in Chicago, HPE announced that Lux, an AI cluster built with AMD for Oak Ridge National Laboratory, debuted at No. 14 on the TOP500 with 220.79 petaflops of measured HPL performance. HPE said the system, purpose-built for AI training and inference, placed ahead of machines designed for traditional supercomputing workloads. Lux is the first dedicated AI system to come online for the U.S. Department of Energy’s Genesis Mission. HPE and AMD co-designed and co-constructed the cluster, which gives researchers across the U.S. multi-tenant, cloud-like access. The debut was announced on November 16, 2026, according to the articles.

Lux runs on direct liquid-cooled HPE ProLiant Compute XD685 systems with AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs, AMD EPYC CPUs, and AMD Pensando DPUs. The network uses HPE Juniper Networking QFX switches running 800G Ethernet, with load balancing and congestion management that HPE says reduce bottlenecks and improve GPU utilization. HPE Networking Data Center Director handles intent-based deployment, management, and lifecycle automation. Half of Lux’s 3.5 million annual node-hours are dedicated to the Genesis Mission, and the other half are available for proprietary use, a total equivalent to about 400 nodes running around the clock for a year. HPE has made a $37 million in-kind investment in the program to support research projects.

Trish Damkroger, senior vice president and general manager of HPC and AI Infrastructure Solutions at HPE, said the company, with ORNL and AMD, had delivered breakthrough engineering innovation and was furthering what it can accomplish as a proven public-private partnership. She said HPE was proud of its continued collaboration and investment in the Genesis Mission to stand up one of its first AI systems. Georgia Tourassi, associate director of computing and computational sciences at the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility, said she was excited for the debut and the opportunities it creates to expand access to advanced computing resources. She said Lux will give researchers additional capacity and flexibility to advance innovative SI approaches in Earth system prediction, materials development, biology, and fusion energy. Thomas Zacharia, senior vice president of global public sector and strategic partnerships at AMD, said Lux shows what is possible when national laboratories, government and industry work together.

AMD said the cluster runs its ROCm software stack, and neither company has published a node or GPU count for the system. AMD said Lux is now open to scientific users. HPE describes Lux as the first deployment of HPE Networking products at a DOE national laboratory, bringing scalable, high-performance, open Ethernet to AI-driven science. The Genesis Mission is a DOE program that applies AI to energy research, scientific discovery, and national security on a platform combining AI, supercomputing, quantum systems, and scientific instruments. Zacharia tied Lux to an open, sovereign AI stack with tools that researchers across the country can use.

HPE announced Lux about a year ago as part of its broader collaboration with ORNL and AMD. The partnership also includes Discovery, a forthcoming next-generation supercomputer developed as the successor to Frontier, which first broke the exascale speed barrier. ORNL has said Discovery will pair AMD EPYC Venice CPUs with AMD Instinct MI430X GPUs on an HPE Cray Supercomputing platform, with delivery expected in 2028. Lux carries the integrated management and Silicon Root of Trust protection found across HPE ProLiant servers. The configuration equips Lux with the performance necessary for large model AI training and deep learning.

The articles do not say when Lux began operating beyond its debut at SC26. They leave open how many nodes or GPUs the system contains. They do not state which proprietary users will take the half of node-hours not dedicated to the Genesis Mission. They do not give a date for Discovery’s delivery beyond 2028. They do not say what the $37 million in-kind investment will fund specifically.

stories.Headline: Ramaphosa pitches South Africa as Africa's AI hub during Silicon Valley visit
stories.Summary:
President Cyril Ramaphosa said South Africa wants to become a leading hub for AI in Africa, pitching expanding energy capacity, telecommunications infrastructure and an established data-centre industry as foundations for attracting investment and developing homegrown technology. He told a delegation to the US that Microsoft, Amazon Web Services and Google had established major data-centre and cloud-computing operations in South Africa. He described their presence as a vote of confidence in the country's infrastructure, skills and institutions. He said the challenge was to build on these investments by moving beyond hosting digital infrastructure to developing homegrown AI enterprises, applications and intellectual property that could compete globally. He addressed a South African delegation in California on the country's AI mission on Monday, November 16 2026.

The delegation's programme includes engagements with Stanford University, Alphabet, Google, Cisco, Palo Alto Networks and Microsoft, as well as investors, academics and technology specialists. It brings together government representatives, business leaders, researchers, academics, technical experts and university students. Ramaphosa said South Africa was generating an electricity surplus and planned to build 14,000km of transmission lines while expanding nuclear and renewable energy capacity. The government was also seeking to strengthen digital connectivity and attract investment in data centres, advanced computing, research and development and technology-driven industries. The visit is intended to help South Africa understand how the technology industry has developed in the US, particularly the role played by venture capital, universities and partnerships between government and private companies in turning research into commercial enterprises.

Ramaphosa said South Africa needed to develop a similar innovation ecosystem, but cautioned against simply copying Silicon Valley. He said the country's approach should reflect its own economic and development needs, creating opportunities for entrepreneurs in townships and rural communities as well as major cities. He identified access to venture capital as an important part of building local technology companies, saying the government needed to understand how innovative businesses could secure funding to grow into globally competitive enterprises. He said universities and research institutions would also need to play a greater role in technological development and commercial innovation. He said South Africa wanted investment partnerships that would support local startups, strengthen universities and provide opportunities for domestic innovators to access international markets.

Ramaphosa called for technology and knowledge transfer, saying the country should not simply become a consumer of technologies developed elsewhere. He cited the experience of Asian economies, including Japan and South Korea, which he said had used technology and knowledge transfer to advance their industrial development. He said attracting investment would depend on the government's addressing constraints that could undermine the country's competitiveness. He called for more reliable and affordable electricity, expanded digital connectivity, stronger skills development and an easier environment in which to establish and grow businesses. He raised concern about risks associated with the technology, including the misuse of personal information, discrimination embedded in automated systems, misinformation and the concentration of technological power in a small number of companies.

According to the presidency, global hyperscalers are planning about $650bn in AI capital expenditure in 2026. Venture capital investment in AI reached $259bn in 2025, with about three-quarters of that investment taking place in the US. The investment drive comes as countries compete to attract capital into an industry requiring substantial computing capacity, data infrastructure and reliable electricity. Ramaphosa said South Africa had raised the need for AI guardrails at the Brics summit in India and should work with other developing countries to ensure that international rules reflected their interests. He argued that technological innovation needed to remain subject to human oversight and democratic accountability.

The articles do not state what agreements, if any, were reached during the delegation's engagements with Stanford University, Alphabet, Google, Cisco, Palo Alto Networks and Microsoft. They do not say what the delegation would do after the week-long programme in Silicon Valley, California. They do not give the outcome of the engagements with investors, academics and technology specialists. They do not say whether the government had set targets or timelines for the 14,000km of transmission lines or for expanding nuclear and renewable energy capacity. They do not say what response the US companies or investors gave to Ramaphosa's pitch.

stories.Headline: Anthropic plans a November 2026 public offering using a governance structure to protect its public benefit mission
stories.Summary:
Anthropic plans to launch an initial public offering on Wall Street during this current month of November in the year 2026. The San Francisco startup intends to go public while maintaining a pledge to prioritize the benefit of humanity during AI development. This transition to a public company will test a commitment the firm has held since the time of its founding. The company wants to balance the new pressure to deliver profits with its original mission to help the general public. This move marks a significant shift as the startup prepares for its official debut on the American stock market.

The company is a public benefit corporation, which is a legal designation used to balance shareholder interests with the public good. Anthropic has sketched out a governance structure that it says will protect its broader mission against various financial interests. This legal status is also used by its rival, OpenAI, to manage the tension between profit and social benefit. Experts say the described mechanisms give the company wide leeway to decide how it measures its benefit to society. The company is operating in uncharted territory as it reaches a potential valuation of many trillions of dollars.

The company is responsible for creating a governance structure that protects its mission from the pull of financial interests. Anthropic says this structure will ensure that the company continues to prioritize humanity as it develops its artificial intelligence. The firm claims that its legal status as a public benefit corporation helps it maintain this specific social balance. These internal mechanisms are designed to keep the company focused on the public good during its growth. The startup maintains that its mission remains central even as it seeks to attract new public investors.

Sarah Kreps is a professor and director at Cornell University who provided an expert perspective on the company's new filing. She stated that the real test emerges if the question of public benefit becomes costly for the business. Kreps believes a conflict may arise when the public benefit clashes with the need to make a profit. Other experts are affected by these developments as they monitor how trillion dollar AI firms handle social responsibilities. These observers are concerned that the company has too much wiggle room in its official IPO filing.

Anthropic was founded as a startup in San Francisco with a core mission to develop artificial intelligence for humanity's benefit. The company chose to incorporate as a public benefit corporation to legally embed this social mission into its structure. This background mirrors the approach taken by OpenAI, which also uses the public benefit corporation legal designation. The firm has spent its early years developing AI while promising to avoid prioritizing profits over the public good. This history sets the stage for the tension expected during its upcoming transition to a public company.

The company will now move forward with its initial public offering to begin trading on the Wall Street stock exchange. This process will determine if the firm can actually prioritize humanity while meeting the demands of its shareholders. The articles leave open exactly how the company will measure whether it is successfully benefiting the global society. It remains unclear if the governance structure will be strong enough to resist the pressure for higher financial returns. The final outcome of this experiment in corporate governance will be seen after the IPO is complete.

stories.Headline: ControlUp launches AI Visibility & Usage Insights for IT to track AI tool adoption
stories.Summary:
ControlUp announced AI Visibility & Usage Insights on November 17, 2026, a new capability giving IT a unified view of AI tools adoption, usage, and experience across the organization. The company said IT teams can see how employees use AI applications including Copilot, ChatGPT Enterprise, Gemini, Claude Enterprise, Cursor, Notion AI, and others. ControlUp described itself as a company reinventing IT operations with its AI platform. The announcement said the capability helps IT get more value from their AI investments. David Marshall published the vmblog.com article on November 17, 2026, and GlobeNewswire carried the release from San Francisco dated November 17, 2026.

Gartner projects generative AI model spending will grow from $13 billion in 2025 to $139 billion by 2030, citing Forecast: AI Spending, Worldwide, 2025-2030, 3Q26. The capability includes a unified AI application inventory showing tools in use, including Copilot, ChatGPT Enterprise, Gemini, Claude Enterprise, Cursor, Codex, and Notion AI, with application type, user counts, and top-used models. It includes adoption and usage insights tracking active employees, total usage, and average usage per user across devices and platforms. It includes AI experience scoring with an average AI score and per-application scores, platform and environment context on browsers, operating systems, and device groups, and comparison of physical PCs with remote desktops including virtual desktop infrastructure and desktop-as-a-service. It includes PII risk visibility tracking sensitive data such as API keys and banking information, and flexible filtering by app, browser, platform, operating system, or device tag.

Bob Johnson, SVP Global Partnerships & Alliances at ControlUp, said employees are adopting AI tools faster than IT can track, leaving admins unable to answer basic questions about shadow AI, adoption, or spend. He said AI Visibility & Usage Insights gives IT a clear picture of AI tool adoption to guide governance, plan training, and optimize AI investments based on real usage, not guesswork. The release said IT teams can drive AI adoption by seeing where licensed users are active and where adoption is lagging. It said they can improve employee experience by spotting underperforming AI applications early. It said they can plan investment with confidence by comparing adoption and performance to decide where to expand, consolidate, or add enablement.

The release said IT teams can establish usage guardrails with a shared, evidence-based view of the AI tools in use across the organization. It said AI adoption is accelerating across the enterprise as employees use a growing mix of AI assistants, coding tools, and embedded AI features. It said IT teams are being asked to manage spend and demonstrate value, yet many lack a clear picture of the AI application footprint, including which tools employees use, on which devices, and where more support would help. It said the capability gives IT a data-backed baseline and a clear view of the AI footprint in their environment. The release said the capability helps IT teams understand the AI tools being used so they can support employees and govern AI adoption.

Attendees can experience AI Visibility & Usage Insights live at the ControlUp booth #5257L at Microsoft Ignite, November 17, 20 in San Francisco. ControlUp experts will demo how IT teams can baseline Copilot adoption and extend that visibility across their AI landscape. The capability is offered as an add-on module available to all ControlUp for Apps and ControlUp for Desktops Advanced customers. ControlUp said it is reinventing IT operations with an AI platform built on real-time data, intelligent decisions, and automated action to help IT teams detect, resolve, and prevent issues before they impact the business. The release described the platform as delivering Autonomous Endpoint Management, unifying Digital Employee Experience capabilities with agentic AI, and said ControlUp ONE integrates real-time signals with AI-driven decisioning and automated remediation.

The Gartner forecast was published October 7, 2026, by Kay Arnott, Jon Erensen, Amarendra ., Adrian O'Connell, and Arunasree Chepa. The Manila Times carried the GlobeNewswire release on November 18, 2026. ControlUp directed readers to request a demo at https://www.controlup.com/schedule-a-demo/. The release included a press contact email address that appeared as [email protected]. The articles did not state pricing for the add-on module or a general availability date beyond its availability to ControlUp for Apps and ControlUp for Desktops Advanced customers.

stories.Headline: Nvidia shares rise 4 percent as global stocks fall amid continued AI trade unwind
stories.Summary:
Global stocks fell on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, as the artificial intelligence trade unwind continued to push markets lower. Nvidia shares rose 4 percent in choppy trade immediately after the company released its third quarter earnings results. Investors prepared for the stock market launch of Anthropic later in the week while monitoring various global economic indicators. Solid retail sales in the United States and hawkish comments from Federal Reserve officials kept interest rate expectations high. The market decline occurred as investors weighed the impact of these economic factors against the latest AI company news.

The S&P 500 tech sector fell 20 percent since October 6, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor index dropped 30 percent. Nvidia shares fell nearly 40 percent since October 6, losing more than 1.7 trillion dollars in total market value. Japan stocks fell 1.3 percent, while Europe and the UK both dropped 1.8 percent, their worst day since March. The Nasdaq fell 0.7 percent, the S&P 500 fell 1 percent, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.6 percent. All 11 sectors in the S&P 500 fell, with financials down 1.9 percent and communications services down 1.3 percent.

Interim CEO Colette Kress hosted the earnings call, while former CEO Jensen Huang said he would be honored to return. Huang has agreed to appear before Congress early next month following reports that the SEC is investigating the company. St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said the economy will likely require several interest rate increases before spring 2027. Musalem believes current policy is a full percentage point too low and expects probably four hikes to achieve price stability. The rates futures curve currently prices in only three full 25 basis point increases by the middle of next year.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said that cancer, Alzheimer's, heart disease, and mental illness will be relics of the past soon. Eli Lilly CEO Dave Ricks disagreed on X, stating that such progress is not likely and will be incremental. Alphabet lost 640 billion dollars, SpaceX lost 450 billion dollars, and Micron lost 300 billion dollars in market value. Eli Lilly added over 250 billion dollars since October 6, gaining 25 percent while Nvidia dropped 32 percent. BofA's Michael Hartnett named healthcare as most vulnerable to downside and semiconductors as most vulnerable to upside soon.

Nvidia's daughter, a senior director of product marketing, helped shape the defense of ties to Singapore based firm Megaspeed. The AI trade lost about 5 trillion dollars in less than a month during the market volatility of October. Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk gained 92 percent on average in 15 months after the October 2022 market low. Novo Nordisk lost about three quarters of its value from its June 2024 peak before the recent AI trade reversal. Lilly now trades at roughly 27 times forward earnings, which is about two and a half times Nvidia's multiple.

Markets await the US FOMC October meeting minutes and scheduled speeches from Michael Barr, John Williams, and Neel Kashkari. Investors are watching for UK and Euro zone inflation data and a speech from ECB President Christine Lagarde. The articles leave open whether the board will actually consider the return of Jensen Huang as the company CEO. It remains uncertain if the Federal Reserve will add a fourth rate hike to the current projected futures curve. The reports do not state if the SEC investigation into Nvidia will lead to any formal charges or penalties.

stories.Headline: Einsia AI releases Visual Cipher Bench to test long-horizon visual reasoning in AI agents
stories.Summary:
Einsia AI's Navers Lab announced the launch of Visual Cipher Bench on November 18, 2026, in Singapore to evaluate long-horizon visual reasoning. This new benchmark tests if AI agents can solve complex problems when instructions are absent and rules must be discovered from visual clues. The evaluation focused on rule discovery, logical planning, and spatial operations across eight frontier models and 29 different reasoning configurations. Researchers recorded 3,480 attempts, but no configuration achieved accuracy above 30 percent, revealing a significant gap in autonomous rule discovery. The top performing model, GPT-6 Astra (max), achieved an accuracy of 26.7 percent, averaging 10.7 correct answers per 40-puzzle run.

The benchmark requires agents to solve 40 original visual puzzles represented by 67 black-and-white illustrations across four distinct reasoning categories. These categories include spatial operations like folding and rotation, logical planning, rule induction for hidden patterns, and knowledge decoding for Braille or Morse. Agents receive only one instruction to examine the images and write the final answer to a file without any immediate correctness feedback. The test includes models like GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6 Luna, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Qwen 3.8 Max, and Kimi K3.1 Pro. These models must independently identify examples, understand the target problem, infer the required output, and solve each task using only visual evidence.

Deyao Hong and 14 other authors are responsible for the research and the resulting paper titled Visual Cipher Bench: Benchmarking LLM Agents. The researchers stated that the primary bottleneck for current agents is not executing multi-step plans, but autonomously discovering rules from visual evidence. They noted that some correct answers resulted from thematic guesses rather than systematic rule discovery, which skewed some of the results. The authors explained that agents often adopted rules that explained only some examples without validating them against all available evidence before submitting. They also found that agents frequently relied on exhaustive combinations and extensive tool calls instead of using visual constraints, leading to timeouts.

The findings affect frontier AI agents, which struggled significantly with rule induction, achieving an accuracy of only 0.6 percent across all attempts. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Qwen 3.8 Max, and Kimi K3.1 Pro failed to solve any puzzles, while GPT-6 Luna and Claude Sonnet 5.5 scored 0.8 percent. GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5 both scored 21.7 percent, while spatial operations were more manageable with a 22.8 percent accuracy. Knowledge decoding and logical planning were also difficult, recording accuracies of 3.3 percent and 2.4 percent respectively across the 3,480 attempts. Even the best model, GPT-6 Astra, failed to exceed 13.3 percent accuracy in any category other than spatial operations during the tests.

The articles explain that language-model agents typically excel at coding tasks because they have explicit text specifications and immediate execution feedback. Real-world problems often lack these conditions, as critical information may exist only in images that resist text transcription or trial-and-error feedback. Existing visual benchmarks often reduce tasks to single-turn question answering, while agent benchmarks focus on text-based environments or interactive states. This creates a gap because agents must observe environments, identify signals, and formulate hypotheses without explicit instructions to solve autonomous problems. Visual Cipher Bench was created to bridge this gap by measuring the ability to transfer long-horizon capability from text to visual reasoning.

Next, researchers conducted a hint experiment on 10 puzzles using GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, and GPT-6 Luna to test rule execution. Providing a one-sentence mechanism hint raised overall accuracy from 12.2 percent to 51.1 percent and rule induction accuracy from 0 percent to 85.2 percent. GPT-6 Astra improved from 23.3 percent to 70.0 percent, while GPT-6.1 Sol increased from 13.3 percent to 66.7 percent with these hints. The articles leave open how agents can improve their autonomous rule discovery without hints, as logical planning accuracy remained low at 22.2 percent. They also leave open how to eliminate premature conclusions and inefficient search patterns to move toward more autonomous AI problem-solving.

stories.Headline: Florida House Speaker Sam Garrison warns lawmakers about AI risks and creates a technology oversight committee
stories.Summary:
The Florida Legislature officially began a new term Tuesday, with new legislative leaders pledging to work on affordability issues and guard against the unwieldy ramifications of the evolution of artificial intelligence. New House Speaker Sam Garrison, R-Fleming Island, encouraged the chamber to have a sense of urgency about the perils of the new technology. Garrison raised the prospect of AI that improves itself so quickly that humans will lose the ability to understand or control it. Garrison said this is not science fiction but a sober reality that many in the tech community predict will arrive as early this year or next. Garrison asked lawmakers to think about that and then ask themselves what they are doing and whether they are AI's tool or it is theirs.

Garrison set up a new panel, the Advanced Technology & Digital Security Committee, to look into AI and other new technologies to oversee state technology services. Garrison said the state faces an estimated $12 billion loss to local governments as the homestead exemption increases from $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and to $250,000 in 2028. Garrison said the measure will save money for homestead owners but presents the biggest fiscal challenge Florida has faced in a generation. Garrison cited his creation of the House Public Integrity Committee to investigate public corruption and hold public officials to account. The next regular session for the Legislature is set to begin March 2.

New Senate President Jim Boyd, R-Bradenton, cited cost-of-living issues as among his top priorities but gave few clues about what his policy prescriptions will be to address them. Boyd said it is imperative to tackle affordability and asked what good a beacon of opportunity is if you cannot build a good life here. Boyd said it is challenging to build a good life when folks are struggling to make ends meet. Boyd said that while we cannot change the national or global economy, we do have an important role to play in keeping Florida affordable. Boyd said families have made hard adjustments and they expect government to do the same.

House Democratic Leader Christine Hunschofsky of Parkland said Democrats are ready to listen, find common ground, build relationships and work with every member who shares a commitment to making Florida better. Hunschofsky, armed with a 50-member-strong Democratic caucus, the largest for the party in decades, warned her caucus will speak up if the Republican majority shuts them out of discussions affecting their districts. Rep. Gallop Franklin, D-Tallahassee, spoke out against proposed changes to the House rules, which include earlier deadlines to file bills and allow bills to be rewritten and passed on the same day. Franklin said constituents' needs do not follow the legislative calendar and that members of the public deserve to read bills before we vote. Franklin welcomed other changes, such as requiring lobbyists to disclose whether they also act as a political consultant or receive any other payment from a member's political committee.

Florida has been at the forefront of AI skepticism, led by Gov. Ron DeSantis, who urged lawmakers to pass an AI Bill of Rights to protect consumers. Garrison's predecessor as Speaker, Daniel Perez, preferred to let the federal government and President Donald Trump take the lead on regulating the new technology, so the measure didn't advance in the House this year. Boyd's remarks came in the wake of the midterm elections, in which Republicans narrowly held onto the governor's mansion, the Cabinet and a U.S. Senate seat, but Democrats flipped several seats while emphasizing the rising cost of living. Some Republicans have pointed to Amendment 3, the property tax cut measure approved by more than 60 percent of voters, as one way they're reducing costs for residents. The amendment faced fierce resistance from a wide range of organizations, including firefighters, police, health care workers, local government officials and some GOP leaders, who argued the property tax cut would be too drastic for rural counties to absorb without affecting essential services.

The new rules were passed on a voice vote, over the objections of Democrats shouting no. The articles do not say what the Advanced Technology & Digital Security Committee will do first or when it will meet. The articles do not say what specific affordability proposals Boyd will put forward. The articles do not say how Garrison's House Public Integrity Committee will be structured or staffed. The articles do not say whether the AI Bill of Rights will be revived in the new term.
