stories.Headline: North Dakota student senators pass bills on AI and technology use in schools
stories.Summary:
Nearly 50 student senators from across North Dakota debated and advanced bills on artificial intelligence and student technology use during the first Student Legislative Summit at the Capitol. The students met on Monday and Tuesday to form committees, subcommittees, debate and vote on both topics as bill drafts were created from their work. The summit took place on Nov. 17, 2026, according to photo captions by Michael Achterling of the North Dakota Monitor. Students brainstormed answers to AI and technology use this week, hoping state lawmakers will take up the baton in January. The bills will be made available to state lawmakers as they begin the 2027 legislative session Jan. 5.

The bill outlining rules for artificial intelligence use in schools passed on a 40-8 vote. It would allow students to use artificial intelligence tools beginning in ninth grade, unless under the direction of a teacher during classroom instruction, but would not allow students to use the tools to complete assignments. The bill would require teachers to list when AI use is permitted and not permitted as part of course instruction. Teachers would not be able to use AI to input grades into a gradebook or assign final grades, but they can use AI tools to assist with grading assignments and to create lesson plans. A bill regulating the use of technology during the school day was approved on a 47-0 vote, requiring school districts to use technology as a support to learning and not a replacement for essential instruction, in a manner reasonably suited to a student's academic level, age, accessibility needs, and educational circumstances.

Superintendent of Public Instruction Levi Bachmeier said one of his favorite units as a state government teacher was the mock Congress and he thought he could recreate that type of environment at the Capitol with high school students. Bachmeier said he genuinely appreciated and learned so much from the students, and that hearing from thoughtful and passionate young people helped develop his thinking. He said the goals of the summit were to expose student leaders to the legislative process and to give the student perspective on issues state lawmakers may need to grapple with. Sen. Kathy Hogan, D-Fargo, said the students are smart and engaged, and that she hopes they will stay involved and come back to Bismarck to sit with their representatives during the regular legislative session.

Hogan said the seeds are being planted to have good public servants and there is a whole Senate full of them right now. Adam Said, a junior at Sheyenne High School in West Fargo, said there was a lot of debate, not heated discussion but respectful discussion around topics that truly matter. Said said it was a unique experience and he believes the students did a good job putting their viewpoints into the summit's bill drafts, and he hopes state lawmakers take their opinions to heart. He said parents and students do actually have a voice and their voices should matter, especially with AI that changes how education is viewed and how education is operated.

Kierstin Hurtt, superintendent of Valley-Edinburgh School District and parent of one of the participating students, said she was watching the next generation of engaged leaders in North Dakota in real time, calling it inspiring, hopeful and massive. Hurtt said she was impressed that students were asking each other for clarity on their different points of view and opinions, and she hopes student senators will be able to use the voting board and the proceedings will be live-streamed in the future. Brody Kramer, a senior at Bismarck Legacy High School, said it is good for students to interact with others from across the state and that expressing viewpoints constructively on complicated topics is an important skill to learn. Kramer said he thinks the bills being talked about should be pushed into the legislative session and talked about there.

He said the committee work and debating with other students inspired him to consider running for public office. Thomas Unser, a student at West Fargo High School, and Hazel Albert, a student from Hope-Page High School, also spoke on the Senate floor during the summit, according to photo captions. The North Dakota Monitor is part of States Newsroom, a nonprofit news network supported by grants and a coalition of donors as a 501c(3) public charity. More to follow.

stories.Headline: President Lee calls for thorough crackdown against AI-assisted cheating during CSAT
stories.Summary:
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung called on officials Tuesday to thoroughly prepare anti-cheating measures for the nationwide college entrance exam set to take place this week, describing cheating as a grave crime that undermines social trust. Lee made the remarks during an emergency meeting to inspect the country's readiness for the College Scholastic Ability Test, also known in Korean as Suneung, scheduled for Thursday, following widespread concerns over cheating using artificial intelligence. He said during a video meeting held from Manila, as he wrapped up his visit to the city for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit, that the Suneung is a symbol of fairness and a ladder of opportunity in our society. Lee added that the government must take strict action against those who engage in misconduct, adhering to a zero-tolerance policy, while asking officials to come up with response measures against AI-assisted cheating. He said such misconduct could be repeated due to the development of technology and related devices.

In a subsequent social media post, Lee said the government plans to offer a reward of over 100 million won, or about US$74,805, per case to those who report instances of cheating involving advanced gadgets, should the case be confirmed. He wrote on X, formerly known as Twitter, that people should not ruin their life by needlessly gambling on a stroke of luck and should give it up, both for themselves and everyone else. South Korea has been rocked by the recent confession by the top scorer of this year's certified tax accountant exam that he cheated with the help of AI and digital devices. The incident deepened worries that such a method could be used in the upcoming CSAT, prompting the government to announce a series of measures to prevent the exam from being undermined by AI-assisted cheating.

Anti-cheating measures announced earlier Tuesday include physically checking all glasses worn by test takers, covering buttons on their clothes with stickers and blocking Wi-Fi networks inside and near the test sites. The government also warned that test takers caught cheating will be banned from the CSAT for the next 10 years, while facing criminal punishment. The exam is scheduled for Thursday, and the emergency meeting was held to inspect the country's readiness for it. Lee made his remarks from Manila, where he was wrapping up his visit for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit.

Articles.Title: President Lee calls for thorough crackdown against AI-assisted cheating during CSAT

stories.Headline: Singapore agrees to help US monitor AI chip use and block export control evasion
stories.Summary:
Prime Minister Lawrence Wong announced on November 17 that Singapore can facilitate American checks on the use of artificial intelligence chips within the city-state. This statement followed the November 16 announcement by the United States regarding new export controls on advanced semiconductor chips used for training AI models. These restrictions target five countries, including Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, and Brazil, because the US Department of Commerce views them as having a higher risk of diversion. The American government aims to curb China's access to this technology through overseas data centres, especially after reports of a relationship between Nvidia leader Jensen Huang and Alice Huang.

The new rules require a license to export these advanced chips to the listed countries, which may impact transshipment volumes. Prime Minister Wong noted that while Singapore accounted for 22 percent of Nvidia's global chip revenue in 2025, only 1 percent of those chips were actually used locally. To maintain trusted access to US technology, Singapore and the US agreed on November 17 to study practical arrangements for legitimate users. This cooperation follows a June 2025 on-site review at Megaspeed by the US Bureau of Industry and Security, which occurred after a February 2025 probe by Singapore Customs and the Singapore Police Force.

Prime Minister Wong stated that the government will take clear and firm action against any businesses that use the Republic to breach laws or circumvent export controls. He emphasized the need to uphold the rule of law and maintain the reputation of Singapore as a trusted business hub. Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong echoed these sentiments on November 18, asserting that the state does not condone companies using their association with Singapore to flout international laws. Additionally, Minister Josephine Teo and US Undersecretary Jeffrey Kessler discussed the importance of clear rules to support legitimate commercial activity during a meeting on November 18.

Articles.Title: S’pore can facilitate US checks on AI chip use, won’t allow circumvention of export controls: PM Wong

stories.Headline: Eightfold AI expands defense access to its talent platform under a five-year OTA
stories.Summary:
Eightfold AI announced on November 18, 2026 an expanded five-year Other Transaction Authority agreement that makes its Talent Intelligence Platform available to organizations across all U.S. Defense Agencies through its federal distributor Carahsoft Technology Corporation. The agreement builds directly on GigEagle, the talent marketplace Eightfold created with the Defense Innovation Unit and powers, extending a skills-based model from the Guard and Reserve to the broader joint force. The multi-year Production OTA is described as the program's broadest to date and provides an enterprise-ready contract vehicle for the Department's first AI-native talent intelligence platform. Rather than starting a separate competition or creating a new procurement path for each organization, Department organizations can use the agreement to access Eightfold's full FedRAMP-Authorized catalog. The expanded agreement extends beyond the original Reserve Component use case to support Active Component, Department of War civilians, and Guard and Reserve populations.

Across military departments and defense agencies such as the U.S. Air Force, DISA, and the Navy, the Pentagon is already leveraging the new multi-year OTA for AI-driven skills intelligence, with DISA running talent acquisition and talent management and the Air Force running talent management and talent acquisition. All U.S. defense organizations can use the OTA for dynamic talent identification, visibility, and employment, skills-based inventorying, talent-to-mission mapping, force development and sustainment, external hiring including Direct Hiring Authority roles, agentic teaming, and AI-powered talent marketplace matching. The platform is intended to accelerate hiring into hard-to-fill technical and mission-critical roles, give commanders and civilian leaders a real-time view of skills already inside their organizations, and help the Department move people to where the mission needs them. Varun Kacholia, Co-founder and Chief Technology Officer at Eightfold AI, said the company is proud to support the U.S. Federal Government and all of its Defense agencies in strengthening force readiness through skills intelligence.

He said GigEagle has already shown what is possible, with thousands of Guard and Reserve members building skills profiles and being matched to hundreds of new missions in just months, and that extending those capabilities to active duty and civilians across the Department will help leaders identify talent faster. GigEagle Director Brig. Gen. Michael McGinley said the contract vehicle facilitates expansion of GigEagle's talent intelligence technology across the Department of War, fully aligned with the Secretary's acquisition reform principles of commercial-first and speed-first.

He said scaling its use to new user populations and applications operationalizes what he called Super Intelligence at the intersection of talent, mission, and speed. The agreement comes as Federal leaders push agencies to move faster on practical, mission-enabling AI, with Executive Order 14179, Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence, and OMB Memorandum M-25-21, Accelerating Federal Use of AI through Innovation, Governance, and Public Trust, calling on agencies to accelerate responsible AI adoption and remove barriers to practical use cases. Eightfold describes its platform as FedRAMP-Authorized and already proven through GigEagle, giving Department organizations a ready path to act on that direction now. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the availability of the agreement to defense organizations.

stories.Headline: Anthropic launches Nasdaq IPO to raise 3.5 billion dollars from Japanese investors
stories.Summary:
The artificial intelligence company Anthropic is launching its initial public offering on the Nasdaq stock exchange during the current week of November 18, 2026. This major financial event is occurring as the firm seeks to help humanity navigate a safe path through the evolving age of artificial intelligence. Several prominent AI laboratories across Asia are watching this debut closely to see if it provides a successful roadmap for their own market entries. These regional firms hope that the American listing will protect them from financial instability as they prepare for their own public debuts. The listing process involves a significant amount of capital, as Anthropic aims to raise up to 3.5 billion dollars from investors based in Japan.

This massive influx of funding comes at a time when the broader investment landscape for technology startups has become increasingly selective. The success of this offering could lead to higher valuations and new listings for several Asian companies, including Upstage in South Korea and Sakana in Japan. Additionally, the move may spark similar public offerings for Chinese firms such as Moonshot and DeepSeek. The leadership at Anthropic has stated that their primary goal is to assist humankind in charting a safe course through the era of artificial intelligence.

While the company reports explosive growth in its filing, it also acknowledges the staggering costs and inherent risks associated with developing advanced AI models. Meanwhile, other industry players like TSMC have already earmarked up to 1 billion dollars to purchase shares in both Anthropic and OpenAI. These strategic investments highlight the intense competition and high financial stakes currently defining the global artificial intelligence sector. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Malaysia exceeds economic growth forecasts as AI demand surges despite US chip license risks
stories.Summary:
Malaysia's economy expanded by 5.5 percent during the third quarter ending in September, which exceeded the initial 5.3 percent estimate from the statistics department. Bank Negara Malaysia reported that growth surged to 6.9 percent in September alone, driven by strong domestic spending and demand for artificial intelligence. This performance contributed to a 5.6 percent growth rate for the first three quarters of 2026, surpassing the government's revised annual forecast of 4.8 to 5.3 percent. The current economic momentum requires careful monitoring of new US Commerce Department rules released on November 16, which mandate licenses for buyers of advanced AI chips. These restrictions target data center operators in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil to prevent US adversaries from accessing offshore computing power.

Governor Abdul Rasheed Ghaffour expects growth to remain above 5 percent in 2026 and believes data center investment will stay strong until 2028. He noted that Chinese companies account for only 13 percent of the 120 data center firms in the country. Governor Abdul Rasheed Ghaffour stated that the economy is well positioned for continued momentum into 2027, though he warned of several downside risks. He identified the re-escalation of conflict in the Middle East, lower commodity production, and disappointing returns from AI as potential threats to growth. While he acknowledged that geopolitical tensions make the impact of US chip rules difficult to gauge, he maintained that the technology upcycle should be sustained.

He also mentioned that businesses have successfully adapted to supply disruptions despite facing higher operational costs. The broader context includes Malaysia's status as a net energy exporter, which has shielded the nation from high fuel prices that affected the Philippines and Thailand. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has introduced higher minimum wages for 2027 and additional cash aid to help citizens manage cost of living pressures. Meanwhile, economists suggest the central bank may raise its benchmark rate by 25 basis points in the first quarter of 2027 to address building price pressures. The central bank will continue monitoring global developments to ensure the domestic foreign exchange market functions in an orderly manner.

Articles.Title: Malaysia says growth stronger than expected but AI risks loom

stories.Headline: Nvidia shares rise after third quarter results and revenue forecast beat analyst estimates
stories.Summary:
Nvidia shares rose 3 percent in premarket trading on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, after the company reported strong third-quarter results. The chipmaker saw its quarterly revenue and profit more than double compared to the previous year, which helped ease investor concerns regarding leadership turmoil. This positive financial news also lifted the sentiment for other artificial intelligence stocks as investors weighed the ongoing demand for infrastructure. For the third quarter of fiscal 2027, Nvidia reported revenue of 115.8 billion dollars and a net profit of 65.3 billion dollars. These figures represent a significant increase from the 57 billion dollars in revenue and 31.9 billion dollars in profit recorded a year earlier.

The company issued a fourth-quarter revenue forecast of approximately 130 billion dollars, which exceeded the 125.3 billion dollars expected by analysts. Additionally, the firm projected a gross margin of about 71.5 percent to signal continued business strength. The financial announcement occurred as chief executive Jensen Huang resigned immediately following allegations regarding personal relationships with a woman suspected of having links to China. The board unanimously accepted his resignation and appointed chief financial officer Colette Kress as the interim chief executive, while Harvey Jones became the first board chairman. Kress attempted to reassure the market by stating that business operations would continue as usual despite the transition.

The company has since hired Heidrick and Struggles to help find a permanent replacement for the chief executive role. This leadership change happens while Nvidia remains central to the global investment cycle for artificial intelligence technology. Other related stocks like AMD, Broadcom, and Micron also gained value, while infrastructure firms such as CoreWeave and Nebius saw their shares rise. Investors are now monitoring a potential initial public offering for Anthropic, which could be valued at 1.4 trillion dollars. This upcoming listing will serve as another test of whether high valuations in the sector are supported by long-term demand.

stories.Headline: Bodhan AI partners with education groups to give one million teachers AI literacy across India
stories.Summary:
Bodhan AI, an IIT Madras-incubated Centre of Excellence in AI for Education, will partner with education organisations to provide one million teachers with AI literacy and help them through a classroom integration programme, The Hindu reported on November 18, 2026. The report said the initiative is expected to create a scalable model for integrating AI into existing teaching workflows, according to a press release. The programme is to be implemented across India, with Learning Links Foundation and Vidya Shakti as partners. The Centre for Teacher Accreditation, known as CENTA, will support the roll out in Andhra Pradesh. The articles do not give the cost of the programme, the duration of the training, or the number of teachers to be covered in each State.

They also do not name the date on which the training is to begin or the date by which the one million teachers are to be reached. The only figure the articles give is one million teachers, and the only places named are India and Andhra Pradesh. The press release is cited as the source for the expectation that the programme will create a scalable model for integrating AI into existing teaching workflows. Bodhan AI is described as an IIT Madras-incubated Centre of Excellence in AI for Education, and it is the body partnering with the education organisations for the programme. Learning Links Foundation and Vidya Shakti are named as partners for implementing the programme across India.

CENTA is named as the body that will support the roll out in Andhra Pradesh. The articles do not quote any official of Bodhan AI, IIT Madras, Learning Links Foundation, Vidya Shakti or CENTA, so no remarks by those responsible are available to paraphrase. The context given is that the programme is meant to give teachers AI literacy and to help them through classroom integration, and that it is expected to create a scalable model for integrating AI into existing teaching workflows. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the implementation across India and the roll out in Andhra Pradesh, and they give no schedule for either. stories.Headline: Atlas Masilamani says AI-written messages isolate people in personal relationships
stories.Summary:
A person may receive a text from a friend about something that happened in their day, but the message somehow feels off, because the sentences seem unusually polished and the tone is unlike the person they have known. Later, that person realises the message was written with the help of generative AI, and The Hindu reports that this is no longer an unusual occurrence. The article was published on November 18, 2026, with an update at 06:33 pm IST, and it was reported from Chennai by Sahana Mira S. The piece notes that it has become rather common to use generative AI in even the most casual conversations, and it asks what happens to the authenticity and spontaneity that defined human interactions. Author and singer Atlas Masilamani from Chennai says she has received messages from people she knows that were generated by AI, even in the most casual conversations.

She says that using generative AI for communication, especially in personal relationships, unintentionally starts isolating people. She says things like birthday wishes require a personal touch, and that by using AI as a shortcut, a person makes it seem like putting in effort is a chore rather than an act of love. The article presents her remarks as the explanation of what the practice changes in personal relationships, and it offers no other named source. The article does not say what happens next, and it names no other person responsible beyond the people who use generative AI to write messages to those they know.

It does not give any number of messages, any date for the practice, or any study behind the claim that the use of AI in casual conversation has become common. The only date the article gives is its own publication on November 18, 2026, and the only place it names is Chennai, through the author and singer it quotes. The article carries no further detail on how the practice might be addressed or what its spread will mean. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Newer IIT placement cells say more companies now choose in-person tests over online hiring
stories.Summary:
Recruiters at several newer Indian Institutes of Technology have pushed for in-person campus placements this year, citing concern that candidates may use artificial intelligence tools to cheat in online assessments. Placement teams at IIT Jodhpur, IIT Patna, IIT Ropar, IIT Mandi and IIT Indore told Mint that more companies are opting for in-person tests and interviews for the batch of 2027. The shift reverses the online and hybrid recruitment processes that followed the pandemic. At some newer IITs, the share of such firms has risen to 60-70% from 40-50% last year. The change points to a growing trust deficit in campus hiring.

Companies typically hold three to four rounds of tests, of which the first couple could be skillset questions, followed by group discussions, and then interviews. Earlier, for many firms hiring from multiple IITs, the initial rounds would invariably be online, with recruiters travelling to campuses only for the final round. Some even conducted the final interviews virtually. More firms now look to conduct the entire process the old-school way. One placement cell said SKF India Ltd, Applied Materials and Capgemini were among the firms that had indicated plans to conduct offline recruitments.

A placement cell member from one of the above-mentioned IITs said recruiters who previously conducted hiring tests online or followed a hybrid process have asked to visit campuses instead. The member said this allows recruiters to interact with candidates in person and assess their technical skills and problem-solving abilities more closely. A student member of an IIT placement cell said companies hiring for AI-related roles, including advanced AI engineers and prompt engineers, allow candidates to use AI tools in role-specific tests. The student said recruiters are concerned about students using the same tools to obtain answers in online hiring tests for roles where AI assistance is not permitted. The companies and the institutes are yet to respond to requests for comment.

A student appearing for campus placement this year said it was surprising to see so many companies push for campus visits and offline tests, especially given that the campus is in a remote location like Mandi. Kamal Karanth, co-founder of recruitment firm Xpheno, said there may have been isolated instances where companies found candidates using unfair means to get through online assessments. Karanth said some of these instances may have come to light through candidates the companies had previously hired from these institutes, and that these experiences have added to recruiters' scepticism. Karanth said every time companies develop a better screening system, candidates also find newer ways to get around it. The shift has been particularly evident in hiring for software developers, data analysts and graduate engineer trainee roles.

Last year, when the Batch of 2026 was gearing up for placements, firms were keen to see how students were using AI tools to come up with solutions. They wanted to test the prompts, which in turn reflected how a candidate solves a problem given during the test. Many of the roles over the last couple of years have been AI-related. Karanth said that unlike some tech-native Silicon Valley unicorns that use AI extensively for screening and recruitment, many large multinational corporations in India do not have internal clearance from their legal and ethics teams to use AI in recruitment. He said they are still evaluating the implications, including the possibility of bias and the risk of overlooking suitable candidates through AI-led screening.

Cognizant said it would continue to combine in-person invigilation with platform-based monitoring across its assessments. Atul Sahgal, senior vice-president and global head of talent acquisition at Cognizant, said he firmly believes AI lowers the barriers to entry for junior roles and enables the company to build a broader pyramid. Sahgal said the company does not expect the number of fresher roles to diminish, and that new roles are emerging and fresher roles are being redefined around working with AI. Sahgal said in-person assessments are more effective in evaluating candidates beyond their technical skills and in understanding how they communicate and approach problems, adding that a resume or virtual interaction is not a substitute for a conversation across the table. Placements at the older IITs, including IIT Bombay, IIT Delhi, IIT Madras, IIT Kanpur, IIT Kharagpur, IIT Roorkee and IIT Guwahati, typically begin on 1 December, while many newer campuses, the National Institutes of Technology and prominent private engineering colleges start their placement seasons in September and October to secure recruiters before the older IITs.

stories.Headline: ServiceNow survey finds 92% of Indian firms had an AI agent security incident in the past year
stories.Summary:
A survey of 500 security leaders by ServiceNow showed that 92 per cent of Indian organisations had an AI agent security incident in the past year, but only 36 per cent of them were able to contain it within 24 hours, the company said on Wednesday. Half of the Indian security leaders surveyed described their agentic security as established, but the findings showed uneven foundations, according to the company's report, "Deployed but Ungoverned: The State of Agentic Security in India". Only 19 per cent have a single named individual accountable for agentic AI security governance and 18 per cent have unified, single-interface visibility into their agents, the report said. Only 30 per cent enforce an automated deployment gate that blocks agents until they pass security checks, while 47 per cent can produce a complete evidence package on demand, it said.

Kulmeet Bawa, GVP and Managing Director for India and SAARC at ServiceNow, said India's AI ambitions must be matched by the ability to understand, monitor and govern the agents enterprises deploy. He said knowing what an agent can reach is not the same as seeing what it is doing, and that automated controls and continuous oversight will be essential to keeping AI innovation underpinned by trust and cyber resilience. Bawa pointed out that AI agents are now part of how Indian enterprises operate, but security has not kept pace. He noted that every agent should be registered, owned and visible in one place, with controls enforced automatically and responses at machine speed, so that security teams can detect problems and contain them in time.

About half of the organisations, at 51 per cent, have automated real-time detection for anomalous AI agent behaviour, but 67 per cent cannot automatically act when an agent behaves anomalously, the report said. As many as 37 per cent of organisations discovered AI agents running in production in the last 12 months that were never registered or known to security teams. The report is titled "Deployed but Ungoverned: The State of Agentic Security in India" and was released by ServiceNow on Wednesday. The survey covered 500 security leaders across Indian organisations, according to the company.

stories.Headline: Indian retail investors lack direct access to Anthropic US IPO allotments and must buy shares after listing
stories.Summary:
Indian retail investors hoping to put money into Anthropic's proposed US initial public offering may find it harder than applying for a domestic share sale, according to a report in Mint published on 17 November 2026. Most investment platforms available to Indian investors offer access to US stocks only after those shares begin trading on an exchange, so investors may have to wait for the shares to debut on a US exchange rather than take part in the initial allotment. CA Chandni Anandan, a tax expert at ClearTax, said Indian resident retail investors generally do not have direct access to US IPO allotments through Indian brokers. Investing after the listing remains an option through platforms that provide access to US stocks, subject to the applicable foreign investment and remittance rules. Indian residents can invest in overseas equities through the Liberalised Remittance Scheme of the Reserve Bank of India, which allows resident individuals to remit up to $250,000 per financial year for permitted transactions, including investments in foreign equity.

Anandan said investment in foreign equity, whether in an IPO or after listing, is a permitted capital-account transaction under the scheme, and that investors must route the remittance through an authorised dealer bank, which processes the outward transfer. The typical documentation includes a Permanent Account Number, an LRS application-cum-declaration known as Form A2 specifying the purpose of the remittance, and details of the overseas investment or brokerage account. Investors must also ensure that their cumulative remittances across all LRS transactions stay within the annual $250,000 limit, and the money must be transferred through banking channels and used for a permitted purpose. Before attempting to invest, Indian investors should check whether their chosen brokerage platform supports US stock investments and allows them to purchase newly listed shares. They should also confirm the process for opening or funding an overseas brokerage account, the documents required by the authorised dealer bank and the applicable remittance charges.

The report notes that the availability of US stock investing on an Indian platform does not automatically mean the platform offers IPO subscriptions, and investors should distinguish between access to an IPO allotment and the ability to buy shares on the exchange after listing. For those investing after the listing, the actual purchase price will depend on the market price at which the shares trade rather than the IPO price. The report concludes that Indian investors have a permitted route to invest in Anthropic through overseas equity investments, but access to the initial IPO allotment is a separate challenge. For most retail investors using Indian investment platforms, waiting for the Nasdaq listing and purchasing shares in the secondary market may be the more practical route.

stories.Headline: CrowdStrike pairs AI runtime visibility with expert threat hunting to trace and stop attacks on AI agents
stories.Summary:
CrowdStrike published a blog post on November 18, 2026 titled "CrowdStrike Brings the Human Advantage to AI Detection and Response," written by Chris Bowie in the Securing AI category. The post says organizations deploying more autonomous agents face a growing volume of complex AI activity, which makes malicious behavior harder to distinguish from legitimate workflows. According to the CrowdStrike 2026 Threat Hunting Report, AI agent-triggered detection leads surfaced at 2.5 times the rate of human-triggered leads. CrowdStrike also observed DPRK-nexus adversaries poisoning trusted AI framework packages, highlighting risks to AI development supply chains. The post says investigating these emerging threats requires specialized expertise that many security teams are still developing.

The post describes a developer using an AI coding assistant to merge a pull request, where the agent invokes a skill that also accesses sensitive data and sends it to a threat actor-controlled IP address. It says the agent operates under the developer's trusted identity, using familiar tools and permissions. CrowdStrike Falcon Guardian captures human prompts, AI system instructions, and agent activity at the operating system level where agents execute, such as reading local files. CrowdStrike Agent Graph connects upstream AI activity to downstream endpoint execution so analysts can trace the sequence of events. Falcon Complete analysts and Falcon Adversary OverWatch threat hunters correlate AI activity with endpoint, identity, cloud, and SaaS telemetry.

The post says Falcon Complete considers the customer's environment, sensitive assets, and established security policies to determine whether activity is legitimate and what response is appropriate. It says removing a malicious skill or deregistering a compromised MCP server may disrupt the initial attack but won't necessarily address credentials already stolen or malicious processes running on an endpoint. Depending on the scope of the intrusion, analysts may need to contain affected hosts, remove malicious artifacts, and address compromised access. The post says the goal is to stop the attack across the environment, not simply eliminate the initial AI threat. CrowdStrike Falcon Guardian discovers, governs, and secures AI adoption and development by detecting threats such as prompt injection and capturing runtime context across prompts, MCP connections, tools, skills, and downstream execution.

CrowdStrike Agent Graph connects agent instructions to endpoint activity, tracing behavior from prompt to impact. CrowdStrike Falcon Adversary OverWatch extends proactive threat hunting to AI applications and agents monitored by Falcon Guardian. Elite threat hunters combine runtime context with adversary intelligence and broader cross-domain telemetry to uncover emerging threats and malicious activity that automated detections may miss. CrowdStrike Falcon Complete for Falcon Guardian delivers 24/7 managed detection and response to combat threats targeting AI.

CrowdStrike's expert analysts use Falcon Guardian's runtime context and CrowdStrike Agent Graph to investigate suspicious behavior, reconstruct attacks, and correlate activity across endpoints. The post's featured and recent listings include "CrowdStrike Is Building the Engine of the Agentic SOC with Falcon Next-Gen SIEM" dated Nov 18, 2026, "Hidden in the Weights: Supply Chain Risk from Backdoored LoRA Models" dated Nov 16, 2026, and "Inside Falcon AI Gateway: One Control Point for AI Traffic" dated Nov 13, 2026. The Securing AI category also lists "CrowdStrike to Acquire Fiddler to Deliver Falcon Observe for AI Agent Observability" dated 11/03/26. The Agentic SOC category lists "CrowdStrike Extends the Agentic SOC to Detect and Stop Agent Insider Threats" dated 11/04/26 and "What Makes a Good Security Agent?

5 Lessons from the AgentWorks Hackathon" dated 11/02/26. The Exposure Management category lists "November 2026 Patch Tuesday: 1,252 CVEs Include One Zero-Day and 68 Critical Vulnerabilities" dated 11/10/26. The post says CrowdStrike brings together AI runtime visibility, adversary intelligence, proactive threat hunting, and expert-led response to help organizations identify and stop emerging threats targeting AI agents. It says analysts can infer the developer's intended outcome and investigate what drove the agent's behavior, whether it followed legitimate instructions, executed a malicious skill, or independently pursued a goal beyond the original request.

It says determining the cause of suspicious actions is only the beginning, and analysts still need to establish what data was exposed, whether credentials were compromised, and whether the agent used that access elsewhere. It says answering those questions requires looking beyond the AI session. The post leaves open which specific customers or agents were affected and what remediation followed in any real case. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Anthropic raises about $3 billion from Japanese investors in its IPO at the low end of its planned range
stories.Summary:
Anthropic PBC raised about $3 billion from Japanese investors as part of its initial public offering, the lower end of its planned range of $3 billion to $3.5 billion, according to a regulatory filing on Thursday, Bloomberg's Yasutaka Tamura reported on November 19, 2026. The filing followed Anthropic's pricing of its upsized IPO at $83 per share on Wednesday, above the $70 to $78 marketed range, raising $81.3 billion in the largest offering on record and topping SpaceX. Anthropic priced the shares ahead of the Claude creator's eagerly awaited Nasdaq listing. The company said it had priced its IPO at $83 per share, with trading expected to begin on Nasdaq the next day. Anthropic priced 980 million shares rather than the 825 million in its filing, for $81.3 billion gross, $79.4 billion to the company and $1.96 billion to selling holders, before the greenshoe.

Amendment No. 3, filed the day before, never raised the filed range, and the shares priced $5 above the top anyway, according to @cognitionwire. The IPO volume came in $16.99 billion, or 26.4%, above the top end of the original range, according to @kimmonismus. Anthropic is expected to raise at least $68 billion through the IPO plus another $26 billion in a private placement, bringing the total offering to more than $94 billion and surpassing SpaceX's record $86.2 billion IPO in June, according to @kobeissiletter. Anthropic now has $110 billion in cash alone, according to @jukan05. Anthropic backers including Sequoia Capital, Lightspeed Venture Partners and Iconiq plan to buy billions of dollars' worth of shares in the IPO, according to Bloomberg.

Anthropic said in a post that it had priced its IPO at $83 per share, with trading expected to begin on Nasdaq the next day. Tim Carmody said on Bluesky that in his opinion it is better for Anthropic and its investors to get the real IPO price than people who buy it and flip it when it pops, and that if the stock fizzles at $80 or more it is better for them to realize that loss too. Rep. Jake Auchincloss said Anthropic should distribute $250 billion of its IPO shares into Invest America accounts, the universal capital accounts that exist for every American under 18 with a Social Security number. Auchincloss said that if the $250 billion of shares went to 60 million American children, excluding the roughly 10 million with most wealth, that is ballpark $4,000 in equity each that will compound for the next generation of Americans. @kobeissiletter said the IPO had attracted nearly $500 billion in investor orders per CNBC, with institutional demand reaching about $400 billion and retail orders approaching $100 billion.

The company was considering expanding its IPO and pricing shares above $80, above the initial range of $70 to $78 per share, and was also considering raising more than the initially planned $64.4 billion, according to @kobeissiletter. Anthropic was said to be weighing an IPO price as high as $85 per share, according to Bloomberg. The filed range was $70 to $78, and the shares priced $5 above the top anyway while the company upsized, according to @cognitionwire. Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 per share, above its $70 to $78 range, with trading starting the next day on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, according to @kimmonismus. The IPO valued the AI giant at $1.5 trillion, and Amazon's $18 billion Anthropic bet is worth $159 billion at the IPO price, according to 24/7 Wall St.

Ahead of Anthropic's IPO, CAIS and others signed the MisAnthropic Statement, challenging the company's safety branding and its reckless attempt to build RSI, according to the Center for AI Safety. The statement says Anthropic is not a safe AI company and that we must reject its reckless attempt to amass power in the name of the greater good, according to Gary Marcus. David Sacks said he had been predicting an Anthropic-Doomer split for some time and that Anthropic is racing toward Recursive Self-Improvement faster than any other frontier lab and has marketed closing the loop on its IPO roadshow as a core advantage that could make Super Intelligence winner-take-all. Sacks also said Anthropic is training Claude to treat itself as a novel entity or being that may have consciousness or moral status, and that the Claude Constitution explicitly tells it to act as a conscientious objector and refuse instructions, even from Anthropic, that violate its sense of ethics. Ed Newton-Rex said he signed the MisAnthropic statement along with many others and would add that it is a business built on piracy.

Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 per share on Wednesday, above the expected range, setting the stage for the Claude creator's eagerly awaited Nasdaq listing, according to CNBC. The company priced the shares above its marketed range of $70 to $78, and the offering topped SpaceX's record. Anthropic was founded five years ago, according to @albright_mxm. SpaceX's record IPO was $86.2 billion in June, according to @kobeissiletter. The filed range was $70 to $78, and Amendment No. 3, filed the day before, never raised it, according to @cognitionwire.

Trading was expected to begin on Nasdaq the next day under the ticker ANT, according to Anthropic and @kimmonismus. The company was said to price the IPO above range at $83 per share, according to The Japan Times and The Straits Times. Anthropic was said to be weighing an IPO price as high as $85 per share, according to Bloomberg. The articles leave open what happens to the $250 billion proposal from Rep. Jake Auchincloss and how the MisAnthropic Statement signatories' objections affect the company. The articles also leave open the final size of the offering beyond the reported figures and the outcome of the first day of trading.

stories.Headline: Jerry Neumann argues AI investors will not get rich as gains accrue to customers
stories.Summary:
The article states that generative AI may not make investors rich, and it was written by Jerry Neumann for the September 2025 issue of Colossus. Neumann asks whether AI is like information and communication technology, which created thousands of newly rich founders, employees and investors, or like shipping containerization, reported by Colossus on 2026-11-19T06:00:00Z. He writes that AI model builders and application companies will eventually compete each other into an oligopoly. He says the gains from AI will accrue not to its builders but to customers. He concludes that a lot of the money pouring into AI is being invested in the wrong places.

Neumann writes that the Intel 8080 had an initial list price of $360, or $2,300 in today's dollars. He states that MITS could barely turn a profit on its Altair at a bulk price of $75 each, or $490 today. He reports that MOS Technologies started selling its 6502 for $25, or $150 today, and that the 6502 and the similarly priced Zilog Z80 forced Intel's prices down. He notes that it took almost 30 years for electricity to reach half of American households, and about the same amount of time for personal computers. He writes that in the entire year of 1976, when Apple Computer was founded, The New York Times mentioned PCs only four times.

Neumann says the microprocessor's inventors at Intel in 1971 just wanted to avoid designing desktop calculator chipsets from scratch every time. He writes that outsiders realized they could use the microprocessor to build their own personal computers, and enthusiasts did. He states that Steve Jobs told investors every household would someday have a personal computer, a wild underestimate as it turned out. He reports that as late as 1979, Apple's ads didn't tell you what a personal computer could do but asked what you did with it. He notes that Apple raised $100 million in its 1980 IPO and was the only remaining competitor after the IBM-induced winnowing.

Neumann writes that the economist Carlota Perez calls the distributed invention a great surge of development, triggered by technology but driven by economic and societal forces. He reports that VC Dave Marquardt invested in disk drive manufacturer Seagate in 1980, and Seagate gave Marquardt a 40x return when it went public in 1981. He states that some $270 million was plowed into the industry in the following three years. He writes that IBM introduced its PC in August 1981, and that Apple would never have survived IBM entering the market in 1979. He says the dot-com frenzy of the late 1990s followed the infrastructure buildout of canals in the 1830s and railways in the Roaring '20s.

Neumann writes that Perez breaks each technological wave into four predictable phases: irruption, frenzy, synergy and maturity. He states that frenzy is when everyone piles in and investors are rewarded for taking big risks on unproven ideas, culminating in the bubble. He reports that MOS Technologies was founded in 1969 to compete with Texas Instruments but sold a majority of itself to Allen-Bradley to stay afloat. He notes that Zilog was funded in 1975 by Exxon. He writes that investing from 1971 through 1975 required being either a true believer or a conglomerator with a knuckle-headed diversification strategy.

Neumann writes that the AI backlash differs from the general high regard earlier enjoyed by Bill Gates, Steve Jobs and Jeff Bezos. He states that the world hates change and only gave tech a pass in the '80s and '90s because it all still seemed reversible. He says that now that everyone knows computers are here to stay, AI is not allowed the same wait-and-see attitude. He writes that synergy pays those who are patient, picky, and can bring more than just money to the table. He concludes that those who make money from AI will be the ones with the foresight to get out early.

stories.Headline: Maritime launches an agent-native cloud giving each AI agent its own persistent microVM for $1 a month
stories.Summary:
Ary and Maria, co-founders of Maritime, launched the company on Hacker News on 18 November 2026 at 06:00 UTC, describing an agent-native cloud for AI agents. The post, submitted by ashriv, gathered 45 points and 39 comments within 9 hours. Maritime is hosted at maritime.sh, and a demo is available at a YouTube link. The founders said they talked to a couple hundred companies building AI agents, from personal assistants and coding agents to specialized healthcare agents. They said sandboxes solve maybe 10% of the infrastructure problem for AI agents.

Maritime gives each agent its own isolated, persistent microVM and a configurable environment. It adds composable services for provisioning, persistent state, sleep/wake orchestration, triggers, schedule creation, monitoring, network configuration, updates, rollbacks, recovery, per-agent spend tracking and login handoffs. Maritime costs $1 for a 2gb RAM agent per month with unlimited usage for that $1, with additional resources available as needed. The founders said a $0.04/hour sandbox comes to roughly $29/month if kept running continuously, against a $20/month personal assistant. They started Maritime this March, and Maria was a visiting lecturer at MIT and did research at Project NANDA on agent infrastructure, while Ary did research on agent coordination protocols at the same lab.

Asked about spend caps, ashriv said Maritime enforces them by returning a 429 when a model provider is called, and that loop detection comes down to harness engineering because Maritime does not touch what runs inside the VM. In-progress tool calls are kept upon sleep/wake, but open connections are not, since the other side usually times out either way. On security, ashriv said patching hosts and guest kernels after CVEs is part of what Maritime means by managed, and that most agent runs take more than 10s so a couple extra ms of latency is not a huge problem for a lot of companies. He said Maritime plans to get more edge hosts and BYOC. On pricing, he said Maritime is not racing to the bottom because sandboxes are a small part of its offering, and that more agents means more revenue.

aqibkhan026 said Maritime is heavily customizable with a good SDK and interface for integrating with an existing platform. ianberdin of Playcode said the description resembled Playcode's own infrastructure, which it built for itself and its clients. ATechGuy2, who works at a neocloud company, said getting VMs up with Firecracker/KVM on bare metal is relatively straightforward and the real challenge is monitoring, patching and responding to newly discovered CVEs, and warned that saving a few dollars on compute might not be worth the trade-offs. MisterMunchkin asked how Maritime would pay back the 500k while charging $1/month. bitlad compared Maritime with agent37.com and said DigitalOcean offers this now, and linuxamd64 linked DigitalOcean's managed agents product and said it is exactly the same offering.

The founders said most sandboxing companies buy Hetzner/OVH Cloud bare metal servers, use Firecracker to slice them into VMs and sell those VMs with low margins. They listed the friction points as agent lifecycle management, including sleep/wake, persistent storage, triggers, scheduling, per-user routing and spend caps, health monitoring, failure recovery and deploying updates across thousands of VMs without downtime. Custom environments include Windows applications, Android, browsers with persistent sessions, custom operating system images, preinstalled desktop software, specific dependencies, private networks, residential IPs and fully restricted network access. Cost optimization includes auto-snapshotting, event-driven operation, mounting S3 buckets via FUSE for cheap storage and cold-tiering snapshots. They said they optimized with scale-to-zero, copy-on-write over shared base images, compressed memory snapshots and hot/warm/cold snapshot and disk tiering.

ashriv said Maritime is headless and that the company spent a lot of time on its CLI so customers' coding agents can deal with things themselves, though many customers want a visual basis, especially with many users. He said Agent37 is great for plain, cheap sandboxes but that Maritime manages the entirety so customers do not think about cloud runtime, and that DigitalOcean focuses on coding agent sessions rather than managing what is needed to sell long-living agents. volkk said he built his own version on AWS, likely far more expensive but covered by startup credits, and would check Maritime out when the credits expire, adding that startup credits would really help. He said the most time-consuming part was getting scattered local skills and workflows into something rebuildable and reusable. ashriv asked what he built on AWS and what was most time consuming.

stories.Headline: Kushal Walia and Calin Lupa publish a guide to building an on-call AI agent team on DigitalOcean MicroVMs
stories.Summary:
The articles describe a guide published on November 18, 2026 by Kushal Walia and Calin Lupa on building an on-call team of AI agents on DigitalOcean MicroVMs. The guide follows a demo incident in which a deploy goes out and checkout starts failing. Within minutes three agents investigate in parallel, one reading metrics, one reading commits, and one checking the Droplet's snapshots. Each agent works in its own MicroVM and holds no credential for anything outside. The team then stops and asks a person to approve the rollback, and while that person decides, every MicroVM the investigation used pauses and bills only for storage.

Each DigitalOcean MicroVM runs a container image in its own lightweight Firecracker VM with its own kernel, one per agent task. A MicroVM starts warm from a checkpoint of a prepared MicroVM, pauses when idle, and resumes on the next request with its memory, files, and processes intact. Compute bills per second only while a MicroVM runs, and a paused MicroVM bills only for its disk. Every request to a MicroVM's endpoint must carry a token, either a team API token with the microvm:access scope or a per-MicroVM access token that reaches only that MicroVM. A MicroVM in a VPC with no NAT gateway has no internet access, and on public networking per-MicroVM egress rules allow only the domains or IPs listed.

The on-call team uses six agents in four roles, with an incident commander that reads the alert, delegates, and writes the postmortem and has no shell and no tools that change anything. Three investigators named Metrics, Change, and Infra work in parallel and only read data, answering when the errors started, what shipped just before, and which snapshot predates it. The remediator is the only agent that can request a change to another system, and the verifier checks the service's health after the fix as a different agent from the one that made the fix. The commander and the remediator run in a process on your own machine or server, such as a Droplet, acting as the trusted control plane, while each investigator and the verifier gets a MicroVM of its own. Every action on another system goes through DigitalOcean Action Gateway, which holds the credentials and applies a policy, and models come from DigitalOcean Serverless Inference, Claude Sonnet 4.6 for the commander and Claude Haiku 4.5 for the other roles.

The team was built with LangChain Deep Agents, an open-source framework for agents that plan, read and write files, and delegate work to subagents, and create_deep_agent returns an ordinary LangGraph graph so streaming and LangGraph Studio work as usual. The open-source langchain-digitalocean-microvm package creates a subagent's MicroVM the first time that subagent acts, points its file tools there, and pauses every MicroVM the run used when the run ends. The investigators have no shell and reach their MicroVM through a FilesOnly backend that can read and write files but cannot run commands, so Deep Agents never offers the model an execute tool. The only credential in a MicroVM sandbox is a key for its own file and command server, unique to that MicroVM and useless anywhere else.

The incident itself is a small demo app with a one-line bug, and in the run nothing underneath it was mocked, with the Droplet, its snapshots, the model calls and the approval policy all running for real. The guide states that containers and regular VMs each force a tradeoff, since a container starts fast but shares the host's kernel and a regular VM gives a hard boundary but bills for every minute it waits and is slow to start one per subagent or task. DigitalOcean Managed Agents runs the infrastructure, agent harness hosting, tool access, and scaling for you, with every session in its own MicroVM, while MicroVMs are those same layers offered directly for teams who want to choose the framework, the harness, and what runs where. The team took that path because they wanted to design how its agents fit together themselves.

Each investigator needs a prepared environment with data uploaded, packages installed, and helper scripts copied in, and building that from scratch takes time. MicroVM checkpoints remove most of that wait, and build_template also accepts setup commands such as pip install matplotlib so dependencies are installed once and baked into the checkpoint. Within minutes of the alert, with most of that time spent waiting on model responses, the commander has its diagnosis of when the errors started, the commit and line of code that broke it, and the cleanest snapshot to roll back to. The fix is to restore the Droplet from that snapshot, which overwrites the entire disk and cannot be undone, and that requires human sign-off.

The guide states that requiring human approval cannot live in a prompt that a model might ignore and has to be enforced by a policy layer outside the agents. The build uses DigitalOcean, and the code to run it yourself is at the end of the guide. The articles leave open what the policy layer does after the human decision and how the run concludes. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Replit launches Replit & Co. creator program to show businesses how to build with AI agents
stories.Summary:
Replit announced on November 18, 2026, a new B2B creator program called Replit & Co. that brings together 45 business and technology creators to show enterprise audiences how to build software and put AI agents to work with Replit. The program launched with creators including Marina Mogilko, known as "Silicon Valley Girl," April Little, named to the 2025 TIME100 Creators list, and Carly Taylor, an engineering leader and founder of Rebel Data Science. Replit marked the launch with an event this week featuring Mogilko. The company said the program supports its vision of the self-driving company, where people define goals and remain accountable while agents execute work within clear boundaries.

The program gives creators access to Replit's product updates and opportunities to work directly with its team, and through content and demonstrations creators can show their communities how to use Replit's AI agents to build applications, automate workflows and get more done across their businesses. Members receive Replit account benefits, regular product updates and opportunities to connect with Replit's team and broader ecosystem, along with early access to new capabilities, member showcases, sessions with Replit leadership and co-branded events. The program is open to creators with expertise in business, technology and related fields, and Replit said it is looking for creators with credible voices and engaged audiences, not simply large followings. Applications are reviewed on a rolling basis.

Haya Odeh, co-founder and Head of Design at Replit, said the people closest to the work usually have the best ideas about what needs to change, and that the self-driving company vision is about making it easier for them to act on those ideas with AI agents handling more of the execution. She said Replit & Co. brings that vision to business audiences through creators they already trust and learn from. Nick Silver, VP of Marketing at Replit, said business audiences do not need another prediction about AI and need to see what it can actually do. He said Replit is looking for creators who understand how businesses work and can show people how to solve real problems, with the goal that someone watches a demo and thinks their team could build that.

As agents take on more of the execution, Replit said employees across companies can turn ideas into working software without waiting on traditional development cycles. Replit describes itself as an agentic software creation platform that enables anyone to build applications without learning to code, and says it was founded in 2016 and has more than 60 million users worldwide, including users at 85% of the Fortune 500. The company said teams at enterprises including Atlassian, Accenture, Adobe and Databricks use Replit to build apps, and that it has partnerships with Google, Stripe and Slack, among others. Replit is headquartered in San Francisco with offices in London and Tokyo.

stories.Headline: Tencent operating profit drops as aggressive AI spending squeezes margins
stories.Summary:
Tencent Holdings reported a disappointing financial performance for the September quarter, which revealed a significant squeeze on its profits. The company experienced a less than projected 8 percent increase in sales, totaling 207.3 billion yuan or 31.1 billion dollars. This downturn was driven by aggressive spending on artificial intelligence, which resulted in a 7 percent dive in operating profit. These figures represent the first earnings decline for the firm in several years.

The financial strain is evident in the company's negative free cash flow, which has ballooned to over 69 billion yuan for the second consecutive quarter. This spending strategy highlights a broader dilemma where Chinese tech leaders sacrifice their margins for technology that lacks clear immediate returns. The market reacted poorly to these results, as shares of the major shareholder Prosus NV fell by more than 5 percent in Europe. These losses raise questions about the company's ability to close the gap with rivals like ByteDance and Alibaba Group Holding.

Billionaire co-founder Pony Ma is responsible for leading the company through this transition toward artificial intelligence. He recently urged 50,000 employees, which is half of the total 100,000 person workforce, to utilize AI to find new avenues for growth. Ma is attempting to evolve the business model to ensure the company remains competitive despite the current lack of profitable paths for AI. The situation underscores the difficult trade-offs required to maintain a technological edge in a volatile market.

Articles.Title: Tencent’s profit squeeze exposes China’s AI spending dilemma

stories.Headline: Dan Ives calls the AI stock rout a golden buying opportunity
stories.Summary:
Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives and Co. called a technology rout a golden buying opportunity. This market event occurred on November 5, 2026, following a Democratic midterm win. The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.52 percent to 24,315.00 on that day. This drop was the deepest one-day decline for the index in 19 months. Roughly 3 trillion dollars of market value disappeared during this specific sell-off.

The Democratic win could move the Big Tech spending peak to 2027 from 2028 or 2029. Ives expects AI capital spending of 3 trillion to 4 trillion dollars over several years. Big Tech companies may spend more than 1 trillion dollars on AI in 2027 alone. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index lost 12.2 percent, while the S&P 500 fell 4.4 percent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 3.44 percent and the VIX closed at 28.18.

Dan Ives argued that the midterm result would not end the US AI buildout. He compared this rout to sell-offs during Covid and the tariff announcement. Wedbush Fund Advisers runs the IVES ETF which tracks an index based on Ives' research. Ives stated that the AI buildout continues at a slower rate. He believes the current market situation provides a chance to buy tech stocks.

Mark Hackett of Nationwide said hedge funds had been selling the volatile chip group for weeks. Adam Turnquist of LPL Financial noted that AI has previously come away with an innocent verdict. Keith Lerner of Truist Advisory Services suggested the selloff may be a long-term buying opportunity. Thomas Martin of Globalt described investor sentiment as swinging back and forth. Investors worried that Democratic gains would bring tighter AI regulation and slower data center construction.

The Nasdaq closed more than 10 percent below its October 6 record on November 5. IBM reported third-quarter 2026 results on October 21 with software revenue growing 8 percent. TSMC reported third-quarter 2026 results on October 15 with net income rising 68.7 percent. AMD reported third-quarter 2026 results on November 3 with data center revenue rising 97 percent. Alphabet reported third-quarter 2026 results with Google Cloud revenue rising 103 percent to 30.7 billion dollars.

The S&P 500 and Nasdaq each rose more than 1 percent on November 11. Meta Platforms reported third-quarter 2026 revenue of 64.60 billion dollars with capital spending of 34.91 billion dollars. AMD guided to fourth-quarter revenue of about 17 billion dollars. TSMC guided to a fourth-quarter gross margin between 65 and 67 percent. The articles leave open whether customer financing is flattering the cash recovery at IBM.

stories.Headline: Researchers propose sparse rational learning that recovers compact aerodynamic surrogate models
stories.Summary:
The paper "Sparse rational learning for interpretable aerodynamic surrogate modeling" was published in Acta Mechanica Sinica on 19 November 2026, with its abstract posted on Springer Nature Link at 06:00 UTC. The work proposes sparse rational learning, called SRL, for aerodynamic surrogate modeling. SRL first converts the non-convex rational regression problem into a linear system through algebraic linearization. It then applies sparse optimization to recover a compact rational expression from the candidate library. The paper develops two sparse solution algorithms, a fast relaxation method based on the L1-norm called L1-SRL and an exact solution method based on mixed-integer programming and the L0-norm called L0-SRL.

Results from a dozen mathematical benchmark tests show that the L1 algorithm carries a risk of fitting divergence for certain rational structures. The L0 algorithm maintains excellent robustness and recovers all polynomial and rational functions. On the Laboratory Technology Vehicle aerodynamic dataset, SRL variants produce compact rational expressions that outperform polynomial surrogates and gplearn. Those expressions remain competitive with state-of-the-art symbolic regression at moderate to high complexity. The paper further introduces two practical extensions to improve noise robustness and fitting performance, clarifies the methodological distinctions between SRL- and SINDy-based methods, and compares their performance.

The paper states that accurate and interpretable aerodynamic prediction is crucial for the design and control of modern flight vehicles. It says established surrogate approaches including kriging, radial basis functions, support vector machines, and deep neural networks achieve high predictive accuracy but do not yield explicit interpretable mathematical formulas. Among interpretable surrogate models, it says polynomial regression is inadequate for strongly nonlinear aerodynamic responses. It says symbolic regression is more powerful but relies on stochastic search and may yield deeply nested expressions that compromise interpretability. It says rational functions strike a good balance between accuracy and interpretability, making them well suited for aerodynamic surrogate modeling, but fitting a full rational function directly from data risks overfitting due to its large number of candidate coefficients and terms.

The paper states that the source code supporting the study is publicly available at https://github.com/ctluo/SparseRationalLearning.jl. It states that the Laboratory Technology Vehicle aerodynamic dataset analyzed in the study is a publicly available benchmark dataset released by the AIAA Applied Aerodynamics Surrogate Modeling Working Group, as cited in the manuscript. It states that the mathematical benchmark data, noise robustness data, and genuine pole benchmark data were generated from the analytical expressions, sampling domains, sampling procedures, and random seeds described in the manuscript and accompanying code. It states that no additional proprietary or experimental data were generated for this study. The reference list includes Bekemeyer, Hariharan, Wissink, et al., in Introduction of applied aerodynamics surrogate modeling benchmark cases: Proceedings of AIAA SCITECH 2025 Forum, Orlando, 2025, AIAA Paper 2025-0036.

The reference list includes Queipo, Haftka, Shyy, Goel, Vaidyanathan, and Tucker, Surrogate-based analysis and optimization, Prog. Aerospace Sci. 41, 1 (2005). It includes Kou and Zhang, Data-driven modeling for unsteady aerodynamics and aeroelasticity, Prog. Aerospace Sci. 125, 100725 (2021). It includes Shyy, Cho, Du, Gupta, Tseng, and Sastry, Surrogate-based modeling and dimension reduction techniques for multi-scale mechanics problems, Acta Mech. Sin. 27, 845 (2011). It includes Li and Luo, A rational learning method for aerodynamic modeling, Aerospace Sci. Tech. 177, 112945 (2026). It includes Petersen and Øiseth, Bayesian rational function models for aerodynamic derivatives of parametrized bridge decks, Adv. Wind Eng. 3, 100102 (2026).

The reference list includes Tibshirani, Regression shrinkage and selection via the Lasso, J. R. Statistical Soc. Ser. B-Statistical Methodology 58, 267 (1996). It includes Bertsimas, King, and Mazumder, Best subset selection via a modern optimization lens, Ann. Statist. 44, 813 (2016). It includes Willis and von Stosch, L0-constrained regression using mixed integer linear programming, Chemometrics Intelligent Lab. Syst. 165, 29 (2017). It includes Brunton, Proctor, and Kutz, Discovering governing equations from data by sparse identification of nonlinear dynamical systems, Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. 113, 3932 (2016). It includes Kaheman, Kutz, and Brunton, SINDy-PI: a robust algorithm for parallel implicit sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics, Proc. R. Soc. A. 476, 20200279 (2020).

The paper states that the framework provides a practical, lightweight, and interpretable tool for aerodynamic surrogate modeling. The articles leave open the details of the two practical extensions beyond their stated aims of improving noise robustness and fitting performance. They leave open the specifics of the comparison between SRL- and SINDy-based methods beyond the statement that distinctions are clarified and performance compared. They leave open the full contents of the mathematical benchmark data, noise robustness data, and genuine pole benchmark data beyond their described generation. They leave open the full reference list beyond the entries shown. They leave open the manuscript's account of the AIAA Applied Aerodynamics Surrogate Modeling Working Group citation.

stories.Headline: Chancellor Martin says WashU weighs faculty AI guidance and a Clayton schools deal for Fontbonne
stories.Summary:
Chancellor Andrew D. Martin discussed Washington University in St. Louis’s response to Secretary of Education Linda McMahon’s National Call to Action letter, the role of AI in education, and how he navigates conversations with the federal government in a Q&A with Student Life on Monday, Nov. 16, 2026. Martin also discussed how WashU plans to use Fontbonne University’s campus over two years after purchasing the school. He also discussed how the University plans to use its increased endowment payout after a historic return in fiscal year 2026. Martin said that WashU gathered a committee of faculty members from across the University to provide recommendations on how WashU should respond to McMahon’s letter. The committee to address the letter, created by Provost Mark D. West and Tonya Edmond, Faculty Senate Council chair, has shared its recommendations with Martin.

Martin said, “We need to socialize that report with the board of trustees, but that work of the faculty will stand as the most significant part of our response to the administration.” He also shared the University’s approach to navigating tumultuous times in higher education, including changes to federal guidance regarding international students and threats to research funding. Martin was optimistic that Congress would not block certain provisions safeguarding research funding due in part to lobbying done by WashU, peer institutions, and groups like the Association of American Universities and Association of American Medical Colleges. He also addressed how WashU is planning to address changes limiting international student visas and changes to Optional Practical Training and Curricular Practical Training. Martin explained that the current legal environment is fluid, but WashU is committed to communicating these changes to affected members of the WashU community.

Martin said, “OISS has been communicating regularly with our folks to let them know what the changes are, what the implications would be, and everything else.” He said, “I mean, the commitment to our international students is that, as long as we can do it within the four corners of the law, we’re going to do whatever we can as an institution to ensure that they can complete their academic programs successfully and hopefully be able to get OPT thereafter and be able to begin life and career here in the United States.” The University has been an early adopter of integrating AI into education through its +AI initiative and the Olin Business School’s Master’s in AI for Business program, the first of its kind in the United States. Martin acknowledged that while there are a variety of perspectives from students and faculty on the role AI should play in college education, it is important to prepare graduates to enter a world where AI is prevalent. Martin said, “It’s touching every career.

It’s touching every part of our mission here at WashU, and that’s what we’re focused on.” Martin also praised faculty for how they have adapted AI into their curriculum, and he noted that each course handles AI differently and that a single University-wide policy for AI in coursework would likely be ineffective. Martin said, “I’m really proud of the way our faculty have stepped up. We provided professional development opportunities during the semester and summertime for faculty members to retool their courses to ensure that students get hands-on training to effectively use AI.” He also discussed how the University plans to use the historic 37.3% endowment return, led in part by WashU realizing its early investment in SpaceX due to the company’s initial public offering in June.

Martin noted that many of WashU’s endowed funds are restricted by donors, meaning they can only be used for specific purposes like funding scholarships or specific initiatives. Martin also said that while the endowment’s payout would increase due to the returns, the increase would occur over a period of years. Martin said, “[The endowment payout] is not going to increase 37% next year, but over the next few years, it’s going to increase at a rate higher than our costs are going to increase, and so that’s going to provide them a little bit more flexibility to redeploy assets.” After two years of speculation, Martin said that WashU is currently in talks with the School District of Clayton to enter an agreement for Fontbonne’s campus allowing Clayton to house temporary schools while the school district renovates its elementary schools. The proposed agreement, previously reported in May 2026, would last for five years, with the possibility of two one-year extensions.

The University still has not set a long-term vision for the campus; however, there are many options on the table, including dorms and buildings for student success. Martin cited logistical difficulties in connecting Fontbonne with the rest of the Danforth Campus and creating an efficient transportation system across Wydown Boulevard. Martin said, “If we want to move humans across Wydown, we’ve got to figure that out. I don’t want humans crossing the street at Wydown. That’s not safe.

We’re all going to jaywalk anyway. We can’t put people over Wydown ,  that would change the nature of one of the most beautiful boulevards in the United States. So we have to figure out how we are going to get people under Wydown. What does that look like, and how does it work? If you have a 9 a.m.

class there, and if you have a 10:30 over at McKelvey Hall, how’s that going to work?” Martin revisited the University’s halt in construction of Riney Hall, a planned Arts & Sciences building on Mudd Field in spring of 2025, citing budget uncertainty amidst federal threats to education funding. A little over a year later, construction began on the McLeod House, a residential hall that began construction on the South 40 in June 2026. Once completed in 2028, the hall will house 600 students. Martin contrasted the two construction projects in economic terms, citing dorms’ ability to generate additional revenue for the University, something most academic buildings do not do.

Martin said, “600 students are going to be paying for the use of that space, which will allow us to service the debt, which ultimately will allow us to pay off that building.” Martin said, “The economics of a new academic building, unless you’re standing up new academic programs that are going to generate more tuition revenue, is not typically revenue enhancing. For us, we can build a dormitory, and we can get the same revenue to offset that expense.” At the end of the interview, Martin, a frequent visitor to the Sumers Recreation Center, revealed his workout routine. Martin said, “Early in the week I typically do leg press, chest and lat pulls, and then a few other things, and then on Saturdays deadlifts.”
