stories.Headline: Palmer Luckey says AI cyberattacks outpace outdated defenses and urges faster action
stories.Summary:
Palmer Luckey spoke at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, regarding the current state of digital security. The Oculus founder and Anduril Industries co-founder warned that AI-powered cyberattacks are now moving faster than outdated technology systems can defend against them. He explained that advanced AI tools are allowing for the creation of various exploits that target these older systems. Luckey noted that adversaries of the United States, including North Korea, are exploiting this mismatch for both strategic and financial reasons. The current situation requires organizations to quicken the pace of securing their defenses to keep up with new hacking capabilities.

Luckey argued that while some believe everything can be hacked right now, the long-term advantage will go to whoever uses AI for defense most effectively. He emphasized that people must pick up the pace and start running to close the gap between attackers and defenders. This urgency comes as government officials attribute recent technical outages to companies rushing to patch systems against vulnerabilities discovered by AI. Luckey told interviewer Andrew Ross Sorkin that the level of worry depends on how well prepared an organization is.

He suggested that the public would soon find out more about the ongoing security challenges facing the country. Sorkin mentioned that Vice President J.D. Vance canceled his appearance at the conference to attend meetings about the recent tech outages. Luckey maintained that the primary issue is the inability of old systems to adopt new technology as quickly as it is developed. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Palmer Luckey warns AI-powered cyberattacks are outpacing defenses: 'It's time to start running'

stories.Headline: FBI warns that attackers use the ARTEX AI tool to breach organizations in under three hours
stories.Summary:
The FBI issued a FLASH advisory this week warning that state actors and cybercriminals have been using AI-based software called ARTEX to target businesses and organizations, according to an advisory posted to X by the FBI Dallas office. The advisory described ARTEX as a super intelligence-powered penetration testing framework used to automate attacks, and it stated that the tool can accelerate intrusions from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours. Adam Marre, the chief information security officer for cybersecurity firm Arctic Wolf, told KSL on Wednesday that ARTEX was intended as a penetration testing tool that good guys use to break into companies and organizations to find vulnerabilities. He said that practice lets defenders hack an organization before a threat actor does, allowing them to prepare for an attack and prepare their defenses so they cannot be attacked in that way. Marre said some threat actors, state-sponsored actors and cybercriminals got ahold of the tool and have been using it to attack organizations.

Marre said the developer has since taken ARTEX down, but copies of the open-source software still exist. He said people are using AI tools to find vulnerabilities at an incredible scale, much more than they have in the past, and that vulnerabilities found by attackers this year are orders of magnitude above last year and the year before. Marre said the latest advisory underscores the need for businesses and organizations to use best practices in cybersecurity, like having good passwords, utilizing password managers, and being wary of potential phishing and other social engineering attacks. He said it was also imperative that companies invest in their cybersecurity defenses, including by possibly employing cybersecurity firms that use AI to counter AI, since advancements in artificial intelligence have made cybercriminals faster, more efficient and capable of going after a wider variety of targets.

Marre said the days are gone when you can just have security through obscurity and think you are too small for attackers to want to come after you or your small business and organization. He said everybody now has to take cybersecurity seriously. The advisory was posted to X by the FBI Dallas office, and the KSL article was posted on Nov. 18, 2026, with an estimated read time of two to three minutes. The article's key takeaways state that the FBI warns of AI-based software targeting businesses in a FLASH advisory, that ARTEX was initially a penetration testing tool used by cybercriminals for attacks, and that Marre stresses the importance of robust cybersecurity practices and AI defenses.

Articles.Title: Expert: FBI FLASH advisory highlights AI developments in cyber threats

stories.Headline: Scammers use AI to build fake stores in minutes as Houston shoppers lose money
stories.Summary:
Scammers are using artificial intelligence to build fake stores that look almost identical to legitimate retailers as Black Friday approaches and holiday shopping shifts online, and Houston-area shoppers are already losing money, KPRC 2 reported on November 18, 2026. KPRC 2 demonstrated that it built a convincing fake storefront using AI in less than five minutes. Leah Napoliello, vice president of investigations and public affairs at the Better Business Bureau of Greater Houston, said people cannot just go by how a website seems or looks nowadays. The article was reported by Kayla McDermott with photojournalist Jeovany Luna and published at 6:46 PM on November 18, 2026. The BBB's Scam Tracker database shows how widespread the problem has become and how convincing these fake stores can be.

One Houston-area shopper reported losing $43.90 after spotting what appeared to be a going out of business sale on Instagram offering free bags for just the shipping cost, and the shipping cost turned out to be exorbitant. By the time the shopper realized something was wrong, the bank debit had already processed and could not be stopped, and the site was flagged as an imposter of a business called Jennifer Bags. Another shopper lost $49.99 attempting to buy a scooter from a site impersonating Costco, where the red flag was a price that did not add up, a scooter originally worth more than $100 listed for just $50. The order was never fulfilled and the shopper's credit card was later used to attempt an unauthorized purchase, and that site was flagged as an imposter operating under the name Fluva Shop. According to the Federal Trade Commission, nearly 30% of people who reported losing money to a scam said it began on social media, with total losses reaching $2.1 billion.

Napoliello said her office hears these kinds of stories regularly, particularly in the weeks leading up to the holidays, and that victims never receive those items and then cannot get their money back, or they receive an inferior version of what was featured online. She said it is very common and unfortunately people lose a lot of money. Napoliello said her office has seen complaints from shoppers who believed they were purchasing from Costco or an official offshoot of the retailer only to discover they had been deceived, and that scammers may change the spelling just slightly on the web address, enough to fool people. She said shoppers wind up on a fake scam site that can look very professional and polished too. Napoliello said that if a shopper did provide sensitive information on a scam site, they may want to go to their credit card company and get a new credit card or change their passwords.

Napoliello warned that scammers frequently request payment through untraceable methods including prepaid debit cards, gift cards, Cash App or cryptocurrency, making it nearly impossible to recover lost funds. Chase customers recently experienced a technical outage that prevented some from accessing their accounts. Hackers targeted software supplied by a company called Optimizely, whose technology is used on websites connected to 178 organizations including Salesforce, Equifax, Zoom and IKEA, and the attackers attempted to steal personal information including credit card details. The article states it does not mean all 178 companies' internal systems were compromised, and the extent of any customer information stolen remains unclear. Napoliello said scammers are already using the anxiety surrounding these kinds of events, sending phishing emails and text messages claiming something is wrong with a victim's account and urging them to hand over passwords or sensitive information.

Napoliello said that whenever there is something everyone is talking about, the outages, the scammers adapt their scams accordingly and take advantage in various ways, and that right now everyone should be on even heightened alert. She offered five tips for shoppers heading online this Black Friday and throughout the holiday season, the first being not to impulse buy because scammers rely on countdown clocks and limited-time offers to pressure shoppers into fast decisions. She said shoppers should take time to research any unfamiliar website or business before purchasing and search the company name on the BBB's website at bbb.org to check for complaints, reviews or scam reports, and that searching the company name alongside words like scam or reviews can also surface red flags quickly. She said shoppers should check the web address carefully, not rely on logos or branding alone, verify the URL matches the retailer's official site, watch for subtle misspellings, and treat an unfamiliar name in the browser bar, like Fluva Shop instead of Costco, as a red flag. She said shoppers should look for a secure connection by checking the browser for a lock icon and https in the address bar before entering any personal or payment information, and find real contact information, since a legitimate business should have a verifiable address and a customer service line listed on its site, and if that information is missing, don't buy.

The article states that online purchase scams are nothing new but artificial intelligence is raising the stakes, and that scammers can now generate polished, professional-looking websites complete with product photos, detailed pages and functional checkouts in minutes. It states that this is a dramatic shift from just a few years ago, when red flags like misspellings or low-quality images made fake sites easier to spot, and that AI has largely erased those tells. Napoliello said the AI can erase a lot of those errors and make it look very professional. The article describes the problem as part of a larger national trend of complaints flowing into the BBB. It also links the threat to recent technology disruptions that have put consumers on edge, which scammers are taking advantage of.

Napoliello said that if it is a new business to you, take some time and check it out, and her message is that before handing over money, shoppers should take a moment to make sure the deal and the store are actually real. The article lists the five tips as don't impulse buy, search the company name, check the web address carefully, look for a secure connection, and find real contact information. The article does not say whether any of the reported scams have been investigated by law enforcement or whether any money has been recovered. It does not say how many complaints the BBB has received or over what period. It leaves open the full extent of any customer information stolen in the Optimizely incident.

Articles.Title: AI-powered holiday shopping scams are fooling Houston shoppers — here’s how to stay safe

stories.Headline: Anthropic targets a Nov 19 or 20 Nasdaq debut at a reported $1.5 trillion valuation
stories.Summary:
Anthropic is heading toward its long-awaited IPO on the Nasdaq, with the debut reportedly aimed at Nov. 19 or Nov. 20 and a valuation of $1.5 trillion, which the Associated Press called the biggest IPO of all time. The company is seeking a $1.4 trillion valuation, according to a Yahoo Finance report cited in the coverage. The listing arrives as the stocks that fueled the AI boom remain under pressure, with sell-offs this week in CoreWeave, Salesforce and AMD. Truist chief market strategist Keith Lerner noted that tech valuations have fallen 42% over the past year, and the sector has gone from outperforming the S&P 500 by 25% over six months to underperforming it by 6%. Bank of America's latest fund manager survey shows investors have cut tech exposure by the most since June 2006.

The article says the AI build-out is not disappearing, pointing to Nvidia on Tuesday, and that companies are still spending and the technology is still evolving. Lerner pointed out that previous tech pullbacks of more than 10% during this bull market were followed by an average rebound of 47%, though the article says that does not guarantee a repeat and that the AI stock sell-off could get worse. Investors are questioning the AI spending, the valuations, the financing arrangements and whether the returns will ever justify the billions being poured into the technology. The piece frames the moment as one when investors are asking what could go wrong with AI, and it raises the other question of what could go right.

"Shark Tank" star Kevin O'Leary told the article's author on Sozzi Unleashed that investing in Anthropic is like investing in a young Amazon. The article describes Anthropic as potentially giving Wall Street one of the biggest new pure-play AI investment stories in years, and notes that Elon Musk-led SpaceX is not a pure-play AI company but an industrial company with a whole lot of AI bolted on. The piece was written by Brian Sozzi, Executive Editor, and published on Wed, November 18, 2026 at 5:00 PM CST. It carries the ticker symbol ANT and describes the first few ticks in that symbol as the trade the author is watching.

The article says the question before the Anthropic IPO is whether Wall Street is finally getting too negative, and it suggests the biggest opportunity in tech may emerge when Wall Street least wants to own it. It notes that Anthropic's IPO arrives at a moment when investors are suddenly asking what could go wrong with AI. The coverage lists related headlines, including one saying Anthropic's IPO could give AI stocks a needed spark and another calling the listing a key test for the AI boom. It also cites a veteran tech investor warning that Dario Amodei is just setting himself up with the IPO, and a piece describing Anthropic's IPO dilemma after the AI sell-off as damned if you do, damned if you don't.

Articles.Title: Is the AI party over? Anthropic is about to find out.

stories.Headline: Trump administration restricts Chinese companies from accessing advanced AI chips via remote computing power
stories.Summary:
The Trump administration restricted Chinese companies from accessing advanced AI chips this week. These new rules were announced on Monday to stop remote access to computing power. The move follows the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang last week. Huang admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, a businesswoman with suspected intelligence ties. This scandal appeared to motivate the White House to act on these policies.

Overseas data centers providing large computing power to China now need special licenses. Stricter shipment rules apply to five countries, including Malaysia and Singapore, due to smuggling. Alice Huang previously worked at Megaspeed, a Singapore data center company suspected of chip smuggling. The Bureau of Industry and Security had a budget of 235 million dollars in 2026. These agencies must now manage more red tape for overseas computing power rentals.

A White House spokesperson said the rules crack down on smuggling advanced US SI chips. They stated the goal is ensuring advanced chips go to US SI innovators first. The spokesperson added that these chips should not go to Chinese shell companies. Officials wanted to demonstrate they had the situation under control after the scandal. This effort expands on the original 2022 plan to choke off Chinese AI access.

Federal Reserve Bank of New York researchers found that US suppliers struggled to replace business. They estimate restrictions wiped 130 billion dollars from the combined market value of these companies. These policies also hurt the profitability and employment of affected American technology firms. Chinese companies like Huawei and DeepSeek are now finding ways to compete without US technology. Some analysts previously argued that restricting remote access could hurt US technology companies.

The Biden administration started this strategy in the fall of 2022 to limit AI training. Washington used its influence over semiconductors to hold back the world's second largest economy. The Bureau of Industry and Security was tasked with enforcement despite being small and underfunded. Megaspeed imported 136,000 chips into Indonesia and Malaysia in 2024 and 2025, with 50,000 missing. The Institute for Progress estimates China could have 1 million smuggled H100 chips by 2026.

The US is now regulating how Chinese companies use chips that never enter China. It remains difficult to assess the precise impact of these export control policies. The administration may find it has gone too far by controlling global technology use. The articles leave open whether these new licenses will effectively stop remote computing access. It is unclear if the US can maintain its technological lead through these restrictions.

Articles.Title: America’s AI Chip War Is Heating Up in the Dumbest Possible Ways

stories.Headline: Fastly CFO Richard Wong says security drives near-term AI revenue as GTA VI launch clouds Q4 guidance
stories.Summary:
Fastly executives said at a company event that security is its nearest-term way to make money from artificial intelligence, while demand tied to a major videogame launch could add uncertainty to fourth-quarter results, MarketBeat reported on Wednesday, November 18, 2026. Chief Financial Officer Richard Wong said the security business generated about $45 million in quarterly revenue and grew 32% year over year in the latest quarter. He said the company considers that growth rate sustainable, citing a relatively small base and recently introduced products. Fastly's business spans content delivery, security and compute services. Wong said delivery has the broadest adoption among the company's six product suites, followed by its web application firewall.

Wong said newer bot management and distributed denial-of-service protection products posted a second consecutive quarter of triple-digit year-over-year growth, though the company has not disclosed their adoption rates. Vern Essi, Fastly's head of investor relations, said the company sees its first significant AI monetization path in security, including its ContentGuard product. Essi said the service helps customers identify bots, control access to their websites and establish a path to licensing content to AI tools. Essi said Fastly recently announced a seven-figure deal involving security and agentic AI. Over time, the company also sees an opportunity to support orchestration of AI agents at the edge, potentially helping customers use multiple cloud providers and obtain results without relying as heavily on large language models and graphics processing resources.

Essi said cascade inference would require more of the ecosystem to develop, including enterprise orchestration layers for agentic traffic. He also said Fastly has been approached about physical AI applications, where low latency could matter for robotics and industrial processes, but that the opportunity is still in its early stages. Wong discussed Fastly's 2029 revenue target of $1.1 billion to $1.3 billion, saying growth from existing customers and products could provide a substantial foundation. Potential drivers toward the higher end include AI-related traffic, newer security products and international expansion, he said. Fastly has hired go-to-market leaders in Asia Pacific and Latin America and is seeing momentum in customer prospects attending regional events, Wong said.

For the fourth quarter, Fastly's revenue guidance midpoint was about $200 million, a $10 million sequential increase, according to Wong. He said the forecast incorporated seasonal factors such as holiday shopping and streaming, as well as estimates related to the launch of GTA VI. Wong described the game launch as the biggest unknown in the forecast. Fastly worked with game-console distribution partners to estimate download sizes and volumes, subsequent patches, regional traffic and its share of the partners' business. The launch could provide meaningful upside, he said, but also carries risk if demand does not materialize as expected.

Wong said Fastly saw a fourth consecutive quarter of mid-single-digit content delivery network price declines in the third quarter, driven mainly by customers receiving volume discounts as traffic increased. He characterized the pricing environment as healthy, saying customer discussions have shifted toward performance, reliability and security. Fastly's partnership with Comcast embeds its software in Comcast infrastructure, extending its network capacity and allowing it to serve customers using that infrastructure, Wong said. Fastly expects capital expenditures of about 10% of revenue for the current period discussed and has outlined a 10% to 12% range through 2029, though capacity constraints and customer needs could change that outlook. On sales leadership, Wong said Scott Lovett's planned retirement gives Fastly time to evaluate internal and external candidates.

Wong credited Lovett with building a team focused on cross-selling and said the company intends to continue pursuing multi-product adoption. Wong also cautioned against using remaining performance obligations as a revenue predictor because much of Fastly's business is consumption-based. He said current remaining performance obligations are the more useful of the two measures, although they still account for less than half of the company's full-year revenue guidance. Fastly, Inc. provides an edge cloud platform that helps businesses deliver and secure websites, applications, and digital content, and its services include content delivery, web application and API protection, DDoS mitigation, bot management, and tools for monitoring and analyzing internet traffic. The company also offers edge computing through Fastly Compute, which lets developers run code closer to users, and its platform is designed to help organizations improve the speed, reliability, and security of online services, serving customers across multiple industries and geographies.

stories.Headline: Satya Nadella predicts AI agents will reshape web economics and disrupt ad-based business models
stories.Summary:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella spoke at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, regarding the future of the internet. He predicted that the emergence of AI agents will fundamentally reshape the economics of the web and disrupt current business models. This shift will specifically impact companies that currently rely on advertising revenue and traffic generated by human users. Nadella compared this coming transition to the historical move from web portals like Yahoo to search engines like Google.

The transition to an agentic web requires companies to change how they monetize traffic and handle transactions. Nadella suggested that businesses relying on human eyeballs for ad revenue may need to move toward cost-per-click wins or more transactional models. He noted that Amazon has recently decided to block AI agents from browsing its retail catalog or making purchases for users. This creates an opportunity for competitors like Shopify to gain an advantage by allowing these agents to operate on their platforms.

Nadella is responsible for these predictions and argued that companies clinging to old business models will be forced to scramble. He stated that if a company refuses to accept AI agents, another competitor will likely step in to fill that void. The executive believes that those who try to protect existing models may lose out to those willing to embrace the new technology. He described the changing landscape of digital commerce and aggregation as an interesting development for the entire industry.

stories.Headline: Satya Nadella warns AI cyberattacks threaten unpatchable US infrastructure
stories.Summary:
Microsoft Chief Executive Officer Satya Nadella spoke about the dangers of AI cyberattacks on Wednesday, November 18, 2026. During his appearance at the DealBook Summit hosted by The New York Times, he highlighted severe risks to American software systems. He explained that many critical infrastructure components possess software vulnerabilities that cannot be fixed through traditional patching methods. These systems include various transportation networks and hardware that govern everyday operations across the country.

The situation requires a complete modernization of infrastructure to address firmware that remains discoverable but unpatchable. Nadella specifically mentioned that internet connected devices like HVAC systems and data center chillers are now highly vulnerable. He noted that the speed of AI has forced patches to move instantly into production, which often creates system instability. This urgent need for remediation follows recent large scale outages affecting the NSA, the FFA, Apple, and Microsoft Outlook.

Nadella stated that the smartification of the economy has created tremendous headaches by connecting dumb devices to the internet. He described the recent Microsoft Outlook outage as a perfect storm caused by a latent bug in the system. The executive promised that his company would apply operational and architectural learnings to prevent similar future incidents. He emphasized that companies must now assess their threat vectors and improve their ability to detect and defend attacks in real time.

The current environment is shaped by a wave of outages that some fear are the result of sophisticated cyberattacks. While government officials have denied these claims, the rise of AI makes it much easier for attackers to exploit weaknesses. Companies previously had more time to test and deploy patches before a vulnerability was exploited in the wild. Now, the process of finding and fixing vulnerabilities has escalated to a speed that threatens the stability of critical systems.

Articles.Title: Amidst fears of AI cyberattacks, Satya Nadella says lots of critical infrastructure is 'unpatchable'

stories.headline_source: Amidst fears of AI cyberattacks, Satya Nadella says lots of critical infrastructure is 'unpatchable'

stories.Headline: Anthropic prices its historic IPO at $83 per share as investors bet on the AI boom
stories.Summary:
Anthropic priced its historic initial public offering at $83 per share on Thursday, a move that signaled investors are willing to bet on the artificial intelligence boom, CNN reported. The offering was described as historic in the CNN coverage, which was published on the evening of Wednesday, November 18, 2026, and updated early the next day. CNN's Hadas Gold reported on the pricing in a video segment that ran one minute and twelve seconds. The coverage was credited to Austin Mabeus of CNN and carried a headline saying the pricing came in higher than expected. The articles do not give the total amount Anthropic raised, the number of shares sold, or the valuation the $83 price implies, so those figures cannot be reported here.

They also do not name the exchange where the shares will trade or give the first day of trading. What the coverage does say is that the price of $83 per share was set on Thursday and that the company described the listing as historic. The reporting frames the pricing as evidence of investor appetite for AI companies rather than as a verdict on Anthropic's own finances. The articles do not include direct statements from Anthropic executives, underwriters, or investors beyond the paraphrased framing that investors are willing to bet on the AI boom. No named official is quoted saying anything about the pricing, and no explanation is given for why the price came in above expectations.

Responsibility for the offering rests with Anthropic as the issuer, but the articles do not identify its bankers, advisers, or board members. The context the articles supply is limited to the AI boom and the suggestion that Wall Street is eager to bet on it. They do not say what Anthropic plans to do with the proceeds, how the company will be governed after listing, or what happens on the first day of trading. No date is given for when the shares will begin trading or when the company will report results as a public company. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Dpaccel: accelerating the training of machine learning interatomic potentials with efficient data loading and distributed memory management
stories.Summary:
The articles report that a framework called DPAccel was proposed to accelerate the training of machine learning interatomic potentials, and that Jacob Andreas, a newly tenured associate professor, develops techniques enabling artificial intelligence models to communicate accurately about what they learned from their training data. The DPAccel work was published in CCF Transactions on High Performance Computing on Springer Nature Link, with a date of 2026-11-18T06:00:00Z given for the article. The MIT News article on Andreas was published on November 17, 2026, written by Adam Zewe. Andreas is an associate professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS) and a member of the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL). DPAccel is described as a model-agnostic framework that accelerates MLIP training through two innovations, a high-performance data loading system that eliminates I/O bottlenecks and handles heterogeneous datasets, and a load-balanced distributed second-order optimizer memory management system.

That memory management system reduces the memory usage of the Kalman filter optimizer by 71.84% and increases its speed by 6.27×. As representative MLIPs, the DPA series model throughput increases by 2.43× on 64 GPUs. The datasets analysed during the current study are available in the DeepMD repository at https://github.com/deepmodeling/deepmd-kit. The article states that tax calculation will be finalised during checkout. Andreas says that rather than needing to use all these external tools to try and understand what is going on under the hood, maybe we can train models to talk about themselves in a way that is accurate.

He says he tries to impress upon the students that having a really deep foundation in how all this technology works under the hood is the only way they are going to understand it, and will differentiate them in a world where everyone has access to a coding agent. He says that we used to debug systems just by looking at their parameters and figuring out whether they make sense or not. He says that now we need “mind-reading tools” that can take this really complicated neural computation and translate it for us because it is just not in a language that we, as humans, know how to speak. The article states that Andreas’ fascination with language blossomed at a young age, and that as a child growing up in the San Francisco Bay Area he was a voracious reader of any book he could get his hands on. The articles state that machine learning interatomic potentials are essential for computational materials science, but their training is time-consuming, and existing acceleration techniques are model-specific.

The MIT article states that when deploying deep learning models in high-stakes scenarios, researchers would like to understand how they work, and that today this requires unraveling an enormously complex network of internal processing nodes to understand what the model knows and how it will likely behave in practice. Andreas and his group work toward building intelligent systems that can learn about the world from human guidance and communicate effectively with human collaborators, and they develop methods to make the training process more natural and efficient, so AI models learn in a way that is more like human learning. Ultimately, he and his group want to help people design more accurate and robust deep-learning models that are better suited for their intended application. stories.Headline: Jing and colleagues present provenance-gated tool invocation to defend LLM agents against indirect prompt injection
stories.Summary:
A paper by Jing, Chen, Sun, He and Si published on 18 November 2026 in Advances in Engineering Innovation, volume 17, issue 12, pages 1 to 7, sets out a method called provenance-gated tool invocation for defending LLM agents against indirect prompt injection. The authors are L. Jing, N. Chen, Z. Sun, C. He and F. Si, and the work appears under the EWA Publishing imprint in Oxford in the United Kingdom. The paper is open access, and the datasets used or analyzed during the study will be available from the authors. The statements, opinions and data in the publication belong to the individual authors and contributors and not to EWA Publishing or its editors. EWA Publishing and its editors disclaim responsibility for any injury to people or property resulting from any ideas, methods, instructions or products referred to in the content.

The paper sits among prior work it cites on tool use and prompt injection, including Toolformer by Schick and colleagues in 2023 and the indirect prompt injection study by Greshake and colleagues, also in 2023. It also cites a 2025 survey by Deng and colleagues on security challenges for AI agents in ACM Computing Surveys, volume 57, issue 7, pages 1 to 36. Zhan and colleagues are cited for InjecAgent in the Findings of ACL 2024, pages 10471 to 10506, and for adaptive attacks that break defenses in the Findings of NAACL 2025, pages 7101 to 7117. Yi and colleagues are cited for benchmarking and defending against indirect prompt injection in the KDD 2025 proceedings, pages 1809 to 1820.

The reference list also includes AgentDojo by Debenedetti and colleagues in the 2024 NeurIPS proceedings, pages 82895 to 82920, and PlanGuard by Gong and Deng at the 2026 International Joint Conference on Neural Networks, pages 1 to 6. Debenedetti and colleagues appear again in 2026 for defeating prompt injections by design at the IEEE Conference on Secure and Trustworthy Machine Learning, pages 587 to 618. Wang and colleagues are cited for DataFilter at the 2026 IEEE Conference on Secure and Trustworthy Machine Learning, pages 139 to 157, and Abdelnabi and colleagues for catching task drift with activation deltas at the 2025 IEEE Conference on Secure and Trustworthy Machine Learning, pages 43 to 67.

Denning's 1976 lattice model of secure information flow in Communications of the ACM, volume 19, issue 5, pages 236 to 243, is cited, as is a 2026 critical evaluation of defenses by Jia and colleagues at the ACM Symposium on Access Control Models and Technologies, pages 265 to 270. stories.Headline: Researchers introduce DeltaChargeNet to simulate electronic structures in materials and devices
stories.Summary:
Qingyun Zhang and twenty-one other researchers introduced a machine-learning charge density model called DeltaChargeNet on November 18, 2026. This new system integrates with the full-potential tight-binding muffin-tin orbital method to simulate electronic structures and quantum transport in materials. The team developed this tool to predict electron density from atomic structures while maintaining a low linear-scaling cost. They specifically designed the model to handle complex devices that contain interfaces and disorder.

The framework requires an equivariant graph convolutional network to predict the difference between density functional theory and atomic superposition densities. This process includes a charge neutrality constraint and a secondary residual charge model to correct remaining potential mismatches. The researchers validated the system using bulk HgCdTe disordered alloys and Au/HgCdTe/Au disordered devices. They found that the maximum band energy error for bulk HgCdTe remained below 10 meV. The charge neutrality constraint prevented electrostatic potential distortions of 0.68 to 1.88 eV, while residual compensation fixed errors of 0.16 to 0.46 eV.

The authors, who represent ShanghaiTech University and the Chinese Academy of Sciences, stated that these corrections reproduce the layer-resolved potential within 0.1 eV of fully self-consistent density functional theory. They explained that the model allows for large-scale device simulations without needing the full self-consistent field loop. To demonstrate the practical application of this technology, the team simulated quantum transport in an infrared detector containing 11,220 atoms. This combination of first-principles accuracy and linear-scaling inference enables the study of much larger electronic systems.

stories.Headline: Letta proposes a three-tier memory architecture to address stateless AI agents
stories.Summary:
Memory is the hardest unsolved problem in AI agents, and existing techniques offer only subtle trade-offs and incomplete solutions, according to a TechGig report published on November 18, 2026. Modern large language models operate as stateless systems, which means all relevant information must be re-inserted into the prompt on every call. That stateless nature creates a structural problem for agents that carry out work across multiple turns, sessions, tasks or weeks. The Letta team, which developed MemGPT, proposes a three-tier memory architecture for agents that draws an analogy to an operating system's memory hierarchy. That architecture includes core memory for persistent blocks within the context window, recall memory for searchable interaction history, and archival memory for structured knowledge held in external databases.

Agents are designed to move data between these tiers using tools such as memory_replace, archival_memory_insert and conversation_search. The approach shifts memory design from simple prompt injection to an agent-managed hierarchy, which the report describes as a significant architectural change in stateful agent development. Working memory covers information an agent uses immediately within the context window, episodic memory records past interactions chronologically like a journal, and semantic memory stores durable, context-independent knowledge such as user preferences or team processes. Common memory features often rely on vector stores for semantic search, embedding all user and agent interactions as vectors and retrieving the relevant ones. That method struggles in production with contradictions, retractions, salience and the decay of stale facts, the report says.

Effective memory systems instead integrate layered approaches, including a scratchpad for current tasks, file-based memory for durable preferences, episodic logs of full conversation transcripts for on-demand retrieval, and recursive summarization that compresses older context into brief synopses. Vector stores suit searching large corpora for semantic similarity but are not ideal for precision, mutability or expiry. The most robust design has the agent itself manage its memory, with tools for reading, writing, updating and deleting information, so it can decide what to remember and what to forget. The report notes this could potentially include sleep-time agents that consolidate memory between sessions. The articles do not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: US restricts AI chip exports to China as Australia joins technology security alliance
stories.Summary:
The United States administration announced new Commerce Department restrictions on November 18, 2026, to limit China's access to advanced AI accelerators from vendors like Nvidia. These measures specifically target chip smuggling and overseas data centres to increase geopolitical oversight of silicon flows and data centre capacity across the Asia-Pacific region. Simultaneously, Australia joined the United States and eight other allied nations, including India, by signing the San Francisco Declaration. This international agreement focuses on coordinating the security of critical technologies and infrastructure that support artificial intelligence supply chains.

The new restrictions require tighter control over advanced hardware, while the San Francisco Declaration establishes resilient corridors for compute, semiconductors, and AI infrastructure. These geopolitical shifts occur as Fujitsu research shows that 70 per cent of Australian firms are sharing data more widely than their governance frameworks allow, surpassing the 60 per cent rate in the United States. Additionally, BlueFlag Security reports that 83 per cent of organisations are running unapproved AI agents, many of which possess administrative privileges. These figures highlight a growing gap between the rapid deployment of enterprise AI and existing data sovereignty controls.

The US administration is responsible for the export controls, which they intend to use to monitor the movement of high-end silicon. Regarding the supply chain alliance, the participating nations aim to ensure that the infrastructure underpinning artificial intelligence remains secure and resilient. In the private sector, TechnologyOne is challenging its research and development teams to double their output to avoid the AI-driven redundancies seen at companies like Canva and WiseTech. This approach seeks to combine higher engineering productivity with revenue expansion to combat competition from direct-to-consumer AI tools.

stories.Headline: Razorpay expands Agent Studio to offer Indian merchants AI agents for cart recovery and EMI collection
stories.Summary:
Razorpay is expanding its artificial intelligence agent platform, Agent Studio, beyond transaction processing so that it can offer new merchant services to businesses across India. The company announced the expansion on November 18, 2026, according to a TechGig report published that morning. The platform is designed to help businesses recover abandoned carts, collect overdue loan instalments known as EMIs, and automate customer interactions. Razorpay is positioning Agent Studio as a marketplace and builder platform where businesses can deploy specialised AI agents for their daily operations. Agent Studio recorded around five lakh monthly agent runs as of September and is live on 350 brands, according to Khilan Haria, the chief product officer at Razorpay.

Voice-led commerce has gained momentum among customers, with an AI agent calling a customer on behalf of a business to complete a transaction or recover a payment. Haria said conversion rates in some voice-led use cases ranged from 8 to 10 per cent in most scenarios and reached as high as 20 per cent for dropped-off opportunities. Razorpay announced a partnership with Meta on November 17 to enable payments through Meta Business Agent on WhatsApp, letting customers discover products, interact with businesses, and complete purchases using UPI, cards, or net banking within the same conversation. Haria said AI enables a decision layer across the buyer and merchant journey, moving beyond basic chatbots, and the platform lets businesses build customised agents by describing desired automated tasks without writing code. The initial applications included abandoned-cart recovery, subscription payment recovery, dispute responses, and cash-flow forecasting.

In September, Razorpay launched RAY, an AI account manager on WhatsApp that lets businesses check payment information and initiate refunds through messages or voice notes. Last month, Razorpay also partnered with OpenAI to help Indian brands advertise on ChatGPT through its growth marketing platform, Engage, which assists brands in preparing product catalogues and managing advertising campaigns with an AI agent. These initiatives are part of Razorpay's strategy to become more involved in merchants' day-to-day operations, extending the company's role past core payment processing. The expansion taps into the growing use of conversational and voice-led commerce among businesses, which the company sees as a significant application of its agent platform. The articles do not say what further products or markets Razorpay plans to enter next, or how the platform will be priced for merchants.

stories.Headline: Railway reports attackers stole AI keys and ran up $740,000 in usage
stories.Summary:
Attackers breached the cloud hosting platform Railway in October and used stolen AI provider credentials to run up an estimated US$740,000 in unauthorised AI usage, according to Railway's incident report published on November 10. The company said the attacker specifically targeted AI provider credentials and believes they were passed to distributed transfer stations for model distillation. The attacker decrypted stored environment variables for at most 1.85 per cent of Railway's workspaces, affecting about 100,000 accounts. Database logs showed queries selecting variables matching AI provider keys, favouring customers with many stored variables. Developers on platforms like Railway store app settings as environment variables, which can include secrets such as API keys, and an AI provider's API key works like a password tied to a billing account, letting anyone holding it charge usage to the owner.

Refund handling varies by provider: AWS Bedrock and Google Gemini have begun refunds under existing fraud policies, while OpenAI and SpaceXSI are reviewing claims case by case through a shared channel with Railway. Railway committed to covering Anthropic-related costs while discussions continue, and said it would also cover OpenRouter, which enforced its no-refund policy. That commitment marks a shift from October 26, when Railway initially told customers it could not refund spend from compromised API keys. The decrypted data also included linked-account tokens for 1,852 users, covering AI agents and GitHub OAuth tokens, and Railway reset all affected tokens, notified users, and found no logins to Railway accounts using the stolen credentials. Railway's report identified similar thefts at OpenCode, Warp and Fireworks AI between October 6 and 23, describing the incident as part of a series of attacks on platforms holding AI keys.

Fireworks AI disclosed two linked incidents: the first, on October 6, involved misused internal credentials exposing secrets for evaluation jobs for a limited number of accounts, and a November 9 update said attackers reached its development machines on October 24 via a third-party cloud provider breach, exposing customer account and billing information and, for some accounts, secrets, datasets and incomplete model weights. Fireworks believes a financially motivated group is selling large language model access through illicit routing gateways, a practice known as LLMjacking. The Fireworks breach also affected Notion, which used Fireworks for its Notion AI Insights feature; Notion said fewer than 1 per cent of its workspaces might have been affected, disconnected its systems from Fireworks and deleted its data by November 3, and has since disabled Insights and advised affected customers to rotate passwords or API keys used with Notion AI. In both the Railway and Fireworks incidents, customer systems were not breached directly, and exposure occurred through platforms or vendors between customers and AI models. Railway filed a complaint with the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center and engaged a forensics firm, while Fireworks engaged Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42.

stories.Headline: Oncologist Avishek Kumar warns that chatbot cancer answers need clinical validation
stories.Summary:
Avishek Kumar, MD, an oncologist, wrote an article published by Onco'Zine on November 18, 2026, about AI in cancer care. He described a person at almost midnight looking at blood work on a phone, with one result flagged in red. The person copied the numbers into an AI chatbot and asked what they meant. The response came back in seconds saying the findings could suggest cancer, and the person began looking up survival rates. Nobody had diagnosed the person with cancer.

Kumar wrote that AI can help detect cancer earlier, as shown by AI-assisted mammography, but findings require clinical validation and physician interpretation. In the 2026 GEMINI study, researchers examined AI-assisted mammogram reading in more than 10,000 women in the United Kingdom. The AI system flagged scans that standard human reading had not led to recall, and after additional review by clinicians, 11 more cancers were diagnosed. In a 2023 JAMA Oncology study, investigators asked an earlier version of ChatGPT for cancer treatment recommendations. Among responses that offered a recommendation, 34.3% included at least one treatment not consistent with the oncology guidelines used in the study.

Kumar said AI could be one of the most useful developments in medicine in his lifetime and is already helping identify suspicious findings on scans. He said he worries when a patient mistakes an AI-generated possibility for a medical conclusion. He said the machine has no idea what that sentence did to the person reading it. He said a dedicated mammography algorithm is not the same thing as a general-purpose chatbot and the two should not be lumped together. He said the 2023 study tested an older system, not every AI model available today, but the broader concern remains.

Kumar wrote that an elevated white blood cell count could reflect infection, inflammation, medications or a blood disorder, and a small lung nodule may need follow-up but is not automatically cancer. He said he looks at the person, their symptoms, medications, prior scans, medical history and family history, and sometimes a trend over several years tells more than one alarming result. A 2026 Nature Medicine study involving 1,298 adults found that people using large language models for medical scenarios did not make better decisions about identifying conditions or seeking appropriate care compared with a control group. Another 2026 study, in npj Digital Medicine, found potentially unsafe advice in responses from several widely used chatbots. A 2024 JAMA Oncology study found that oncologists evaluating written answers to cancer questions rated chatbot responses as more empathetic than physician responses.

Kumar wrote that two people can have the same cancer and the same stage and very different ideas about what they are willing to go through. He said AI can summarize survival curves and treatment options but cannot fully understand what it means to this particular person to miss a family wedding, to lose the ability to work, or to spend another week in the hospital. He said doctors are often rushed and could communicate better, but empathy in a paragraph is not the same as a relationship or accountability for the recommendation. He advised starting with the original result and asking whether the concern was raised by a radiologist or pathologist, by a clinically validated tool, or by a chatbot interpreting something uploaded. He advised contacting the clinician who ordered the test, especially if the finding is described as urgent or there are concerning symptoms, and being thoughtful before uploading personal medical records into an app.

Kumar wrote that patients should not ignore a real abnormality, schedule an expensive scan, assume the worst, or make treatment decisions based only on a chatbot response. He gave the question he would ask a doctor, beginning with what the actual medical evidence suggests in the case. The article ends there, and it does not say what answer a doctor would give or what happened to the person at midnight. It does not say whether any of the studies led to changes in how chatbots are regulated or used. It does not say what Kumar advises beyond contacting the clinician who ordered the test.

stories.Headline: Palo Alto Networks beats estimates and agrees to buy Applied Compute for $4.5 billion as shares surge
stories.Summary:
Palo Alto Networks reported a beat-and-raise quarter on Wednesday evening, 18 November 2026, and its stock surged as all signs pointed to how important cybersecurity is in the AI age. Revenue in the company's fiscal 2027 first quarter increased 39% year over year to $3.45 billion, exceeding the Wall Street consensus estimate of $3.31 billion, according to LSEG. Adjusted earnings per share rose 13% to $1.05 in the quarter ended Oct. 31, ahead of the 97-cent LSEG consensus estimate. In after-hours trading shares soared 9%, after a regular Wednesday session rally that saw the stock surge nearly 10%. Palo Alto also announced an acquisition that should get the company even more deeply embedded with customers.

The quarter's next-generation security annual recurring revenue increased 66% year over year in fiscal Q1, a sequential acceleration from the 63% growth rate in the prior quarter, which was itself an acceleration from the 60% in the quarter before that. Net new NGS ARR more than doubled versus the year-ago period. Net new platformizations came in at about 170 in the quarter, more than the previous two first-quarter reports combined, a 2.5 times year-over-year increase. Total remaining performance obligation increased 35% year over year to $21 billion, also ahead of expectations. Palo Alto will acquire Applied Compute for $4.5 billion in an all-stock transaction expected to close in the fiscal 2027 third quarter.

CEO Nikesh Arora said on the call that many of the major disruptions over the last few weeks, including outages across major enterprises and governments, were partially due to unintended consequences of patching and configuration changes, as IT teams cannot patch vulnerabilities fast enough without compromising production environments. He said bad actors are using open-weight models and new frameworks to find and exploit vulnerabilities at unprecedented speed and scale. He said the increased levels of security patches needed now will continue for at least another 18 months, with the same risk of collateral damage, before the risk decreases as customers get smarter about how and when to patch. He said no patch will prevent the bad guys from trying to breach systems, and that every organization must expect and prepare for attacks. He said the most important thing is to modernize the north of $1 trillion of legacy security and IT infrastructure onto real-time platforms.

Arora said open-weight models grew from under 5% of token traffic to more than 60% over the past year, and Palo Alto expects a future with a serving opportunity in the hundreds of billions of dollars of enterprise applications driven by open-weight and open-source adoption. He said Palo Alto landed on Applied Compute because no other team matched the technical pedigree in post-training open-weight models, and expects to reach 100 researchers by year-end. He said, "We have to get in the training business to be able to build a good supervision business," and that if it works the deal could dwarf Palo Alto's cybersecurity abilities. The team expects Applied Compute to add over $1 billion of annual recurring revenue to next-gen security ARR by fiscal 2029, requiring about $3 billion, or less than half a year of free cash flow, in one hundred-plus megawatts of compute capacity over the next three to five years. CFO Dipak Golechha said Palo Alto intends to remain capital light and will maintain strong free cash flow margins through and beyond the capex cycle.

Palo Alto has been volatile with sharp ups and downs since its record-high close of almost $420 on Oct. 6. The Club reiterated its hold-equivalent 2 rating and kept its price target at $400, saying it is not its discipline to chase huge rallies. Jim Cramer's Charitable Trust is long PANW and CRWD. For fiscal 2027 Q2, revenue is expected in the range of $3.53 billion to $3.55 billion, above the consensus estimate of $3.42 billion, according to LSEG. Adjusted EPS is seen in the range of $1.01 to $1.03, which at the $1.02 midpoint beats the LSEG consensus estimate of $1.01 per share.

NGS ARR for fiscal Q2 is projected between $10.2 billion and $10.22 billion, above the FactSet consensus estimate of $9.91 billion, and RPO is expected in the range of $21.5 billion to $21.6 billion, above the consensus estimate of $21.49 billion. For the full fiscal year, total revenue is seen in the range of $14.52 billion to $14.57 billion, well ahead of the $14.17 billion expected, according to LSEG. Adjusted EPS is expected between $4.26 and $4.30, ahead of the $4.18 LSEG consensus estimate and up from the prior range of $4.16 to $4.19 per share. NGS ARR is projected between $11.48 billion and $11.53 billion, ahead of expectations of $11.13 billion and up from the previous range of $11.075 to $11.175 billion, and RPO is expected in the range of $25.3 billion to $25.5 billion versus estimates of $25.3 billion and above the prior outlook of $25.2 billion to $25.4 billion.

stories.Headline: Agentic AI systems act autonomously, forcing security teams to monitor five new surfaces
stories.Summary:
Agentic AI systems that can read repositories, query databases, modify code and start workflows are changing what enterprise security has to cover, according to a TechGig report published on November 18, 2026. Unlike earlier AI that mainly produced content or recommendations, these agents build their execution plans dynamically, so security teams cannot predict the sequence of actions in advance. The report says this gap calls for a new class of security tools built specifically for autonomous agents. It lists five security surfaces that enterprise teams must address as these systems move into production. The first surface is the agent estate, which means continuously finding every approved and unapproved agent, AI platform and extension, including shadow AI.

The second is the agentic supply chain, where models, skills, plugins and tools can change what an agent is able to do. Identity and permissions form the third surface, because an agent holding legitimate credentials can still cause a breach if it combines permissions in unexpected ways. Runtime behaviour is the fourth, requiring controls with enough context to watch tool calls and data access as they happen. The fifth is intent, which traditional tools struggle to represent, making it important to detect when an agent's behaviour drifts from its original objective. Several platforms are named as addressing these problems.

Dash Security focuses on continuous discovery of the agentic layer, supply-chain risk assessment, and session- and intent-aware monitoring. Zenity secures AI agents across their lifecycle, with discovery, posture management, runtime detection and prompt-injection protection. Palo Alto Networks Prisma AIRS folds agent security into a broader enterprise AI security architecture, offering visibility and control as agents enter production. HiddenLayer extends visibility into autonomous execution through Agentic Runtime Visibility and Threat Hunting, while Check Point AI Security, enhanced by Lakera's technology, pairs controls over AI interaction with defenses for agent actions, especially tool use in workflows.

Noma Security treats agentic AI as part of a wider AI and data security platform covering discovery, posture, supply-chain risk and runtime protection, and Prompt Security, now part of SentinelOne, provides visibility and controls across employees, applications and agentic systems, with a focus on sensitive-data exposure and prompt injection. The report frames this as a shift in enterprise security requirements rather than a single product fix, since agentic tools act instead of only advising. It does not give adoption figures, pricing or a timeline for when companies are expected to put these controls in place. The tools it describes are presented as available options from the named vendors, and the article closes by inviting readers to share their thoughts on the subject.

Articles.Title: Agentic AI tools demand new enterprise security strategies

stories.headline_source: Agentic AI tools demand new enterprise security strategies

stories.Headline: OpenAI offers Indian faculty and postdocs free ChatGPT Plus for twelve months
stories.Summary:
OpenAI extended its ChatGPT for Academic Researchers programme to India on November 18, 2026, offering free ChatGPT Plus access for twelve months to eligible college faculty and postdoctoral researchers. The programme is meant to accelerate daily scientific work, from analysing complex data to writing research code, according to TechGig. The India expansion is part of a global rollout in which OpenAI is offering 50,000 new grants to eligible researchers worldwide on a first-come, first-served basis. Each grant includes three ChatGPT Plus seats in a shared research workspace for the main applicant and up to two collaborating partners. OpenAI aims to provide free ChatGPT access to up to 200,000 researchers globally, doubling its initial target announced during the pilot launch in July.

Eligible applicants must be research faculty members or postdoctoral researchers at a qualifying college or university, and they must prove institutional affiliation. They must also have authored a research paper on an accepted platform within the past three years. OpenAI has clarified that, by default, it does not use private data shared through this programme to train its AI models. The company also published a study titled Science at the Frontier: How Scientists Use ChatGPT, which surveyed over 1,800 researchers who used the tool during the summer test run.

Scientists estimated that doing the same quality of research work would have taken nearly twice as long without AI. Raghav Gupta, Head of Education for India and Asia Pacific at OpenAI, noted high interest from Indian universities since the summer pilot. He said India's research institutions are home to individuals asking important questions across science and engineering. He stated that the initiative will equip those creating new knowledge with appropriate tools and practical support.

Indian universities showed high interest in the summer pilot programme, according to TechGig. The expansion follows OpenAI's growing focus on India, including a previous $500,000 grant to IIT Madras for studying AI's impact on teaching and learning. The programme provides free ChatGPT Plus access for twelve months to eligible faculty and postdoctoral researchers in India. OpenAI is offering the 50,000 new grants worldwide on a first-come, first-served basis as part of the global rollout.

Articles.Title: OpenAI expands free ChatGPT to Indian academic researchers

stories.Headline: Bishop Cantú updates bishops on a task force for human dignity in the age of AI
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops held its fall plenary assembly in Baltimore from Nov. 16 to Nov. 19, 2026, and the second day of public sessions was Nov. 18. On the morning of Nov. 18 the bishops quickly approved items they had discussed the day before, the first day of public sessions. The bishops voted overwhelmingly to approve a new Mass lectionary and Book of the Gospels without any amendments. The bishops also voted overwhelmingly to approve a resolution on diocesan financial reporting through 2031 and the updated “Socially Responsible Investment Guidelines for the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops.” Archbishop Charles C. Thompson of Indianapolis, chair of the Committee on Evangelization and Catechesis, then introduced Auxiliary Bishop Richard Umbers of Sydney.

Bishop Umbers spoke about the 2028 International Eucharistic Congress in Sydney with its theme “This is my body given for you.” Bishop Umbers said the congress has heavily drawn on the U.S. experience with the National Eucharistic Revival and the 10th National Eucharistic Congress. He said that per Pope Leo’s request the congress will place a special priority on youth. He said the congress touches on the Real Presence and on what Christ does for us and why he does that for us. After breaking for lunch, the U.S. bishops shifted their focus to listening to a panel of experts from The Catholic University of America regarding their own research into young adults under 30.

Brandon Vaidyanathan, a professor of sociology at The Catholic University of America, opened the discussion with findings from Gallup’s 2026 Beauty and Belief survey, which took place in March and April of 2026. He detailed findings that 64% of Catholic young adults say religion is more important to them now than it was five years ago, compared to 41% of Catholic adults over 30. Vaidyanathan and other Catholic University experts did a deep dive into the data and answered bishops’ questions afterward. The presentation made clear that the Church is still “pretty far away in terms of revival.” It noted that 58% of Catholics ages 18-29 are Hispanic, but they attend Mass weekly at a lower rate.

Bishop Oscar Cantú of San Jose, California, home to Silicon Valley and the hub of AI development, gave the bishops an update on the USCCB’s new Task Force on Preserving Human Dignity in the Age of Artificial Intelligence, which he chairs. He acknowledged fears, even among the bishops, that AI poses an existential threat to humanity, and said this moment “represents a significant opportunity for the Church.” He drew a comparison to what the Church achieved following Pope Leo XIII’s 1891 encyclical “Rerum Novarum” during 19th century industrialization and Pope Leo XIV’s 2026 encyclical “Magnifica Humanitas” on the technological revolution driven by AI. He said the task force has begun implementing the USCCB’s mandate in formation opportunities on AI for bishops and diocesan leaders, helping Catholic education with AI literacy and best practices, public policy work with the USCCB government relations team to continue advocating for clear guardrails on the development and use of AI, continued engagement with the tech sector that includes more voices in society as called for by “Magnifica Humanitas,” and developing a “theology of human dignity for the digital age.” Bishop Daniel E. Thomas of Toledo, Ohio, chair of the Committee on Pro-Life Activities, asked the bishops for permission to begin updating their pastoral plan on pro-life activities, last updated in 2001.

He noted dramatic changes since then, with the overturning of the 1973 Roe v. Wade decision and the teachings on human life from three additional popes following St. John Paul II, from the death penalty to other end-of-life issues. He also noted that abortions are on the increase, with pills to procure them widely available, and that in vitro fertilization, or IVF, and other artificial reproductive technologies are on the rise. Archbishop William E. Lori of Baltimore, a former chair of the pro-life committee, spoke in support of developing a new pastoral plan. Archbishop Gabriele G. Caccia, the papal ambassador to the U.S., called for a revised plan to include advocacy for banning human surrogacy, which he described as a new form of trafficking worldwide and “another frontier” for the pro-life movement, and the bishops unanimously voted to update the plan, 205-0.

Bishop Daniel E. Garcia of Austin, Texas, chair of the Subcommittee for the Promotion of Racial Justice and Reconciliation, presented a proposal to designate the last Sunday in October as a day of prayer for racial justice. He noted that this observance would serve as a bridge between October, which is Respect Life Month, and November, which honors Black Catholics and Native American Catholics’ heritage and history. He said the Sunday readings for Mass also fit well with the theme. Bishop Garcia referred to the findings of an Oct. 26 report from the Center for Applied Research in the Apostolate indicating that 60% of adult Catholics in the U.S. believe racism exists within their local community, with about 4 in 10, or 39%, saying they have experienced racial discrimination generally. Before the vote, Bishop Garcia told OSV News that ending racism “first and foremost” begins with prayer, and the bishops voted 180-15 to approve the day of prayer for racial justice, with seven abstentions.

Bishop Brendan J. Cahill of Joliet, Illinois, chair of the Committee on Migration, concluded the day’s presentations with a report marking a year since the U.S. bishops issued their special pastoral message on immigration. Bishop Cahill warned of a “culture of indifference” informing the treatment of migrants in the U.S. and around the world. He called out the U.S. government’s “manipulations of the truth, which dismiss God-given human dignity,” seen in its “emphasis on mass detention and mass deportation to the sudden revocation of legal status and work authorization for millions of people.” He detailed the challenges the Church faced with the government, particularly in providing pastoral and sacramental ministry to Catholics in immigrant detention, but noted substantial relief had been obtained for religious workers from overseas who serve the Church in the U.S. He noted the Justice for Immigrants campaign, the conference’s “You Are Not Alone” initiative, the recent Evangelical-Catholic Dialogue on Immigration, and the Cabrini Pledge, named for St. Frances Xavier Cabrini, as examples of the conference’s ongoing work to advocate for the life and dignity of immigrants. The meeting concluded with the Collect for St. Frances Xavier Cabrini and a reminder for bishops to make sure their tablets were charged for the following day’s closed-door session.

Peter Jesserer Smith is the national news editor of OSV News, and Gina Christian, Lauretta Brown and Kate Scanlon contributed to the report. The articles leave open what the updated pro-life plan will contain and when it will be completed. They leave open what the day of prayer for racial justice will involve beyond its designation of the last Sunday in October. They leave open what the task force will produce from its formation, education, public policy, tech sector engagement and theology work. They leave open what the closed-door session the following day concerned.

Articles.Title: Young adults, AI, migrants, racial justice and updated pro-life plan round out bishops’ meeting

stories.Headline: Penn State student newspaper asks students and faculty to share AI study habits via confidential form
stories.Summary:
The Daily Collegian is seeking to better understand how students view using artificial intelligence to study in their courses, along with faculty policies and opinions on AI usage for studying and notetaking. The student newspaper at Penn State published its request on November 18, 2026, inviting readers to share information through an online form. Students willing to share whether they use AI tools or apps to study or take class notes are encouraged to fill out the form. Faculty members who have policies or opinions on how AI tools and apps can be used for studying in their courses are also encouraged to respond. The forms ask respondents to provide a phone number and or a personal email address if they wish to be contacted by The Daily Collegian to speak further.

All information provided, including name and contact information, will be kept confidential, and the paper says it will not publish any of the information provided on the form without gaining permission first. The Collegian states that it abides by the journalistic Code of Ethics outlined by the Society of Professional Journalists, and that one of those pillars is to minimize harm. The paper describes its utmost commitment as being to its sources. Questions can be directed to The Collegian's science and technology reporter, Jonathon Chiu, at jwc6496@psu.com, with "AI studying" included in the email subject line.

The request was published under the From The Newsroom section of psucollegian.com. The article carries a file photograph of the OpenAI logo on a mobile phone in front of a computer screen displaying output from ChatGPT, taken in Boston. The paper's mailing address is listed as 115 Carnegie Building, University Park, PA 16802. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Anthropic debuts on Nasdaq at $83 a share with a target value above $1 trillion
stories.Summary:
Anthropic is expected to make the largest-ever public market debut when it starts trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange Thursday, NBC News reported on Nov. 18, 2026. The leading AI lab was founded in 2021 by brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei, both former employees of rival OpenAI. Anthropic and its main product, Claude, are seen as the gold standard of AI models, despite lacking the household-name cache of ChatGPT. The offering priced Anthropic at $83 a share, above the company’s intended range, the company said late Wednesday. The debut comes as the AI investment boom stands at a crossroads, with a target market value of $1.5 trillion, larger than SpaceX’s record-setting IPO just a few months ago.

The IPO will make Anthropic worth more than $1 trillion and will serve as a test of current sentiment around AI itself at a pivotal moment for the industry. For much of the past year, the AI investment wave has powered the stock market to new heights and sustained U.S. economic growth. The tech-heavy Nasdaq was up 19% for the year recently, and as of Wednesday it is higher by less than 5%. The latest edition of Claude, dubbed Fable, ranks No. 1 on Artificial Analysis’ leaderboard of top-performing large language models as it is able to handle complex computer engineering tasks. Its Claude Code application, released in Feb. 2025, became the fastest-growing product in enterprise software history by some accounts, hitting $1 billion in revenues within six months of launching.

James McCann, senior economist for investment strategy at Edward Jones, said in a client note Wednesday that investors have over recent weeks become increasingly concerned around the sustainability of the investment boom. McCann said the leadership change at Nvidia adds to short-term uncertainty around the sector, particularly given the important role this giant company has played in financially supporting a range of smaller technology firms in recent years. He said that with the selloff in technology stocks continuing this week, investors will be watching to see how well the Anthropic IPO is received. Dario Amodei has argued that building safe AI and creating the world’s most advanced and valuable AI models are not necessarily mutually exclusive. When a user criticized Anthropic for seeming to plunge ahead with its attempt to create “superhuman” AI despite the risks to humanity, Amodei replied in an X post that a list of things Anthropic did in the past year that were pro-safety and commercially costly to us would be much longer than a list of risks it posed to mankind.

Renée Friedman, global head of research at EXANTE, a Europe-based finance and technology group, said a strong IPO would help resurrect the AI trade, but it does not mean a weaker-than-expected IPO would bury that trade. Friedman said there are significant commitments into the AI cycle by some of the world’s largest companies over a multi-year period, and these are not going to just disappear. Former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon wrote of his concerns about AI shortly before resigning that without international coordination we will incur a risk of causing human extinction. Thursday’s IPO is expected to mint a new crop of billionaires and multi-millionaires as Anthropic’s co-founders and early employees see their interest in the company turned into shares with a defined cash value. According to Vanda Research, a markets consultancy, Anthropic could see approximately $250 million worth of buying among non-institutional or “retail” investors when it starts trading Thursday, double the magnitude of interest following SpaceX’s IPO.

The market gains notched this spring and summer thanks to the AI boom have now largely been wiped out, with fears of over-spending on infrastructure, rising debt loads, ballooning costs and uncertain demand having grown. Public opinion has turned against data centers, and AI-skeptical Democrats won control of Congress earlier this month. The Jensen Huang scandal broke, creating a cloud of uncertainty over Nvidia, a company at the heart of the AI economy. In the first half of 2026, Anthropic saw total revenues of more than $16 billion, compared with $41 million over the same period just three years ago. While Anthropic was technically operating at a loss to start the year, investors expect it to be profitable soon.

Other major winners will include Amazon, Google-parent Alphabet, Microsoft, and Nvidia, which will each own billions-worth of Anthropic shares. Some observers see Anthropic’s debut as more of a major milestone than a make-or-break moment, in their view there are plenty of other investments backstopping the AI boom. Current and former Anthropic employees have also been some of the most vocal proponents of AI safety, giving voice to fears that, should the technology become too advanced, it could start to run amok. Some critics have said those concerns have proven no match for the seemingly unstoppable momentum of creating a company publicly valued at more than $1 trillion. Dario Amodei in September was pictured in Washington, and the article was reported by Rob Wile and published Nov. 18, 2026, at 4:13 PM EST and updated at 4:23 PM EST.

Articles.Title: Another AI company is about to be worth more than $1 trillion. What that means for the rest of us.

stories.Headline: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney proposes a global AI risk monitoring body to China
stories.Summary:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney proposed the creation of a global body to monitor artificial intelligence risks during a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Tuesday. This proposal for a Technology Stability Board was discussed while the prime minister was visiting China to address the dangers of emerging technology. Carney believes that any successful effort to manage these risks must include the nations that are currently developing the most advanced systems. He spoke with reporters in Shenzhen on Wednesday to explain why these specific discussions with the Chinese leadership are necessary for global safety. The proposed Technology Stability Board would bring together various countries with deep artificial intelligence expertise to safeguard the technology for everyone.

This new model is based on the Financial Stability Board, which Mark Carney chaired for a period of seven years. The prime minister noted that the decisions made by that previous board were not legally binding for the member nations. However, he explained that when countries discussed risks together, most of them returned home and implemented the suggested safety measures. Prime Minister Mark Carney is responsible for pitching this initiative because he believes a global solution is impossible without the participation of China.

He told reporters that the goal is to get every major developer around the table to identify where the primary risks are located. By applying a model he has used before, Carney hopes to encourage international cooperation through dialogue rather than strict mandates. He argues that the collaborative nature of such a board is the most effective way to ensure that AI is developed safely. More to follow.
