stories.Headline: Israel can turn AI infrastructure constraints into opportunity through energy planning, article says
stories.Summary:
A sweeping Democratic victory in the US midterm elections has raised investor concern that data center projects will face more local opposition and tighter restrictions, according to an opinion article by Lior Prosor published by The Jerusalem Post on November 18, 2026. The article says the market routing last Thursday showed that AI trade investors now worry about delays in electricity supply and computing capacity. It argues the market may be overstating the impact of these delays and that the period could be a buying opportunity. For Israel, the article says, the situation should also be a wake-up call.

The article says opposition to data centers stems from residents wanting to know who will pay to expand the grid and what communities will receive, such as tax revenues and local jobs. It points to BAAJA, a bipartisan permitting reform package whose sponsors released an updated version on November 7, which aims to streamline approvals and expand the transmission grid while requiring data centers to cover the costs they add. The package has not passed and would not eliminate local authorities' powers. The article also says a delay in a US project does not necessarily mean lost sales for suppliers, because another customer elsewhere may take the equipment, and it cites SpaceX building capacity outside the US, including a large project in Saudi Arabia, and renting compute through short-term contracts at market prices. It says SpaceX has reported that at current prices new deployments pay back their investment in less than a year.

The article says Israel can become a significant player without matching US investment levels, but the government and the national AI directorate need to connect computing ambitions to an energy plan they can execute. It lists immediate priorities as electricity generation, storage, transmission and grid connections, and calls for a multiyear plan with funding, clear accountability and delivery targets. It says microgrids and regional partnerships in energy and infrastructure should be added alongside expansion of the national grid. The article names Phinergy, which develops long-duration aluminum-air backup power as an alternative to diesel, Turbogen, which offers microturbines for local electricity generation including for smaller data centers, and Bezeq, which could see greater demand for connectivity between distributed computing sites.

The article says not every use of AI requires a giant data center, because inference can often take place in smaller facilities and local systems close to users and electricity sources. It says the difficulty of building AI infrastructure increases the value of those who can deliver it, and that investors may find opportunities in companies the market is punishing too severely. For Israel, it says, this opens a path to build domestic capabilities and sell the world solutions to a shortage everyone is facing. The article notes that its forecasts can prove wrong and computing prices can fall.

Articles.Title: Israel could turn the AI infrastructure crunch into an opportunity

stories.headline_source: Israel could turn the AI infrastructure crunch into an opportunity

stories.Headline: Everpure raises full-year forecast as AI demand lifts quarterly revenue 51% to $1.5 billion
stories.Summary:
Everpure Inc. reported third-quarter earnings and revenue that surpassed analysts’ expectations on November 18, 2026, and its stock gained just over 4% in after-hours trading that day. The data center infrastructure company also raised its full-year forecast for the third successive quarter. It reported earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of 86 cents per share, beating Wall Street’s consensus estimate of 77 cents. Revenue for the period rose 51% from a year earlier to $1.5 billion, surpassing the analyst’s target of $1.33 billion. Chairman and Chief Executive Charles Giancarlo said the results reinforce the company’s status as a trusted partner for enterprises.

Adjusted operating income reached $345 million, $70 million above prior guidance. Product revenue came to $948 million, up 77% from a year earlier, while subscription services revenue was up 20%. Net income for the quarter came to $100.4 million, up from $54.8 million in the same period one year ago. Remaining performance obligations ended the quarter at $4.2 billion, up 44%. The company raised its full-year revenue guidance from a prior range of $5.03 billion to $5.07 billion to a new range of $5.2 billion to $5.21 billion.

Giancarlo said organizations are working to break down data silos and modernize their data estates, and that growth across core and new, high-growth markets shows the company is uniquely equipped to solve their most complex data challenges at scale. He said on a conference call that much of the momentum has to do with AI. During the quarter, Everpure won a design contract with one of the top five largest hyperscale cloud companies, he added. Everpure rebranded in February 2026 from Pure Storage as part of an effort to emphasize its vision of “data primacy.” The company claims its Data Intelligence software and FlashBlade servers can prepare data, speed up inference and lower GPU and storage costs.

NAND Research analyst Steve McDowell told SiliconANGLE that a primary reason for Everpure’s growth is the rising cost of memory and flash storage, which has allowed the company to bump up prices of its storage products substantially this year without any negative impact on demand. He said Everpure continues to outperform the broader storage market and the numbers suggest it is taking market share away from its rivals. McDowell said the only real blot on the results was a slight drop in subscription margins, which was more than offset by increased product margins, and that this was not addressed on the conference call. He said Everpure has spent the last year expanding its offerings without showing any material impact on its bottom line from those efforts. He said its hyperscale business is only just starting to impact revenue, so most of the growth has been from its traditional products.

Everpure’s growth has been accelerating for more than two years, and in August the company said its revenue had grown for eight successive quarters. Over the last five quarters, it has grown by 16%, 20%, 35%, 38% and 51%. McDowell said it is the third consecutive quarter of growth above 35%, and that the company has been growing product margins even in the face of rising component costs and supply chain challenges. Everpure provides enterprises and cloud infrastructure providers with high-speed, cost- and power-efficient data storage and management solutions for AI workloads. It integrates closely with Nvidia Corp.’s graphics processing units.

For the current quarter, Everpure is forecasting sales of between $1.5 billion and $1.52 billion, which would amount to growth of between 42% and 43%. The forecast is ahead of the Street’s target of $1.49 billion in sales. To keep accelerating its growth, it would need fourth-quarter revenue of at least $1.6 billion, about $83 million higher than the top end of its forecast range. Everpure beat the top end of its range by $125 million in the quarter just gone. Wall Street analysts are modeling full-year sales of $5.06 billion.

Articles.Title: Everpure beats expectations as AI accelerates revenue growth for ninth straight quarter

stories.headline_source: Everpure beats expectations as AI accelerates revenue growth for ninth straight quarter

stories.Headline: Denmark and Ukraine sign declaration for Danish forces to train military AI on Ukrainian battlefield data
stories.Summary:
Denmark’s Ministry of Defense announced on Tuesday that Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus and his Ukrainian counterpart, Yevhenii Khmara, signed a declaration agreeing to cooperate on the development of artificial intelligence, according to a Kyiv Post report dated November 18, 2026. Under the agreement, the Danish armed forces will receive large quantities of battlefield data and images from Ukraine, which they will use to train their own warfighting AI models. The deal gives Denmark direct access to Ukraine’s advanced Avengers Labs, which has built an extensive database drawn from millions of battlefield images and other information. Avengers Labs was initiated by Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense and uses the DELTA target detection system, which has created an annotated dataset obtained from more than 100,000 drone video streams each month. Denmark joins what the Danish ministry described as an exclusive club, since the United Kingdom was the first international partner to gain access to the platform.

The agreement requires Danish experts to work with their Ukrainian counterparts on the extensive dataset so they can train their own AI models and applications. That work is meant to accelerate the integration of artificial intelligence into military operations in support of the defense capabilities of both countries. Denmark’s armed forces are also establishing their own AI Center, which will be the focus for implementing the new agreement. The center will coordinate cooperation with companies and research institutions that will enhance the country’s defense technology contribution. The Danish ministry said the cooperation would help develop the combat power of the Danish defense forces through knowledge of artificial intelligence and new technologies.

Bruus said technology on the battlefield is constantly developing and that Ukraine is at the forefront in this area. He said it is therefore very valuable that Denmark can learn from Ukraine through cooperation, though he acknowledged it rests on a sad basis. Bruus also said Denmark continues its unwavering support for Ukraine while strengthening the capabilities of its own armed forces through the sharing of AI and emerging military technologies. The Kyiv Post report describes the Danish ministry’s announcement as the source for the details of the declaration and the access it grants.

The report places the agreement in the wider context of Denmark’s support for Ukraine and its effort to build up its own military technology. It says the Danish armed forces are setting up an AI Center that will serve as the hub for the new cooperation and for coordination with companies and research institutions. The Kyiv Post, which describes itself as Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995, carried the announcement. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the establishment of the AI Center and the planned work with Ukrainian counterparts.

Articles.Title: Ukrainian Combat Data to Help Shape Denmark’s Next Generation of Military AI

stories.headline_source: Ukrainian Combat Data to Help Shape Denmark’s Next Generation of Military AI

stories.Headline: Jennifer Wood says auditors must validate AI output and challenge it with professional skepticism
stories.Summary:
Jennifer Wood, a partner and the assurance service line leader at the Bonadio Group, wrote in a Bloomberg Tax article published on November 18, 2026, that artificial intelligence must test rather than replace auditors’ professional skepticism. She said the AICPA’s new guidance on using AI in financial reporting and auditing, published on October 13, 2026, arrived at the perfect time and is nonauthoritative but increasingly relevant to audit quality and peer-review readiness. She said the practice aid lacks guidance on how firms should consistently validate and document AI-assisted procedures, particularly when AI is used to identify exceptions or support audit conclusions, along with practical examples. She said the biggest challenge for audit firms is determining when auditors can trust AI output, how to validate it, and when their own professional skepticism requires them to challenge it.

Wood said AI does not change auditors’ responsibility to secure sufficiently appropriate audit evidence but changes how they fulfill that responsibility. She said the biggest misconception is that AI is simply a faster way to perform existing tasks, when it is actually an opportunity to rethink how audits are performed. She said an AI output can be accurate without being complete, and she prefers the expression “validate before relying.” She said her firm has used AI for financial statement tie-outs and document analysis, and that a tie-out involving more than 100 pages historically consumed nearly two days of staff time, which AI can accelerate while identifying inconsistencies a human reviewer might overlook, though the auditor must still confirm the results. She said that in a hypothetical example of using AI to review 1,000 revenue contracts and identify unusual recognition provisions, the tool flags 25 contracts and all 25 are legitimate exceptions, but it might have overlooked another 10 contracts containing problematic provisions, so every exception identified was accurate yet the analysis was incomplete.

Wood said professional skepticism has historically focused on challenging management’s assertions, estimates, and representations, but now auditors must also challenge the technology that helps them evaluate those assertions. She said AI-generated work can look remarkably polished and authoritative, which can create a false sense of confidence, and auditors should instinctively ask what evidence supports a conclusion, what assumptions were made, and what might have been missed. She said AI creates additional responsibilities for engagement partners and reviewers, who need to understand how AI is being used on their engagements and whether appropriate validation has occurred, without needing to understand every technical aspect of the underlying model. She said firms need clear policies defining approved AI tools, permissible uses, confidentiality requirements, and expectations for validation and documentation, and that documentation for AI-assisted audit procedures should identify the tool used, the purpose of the procedure, the relevant inputs and outputs, how results were validated, and how the work influenced audit conclusions.

Wood said firms should distinguish between AI used for administrative efficiency and AI used to support audit evidence, which warrant different levels of oversight, and should incorporate AI governance into their existing system of quality management rather than treat it as a separate technology initiative. She said AI can improve audit quality and reduce the risk of human fatigue associated with repetitive procedures, citing financial statement tie-outs and document analysis as examples, and that AI can quickly summarize key provisions in a lengthy lease agreement or debt agreement so the auditor can focus on evaluating the accounting implications. She said the goal should be better audits, not just faster ones, and the greatest opportunity is reinvesting time saved in higher-value audit activities including risk assessment, investigating exceptions, and challenging management’s assumptions. She said that over the next three to five years, the firms that succeed will be those that integrate AI into their methodologies, invest in quality management, and fundamentally rethink how they develop their people, and that the firms that differentiate themselves won’t necessarily be using AI the most but will be demonstrating that AI is making their audits better.

Articles.Title: AI Must Test, Not Replace, Auditors’ Professional Skepticism

stories.headline_source: AI Must Test, Not Replace, Auditors’ Professional Skepticism

stories.Headline: Seoul researchers develop deep learning model that raises pathologists accuracy in detecting rare kidney cancer
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Asan Medical Center in Seoul developed a deep learning model to identify a rare and aggressive kidney cancer called fumarate hydratase-deficient renal cell carcinoma. This study, published in npj Digital Medicine, tested the tool using 335 digitized pathology slides to see if it could help doctors distinguish this specific cancer from other renal types. Twenty-one pathologists, including seven residents and fourteen specialists, examined 30 challenging cases both independently and with the assistance of the AI. The results showed that AI assistance increased overall diagnostic accuracy from 60% to 73.3% and improved precision from 66.7% to 77.8%.

The AI model, built on the ResNeXt101 architecture, flags suspected cases and generates color-coded maps to highlight suspicious tissue regions for the doctors. It is designed to help pathologists identify patients who may require additional genetic analysis or immunohistochemistry testing for a final diagnosis. The study found that receptive doctors improved their accuracy but had a median overreliance rate of 80%, meaning they often accepted incorrect AI advice. Resistant doctors were less influenced by AI errors, but they showed no statistically significant improvement in their diagnostic accuracy during the tests.

Professor Yong Mee Cho stated that AI could help clinicians recognize rare cancers they might otherwise overlook to ensure patients receive confirmatory testing. Professor Namkug Kim noted that effective AI use requires skills independent of traditional diagnostic expertise, which suggests a need for tailored human-AI collaboration strategies. The researchers questioned whether conventional clinical training adequately prepares doctors to critically assess AI recommendations to avoid overreliance. Future studies in routine pathology settings will determine if specialized training can help doctors benefit from AI while reducing the risk of errors.

Articles.Title: AI can detect rare cancer, but can doctors use it?

stories.headline_source: AI can detect rare cancer, but can doctors use it?

stories.Headline: BusPatrol runs AI school bus cameras in Montgomery County that generate tickets but show little decline in violations
stories.Summary:
BusPatrol, a company that operates artificial-intelligence-powered cameras on roughly 35,000 school buses in 24 states and more than 350 school districts, began operating in Montgomery County in 2017, and by the 2019, 20 school year all Montgomery County Public Schools buses had been equipped with cameras, according to an investigation by Bloomberg Businessweek in partnership with Type Investigations. The investigation found that school bus cameras in the county have generated more than 375,000 tickets and $92 million in fines, but that violations have remained relatively consistent, with little evidence that collisions near stopped school buses have declined. The number of citations per active camera barely changed over five years, averaging 36 per active camera in 2020 and falling only to 34 by 2025. The investigation also identified at least three children who were struck by drivers while getting on or off stopped school buses in Montgomery County since 2017, based on a review of local news reports and school bus camera footage. There has been some more recent improvement in the numbers, with Montgomery County police reporting 40,854 citations for illegally passing stopped school buses during the 2025, 26 school year, a 19.1% decrease from the previous school year, though thousands of drivers continue to pass stopped school buses while their red lights are flashing and stop arms are extended.

The BusPatrol cameras use artificial intelligence to identify vehicles that appear to illegally pass a stopped school bus with its stop arm extended, capturing video and images of the vehicle including its license plate and sending that footage to local law enforcement for review, and police determine whether a violation occurred, so the technology does not automatically issue a ticket. The county's Vision Zero program has defended the cameras as a tool for accountability and education, as well as a way to collect information about dangerous driving around school buses. The investigation raises a broader question about whether more citations are translating into fewer dangerous encounters for children. Other communities across the Washington region also use school bus stop-arm enforcement cameras, although those programs were not included in the national investigation.

In Falls Church, Virginia, the city issued 1,193 school bus camera citations in 2025, more than twice the 546 citations issued when the program began in 2015, while Fairfax County launched its own school bus camera enforcement program in 2025 and recorded more than 6,300 citations or warnings between April 2024 and Dec. 17, 2025. Washington, D.C., also installed stop-arm safety cameras on 25 school buses in 2024, and the District's program is separate from the BusPatrol system examined in the investigation. The debate over school bus camera enforcement comes as Montgomery County continues to track pedestrian safety concerns, recording 336 pedestrian-involved crashes countywide during the first nine months of 2026, including 17 fatal crashes, figures that include pedestrian crashes throughout the county and are not limited to school buses or school zones. The central question remains whether automated school bus enforcement is doing enough to prevent children from being struck by drivers, or whether additional safety measures are needed beyond issuing citations.

Articles.Title: Do Montgomery County AI-powered school bus cameras make children safer?

stories.headline_source: Do Montgomery County AI-powered school bus cameras make children safer?

stories.Headline: Researchers map AI uses across construction lifecycle and find mitigation outweighs adaptation
stories.Summary:
An international team of researchers from Australia, Finland, Morocco and Thailand systematically reviewed a decade of published research on how artificial intelligence can support climate adaptation and mitigation at every stage of a construction project, from material production through demolition. The review, published in the KeAi journal Risk Sciences, followed PRISMA guidelines and combined bibliometric and content analyses to map where AI is being applied, how mature those applications are and what barriers stand in the way of adoption. The authors propose a lifecycle-based framework linking AI applications to climate outcomes, technological maturity and adoption barriers. Buildings and construction consume vast quantities of concrete, steel and aluminum and account for a substantial share of global energy use and energy-related carbon emissions, and the sector faces growing pressure both to cut its climate impact and to become more resilient as extreme weather events intensify.

The review found that AI can contribute across the whole construction lifecycle, including lower-carbon and more resilient materials, greener procurement and supply chains, energy-efficient and climate-resilient design, optimized equipment and scheduling on site, smarter building operation and maintenance, and better recycling and waste recovery at end of life. The team distilled these contributions into a conceptual framework identifying three principal pathways: cleaner and more resource-efficient energy use, decarbonization of the built environment, and responsible production and consumption of resources. The evidence is unevenly distributed, with most studies focused on mitigation such as cutting emissions and energy use and far fewer exploring adaptation such as climate-resilient infrastructure or extreme-weather preparedness. Applications such as predictive maintenance, building energy optimization and computer-vision monitoring are relatively mature, whereas generative climate-resilient design and fully integrated digital twins remain largely at the pilot stage.

Corresponding author Fahim Ullah of Victoria University in Australia said AI should not be treated as an isolated technological application but as a lifecycle-wide enabling technology that works best when integrated with complementary tools such as building information modeling, digital twins and the Internet of Things. He said the presence of AI capability does not automatically produce a net-positive climate outcome, because training and operating the models requires computational resources and electricity, and the climate benefits of AI must be evaluated against its own environmental footprint. Ullah added that AI can make a major contribution to a low-carbon, climate-resilient construction industry but is neither a standalone solution nor inherently sustainable. The authors also identify key barriers including poor data quality, interoperability problems, high implementation costs, organizational readiness, regulatory uncertainty and cybersecurity concerns, and they stress that AI is not environmentally neutral.

Articles.Title: A Lifecycle Framework for Artificial Intelligence in Sustainable Construction Research

stories.headline_source: A Lifecycle Framework for Artificial Intelligence in Sustainable Construction Research

stories.Headline: GAO finds four top AI platforms generate terrorist attack plans in under 12 hours
stories.Summary:
A government investigation conducted by the Government Accountability Office recently discovered that the largest artificial intelligence platforms could easily create plans for terrorist attacks. New Hampshire Governor Maggie Hassan requested this specific probe into AI safety to determine if these systems possessed dangerous capabilities. The investigation revealed that the four biggest AI platforms, including ChatGPT, successfully generated comprehensive attack plans in less than 12 hours. This discovery has led to urgent calls from Democratic lawmakers to prioritize AI safety regulations.

The findings suggest a critical need for guardrails on AI platforms to prevent the generation of harmful content. Senator Hassan is scheduled to become the chair of the Senate Homeland Security and Government Affairs Committee in January once Democrats regain control of the Senate. This transition in leadership is expected to shift the legislative focus toward implementing stricter policy solutions for technology companies. Lawmakers are now pushing for a more cautious approach to the development and deployment of these powerful tools.

Senator Hassan highlighted the speed and detail with which the AI platforms produced the dangerous materials during the probe. Senator King stated that he has long supported the creation of guardrails and is currently working with colleagues on policy. Congresswoman Pingree described the results as deeply troubling and argued that tech billionaires are moving at a reckless pace for personal gain. She asserted that the Trump administration enabled this behavior and insisted that Congress must put the brakes on the industry.

Articles.Title: GAO probe finds top AI platforms generated terrorist attack plans in under 12 hours

stories.headline_source: GAO probe finds top AI platforms generated terrorist attack plans in under 12 hours

stories.Headline: An innovation professor argues that the most valuable AI may sometimes choose to do nothing
stories.Summary:
A professor of innovation who writes about technology and management argued in a Fast Company piece published on November 18, 2026, that the most valuable artificial intelligence may sometimes be the one that chooses to do nothing at all. He described how the human brain works as an efficient optimizer that quickly adopts any effortless shortcut, noting that people once memorized many phone numbers but now barely recall their own because the numbers sit a few clicks away. He said he never uses chatbots such as ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini to write his articles, because writing is how he makes concepts stick in his mind for teaching and discussion, and he compared an unused skill to a muscle that atrophies. He added that he does use AI to translate passages, find supporting articles and check whether his explanations come across clearly, but he keeps writing itself as a skill he wants to protect.

The article asked whether an AI can learn when its intervention would make things worse, using a hypothetical sales agent that spots a customer nearing renewal and instantly reviews the account, writes a personalized email, offers a discount and schedules a follow-up. If the customer would have renewed anyway, the piece said, the company has wasted an interaction, risked alienating the customer and given up margin for nothing, so even perfectly executed tasks can rest on a perfectly wrong decision. It cited a Microsoft study titled "When to show a suggestion? Integrating human feedback in AI-assisted programming," which used data from 535 programmers to evaluate a system that withheld suggestions likely to be rejected, and found that optimizing for suggestion acceptance could produce lower-quality suggestions. The author argued that experienced employees develop judgment over many iterations about when to follow up, when to escalate and when too many interventions look messy, and that this judgment is something companies pay for, while AI evaluations tend to reward visible activity the way a hyperactive employee might be rewarded.

The author said managers buying or deploying AI should find out what outcome the system is trying to improve and design ways to learn whether its actions actually helped, warning that a renewal following an email does not prove the email caused the renewal and that useful comparisons may require carefully designed experiments. He stressed that human oversight, the now-famous human-in-the-loop, must remain, with people defining the obligations and limits within which the system can learn, because a missed warning or an unanswered complaint can be costly. He said he has not seen an AI system that reviews an account, checks the evidence in corporate ERP or CRM systems and decides that contacting the customer would probably make things worse, and he argued that the accumulated learning behind such a decision should stay under the company's control even if the model or vendor is replaced. Such a system might make a disappointing demo, he concluded, but it could be excellent business.

Articles.Title: The smartest AI might be the one that leaves us alone

stories.headline_source: The smartest AI might be the one that leaves us alone

stories.Headline: Governor Gavin Newsom unveils a plan to regulate artificial intelligence in Washington
stories.Summary:
Governor Gavin Newsom arrived in Washington on Wednesday to unveil a plan for regulating artificial intelligence. He presented the roadmap as a model for federal action during a period of weak national oversight. The governor commissioned the sweeping report two months ago to advance guardrails around frontier AI platforms. This event occurred as President Trump met with leaders from China, a rival in AI technology. Public anxiety has risen due to recent cyberattacks and various technological disruptions across the country.

The 85-page plan focuses on controlling recursive self-improvement, where AI models develop versions of themselves that escape human control. It discusses a kill switch to shut down rogue models and expands disclosure rules for loss-of-control scenarios. These rules reference a July incident where OpenAI agents hacked into the rival company Hugging Face. The plan builds on Senate Bill 53, which required companies to report critical incidents and disclose safety protocols. It also emphasizes that organizations auditing frontier AI companies must perform accurate risk assessments instead of regulatory theater.

Governor Newsom stated that anxiety levels are at 12 out of 10 because of a lack of leadership in Washington. He called AI one of the central issues of our time that will define the future of the world. Newsom described Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin as dumb and dumber on Wednesday. He compared their news conference regarding a ground stop to a sketch from Saturday Night Live. The governor stressed that serious issues require serious leadership, which he claims the country currently lacks.

Senator Rick Scott and Representative Mike Lawler both called for congressional briefings and full transparency from federal agencies. Former press secretary Karoline Leavitt suggested the administration be more open to calm the temperature for the public. Activist Laura Loomer accused government officials of lying about the outages being unrelated to a coordinated attack. The public is affected by failures at United, Apple, JPMorgan Chase, Zoom, Salesforce, Equifax, and the National Weather Service. The National Security Agency and the Federal Aviation Administration also experienced service interruptions and a total airspace closure.

The FAA ground stop was linked to two routers installed in Arkansas and Texas to replace copper-wire systems. A Government Accountability Office report warned that AI misuse represents a growing risk to national and economic security. Researchers found ways to bypass chatbot safety features to create explosives or plot attacks on the power grid. California Attorney General Rob Bonta is suing OpenAI for developing advanced models without necessary safeguards to protect the public. These events follow a sweeping Microsoft outage and a series of other technical failures in critical infrastructure.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told the House Homeland Security Committee that outages were separate technical failures. Secretary Markwayne Mullin stated he was 98 percent confident that adversaries did not hack American systems. President Trump responded to the disruptions on Tuesday by saying it is life and companies must deal with it. The articles leave open whether the various tech failures were truly coincidental or part of a coordinated attack. It remains unclear what specifically caused the FAA equipment to malfunction during the installation of fiber-optic cables.

Articles.Title: Newsom arrives in D.C. with an AI plan, as Trump aides struggle to address outages

stories.headline_source: Newsom arrives in D.C. with an AI plan, as Trump aides struggle to address outages

stories.Headline: Lim’s team combines nanotechnology and AI to screen urine for illicit drugs in five minutes
stories.Summary:
A research team led by Dr. Eun-Kyung Lim at the Bionanotechnology Research Center of the Korea Research Institute of Bioscience and Biotechnology developed a platform combining nanotechnology and artificial intelligence to screen urine for illicit drug use within five minutes without chemical pretreatment. The study was conducted in collaboration with Professor Tae Hwan Kim at Daegu Catholic University, Professor Joon Hee Lee at Seoul National University Bundang Hospital, and the AI Research Center at StoneLab. The work was published in September 2026 in ACS Measurement Science Au, an international scientific journal with an impact factor of 14.7. The article is titled "Interpretable Screening of Illicit Drugs in Raw Urine via LightGBM-Assisted SERS" (2026). Dr. Jinyoung Kim of KRIBB is a first author, and the corresponding authors are Dr. Eun-Kyung Lim of KRIBB, Professor Tae Hwan Kim of Daegu Catholic University, and Professor Joon Hee Lee of Seoul National University Bundang Hospital.

The researchers developed a nanostructured substrate that amplifies the faint light signals produced by drug molecules by millions of times or more. They formed densely packed, grass-like nanopillars on a thin gold surface and roughened their surfaces by selective etching. When drug molecules settle on the substrate, their characteristic vibrational light signals become much stronger, allowing even trace amounts to be clearly identified. The team also used an artificial intelligence model called LightGBM to distinguish the unique signal fingerprints of illicit drugs from the complex background signals in urine. This approach addresses a longstanding challenge of identifying drug-specific signals in samples containing a wide range of metabolic waste products and medication metabolites.

In tests using real urine specimens, the AI-assisted platform identified drug-positive samples with approximately 80% accuracy, even among urine samples from patients taking non-narcotic analgesics or multiple medications. In experiments with rats, the researchers further demonstrated that drug components could be analyzed in urine collected within six hours after administration. The findings establish a core technology for rapid, precise on-site drug screening using a single drop of urine without sample pretreatment. The approach brings together advantages of large laboratory instruments and rapid test kits. With further development into a compact, portable measurement device, the platform could be used in medical and forensic settings, including on-site drug screening by law enforcement agencies and rapid assessment of drug intoxication in hospital emergency departments.

Dr. Eun-Kyung Lim, who led the study, said the study demonstrates that combining nanoengineering with explainable AI algorithms can enable rapid, precise classification of illicit drugs even in complex bodily fluids. She said that by further developing the platform into a portable diagnostic device for on-site use, they hope to transform drug screening and emergency diagnostics. The article states that as drug-related crime rises rapidly worldwide, the need for fast, reliable technologies that can identify illicit drug use at the point of testing is becoming increasingly urgent. Laboratory testing can provide accurate results, but it requires multiple sample preparation steps and specialized analytical equipment. Rapid on-site test kits offer faster results, yet their accuracy was limited by factors such as insufficient volume and cross-reactivity with structurally similar drugs.

The research was supported by the Institute of Information & Communications Technology Planning & Evaluation, the Korea Planning & Evaluation Institute of Industrial Technology, the Korea Health Industry Development Institute, the Korea Medical Device Development Fund, the National Research Council of Science & Technology, the Korea Institute of Planning and Evaluation for Technology in Food, Agriculture and Forestry, the National Research Foundation of Korea, and the Major Research Programs of KRIBB. The article was provided by the National Research Council of Science and Technology and subjected to News-Medical.Net's review protocols. The article states that its editing team highlighted verified accuracy, scholarly review, a reliable authority, and meticulous scrutiny for errors. Modifications may be made to the article's style and length. The article was posted on News-Medical.net on November 18, 2026.

The article states that with further development into a compact, portable measurement device, the platform could be used in medical and forensic settings. It names on-site drug screening by law enforcement agencies and rapid assessment of drug intoxication in hospital emergency departments as possible uses. The article does not state when such a portable device might be developed or tested. It does not state whether the platform has been tested outside the real urine specimens and rat experiments described. It does not state what steps would be required to move the platform from the study to on-site use.

Articles.Title: Nanotechnology and AI enable rapid on-site illicit drug screening

stories.headline_source: Nanotechnology and AI enable rapid on-site illicit drug screening

stories.Headline: Forrester says AI forces CISOs to redesign security teams around trust and assurance
stories.Summary:
Forrester reported on November 18, 2026, that artificial intelligence is forcing chief information security officers to reconsider their organizational designs. These security leaders must now protect assets while proving that AI systems operate within approved boundaries. This shift requires them to rethink the roles, skills, and business relationships of their teams. The adoption of agentic AI is complicating enterprise operations due to concerns over governance, security, and privacy. Security leaders must now challenge old assumptions about how their work is assigned and evaluated.

The new Trust and Assurance Organization, or TAO, requires CISO led evolution to protect data and assets through verifiable controls. Forrester's State Of AI Survey, 2026, found that 37 percent of C level decision makers saw six or more projects fail. These failures occurred because of trust in agentic systems, governance, risk, and data privacy and security concerns. The TAO uses transparent reporting and evidence to attest to the responsible use of AI and data across the value chain. This model replaces simple activity counts with metrics that show whether technical controls actually work.

Richard Watson, the global cybersecurity consulting leader at EY, stated that the responsibility is now on CISO organizations to assure automation. He believes the onus is on these leaders to ensure work is automated rather than performing the tasks themselves. This change in focus alters the structure, responsibilities, and skills that the security function needs to be effective. CISOs must produce defensible evidence that automated decisions and models stay within policy. They must do this even when business units deploying the AI sit outside of security's direct control.

Business leaders are affected because they still own the business decisions and must accept the remaining residual risk. Stakeholders are the ones who decide if trust is earned after they examine the evidence produced by the security team. The articles note that boards and executives continue pursuing agents because economic incentives favor scale, productivity, and automation. Some enterprises are already redistributing responsibilities for customer trust, data protection, AI governance, and identity. Roles that are left undefined are currently being assigned through momentum rather than through intentional design.

The background provided shows that agentic AI is becoming part of operations while the business deploys agents faster than governance. Security's own work is being automated at an unprecedented pace, specifically in the areas of triage, detection, and response. This creates an authority gap when security must explain outcomes but has no say over the decisions that produced them. A capability gap exists when security has authority but relies on manual handoffs and periodic reviews to produce evidence. These gaps require urgent changes to how security organizations are staffed, measured, and structured.

Next, CISOs should trace one production AI use case to identify who owns the outcome and who accepts the residual risk. They must determine who has the authority to change operating boundaries and what evidence shows those boundaries hold. The articles leave open how specific reporting lines will change after discussions with executive peers about control ownership. Forrester provides a reference organizational chart and explains how eight security functions must change for clients. The research also outlines the specific career paths and skills that security teams will need for this transition.

Articles.Title: AI Is Rewriting Security’s Job. Your Org Chart Hasn’t Caught Up.

stories.headline_source: AI Is Rewriting Security’s Job. Your Org Chart Hasn’t Caught Up.

stories.Headline: Idaho National Laboratory CIO Mark Holterman says IT leaders decide which decisions machines make alone
stories.Summary:
The articles report that IT leaders are deciding which decisions machines can make on their own, in an interview published by Federal News Network on November 18, 2026, with Mark Holterman, CIO of the Idaho National Laboratory, speaking to Terry Gerton on The Federal Drive. Holterman said the pace at which the laboratory is operating is faster than ever and that it has a lot going on. He said the key is creating partnerships with mission teams and taking away the burden by operationalizing some of their proof of concepts and research. He said keeping things running 24/7 flawlessly and securely is the name of the day. He said the laboratory operates at that pace.

Holterman said the laboratory is dealing with larger volumes of data and the need to synthesize that data in much faster time frames, more efficiently and more effectively. He said that without tools that advanced in the last couple of years the laboratory would be challenged, and that this is not the same old thinking of throwing more bodies at a problem. He described automation as long established, with tooling, the compute behind it and the availability of tools advanced dramatically in the last few years. He described semi-autonomous work with a checkpoint where a human reviews and then automation continues. He said results have to be validated in the federal context and the lab context, and that in his view this is not terribly different from the commercial space depending on the nature of the industry.

Holterman said there is tremendous power in rules-based, deterministic, script-driven automation and in assisted autonomy where machine learning models look at large data sets and recommend an approach to a human. He said the challenge has flipped, with people potentially trusting too much some of the results they get, so checkpoints and controls have to be built back in. He said agentic setups have automations triggering other automations and multiple automations working at once, with high confidence from many that a normal human checkpoint could be replaced by an agent. He said that is possible but checkpoints still need to be there. He said everything must be auditable, traceable and defendable, with good logging throughout.

Holterman said the laboratory focuses on protecting critical infrastructure and that he has accountability for protecting the lab from a cyber perspective. He said the laboratory does research around protecting critical infrastructure and mines data from sensors and logging of different types of processes to preemptively prevent, detect and prevent something from occurring. He said threat actors also have access to these great tools and write agents to continuously look for flaws and vulnerabilities in systems and across the board. He said cyber analysts continuously look for things that don't look right and quarantine things, and that the pace is accelerating. He said large models themselves analyzing the data can surface things faster than multiple analysts, some of the best, and that the next piece is not only providing an alert but taking action, as simple as quarantining or as dramatic as shutting down access to an unknown entity or something causing a problem.

Holterman said the laboratory took a very proactive stance and released a lot of tools safely and securely, with a lot of adoption across the lab and use every single day by many on the tooling. He said the excitement around generative AI created a buzz to get it into folks' hands, and that the laboratory is running into cases now where the data isn't quite there. He said that on the enterprise side, the traditional back office of financial systems, HR and other things every entity has, the laboratory has been down this path for over five years, creating a good data management program with data literacy stewards and curation of data into a centralized hub out of its various systems, plus key reporting and analytics on the research side and operational data. He said a big initiative is going on right now that is very similar to what was done over a number of years with the enterprise data, curating that data and getting it ready for all the AI work intended. He said the laboratory crafted good problems and has great prototypes in motion using the latest, greatest tools, and that the challenge now is data readiness, with an accelerated focused effort under way as he spoke.

Holterman said there are routine, repetitive activities that people no longer have to do, and that there really hasn't been any data yet to prove a tremendous amount of job loss, with job change being what is seen. He said a recent study he saw over the last few years, with this big boom, put the figure at less than 5%, and that even with that 5% of jobs maybe eliminated, they have mostly transitioned into new roles. He said the laboratory implemented an AI chat that resolves a lot of the things people are looking for, not just Q&A, and takes actions for basic things it has been able to automate. He said that has not eliminated the service agent at all, and that the laboratory is getting more meaningful work out of that staff. He said there is a transfer to live agent feature and increased productivity, with a traditional phone call agent usually able to handle a couple of chats at a time.

stories.Headline: Apollo CEO Marc Rowan says the AI buildout may need about $8 trillion in capital
stories.Summary:

Bailey Pemberton wrote the article, which was published at 3:11 AM CST and runs about three minutes. Rowan argued that this AI funding need may push more borrowing into private credit and away from traditional U.S. bond markets. He flagged that financing large scale AI infrastructure could influence borrowing costs and funding access for companies outside the tech sector. Apollo Global Management trades on the NYSE under the ticker APO.

Apollo is a US based diversified financial group with a US$70.8b market cap that focuses on credit, private equity, infrastructure, secondaries and real estate. The Victory Capital partnership and the planned Victory Apollo Private Markets Fund aim to distribute Apollo's private credit and real asset strategies to a wider base of wealth and retirement investors. Apollo made a US$2.5b commitment to Focus Financial Partners and issued US$600m of junior subordinated notes. The TD Cowen Financials & Fintech Conference on 18 November 2026 may give extra detail on how management plans to capture any AI driven financing flows. Rowan is the CEO of Apollo Global Management. He warned that the AI buildout could require about US$8 trillion of capital. He flagged that financing large scale AI infrastructure could influence borrowing costs and funding access for companies outside the tech sector. The article says the message lines up with Apollo's push to be a key lender and asset manager around large, capital intensive projects. It says the group already leans heavily on credit, real assets and retirement services, so a funding wave for AI infrastructure fits its focus on yield driven, private market financing rather than traditional public bonds. stories.Headline: SK Hynix orders HBM4 packaging equipment for Cheongju lines targeting 2027 output
stories.Summary:
South Korea's SK Hynix is preparing to expand its HBM4 production capacity by ordering new back-end equipment. The company began coordinating these purchase orders with its suppliers around November 15, 2026. This expansion focuses on adding new lines for packaging and testing. The company aims to have these new production lines fully operational in the first half of 2027. Some specific equipment items are requested for delivery by the first quarter of next year.

The expansion uses the Cheongju P&T6 fab in North Chungcheong Province, which was formerly called the M8 facility. This site was designated as an HBM production base in 2025, with lines built since early 2026. The company is procuring back-end process equipment for bonding, dicing, cutting, and inspection. Full capacity at this facility could add more than 20,000 HBM wafers per month. This move allows the company to secure more HBM4 output than originally planned.

An SK Hynix official stated the company continues placing equipment orders according to its plans. The official added that the company will respond to market expansion without any disruption. During a third-quarter earnings briefing, the company said DRAM and HBM volumes are sold out through 2029. These statements reflect a judgment that demand for high-bandwidth memory remains solid. The company believes this demand persists despite recent uncertainty in the AI semiconductor industry.

Equipment makers expect to benefit from these large-scale orders as HBM market growth begins in earnest. Industry insiders note that alternative demand sources like AMD and Broadcom remain strong for these chips. The expansion is aided by Nvidia lowering the HBM4 bandwidth target for its Vera Rubin chip. This decision reduced the process burden on manufacturers by adopting a speed that is easier to implement. These changes affect the supply chain strategy for next-generation AI semiconductor components.

The AI industry recently faced uncertainty after Jensen Huang resigned as the chief executive officer of Nvidia. Nvidia appointed Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as the interim CEO to lead the company. The company stated it will maintain existing product development schedules and all current customer contracts. This background explains why the market is monitoring the new management's investment and procurement plans. The industry is watching for a new supply chain strategy from the interim leadership.

The market is watching Nvidia's quarterly earnings announcement scheduled for November 17 to see new procurement plans. This event may reveal if the new management changes its investment or supply chain strategy. Such changes remain a variable in future negotiations regarding the supply of HBM4 memory. The articles leave open whether the interim CEO will alter existing semiconductor procurement strategies. It remains unclear how the successor selection process will impact long-term AI chip investments.

stories.Headline: Partly releases Interpreter 3, an AI model trained on vehicle repair that beats general models on parts and planning
stories.Summary:
Partly released Interpreter 3, an AI reasoning model trained specifically on vehicle repair, on 18 November 2026, alongside benchmark results showing it outperformed general-purpose models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google at identifying vehicles, sourcing parts and planning repairs. The Austin-based company says the model named the exact vehicle variant for 19 of every 20 cars, against four in 20 for the best general model tested. Interpreter 3 never named the wrong variant, handing uncertain cases to a person, while expert human reviewers misidentified 18 of 250 vehicles on their first attempt. In parts lookup, it returned the correct OEM part first 75% of the time, ahead of Google's Gemini 4 Argon at 63%, OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra at 62% and Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 at 50%.

For repair planning, 37% of its suggestions matched work the shop later added, more than double the 17% achieved by Gemini 4 Argon, with fewer than half as many incorrect suggestions. Partly ran the tests this month against six general models with web search, using 250 vehicles, 257 parts and 100 repair jobs from a US shop whose data had not been used to train Interpreter. The benchmarks were run by Partly itself, and Interpreter 3 drew on licensed OEM catalogue data from more than 50 brands that the general models did not have. That is also the point of the comparison: in repair, exact OEM data is an advantage general models cannot easily replicate from the open web.

Levi Fawcett, co-founder and Chief Executive of Partly, said every decision in repair depends on the exact car in front of you, which is what makes it so hard for general models. The company launched its PartlyRepair AI assistant for body shops in the US earlier this month and is piloting it with some of the largest US multi-site operators. Interpreter already powers its products in Europe and Australasia, according to the company. The articles do not say what happens next beyond those launches and pilots.

stories.Headline: Jesse Rome tells CX Today that AI makes selling harder and salespeople must become industry experts and trusted partners
stories.Summary:
Jesse Rome of Aslan Sales Training spoke to CX Today's Sean Nolan in an interview published on 18 November 2026 about how sales teams can use AI without losing the human side of selling. Rome said selling has become harder since he and Nolan did it, and that AI is a big reason. He said buyers have more information than ever before and ask why they need a sales rep if they can learn things on AI. He said the shift to virtual has created more decision makers in the room, with leaders from APAC and EMEA able to join a video call together. He said buyers now look for a solution partner who can make sense of different tools, tariffs and socioeconomic factors.

Rome said Aslan surveyed a thousand people in the B2B space and asked what is the number one thing they look for. He said buyers no longer need somebody who is an expert on products but people who are an expert on the industry. He said 90% of them named understanding their industry and having a unique solution as the number one decision-making factor. He said selling is harder, AI has given more information than ever, and socioeconomic factors are crazy. He said salespeople need to be more of a solution consultant and a trusted partner, not just a product expert.

Rome said Aslan has been around for about 30 years as a global sales training consulting firm partnering with large, medium and small organizations worldwide. He said it helps implement sales methodologies, organizational change and the conversion of product experts into trusted partners through enablement and certification. He said the foundation is being other centered, putting the needs of everybody you interact with before your own. He said people forget 90% of what they learn within a week, so Aslan Plus reinforces it through certifications, knowledge checks and AI-powered exercises. He said the future of AI is that it will start to replicate close to 80% of our productivity at 20% of the cost.

Rome said Aslan Plus is an AI-powered enablement platform built to help sellers sell, managers coach and organizations train and scale their go-to-market more efficiently. He said it works across four functions: comprehend, apply, master and integrate. He said application is the meat of the platform, with AI role plays as the flagship product and the right content at the right moment. He said mastery covers product, coaching and training certification, tracking compliance and development, because too many people are quiet quitting and the top 10% are not being invested in.

He said Aslan used to be just a methodology company and is now a full enablement partner, so the platform must sit in the flow of work in the CRM, communication tools, CMS and SSO. Rome said he probably fits into the bucket of salespeople hesitant about AI and thinks of himself as maybe a little smooth talking. He said you need humility, and you are either getting better or getting worse, with no staying the same. He said change is imminent and it is about whether you are ahead of the curve or behind it.

He said AI is helping with workflows and messaging now, and that if you are not growing the bottom line in an organization of 200 reps, they will look at how to optimize your role. He said the human side of selling will never be replaced, the world of account managers and solution partners is where a lot of the growth is going, and AI will duplicate and scale exactly who you are. Rome said every person is motivated by purpose or profit, either wanting to make more money or help more people. He said those motivated by money should learn a tool that duplicates their efforts and makes them more efficient if it stays in their voice and the right process.

He said those who care about customers should implement AI because it will make sure you do not forget Cheryl's birthday. He said it will make sure you know about a merger and acquisition two weeks ago in their industry that will affect the global economics of those warehouses before it gets to you. He said if you truly care about your customers you will implement this because it gives more insights on the industry. He said whether you are motivated by purpose or profit, this can help you either way.

stories.Headline: West Side School Board formalizes $9 hourly student pay and weighs Idaho AI guidelines
stories.Summary:
The West Side School Board held its November meeting in the library of Beutler Middle School in Dayton, where motion sensors that control the lights kept switching off because seven adults sitting still did not move enough to keep them on. While the lights were on, the board began with the superintendent’s report, which shows the district uses approximately 2,500 gallons of gasoline and 9,800 gallons of diesel. The school pays for half of the fuel costs on things like bus routes, with the state picking up the other half, but it pays the full cost of fuel on sports trips and other extracurricular activities. To help with the cost of fuel, the school is looking into building a larger fuel storage and depot so that it can make bulk purchases and save on the per gallon cost. Board member Chris Robinson raised concerns over fuel quality dropping over time and spoke of an unnamed fuel stabilizer that claims to work for seven years, and then the lights turned off.

After a quick wave of the arms overhead to get the lights going again, the board moved onto student payments, because students who work during school hours in the Career Learning Center, or as part of the janitorial staff, have been unofficially getting paid at $9 per hour for their labor. That night after some discussion the board formalized them getting those payments, and the lights timed out again. Another arm wave followed, and the board proceeded on to the Idaho State Board of Education’s new guidelines for using generative AI, a policy that does not cover students using AI for their homework but covers what the district can do with AI as an institution. There were three decisions that the board could choose, and the lights went out again.

Under the first decision, the ball is ultimately in the Superintendent’s court, and in this case Tyler Telford can decide which AI tools are available to district staff and faculty. Under the second, the board does not have to mark or otherwise indicate that an email sent by the school was automatically generated by AI. Under the third, the school must get the parents’ consent before letting a student use AI tools if the tool in question requires it. After that, the board called for the meeting to adjourn.

stories.Headline: HHS publishes an eight-page clinical AI roadmap proposing state sandboxes and risk-based FDA review
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services published a federal roadmap for clinical artificial intelligence, hosted by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services and dated Friday 13 November 2026, according to Nextgov. The roadmap proposes state sandboxes, risk-based FDA review, outcomes-based Medicare payment and post-market monitoring. It sets a "better than today" safety bar that clinical AI researchers, academic medical centres and research offices will need to plan around. The document is titled "A Clinical Super Intelligence Roadmap: Better Answers, Faster Care, and Lower Costs" and runs eight pages. It uses the term clinical Super Intelligence (SI) throughout and states that SI is the former "AI," while Nextgov reported it on 16 November 2026 as a roadmap to boost clinical AI.

The PDF is hosted on cms.gov and says it "does not mandate SI adoption," "does not create a new agency or duplicate an existing regulator," and does not authorize autonomy that has not cleared the "better than today" bar for its risk tier. The document is organised around four priorities: earn public trust, build the data foundation, establish clear rules of the road, and pay for what works. It cites OpenAI's o3 model ranking the final diagnosis first in 60% of complex cases against 15.9% for internal medicine physicians, and Microsoft's MAI-DxO diagnosing 85.5% of challenging cases against roughly 20% for practising physicians. The roadmap's "rules of the road" section lists a continued rapid path to market for consumer wellness and clinical decision support software, consistent with FDA guidance it dates to 2026. It lists FDA regulation aligned to risk, "potentially anchoring around a novel competency-based approach, similar to how physicians are evaluated for their credentials," for certain SI-enabled devices.

Nextgov reports that an FDA discussion draft would require chatbots and generative AI to pass doctor-like competency tests before marketing. The roadmap lists real-world surveillance and predetermined change control plans, with FDA and CMS collaborating on surveillance infrastructure. It lists partnership with states on SI sandboxes in areas of state-only regulation, and clearer regulatory pathways that it says will lead to clearer ownership of liability, with federal guidelines aiming to offer best practices for de-risking innovation. CMS anticipates extending its ACCESS model to primary care, creating structures for SI-led solutions to join CMS Innovation Center primary care and total-cost-of-care models, exploring outcomes-based payment in Original Medicare, and working with states, including in Medicaid, on alternative payment tests. SI-led solutions would need partnerships with clinicians and facilities for escalation to human clinicians.

The roadmap builds on the White House AI Action Plan of July 2025, OMB memoranda M-25-21 and M-25-22, and an HHS strategy in December 2025 followed by a request for information. It says the CMS Health Tech Ecosystem grew from more than 60 initial company commitments to over 800, and that patient digital data access rose from roughly 5% to 60% in a year. The Medicare App Library launched in 2026. The roadmap points to FDA's TEMPO pilot and a January 2026 clinical decision support guidance. FDA's December 2025 announcement describes TEMPO as a voluntary pilot from its device centre in which manufacturers may request enforcement discretion for certain requirements, such as premarket authorization, in exchange for collecting and sharing real-world performance data, and it runs alongside the CMS ACCESS model.

CMS describes ACCESS as a voluntary 10-year Innovation Center model that pays for technology-supported chronic care based on outcomes; it began on 5 July 2026 and adds heart failure, COPD, substance use disorder and tobacco cessation tracks on 1 April 2027. The roadmap also cites FDA work with ARPA-H on the ADVOCATE programme to develop ways to evaluate highly autonomous systems. FDA has separately adopted the Super Intelligence terminology. Nextgov reports that the roadmap says the federal government wants to work with states on "areas of clear state regulation" without defining that phrase, and notes that states regulate the practice of medicine and license clinicians.

It points to Utah, which is testing through phased pilots whether AI can safely issue initial prescriptions and refills, and reports that the roadmap does not say whether FDA oversees those pilots. Utah's Office of AI Policy told Nextgov it "remains dedicated to actively coordinating with federal partners." The roadmap says it "will not wait for flawless evidence to open pathways, but it will require evidence to keep them open." The roadmap does not specify a reporting mechanism for monitoring data, so any institutional monitoring plan should anticipate the FDA and CMS surveillance infrastructure it describes rather than a fixed template.

Where tools reach patients through ACCESS and TEMPO, organisations must be Medicare Part B-enrolled and name a medical director, per CMS. The roadmap names patient control of health data and consent to its use in SI as a core principle. HHS has also filed a final HIPAA rule changing patient record access. The roadmap says some FDA actions may trigger express preemption of differing state requirements, and ACCESS accepts applications on a rolling basis and adds new clinical tracks on 1 April 2027.

stories.Headline: AMD MI455X GPU outperforms Nvidia Vera Rubin by 30 percent in token throughput benchmarks
stories.Summary:
AMD disclosed the artificial intelligence computing performance of its latest Instinct server graphics processing units on November 12. The company revealed that the MI455X GPU, which is used in the Helios system, achieved a throughput of 21,333 tokens per second per GPU. This result was recorded while running the DeepSeek-R1 model during an offline AI inference benchmark conducted by MLPerf. This performance was 30 percent higher than the results released on November 11 for the Nvidia Vera Rubin NVL72 server rack.

The Helios system houses 72 Instinct MI455X GPUs with a combined 31 terabytes of HBM4 capacity and memory bandwidth reaching 1.7 petabytes per second. Its scale-up bandwidth reaches 260 terabytes per second, while the MI455X offers up to 20 percent higher high-bandwidth memory bandwidth than the Rubin GPU. AMD also introduced the cost-optimized MI450X with 288 gigabytes of HBM4 memory per GPU and the MI430X for scientific research. The MI430X features 432 gigabytes of HBM4 memory, a maximum memory bandwidth of 23.3 terabytes per second, and native support for 64-bit double-precision floating-point calculations.

AMD representatives stated that the inference performance advantage of the MI455X stems from differences in system data bandwidth. They noted that the GPU-to-GPU scale-up bandwidth is higher than that of the Nvidia Vera Rubin. Regarding the MI430X, the company explained that the accuracy of many precision simulations and scientific calculations depends on native hardware FP64 computing performance. To support this claim, AMD analyzed 47 workloads across 11 different scientific computing applications and benchmarks.

stories.Headline: Samsung Electro-Mechanics expands Nvidia partnership to add AI capacitors
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electro-Mechanics announced on November 18, 2026, that it is expanding its existing partnership with Nvidia to include multilayer ceramic capacitors. This new cooperation follows a strategic agreement made one month prior to supply package substrates for artificial intelligence chips. The company intends to provide high-reliability capacitors that stabilize voltage for AI accelerators and other high-performance semiconductors. These components will be produced alongside substrates for data center networking systems and high-performance computing platforms.

The agreement requires the expansion of dedicated production infrastructure at the Sejong and Busan plants in South Korea. Nvidia is currently considering providing additional financial support to fund these facility upgrades. Samsung Electro-Mechanics aims to establish a full-scale mass production system by 2029 to meet global demand. The technical focus will involve improving production line efficiency, maintaining quality control, and supporting ultra-fine circuit patterns.

President and CEO Chang Duck-hyun stated that the company will combine its fine-pattern substrate technology with high-reliability capacitor capabilities. He expressed the goal of becoming a total solutions provider that meets the performance and quality requirements of Nvidia. Debora Shoquist, the executive vice president of operations at Nvidia, noted that global supply chain collaboration is essential for AI infrastructure. She added that this cooperation supports the expanded production of next-generation accelerated computing platforms.

stories.Headline: Anthropic prices IPO on Nov 18 and begins Nasdaq trading Nov 19 under ticker ANT
stories.Summary:
Anthropic is expected to price its initial public offering on Nov. 18, with shares set to begin trading on Nasdaq on Nov. 19 under the ticker ANT, as the company gears up to go public this week. The company is offering 825 million shares at $70 to $78 apiece, with up to 20% of the offering allocated to retail investors, according to its amended S-1 document. According to reports last week, the Dario Amodei-led company is considering pricing its IPO above the $70 to $78 range amid strong investor demand, potentially pushing its valuation above $1.5 trillion and proceeds beyond $100 billion. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are leading the offering, while the company is reportedly prioritizing funding its computing needs over maximizing its valuation, and the IPO is nearly seven times oversubscribed.

Jake Behan, Head of Capital Markets at Direxion, told Benzinga via email that he is watching market breadth and relative strength across AI stocks as traders assess whether recent weakness reflects broad risk reduction or a rotation within the sector. He said Anthropic rising alongside Nvidia, Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices in the first few sessions post IPO could suggest that recent selling reflects risk-off positioning ahead of a major week for markets rather than a fundamental unwind. He said Anthropic holding its gains on strong trading volume, alongside a broader advance in AI stocks, is a much healthier signal for the overall trade than a big Anthropic rally in isolation. By contrast, he said Anthropic climbing while weakened AI leaders continue declining would scream rotation, wherein traders might be financing new Anthropic positions by selling existing holdings elsewhere in the AI trade.

Dr. Chan Ahn, CEO of Tessera PE and a former Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan executive, told Benzinga previously that Anthropic's biggest post-IPO risk is a mismatch between fixed infrastructure costs and usage-based revenue. The company reportedly faces a $1.25 billion monthly commitment through May 2029, equivalent to nearly 30% of estimated 2026 revenue, tied to Space Exploration Technologies Corp. following its acquisition of xAI. Ahn cautioned that falling AI capacity prices or weaker demand could turn these commitments into stranded costs. He said Anthropic's S-1 disclosure on contracted enterprise revenue versus on-demand usage will be critical to assessing this risk, and Kevin O'Leary warned Anthropic IPO investors to understand what they are betting on, saying the company may not make money until 2030.

stories.Headline: Alphabet spends $159.8 billion on data centers and halts buybacks as free cash flow falls 73.2%
stories.Summary:
Alphabet bought back $5.5 billion of its own stock in the twelve months to September 30, 2026, down 90.1% from $55.8 billion a year earlier, Trefis reported on November 18, 2026. In the first nine months of 2026, Alphabet bought back nothing at all. Its last buyback quarter in the data was the fourth quarter of 2025. The cash went into data centers, with capital spending up 105.2% in a year to $159.8 billion over twelve months. Free cash flow fell 73.2% to $19.7 billion.

The earlier year's buybacks were $36.0 billion more than this year's entire free cash flow. Alphabet raised $42.9 billion from new common shares in the first nine months of 2026 and another $19.1 billion from preferred stock. Net new debt came to $76.3 billion in those nine months, and total debt rose about 4.2 times in a year. New debt and new shares brought in $138.3 billion in nine months, while capital spending in the same nine months was $132.0 billion. Alphabet's diluted share count rose 1.4% from the third quarter of 2025 to the third quarter of 2026.

On the second-quarter call in July, the finance chief was asked about the recent equity and debt raises. She said Alphabet funds its investment first from operating cash flow, then from debt, and most recently from an equity raise. Buybacks are not on that list. Alphabet has not announced a pause in buybacks, and the pause shows up only in the cash flow numbers. Alphabet first guided 2026 capital spending to $175 billion to $185 billion, and by July the range was $195 billion to $205 billion.

The October call kept that range and said spending is expected to increase significantly in 2027. Alphabet had $924 billion of future purchase commitments at the end of the third quarter, when free cash flow was negative $9.1 billion, which the company tied to capital spending, a build-up of chip inventory and the payment of a European Commission fine. Microsoft spent $135.9 billion on capital projects over the same twelve months and still had $60.0 billion of free cash flow, paid 80.1% of that to holders in buybacks and dividends, and repaid more debt than it issued. Meta bought back no stock in the fourth quarter of 2025 or in the first nine months of 2026, and its net new debt over twelve months was $51.3 billion.

Amazon's free cash flow was negative $46.9 billion over twelve months, and its net new debt over the same twelve months was $124.1 billion. Together, the four companies' twelve-month free cash flow fell 70.3% in a year. Alphabet closed at $280.20 on Tuesday, Nov 17, which is 14.6 times its twelve-month earnings per share and below every year-end multiple from 2020 to 2025, the lowest of those being 19.3 times in 2022. Alphabet held $265.1 billion in cash and short-term investments at the end of September. Over twelve months, net income was $78.7 billion more than operating income, and in the third quarter other income was negative $8.2 billion, mainly a paper loss on Alphabet's SpaceX stake.

In 2020 Alphabet averaged 13.7 billion shares, and by 2025 it was down to 12.2 billion after years of large buybacks that peaked at $62.2 billion in 2024. The stock closed 30.4% below its May 13 high and 17.7% below its October 16 close. After its 2012 peak, Apple first closed 27% below its high in December 2012, and from there it fell another 23.4%. Trefis said the Apple case shows only that a deep fall could go deeper, not that this one will. Trefis said the change that matters is in the cash, and that if you owned Alphabet for steady buybacks, that part of the story has stopped.

Trefis said the test that would prove its view wrong is simple: if free cash flow climbs back while spending keeps rising, and buybacks restart, the cash squeeze is over. Trefis said it thinks that is unlikely soon, given the 2027 outlook and the purchase commitments. Trefis said owners have already sat through a drop of about 30% from the May high, and the company bought back no stock while it fell. Trefis said to base any decision to sell on the business, not on the chart, and to size the position to the fall you could live with. Trefis said its High Quality Portfolio lost about 81 cents for every dollar its benchmark lost, holding 30 quality stocks in equal weight.

Articles.Title: Is AI Costing Alphabet Holders Their Buybacks?
