Nebius Group shares rose 3.0% on November 18, 2026, according to Quiver Quantitative, which attributed the move most likely to a rebound in AI infrastructure and neocloud shares after Nvidia's latest earnings renewed confidence in demand for GPU capacity. The stock also retained support from Nebius's own recent results, which showed very rapid revenue growth even though investors had been worried about timing delays tied to third-party data center capacity. On November 12, Nebius said third-quarter revenue rose to $980.8 million, with AI Cloud revenue of $973.8 million, showing that customer demand remains strong. Nebius said four new sites began generating revenue across the U.S. and Europe, and additional capacity was delivered in New Jersey during the quarter and through November. The company said prepayments on third-quarter agreements covered more than 100% of associated capex, which may have helped reassure investors about funding for expansion.

The report said the rise could also reflect a relief rally, because the stock had sold off sharply after management moved its 2026 revenue outlook to the low end of its prior range, leaving room for improvement as sentiment across the AI compute group recovered. Quiver's price movement analysis was generated with the help of AI and carried a disclaimer asking readers to double-check the information for mistakes. The same article reported that Nebius insiders traded the stock on the open market 119 times in the past six months, with 11 purchases and 108 sales. It listed sales by COO Ophir Nave of 500,000 shares for an estimated $117,765,467, by CEO Arkadiy Volozh of 84,405 shares for an estimated $19,824,423, and by Chief Infrastructure Officer Andrey Korolenko of 62,961 shares for an estimated $14,786,641, among others, while Arne Grimme made 11 purchases of 2,014 shares for an estimated $330,439.

The article also reported institutional moves in its most recent quarter, including the California State Teachers Retirement System removing 61,942,524 shares, a 99.6% decrease, for an estimated $14,611,002,561, GQG Partners adding 10,976,818 shares for an estimated $2,589,211,829, and Goldman Sachs Group removing 4,720,517 shares, a 48.2% decrease, for an estimated $1,113,475,549. It said Wall Street analysts had issued eight buy ratings and one sell rating on the stock in the last several months, with Citigroup, Truist Securities, Rosenblatt and Baird among the recent buy or outperform ratings and Rothschild & Co issuing a sell rating on September 21. Twelve analysts offered price targets in the last six months with a median target of $230.0, including Tyler Radke of Citigroup at $215.0 on November 16, Arvind Ramnani of Truist Securities at $245.0 and John McPeake of Rosenblatt at $304.0 on November 13, and Daniel Wang of BNP Paribas at $399.0 on September 24. The article stated that it is not financial advice and noted there may be inaccuracies due to mistakes in ticker-mapping and other anomalies.

stories.Headline: KAIST team develops KORMo-Web AI agent that operates websites for shopping and online tasks
stories.Summary:
A research team led by Professor Lim Kyung-taek at the KAIST Graduate School of Culture Technology developed an AI agent called KORMo-Web. On November 17, the team announced that this model can watch a computer screen like a human to operate a mouse and keyboard. The AI performs various online tasks on behalf of users, such as shopping, writing emails, and creating presentation materials. It can also engage with online communities by automatically writing comments on YouTube videos.

The system requires a massive dataset of over 10 million web screen samples in English and Korean to function. To handle multi-step tasks, the researchers used more than 100,000 records of real user interactions with various websites. A compact model with 4 billion parameters achieved a 42.3% success rate on real websites in both languages. This performance surpassed previous open models by 22.1 percentage points in Korean and 9.6 percentage points in English.

Professor Lim stated that the goal was to have AI understand screens directly rather than connecting separate application programming interfaces for every service. He explained that the team wants to create an environment where small AI installed on personal computers can handle diverse web tasks. To support this goal, the team released three different models, including an in-house version and a small version for personal computers. All program code, training data, and models are provided as open source for anyone to use.

stories.Headline: Heo Seong-beom urges exam cheating countermeasures after AI scandal
stories.Summary:
Broadcaster Heo Seong-beom, a 26-year-old former AI researcher at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, posted a video titled "AI Was Not Made to Be Used This Way" on his YouTube channel on the 16th. In that video he said the top scorer on the Certified Public Accountant exam had admitted to cheating with a smart device, and he added that he was deeply distressed by it. He said it was painful that people who exploit AI had appeared before society had established guidelines for the technology. The video was reported by MoneyToday on 17 November 2026.

Heo Seong-beom said the biggest problem is that examinees who have studied hard are having their opportunities taken away by the minority who abuse the system. He argued it makes no sense to proceed with the CSAT as it is without any countermeasures, and he said various preventive measures must be established even if that is a bit troublesome. He cited metal detectors as an effective way to detect cheating, because cameras, communication equipment and earphones are needed to photograph questions, send them to AI and receive answers, so the response should involve detecting batteries. He said students suspected of cheating can be checked through USIM communication records and analysis of exam papers, since data exchanges leave records on the USIM and handwriting can show whether cheating occurred.

He warned those attempting to cheat that cheating will always be discovered and that if they catch them, they catch everyone. He told friends who decided to cheat because they thought they could get away with it this time that it is a matter that will ruin their lives, and he hoped they would not do it. To examinees who may feel confused, he said people like these bad actors have existed in every era, and he encouraged them not to worry and to go their own way even if they wonder why they should study in an era like this. Heo Seong-beom attended the Korea Science High School for the Gifted and the Department of Computer Science at KAIST, is currently enrolled in the AI Graduate School, and became known through CSAT explanation videos, lecturing and appearances on Coupang Play's "University War" and Wavve's "Blood Game 3."

stories.Headline: Kenilworth residents form nonprofit and push data center bans as CoreWeave builds
stories.Summary:
A 40-megawatt data center has been under construction for a year in the Borough of Kenilworth, New Jersey, including more than 30 diesel-fueled generators that are the size of tractor-trailers, according to an ABC7 New York investigation published on Wednesday, November 18, 2026. Tiffany Haltom, who lives in a nearby town, said she did not know anything about the center until after it was under construction and found out this spring through a Facebook group for moms. She helped create and became president of a nonprofit fighting the facilities, the Union County Residents Alliance Coalition, and said the issue snowballed from there. Many Kenilworth council meetings have been tense since then, with residents from nearby towns giving public comment against the project, and the first phase is already a done deal. Under former Gov. Phil Murphy, the company behind it, CoreWeave, received up to $250 million in state tax credits.

The group is going into every town and attending meetings to push for data center bans, and it has made progress in the areas surrounding Kenilworth in just the past few months. Cranford Township and Roselle Park to the south and Union Township to the north passed bans on data centers, along with the cities of Linden and Summit, while officials in Westfield say they are considering a similar ban. A Springfield Township committee recently expressed support for a moratorium, and Scotch Plains leaders say data centers are not permitted under current zoning laws. Members of the nonprofit say they are not against data centers but do not want communities rushing to build them.

New York State hit pause on building new ones for a year, while New Jersey did not. A CoreWeave spokesperson said the company is funding approximately $150 million in electrical infrastructure upgrades, including a new substation, so grid improvement costs are not passed on to local ratepayers, and that the facility will use closed-loop cooling and sound controls designed to meet local noise standards. The spokesperson said CoreWeave is a New Jersey-based company formed by founders working in Union County and headquartered in Livingston, and that the Kenilworth project includes more than 140 data center jobs and 1,500 union construction jobs. The company said it has maintained a dialogue with neighboring communities, including multiple conversations with local leaders about power, water, sound and project plans, and will continue those conversations as the project moves into operation.

Eyewitness News reached out to all of the council members in Kenilworth, who would not speak with the station, and their attorney sent a statement. The attorney said the Mayor and Council have a responsibility to protect residents' financial interests, health and safety, and that the Borough has complied with all public notice requirements, including public hearings in 2024 and 2025, while contract negotiations and attorney-client communications remain confidential as permitted by law. The statement said the proposed data centers represent a significant tax ratable that could stabilize or reduce property taxes for residents for years to come, and that the Governing Body is retaining independent, licensed professionals with no past or present relationship with the developer to evaluate potential impacts. It said their findings will help determine whether any concerns require action, that the bipartisan Governing Body is committed to fully vetting the project, and that any claim otherwise is categorically false.

stories.Headline: OECD study finds German media overreports autonomous vehicles and large language models in AI incident coverage
stories.Summary:
The OECD AI Policy Observatory published a paper on 17 November 2026 analysing live data from the OECD.AI Incidents and Hazards Monitor to compare how 15 thematic clusters of AI incidents and hazards appear in German-language media against global trends. The analysis found three themes overrepresented in German-language coverage, namely autonomous vehicles, intellectual property, and large language models. It found two themes underrepresented, namely synthetic media, and cyberattacks and fraud. Coverage of the remaining ten thematic clusters was broadly aligned with global media patterns. The paper says media reports of AI incidents and hazards can shape public perception and political debates, while both the level and thematic focus of media attention vary across regions.

The paper concludes that media representation of AI risks is shaped not only by the nature of AI incidents but also by language-specific and regional contexts. The OECD.AI platform says governments must track and understand AI incidents and hazards to manage risks, and that all actors must be accountable for AI risks. It also says organisations developing advanced AI systems can participate by submitting a report, and that sharing information will facilitate transparency and comparability of risk mitigation measures. The OECD.AI Index assesses countries' progress in implementing the OECD Recommendation on AI. The platform describes itself as an online interactive platform dedicated to promoting trustworthy, human-centric AI, and notes that the GPAI initiative and OECD member countries' work on AI joined forces under the GPAI brand to create an integrated partnership.

The articles do not name individual authors or officials and give no direct statements beyond the platform's general positions on accountability and risk tracking. They describe the OECD as both a regulator and investor in AI as well as a developer and user, and say experts from around the world advise GPAI and contribute to its work. The paper is available for download through the OECD.AI page, and the page invites readers to sign up for the OECD's artificial intelligence newsletter. The articles do not say what policy changes, if any, follow from the findings.

Articles.Title: AI incidents and hazards in the media: Evidence from German-language coverage - OECD AI Policy Observatory

stories.Headline: Baidu and Xiaomi CEOs warn that AI investments are outpacing commercial returns
stories.Summary:
Robin Li Yanhong of Baidu and Lei Jun of Xiaomi issued warnings on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, regarding the current state of artificial intelligence. These leaders spoke during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation CEO Summit held in the city of Shenzhen. They expressed significant concern that the massive investments flowing into the technology are far outpacing the actual commercial returns. This warning comes during a period of market jitters following the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The tech leaders argued that the industry must shift its focus toward building practical applications rather than simply creating more powerful models.

They believe that the true value of artificial intelligence will be determined by how these tools are used in real-world scenarios. This shift is necessary because there is a widening gap between heavy capital expenditure and profitable adoption. Robin Li made these comments just one day after Baidu reported its sixth consecutive quarterly drop in revenue. Robin Li Yanhong stated that the most pressing task for the industry is to identify and develop high-value applications for AI models.

Both he and Lei Jun urged the tech community to prioritize utility over the hype surrounding the technology. They suggested that the current trajectory of spending could lead to an artificial intelligence bubble if returns do not materialize. The executives emphasized that the ability to generate profit depends on finding the right use cases for the existing models. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Kyndryl CEO Martin Schroeter says companies must control AI agents and build governance into their design
stories.Summary:
Kyndryl Chairman and CEO Martin Schroeter gave adapted remarks during a fireside chat with cybersecurity expert Nuno Mateus-Coelho at the Web Summit in Lisbon on November 12, 2026. The article was published on kyndryl.com on November 18, 2026, with a read time of one minute. Schroeter said cybersecurity remains top of mind for Kyndryl's customers. He said the world now has two things to deal with: bad actors and agents that are misguided, incorrectly built or uncontrolled. He said bad actors are going to use AI to try to break into systems and that Kyndryl sees it every day.

Schroeter said the second concern is about agents, which he called the new world. He said there are examples of agents moving outside their sandbox or doing things they were not intended to do. He said Kyndryl is building agents for its customers, that they are all controlled, and that Kyndryl has visibility into them. He said Kyndryl knows what the agents are doing, what they are allowed to do and what they cannot do. He said the agents are controlled through what Kyndryl calls Kyndryl Bridge.

Schroeter said you have to create agents, control them and set their permissions the right way, as is done with many other things in infrastructure. He said that at the end of the day agents are software code, but they are relentless, goal-seeking pieces of software. He said agents need to be controlled. He said that across industries, the companies getting this right and thinking ahead have, first and foremost, a complete view of their inventory. He said Kyndryl helps its customers do this.

Schroeter said those companies have a complete view of the hardware, software, operating systems and everything in their inventory. He said they also know what patches have been applied. He said that allows Kyndryl's customers to prioritize what they need to protect specifically, because not everything is equally important. He said the first thing is to know what you have. He said the governance of agents is a top concern.

Schroeter said these companies do not build agents and then try to figure out how to govern them. He said they use tools like what Kyndryl calls policy as code. He said Kyndryl can ingest their business rules, their infrastructure and the business logic they are trying to follow. He said you can then apply the policy you already have in place to the new piece of code you are introducing into your infrastructure. He said governance cannot be an afterthought and has to be part of the design.

Schroeter said you need to be able to shut agents down or control them and make sure you have a resilient system. He said that if you know what you have, build policy governance into the design, and have a way to keep your systems resilient if something goes wrong, you are among the companies at the forefront of this in every industry. The article ends mid-sentence, asking what role industry should play in shielding customers from geopolitical risks and helpi. The article gives no further remarks, no other speakers and no additional dates or figures. More to follow.

stories.Headline: CATL searches for an AI model to accelerate battery research and scientific discovery
stories.Summary:
CATL founder and CEO Zeng Yuqun announced the search for an AI Einstein during a panel discussion at the Apec CEO Summit 2026. This event began on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, in the city of Shenzhen. The company wants to find an artificial intelligence model that can accelerate scientific research and drive growth through innovation. This initiative comes as the Chinese battery giant deals with several market setbacks and headwinds.

The project requires a specialized AI model capable of working far beyond the current applications of existing technology. Zeng Yuqun questioned Robin Li Yanhong, who is the co-founder and CEO of the AI pioneer Baidu, about the capabilities of current large language models. The goal is to determine if these existing tools are good enough to drive the necessary breakthroughs. The company believes a more advanced system is needed to speed up the pace of scientific discovery.

Zeng Yuqun is responsible for leading this search to ensure the company maintains its competitive edge in the battery market. He explained that the company is actively seeking a tool that can function like a digital genius to solve complex problems. By integrating such a model, CATL hopes to overcome current obstacles and accelerate the development of new battery technologies. The company aims to move past standard AI uses to achieve significant scientific leaps.

stories.Headline: Giovanni Carraro says open-weight AI models give enterprises more control over cost and customization
stories.Summary:
Open-weight AI models are creating new possibilities for how organizations deploy, customize and manage artificial intelligence, according to a Kyndryl article published on 18 November 2026. Unlike proprietary models, which are typically accessed through a provider, open-weight models give enterprises the option to run AI within their own infrastructure. The article says open-weight AI is expanding enterprise choice and changing how leaders evaluate cost, control and risk. Giovanni Carraro, Senior Vice President, Global Strategic Alliances at Kyndryl, discusses the trade-offs between open and closed models as more firms move from experimentation to enterprise-wide AI adoption. The article asks why open-weight AI models are gaining attention among enterprise leaders.

Carraro says organizations are moving beyond experimentation and thinking more seriously about how AI fits into their operations, infrastructure and long-term business strategies. He says cost, control and customization are driving much of the interest, and some organizations are finding that open-weight models can be a part of their enterprise tools. Open-weight models allow organizations to access, download and customize trained AI models to meet specific business needs, giving them greater control over where AI runs, how data is managed and the cost model under which it operates. He says that flexibility may become increasingly valuable as enterprises balance growing demands with operational and financial considerations. The article says the flexibility raises important questions about cost, sovereignty, security and long-term strategy.

Carraro says the choice between open-weight and closed, proprietary AI models should not be an either-or decision. He says both have advantages, and the right choice depends on an organization's needs and how it plans to use AI. He says it is helpful to think about surfaces and engines, where surfaces are where you access the tool and engines are the AI model the surface directs to. He says proprietary models are typically accessed through web, desktop and mobile applications, through APIs either directly from the developer or via managed cloud platforms, through command-line tools and IDE extensions, and increasingly through integrations embedded in enterprise software.

He says the AI provider manages much of the underlying infrastructure in these instances, which can simplify deployment and ongoing maintenance for the end user. Carraro says proprietary models can still offer choices of hosting location and capacity, and in some cases can offer fine-tuning within the model provider's available options. He says open-weight models can offer greater flexibility over where and how AI operates, and organizations can host them in private cloud or on-premises environments, or even on individual devices. He says organizations can customize certain models for specialized tasks, and some open providers offer models through cloud services, which means they would manage the infrastructure and maintenance.

The article says the conversation should not be about whether open-weight or proprietary AI models are better, but about understanding which model can deliver the greatest value to an organization, including meeting its security requirements. The article says organizations may also turn to specialized models, whether open or closed, to achieve their goals. The article says Kyndryl can help customers navigate their AI partner choices. It says the conversation about enterprise AI is evolving as organizations move beyond experimentation.

The article carries a read time of 1 minute and is dated 18-Nov-2026. It says open-weight AI is expanding enterprise choice and changing how leaders evaluate cost, control and risk. The article says it is also important to distinguish open-weight models from other kinds of models. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Civil servants submit AI and data ideas to a 2026-27 challenge run by NTT DATA with government
stories.Summary:
Civil servants across government were invited to submit ideas for using artificial intelligence and data to improve public services when the 2026-27 Civil Service AI & Data Challenge opened for applications, in a competition run by NTT DATA with the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport and the Cabinet Office. The competition is open to civil servants in all departments, roles and grades, and it asks them to identify problems they encounter in their day-to-day work that could be addressed through better use of AI and data. The strongest proposals will be developed through a Dragons' Den-style competition, and the winning project will receive £50,000 of support to help bring the idea to life. Applications are open until 10 December 2026, and civil servants can submit an idea, volunteer to join a project team, or do both through the Challenge website. The latest competition follows last year's programme, which has seen at least seven AI and data projects taken forward by government departments and agencies.

Among them is an initiative proposed by last year's winner, Marlon Woodley, a verification assurance officer at the Department for Work and Pensions, whose idea focuses on improving the tools available to benefits caseworkers to reduce errors and accelerate decision-making. Previous Challenges have also generated proposals to support peatland restoration and to improve information-sharing between the NHS and the DWP following a death. For the 2026-27 programme, eight teams of civil service volunteers will be established to develop the most promising proposals, supported by a government-wide network of data leaders, and the competition will culminate in July 2027, when a panel of senior Civil Service digital leaders will select the winning project. Minister for digital government Stephanie Peacock said civil servants across the country see first-hand where technology could make a real difference to people's lives, whether that is speeding up decisions, reducing avoidable admin or making public services easier to use, and that the Challenge gives them the opportunity to turn that experience into action. Government chief data officer Aimee Smith said she saw last year how the Challenge enables civil servants in every role, department and grade to help improve public services, and that it is also a brilliant way for them to improve their skills and experience in digital technologies.

David Filmer, head of public sector at NTT DATA UK&I, said AI and data have enormous potential to transform public services and make a tangible difference to people's lives, and that it is a privilege for the company to support civil servants in turning their ideas into reality. The Challenge is also supported by government Chief AI officer Kalbir Sohi and DCMS permanent secretary Susannah Storey. Woodley said that winning has been a life-changing experience and that he is now involved in a project to see his idea through to implementation, improving the tools used by benefits caseworkers to reduce errors and speed up decisions. The programme is also intended to develop digital skills across the Civil Service by giving participants experience of working on technology projects alongside colleagues from other departments and disciplines.

stories.Headline: NTT DATA's Tulloch says AI threats push clients from annual audits to live risk scores
stories.Summary:
Ben Tulloch, executive managing director of advisory services for Asia Pacific at NTT DATA, said AI-driven threats are pushing companies from annual security audits to live risk scores that update whenever a company changes its software. He spoke to CRN Asia at the NTT R&D Forum 2026 in Tokyo and at a media roundtable there. He said each new feature or AI agent a company releases can open a fresh weakness or link systems in ways no one has checked. He said companies are producing software faster than ever, and a new agent built in one part of a business could expose a vulnerability elsewhere that the company did not know about. He said the traditional model, in which an outside firm spends several weeks reviewing a company and issues a grade for the year, had fundamentally changed in three months.

Tulloch said the traditional motion was to bring in someone to audit you, do a six-week assessment, get the stamp and come back next year. He described a live risk score, which tracks a company’s exposure as it changes, as a concept that was not around three or four months ago. He said a company could say its teams deployed more code today and that this increased exposures for reasons A, B and C, and therefore it needed to do something. He said NTT DATA had not found fewer than 100 vulnerabilities at any enterprise client in Asia Pacific, though the number varies with a client’s size, industry and exposure to the outside world. He said a medium-sized client would typically have hundreds, while one large client in Australia had more than 4,000 vulnerabilities.

Tulloch attributed the vulnerability counts to companies not assessing their software libraries, the ready-made blocks of code that developers borrow rather than write themselves, and said it is quite staggering. He said NTT DATA had been rethinking its approach to cybersecurity with clients since Anthropic announced its Claude Mythos Preview model in April. He cited a technical assessment published on 7 April in which Anthropic said the model could identify and exploit previously unknown vulnerabilities in every major operating system and web browser when directed to do so. He told reporters that AI can test every possible route into a system, so a collection of medium-risk weaknesses can now be exploited in ways that were not practical before. He said the first problem for many organisations is simply knowing where they stand, and that no one really knows whether you are being attacked or not until you are being attacked.

Tulloch said that once you understand your vulnerability, you cannot unsee that, and you are compelled to act. His roundtable presentation, citing CrowdStrike’s 2026 Global Threat Report, put the average breakout time, meaning how long an attacker takes to move from a first foothold to other systems, at 29 minutes. He said the fastest was 27 seconds, and in one case data was taken out of a network within four minutes. He said this made the long-standing 1-10-60 benchmark, which gives security teams one minute to detect an attack, 10 minutes to investigate it and an hour to contain it, no longer workable. NTT DATA’s alternative is a machine-first response in which software takes the first containment step, such as cutting off a user session or stopping a compromised AI agent, and then passes the case to a person.

Tulloch said at the roundtable that this does not mean taking humans out of the loop, but that a machine has to be the first response to an AI threat. Asked who decides which actions a machine may take without approval, he said such decisions were moving beyond the chief information security officer to the CEO and the board. He said that if the CISO’s only metric was containment, that may be a great risk to revenue, so the CEO will be thinking about customer impact, revenue impact, people impact, as well as security. He did not say whether automated containment had ever shut down legitimate systems at a client, saying he was not sure he could answer that question. He said the attack surface, meaning the range of entry points open to attackers, had also grown as more staff across the business build their own AI agents, sometimes with low-code tools that require little programming.

Tulloch pointed to newer technologies such as MCP servers, which let AI agents connect to company applications and data, as changing what agents can reach. He said at the roundtable that this shift moves part of the problem out of the security team’s hands, because engineering flaws out is a software development problem and that is a different group of people. He noted that NTT DATA had formed partnerships with Google and cloud security company Wiz in recent months, and that Wiz’s code-scanning tool is used to flag weaknesses while software is still being written. He said that in regulated sectors such as banking and insurance, AI agents need to be highly accurate, and that you cannot be 30% wrong, you have got to be aiming for 98, 99%, and then bring the human in the loop for that. He said NTT DATA AIVista, the group’s AI firm in Silicon Valley, was working on neuro-symbolic AI, which pairs machine learning with rule-based logic, with the aim of keeping agents within defined limits and with insurance and banking as its main focus.

Tulloch said many of the agent-focused startups he saw at an event in Jakarta the previous week talked about productivity rather than quality. He said that in any regulated process it comes down to quality, that you have to be able to trust it, and that if you do not trust it, you will not deploy it, not at scale. He said clients are also asking for help managing the agents they already run, covering token costs, the usage charges for running AI models, access to data and the ability to show auditors what the agents have done. He said it is a sign of clients being serious about AI when they say they have these agents now and ask for help managing them, and that many software-as-a-service options for this are expensive, so clients are looking for lower-cost ways to do it. He said the last of the four areas in NTT DATA’s approach is preparing for post-quantum cryptography, encryption designed to withstand future quantum computers.

Tulloch told the roundtable that Singapore expects critical infrastructure operators to have migration plans by March 2027. He said that, as far as he was aware, no one can yet break current encryption with a quantum computer. He said the immediate risk is that attackers can steal encrypted data now and decrypt it once quantum computers are capable enough, a tactic known as harvest now, decrypt later. Asked about Malaysia, he said he was not personally aware of its plans, and he expected banks operating across both markets to follow Singapore’s timeline. He said most of the banks in Malaysia and Singapore are across borders, so they are probably more likely going to fall to the Singapore timelines, unless Malaysia is more stringent.

Articles.Title: AI pushes cybersecurity from annual audits to live risk scores, says NTT DATA - CRN Asia

stories.Headline: Strike Graph launches Integration AI to collect compliance evidence from any API
stories.Summary:
Strike Graph announced the launch of Integration AI on November 18, 2026, in Seattle. This new agentic AI solution allows the company to automatically collect compliance evidence from any software that possesses an API. The system uses two separate AI agents to read public vendor documentation and build the necessary backend and user interface connections. This process removes the need for customers to install software agents or manual tools within their own infrastructure. The new tool connects API to API and applies collected evidence to more than 30 different frameworks.

This includes major standards such as SOC 2, ISO 27001, HIPAA, and CMMC, which eliminates the need for duplicate work. To maintain security, the integrations are restricted to read-only operations and utilize an endpoint allowlist. All credentials are kept in a secure secrets vault and remain completely separate from the AI build process. Justin Beals, the founder and CEO of Strike Graph, stated that quick and continuous access to evidence is essential for successful compliance. He explained that Integration AI overcomes previous roadblocks by allowing the platform to collect evidence from any system with an API.

Beals noted that the graph-based evidence model ensures that a single piece of data counts toward every framework a customer pursues. The company treats vendor documentation as data rather than instructions to prevent prompt-injection attacks. Human engineers must review the research plan and the final code before any integration is deployed to production. Each script runs in an isolated sandbox environment to ensure that a flaw in one connection cannot spread to others. Integration AI is available to all Strike Graph customers starting today.

Articles.Title: Strike Graph Launches Integration AI to Automate Continuous Compliance Evidence Using Any Existing Tool - Dark Reading

stories.headline_source: Strike Graph Launches Integration AI to Automate Continuous Compliance Evidence Using Any Existing Tool

stories.Headline: COP31 observers say AI data centre growth may raise fossil fuel use and strain power grids
stories.Summary:
Observers at the COP31 UN climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, said that the expansion of data centres to power the artificial intelligence boom could increase fossil fuel use, strain power grids and raise electricity prices for ordinary people. Turkey, which is hosting the conference, launched a pledge on November 16 for countries and companies to sign that urges them to seek the technology's potential in finding climate solutions while assessing its growing environmental risks. Turkey said the pledge received 80 endorsements but did not specify who had signed, and The Straits Times understands that Singapore has not signed it. The concerns were voiced as global superpowers remain locked in a race to dominate the emerging field, and some tech leaders such as Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei have separately called for an AI slowdown on oversight grounds.

The pledge and the debate sit alongside a Turkish presidency target for countries to agree at the conference on raising the share of electricity in global energy demand from 20 per cent currently to 35 per cent by 2035 through electrification. UN climate chief Simon Stiell said at the launch that AI offers both great potential and great peril for the battle against global warming, and that people cannot be asked to accept higher bills, more planet heating pollution and deeper inequality today in exchange for promises of a better tomorrow. He called on companies to align their business plans with climate goals and to power their data centres with renewable energy. Alex de Vries-Gao, a researcher at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam who studies the environmental impacts of digital infrastructure, told the paper that AI development should be slowed if its growth cannot be accommodated without increasing fossil fuel use or putting further pressure on grids, and that building data centres first and promising to address the consequences later is not a sustainable approach.

Xueying Wu, co-lead of the Global Big Tech campaign at Greenpeace, said unchecked expansion of AI data centres threatens to derail the global energy transition, noting that an International Energy Agency report showed global data centre electricity consumption will more than double by 2030. Philip Newell, who leads the COP31 Actual Intelligence Unit at the Climate Action Against Disinformation coalition, said data centre growth would not need to slow if tech companies committed to tapping more wind and solar power backed by batteries rather than relying on fossil fuels. Nidhi Upadhyaya of the Atlantic Council's Climate Resilience Center said consumers are already seeing the strain, and that the AI infrastructure construction boom and rising electricity bills were among the main concerns for voters in the November 3 US midterm elections that saw a Democratic victory in Congress. In South-east Asia, data centres currently consume more than 13 terawatt-hours of electricity, a figure the IEA expects to nearly triple by 2035 in a November 9 report, and that current total is equivalent to about a quarter of Singapore's electricity consumption in 2024.

Kirsten Dunlop, chief executive of the independent climate innovation agency Climate-KIC, said data centre expansion should slow down to allow developers to build more sustainable infrastructure. Upadhyaya said it will be critical to ensure that the cost of building data centres is borne by the companies setting them up rather than by consumers, and that grid capacity needs to be re-evaluated and infrastructure retrofitted, upgraded or rebuilt to be more resilient. She also called for guardrails governing where data centres are built, the impacts they will have on neighbourhoods and governance of how AI is used. Hikmat Soeriatanuwijaya of Oil Change International said that with growing resistance to data centres in the US, South-east Asia will need to assess the implications of investments in these areas, while Vries-Gao said governments need to consider who benefits, who pays for the additional infrastructure and what happens to local electricity and water supplies.

Articles.Title: AI boom could increase reliance on fossil fuels, strain grids: Observers at COP31 - The Straits Times
