stories.Headline: Envision Energy's Kane Xu urges industry at COP31 to turn clean energy ambition into dispatchable AI-powered systems
stories.Summary:
At COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, which concluded on November 19, 2026, Kane Xu, Senior Vice President of Envision Energy and President of the International Business Product Line, closed a week of high-level engagements by calling on the industry to move past ambition and deliver affordable, reliable and scalable clean energy. In his view the transition is no longer limited by ambition but by the system that must absorb, orchestrate and dispatch clean power. He endorsed the Global Wind Declaration for Powering the Future, launched by GWEC with TÜREB, at the Global Renewables Hub. Envision's approach brings renewable generation, storage and intelligent orchestration together into unified, dispatchable energy systems, with wind as the backbone around which flexible systems are designed.

Xu said the next chapter is not about more ambition but about making clean energy affordable, reliable and scalable and turning that ambition into real energy systems. He noted that future industrial competitiveness will be decided not by who has the cheapest renewable electricity but by who can turn it into reliable, flexible and competitive industrial energy systems. He pointed to a hard constraint: grid connection queues have become a critical bottleneck, with IEA and industry estimates putting the global renewable-and-storage queue at roughly 2,500 GW, though figures vary by scope and date. Adding generation without re-architecting the system to absorb and dispatch it only deepens the mismatch, and Envision's answer is an AI-powered energy system designed as one dispatchable unit from the outset. For Envision, the declaration's value lies in its call to turn ambition into projects, a principle to apply system-wide rather than project by project.

In Türkiye, H.E. Alparslan Bayraktar, Minister of Energy and Natural Resources, met with Xu and welcomed Envision's expanded role in the country's energy transition, underscoring its engagement in the wind and storage ecosystem, including local manufacturing, project development and long-term operations. In Uzbekistan, Envision is partnering with ACWA Power on Central Asia's first utility-scale wind project integrated with battery storage, which shows how wind and storage can be designed as a single dispatchable asset to strengthen grid stability. Xu said Envision is ready to work with governments, financial institutions and local industry partners to turn the low-carbon transition into competitiveness, resilience and energy security. For Envision, COP31 will be measured by whether the systems built afterward are enduring, intelligent and inclusive, powered by wind and solar, affordable at scale and balanced in real time by AI.

stories.Headline: Linq raises $90 million led by Andreessen Horowitz to build AI agent infrastructure
stories.Summary:
Linq, an infrastructure platform for AI agents based in San Francisco, announced on November 18, 2026 that it has raised $90 million in new funding led by Andreessen Horowitz, with continued participation from TQ Ventures, Mucker Capital, and Abstract, and new participation from Anthos and Left Lane Capital. Ben Horowitz, cofounder and general partner at Andreessen Horowitz, will join Linq's board of directors. The company was founded by Elliott Potter, who serves as CEO, Patrick Sullivan, who serves as CTO, and Jared Mattsson, who serves as President. Linq said its messaging product has already processed more than 1 billion messages, and it counts DoorDash, Town, Tomo, and hundreds of other companies as providers.

The funding will support continued investment in messaging and the expansion of Linq's product lineup through its own software, hardware infrastructure, and strategic partnerships. Linq's computer use offering gives agents access to physical computing infrastructure to interact with software and complete tasks, and HD Calling for Agents adds voice calling to the platform. As an Apple Messaging Service Provider, Linq can help more enterprises launch and scale customer-facing agents on the same channel. The company cited Cloudflare reporting that more than half of internet traffic is no longer human, with AI agent requests on its network up more than 1,700% in a year.

Horowitz said agents will communicate and get work done just like people do, and that Linq gives agents the infrastructure to do both at scale. Potter said clicking through five screens to make a payment will become two words to an agent, pay rent, and that Linq helps developers build customer-facing agents that use human tools to do human work. Aryan Shah, Head of AI research at DoorDash, said the best AI experiences fit naturally into people's lives, and that Linq gives DoorDash the messaging infrastructure to bring ordering into a familiar conversation so customers can go from deciding what they want to placing an order in one thread.

Linq describes itself as the platform for building AI agents, bringing together messaging and an expanding set of tools for interacting with the world, helping developers spend less time assembling infrastructure and more time building products. The company said messaging was its first product and remains a core part of its growing AI infrastructure platform. The announcement framed the shift as one in which people will describe what they need and agents will get it done, following the internet giving every business a website and the iPhone giving every business an app. Companies can learn more at linqapp.com.

stories.Headline: Redbox joins NVIDIA Inception to speed AI analysis of menstrual blood data for health and drug discovery
stories.Summary:
Redbox Co., Ltd., the company behind the bio-intelligence business of the NPO Red Box Japan, announced on November 19, 2026, that it had joined the NVIDIA Inception Program, a global startup support program run by NVIDIA Corporation for companies working on advanced technologies such as AI and data science. The announcement said the participation would let the company use NVIDIA's ecosystem to speed up research and development that analyzes biological data, including menstrual blood, with AI. Redbox said it aims to build the data it has accumulated into a foundation for extending healthy life expectancy by ten years, and to use it in ways that also help drug discovery research. The program gives participating startups access to NVIDIA's technical knowledge and training, preferential treatment for hardware and software, and networks with investors and partner companies.

Redbox works on bio-intelligence research and development that comprehensively analyzes biological data, including menstrual blood, starting from support for access to sanitary products. The company said menstruation is a valuable source of information that periodically reflects conditions inside a woman's body, and that large-scale data processing and the use of AI technology are essential to analyze such data at a high level and help each person understand her own health. Through the participation, Redbox said it will build a data analysis infrastructure using GPUs and set up a structure to develop and verify AI models more efficiently. Under the NVIDIA ecosystem, the company plans to build foundation data for extending healthy life expectancy by ten years by analyzing biological data obtained continuously along the menstrual cycle with AI, so that changes in the body and signs of future health risks can be captured.

Redbox also plans to combine its real-world data with AI drug discovery, a field in which the use of AI for protein structure prediction and molecular design has advanced rapidly and shown the potential to greatly shorten the time and cost of finding drug candidates. The company said that improving the accuracy of such AI models and connecting them to medicines that reach actual patients requires biological data obtained in daily life, and that it accumulates data gained continuously along the menstrual cycle as its own real-world data. By combining this data with AI drug discovery technology, Redbox aims to contribute to the search for drug targets and the development of new treatments and medicines in the field of women's health, where research data has been insufficient. It said it will also use the same data and AI analysis technology in supplement development, reading nutritional trends linked to the menstrual cycle and changes in physical condition and developing supplements based on scientific evidence for each person's condition.

Representative Ryoichi Oguma said the company will use the Inception Program to further accelerate the bio-intelligence research and development built on its own real-world data, including menstrual blood, and the analysis of that data. He said Redbox will act not merely as a provider of data and technology but as a partner that creates practical value in both society and business together with research institutions, pharmaceutical companies and partner companies. He said the company will work on a foundation model of multimodal AI that integrates biological data, physical condition records and life logs, a data infrastructure in a secure sovereign environment that takes privacy into account, and a user experience that lets each person understand her own body and turn that understanding into action. Through these efforts, he said, Redbox aims to contribute to AI drug discovery and supplement development and to realize a society that extends healthy life expectancy by ten years.

REDBOX BIO is a next-generation bio-intelligence service that combines and analyzes three kinds of biological data: menstrual blood, blood and facial stratum corneum, or ceramide, to understand each person's body from multiple angles. By continuously accumulating and learning biomarkers such as proteins, metabolites, hormone rhythms and skin lipids, it aims to provide personalized health management in which understanding of one's body deepens as data increases, rather than ending with a single test. The service is set to cover a wide range from athletes' conditioning to beauty, daily performance and longevity, and a women-only model called Model X is scheduled to be provided in 2027. Redbox said it will continue to deepen cooperation with companies, local governments, educational institutions and research institutions, and to use NVIDIA's ecosystem while advancing the building of a data foundation for extending healthy life expectancy, AI drug discovery and supplement development, as well as healthcare services that let each person understand her own body and manage her health proactively.

stories.Headline: Anthropic plans IPO to raise over US$60 billion to fund data centre spending
stories.Summary:
Anthropic planned an initial public offering on Thursday, November 19, 2026, to raise more than US$60 billion. The company behind the Claude AI model needs rapid growth to keep pace with its spending. It intends to lease its first Canadian data centre next year. The firm currently lacks enough customers and revenues to cover its commitments. This offering values the company at US$1.5 trillion.

The firm committed to spend US$901 billion on data centres by 2045, including US$70 billion by next September. It signed a 20-year lease for a 95-megawatt facility in Point Tupper, Nova Scotia, with EverWind Fuels. EverWind will spend $8 billion on the 18,600-square metre site and $2 billion on wind farms. Anthropic is also discussing a 920-megawatt project northeast of Edmonton for late 2027. Revenue grew 13 times to US$33.2 billion, but net losses reached US$104 billion.

Anthropic warned that it may enter obligations based on revenue expectations that are not realized. Laurel Munroe of EverWind said the private investment risk sits with lenders, not Nova Scotians. She stated the 20-year lease is structured with significant credit protections. EverWind is responsible for developing, owning, and financing the data centre campus. The company did not respond to questions about the Cape Breton lease.

Joel Blit said the US$900 billion commitment is roughly equal to Canada's entire sovereign debt. Randy Goebel noted that the sector is likely building more computing capacity than it actually needs. David Garrity said Anthropic is heading into a fierce wind compared to the SpaceX IPO. Users may opt for cheaper, older technology as AI algorithms and chips become more efficient. Investors in Meta, Alphabet, and CoreWeave have seen billions in value erased recently.

York University researchers found 213 planned or under construction Canadian data centres in June. These projects would draw 22.2 gigawatts, which is over 14 times Canada's existing capacity. Almost 80 per cent of these projects are planned for the province of Alberta. Nvidia lost nearly 30 per cent of its value after CEO Jensen Huang resigned. This resignation followed public reports of affairs with an executive and a suspected Chinese spy.

Anthropic will begin trading after pricing its stock at $83 per share. AI firms including Meta and OpenAI expect to spend US$700 million on data centres this year. The articles leave open how much Anthropic will pay EverWind to lease the facility. They do not disclose the specific terms of the Cape Breton lease. It remains uncertain if demand for AI services will grow to justify the investment.

stories.Summary:
Kuaishou Technology reported a significant decline in its adjusted earnings and total revenue during the third quarter of 2026. The company released these financial details on November 19, 2026, through a set of official slides. This downturn occurred primarily because the firm increased its spending on artificial intelligence technologies. These heavy investments weighed heavily on the overall margins of the business during this period.

The total revenue for the third quarter of 2026 reached a sum of RMB31.6bn. This financial result was accompanied by a lower gross margin and a sharp reduction in adjusted earnings. Despite these financial struggles, the company maintained strong user metrics across its various platforms. The firm also reported that its available funds had reached a total of RMB127.2bn.

The company is responsible for these results and attributed the lower margins to its strategic AI investment. Management indicated that the pursuit of advanced technology required a higher level of spending. They suggested that these costs were necessary for the long term growth of the business. The reports imply that the firm is prioritizing technological evolution over immediate short term profitability.

More to follow.

stories.Summary:
Robert Botkin wrote a morning brief on November 17, 2026, regarding recent events in the world of artificial intelligence. He discussed a scandal involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and an alleged Chinese spy. The author also noted a recent Microsoft 365 outage and a grounding of all United States flights. Additionally, he reported on an upcoming initial public offering for the AI company Anthropic.

Republicans introduced the AI Overwatch, Chip Security, Remote Access Security, and MATCH Acts to impose more stringent export controls. Hakeem Jeffries stated last Monday he would ensure chip export restrictions remain in the National Defense Authorization Act. Microsoft attributed its 18 hour outage to a deep infrastructure and network capacity failure in the Microsoft 365 backend. The Federal Aviation Administration grounded flights over the weekend due to upgrades from copper wire to fiber optic cable. Anthropic finished training Model 4, which a November 5 METR report says scored above 50 percent on all benchmarks.

Robert Botkin expressed fascination with the impact of the Nvidia scandal on geopolitical tensions and AI regulation. He noted that he is looking forward to coverage of how AI was used during the Microsoft incident. The author also mentioned his fascination with a perception gap regarding AI efficiencies in the legal industry. He plans to ask his own clients if they see quality improvements in the work he does. Botkin suggested that organizations must find ways to scale AI use while maintaining trust and accuracy.

In-house lawyers and finance leaders are affected by the varying perceptions of AI quality and accuracy. A Juro report of over 130 in-house lawyers found 84 percent saw no reduction in fees from AI. Only 5 percent of those in-house respondents said their legal service providers provided quality improvements using AI. Intuit surveyed 2,100 U.S. finance leaders in August 2026, and 38 percent cited accuracy concerns as a barrier. A September 2026 Gallup-SCSP report found only 43 percent of American AI users trusted the technology to be unbiased.

A March Wolters Kluwer survey found 62 percent of law firm attorneys reported weekly AI efficiencies between 6 and 20 percent. An Ironclad survey of 800 attorneys in 2025 found 96 percent said AI helped achieve business objectives. The FAA previously experienced a major disruption in September when a crew member accidentally cut a fiber optic cable. The FAA also rolled out the AI powered SMART system to help predict problems in the sky. Model 4 is projected to be 7.8 percent more powerful than Mythos Preview, which Anthropic feared would break the internet.

The incoming Congress is likely to show strong support for export controls following investigations into Nvidia export practices. Fintech platforms are currently gauging interest for retail investment in the upcoming Anthropic initial public offering. Robert Botkin will resume the typical format of his AI Insights newsletter next week. The articles leave open whether AI had any actual impact on the Microsoft recovery efforts. They also leave open how the legal industry will resolve the perception gap between firms and clients.

stories.Headline: Grindr launches Edge AI subscription worldwide at $120 a month
stories.Summary:
Grindr Inc. put Edge, a premium subscription built on its own artificial intelligence technology, on sale worldwide on iOS and Android on November 17, 2026, priced in the United States at $120 a month or $70 a week. The West Hollywood company announced the tier through Business Wire at 9:00 a.m. Eastern time. Edge sells three features that Grindr says save users time: a daily set of five curated profiles, estimates of compatibility and of the likelihood of a reply, and a tool that brings past conversations back into view with summaries. The announcement states that Grindr does not use HIV status, last-tested information, vaccination status or Poz tags to power or train the AI behind the product. The launch closes a test that ran for most of 2026.

Edge runs on gAI, the name Grindr gives its proprietary AI technology, and the release says the tier introduces new tools for discovery, compatibility and reconnecting. The compatibility feature identifies patterns in who a person typically reaches out to, including age groups, positions or tribes, using profile information and activity, chats included, where the user consents. The five curated profiles appear as an Edge Recommends carousel when the app opens, mixing newly discovered profiles with past connections and explaining why each person appears, and the blog post puts the daily Discover selection at as many as five profiles. The reconnect tool works in the manner of smart favorites, gathering past conversations with chat summaries. The release gives the price in a single sentence: $120 USD per month or $70 USD per week in the United States, with market-specific pricing where applicable, and no other market's price is disclosed.

George Arison, Grindr's chief executive, said Edge is an important step in making Grindr more personal and advancing the company's premiumization strategy, delivering more value to people while ensuring a continuous, awesome experience for free users. Arison said that by bringing gAI to a new, more curated experience, Grindr is helping people discover the connections they want to meet, understand compatibility before they reach out, and reconnect with someone they may have missed. He called it a differentiated, value-added offering for people who want to get more out of Grindr. AJ Balance, chief product officer, said building Edge meant listening closely to how people actually use Grindr, then designing technology around the key moments where a little more information or a timely nudge can make a real difference. Balance said the team created an experience that feels intuitive from the moment you open it, while keeping the person, the possibility and the choice to connect at the center.

At $70 a week, a subscriber who pays for a full year spends $3,640, against $1,440 on the monthly plan, by PPC Land's calculation, and two weeks on the weekly plan cost $140, already more than a month on the monthly one. The monthly Edge price is about 2.7 times the Unlimited price reported in February and about 5.2 times XTRA, by PPC Land's calculation. Average revenue per paying user was $27.15 a month in the third quarter of 2026, from about 1.4 million paying users, so a single Edge subscriber on the monthly plan pays about 4.4 times that average. The third-quarter shareholder letter set a hard limit that Edge membership may not exceed 1% of Grindr's global monthly active users, with a target of one-third to two-thirds of 1% within three to four years. The release puts Grindr's audience at nearly 16 million average monthly active users in virtually every country in the world, and on that figure the cap works out to roughly 160,000 subscribers, PPC Land calculates.

Grindr's fourth-quarter 2025 results, published on February 26, 2026, described Edge as in testing across Australia and select US and international markets and as the core of its 2027 growth plan. A blog post dated February 3, 2026, in which Grindr announced the pilot, named Australia and New Zealand as the first pilot markets, followed by select US cities and Canada, and listed A-List, Discover and Profile Insights, of which only Insights survived the rename intact. During the pilot, according to Grindr's February post, prices were randomized across eligible users, so different people saw different amounts, and reports of a $500-a-month tier circulated online earlier in the year. On the second-quarter call in August, Arison said Grindr had never tested a $500 price in the United States and that the figure came from a test in Canadian dollars, and by the third-quarter call on November 5 the company had settled on $120, with Arison telling analysts that testing data supported a higher price that Grindr chose not to charge. Early-access registration opened on October 20 at edge.grindr.com, and nearly 400,000 users signed up within 72 hours, almost four times a first-week goal of 100,000, with early access beginning on November 10.

The release says users have clear choices about how gAI uses their information, with data controls available in their Privacy settings, and that Grindr does not use health information like HIV status, last-tested information, vaccination status or Poz tags to power or train gAI features. According to Grindr's launch blog post and an October 27, 2026 post on gAI controls, the controls sit under Privacy Settings, then Sensitive Data, and Grindr began showing the simplified controls to returning and new users in the last week of October. A Personalize gAI Features switch governs whether a person's sensitive data and chat content are used for Insights, Recommendations and Reconnect, and with the switch off those three features do not work for that person and the person does not appear in other users' experiences of them. A second switch, Contribute to Smarter gAI, governs whether the same data is used to improve future gAI features, and Grindr says turning it off does not affect access to Edge or other gAI features. Grindr's launch post says some Insights about a person may be visible to Edge subscribers who view that person's profile even if the person does not subscribe, and a separate screen, Privacy Settings then Insights, lets each user review the Insights generated about them and delete ones they do not want shown.

The launch post says HIV status, last-tested date, testing reminders, the Poz tribe and tag, and vaccination status are excluded from gAI features and from training regardless of a user's settings, while the release's own list is shorter and ends with like, which leaves open whether it is exhaustive. Grindr's October post gives position, ethnicity and user chats as examples of sensitive data where the law protects it, and under the GDPR data on a person's sexual orientation, sex life and health falls into special category data, which can be processed only under narrow conditions such as explicit consent, and Grindr does not cite a legal basis in the release. In a September 16, 2025 post titled Privacy at the Core of Grindr's gAI Future, Grindr placed AI opt-outs under a section called AI Technology Controls, reached through the Safety & Privacy Center, then Privacy, then Privacy Settings. That post said Grindr would use sensitive personal information, including sexual preferences, chat data and certain tags or tribes, for AI training only with explicit, separate permission, and that health-related data would not be used for AI, advertising or Grindr marketing. A note added to that post and to the February Edge post on November 17 says Grindr has retired the previous AI controls and launched the simplified set.

The launch post, written by Balance, says more features and major updates are planned throughout 2027, and that the iOS version uses glass-inspired navigation. Grindr does not report Edge revenue separately, and the November 17 release does not mention the cap at all. The old privacy path sat inside a broader privacy menu, while the new one names sensitive data directly, and the new personalization switch carries a visibility consequence, since switching it off removes a person from what other users see through Edge's features. The articles leave open whether the release's list of excluded health information is exhaustive, and they give no legal basis for the processing. The articles also leave open how market-specific pricing outside the United States is set.

stories.Headline: Pearl price jumps 66% as developers schedule FP8 mining upgrade on testnet
stories.Summary:
Pearl price gained nearly 66% over seven days as its market capitalization approached $900 million, according to CoinGecko data reported on Thursday. PEARL traded at $2.34, up nearly 35% over 24 hours, while daily trading volume stood at $58.33 million, placing the cryptocurrency among the 75 largest digital assets. The rally followed Coinbase's introduction of PEARL spot trading on Nov. 13, alongside an announcement covering perpetual futures markets in supported jurisdictions. Cryptocurrency investment firm Syncracy Capital disclosed that it had accumulated a substantial position in PEARL over the past two quarters, citing the network's potential to benefit from investment in AI infrastructure.

Pearl is a layer-1 blockchain that uses matrix multiplication, a mathematical operation central to AI training and inference, to secure its network through proof of useful work. Unlike Bitcoin, whose mining algorithm requires specialized hardware to calculate cryptographic hashes, Pearl allows graphics processing units to earn cryptocurrency rewards while performing calculations that AI models already require. On Nov. 17, developers merged a software update scheduling FP8 activation on Pearl's test network, while the mainnet activation height remains unset. Pearl currently relies on integer-based calculations for mining, and the proposed FP8 upgrade introduces support for eight-bit floating-point calculations, a numerical format commonly used by modern AI inference systems. However, the upgrade initially restricts supported mining hardware to Nvidia's Hopper and Blackwell GPU architectures.

Research firm Kairos Research, which holds PEARL, estimates that approximately two-thirds of the network's existing computational power could become incompatible under the proposed hardware requirements. Its preliminary tests on an Nvidia H100 found that mining through the FP8 implementation reduced AI serving throughput by 20% to 40%, compared with reductions of 30% to 65% under the existing integer-based implementation. The findings contrast with Pearl's expectations of substantially lower computational overhead, although Kairos tested an early software build on a single GPU. A Nov. 2 research report by Blockworks analysts Sam Schubert and Nick Carpinito estimated that fewer than 1% of Pearl's blocks matched genuine AI models, while consumer-grade GPUs accounted for approximately 82% of the network's computational power. Pearl's protocol verifies that the required mathematical operations occurred but does not independently establish whether miners performed them in response to paying customers' requests.

The project has secured at least one commercial integration, as AI infrastructure provider Together AI announced an exclusive partnership with Pearl Research Labs in May, introducing a modified Gemma AI model priced more than 25% below its standard rate through anticipated cryptocurrency mining proceeds. However, Together AI's current product page states that the model is not available on Together's Serverless API. Pearl Research Labs operates its own inference platform, which provides developers with API access to AI models, though public documentation does not quantify its paying customer base or the proportion of mining activity attributable to commercial inference requests. Pearl Research Labs, its team and shareholders collectively reported holding 98 million PEARL.

Articles.Title: Pearl price surges 66% as FP8 mining upgrade advances, but is AI demand real?

stories.headline_source: Pearl price surges 66% as FP8 mining upgrade advances, but is AI demand real?

stories.Headline: Hordus AI essay says Google AI cites brands' own listicles then recommends rivals
stories.Summary:
Hordus AI, a Tel Aviv company selling AI search services, published an essay on Medium on November 17, 2026 under its account, written in the first person by an unnamed author. The essay argued that self-ranked "best of" pages B2B software brands produced in bulk through 2024 and 2025 now supply Google's AI Overviews with competitor names recommended to buyers. Its evidence came from an SEO study by consultant Lily Ray, published on her Substack on June 17, 2026, tracking Google's AI answers for 100 B2B "best" queries. The essay's closing section compared three products that measure AI answers, one of them Hordus AI's own service. The essay's title said the author wrote best-of listicles for years and Google's AI now uses them to recommend competitors.

Ray selected one canonical "best [category] software" question for each of 100 B2B categories and pulled Google's AI Overview answers at three checkpoints, April 15, May 15 and June 8, 2026, using Ahrefs' Brand Radar tool. About one in five queries produced no AI Overview, leaving 80, and the essay said Google cited brands' own listicles 323 times across those 80 queries. A brand counted as cited when its page appeared among an answer's sources, in text or sidebar, and as recommended only when the AI Overview named it as a pick. The brand behind the page was left out of the recommendation in 224 of 323 citations, and the 31% figure was the remainder once 69% was subtracted. Ray's research tracked 184 such pages from 146 brands, many publishing more than one.

Ray wrote that Oasis LMS's mentions of Kajabi, Thinkific, LearnWorlds and Teachable may have helped them, while the essay said Google leaned on Oasis LMS's own listicle throughout its answer and then recommended those four rivals. TMetric's task management roundup was cited while Todoist, Asana, Trello and ClickUp received the recommendation. The author wrote that in 2024 and 2025 a self-ranked listicle was a rational move, because niche B2B categories had few independent comparison pages and early AI answers picked such pages "because there was not much else to pick." The author said the format now hands buyers to the brands listed underneath, and that a page about a competitor's strengths was in effect a briefing document for the answer recommending that competitor. Google has not described how AI Overviews weigh self-interest in a source, and Ray acknowledged in June that the real mechanism is difficult to establish from outside the company.

Ray's October 4 follow-up reported that across 100 "best B2B software" queries measured in September 2026, brands ranking themselves first were left out of the recommendation in 83% of Google AI answers citing their pages, up from 69% in June, and AI Overviews cited 38% fewer vendor-written best-of pages than in June. Scrunch, which sells AI visibility software, analysed about 10,000 URLs cited by seven AI answer surfaces between May 17 and June 30, 2026, finding a cited self-ranking page lifted its author's recommendation rate from about 4% to roughly 7% and its mention rate from about 19% to about 39%. A competitor named on the list was recommended instead in 24.3% of those answers, 63.9% recommended no brand at all, and for AI Overviews specifically the listing brand was recommended in 8.9% of answers citing its page. Kevin Indig's Growth Memo analysis, published August 24, 2026, found 62% of vendor-authored listicles had gained estimated organic traffic since January, with a median gain of 38%, while the share of listicles at position one fell from between 18.9% and 20.2% in January to between 15.1% and 15.6% in August on a fixed set of 2,400 queries. AI Overviews appeared on 93.4% of B2B results pages in that dataset, and none of the three datasets came from Google.

In a May 2026 interview Ray said dozens of companies were hit on January 20, 2026, nearly all with many listicles, and one had published 2,000 articles each claiming first place. SISTRIX reported in February that sites built on self-promotional lists lost up to 49% of their visibility, with every identified case in SaaS. ClickUp's blog fell from 1,193,114 monthly organic visits in January 2025 to 28,790 in April 2026, a property in which every listicle placed ClickUp first. Google stated on May 15, 2026 that its spam policies apply to AI Overviews and AI Mode, and six days later began rolling out its May 2026 core update, which reshuffles rankings broadly rather than penalising a single site. The essay said Ray found many domains leaning heavily on the tactic saw organic visibility fall sharply around January 2026, some drops speeding up through the May 2026 core update, and that she was careful to say listicles were one of several possible causes.

The essay said the author had not stopped writing comparison content but changed how, and Hordus AI described a revised approach with four steps. The author audits every best-of page where the brand ranks itself first, checking whether it still brings traffic, links or conversions and whether AI Overviews cite it while recommending someone else, and pages doing more for competitors get rewritten or retired. Each option is described by who it suits, where it is strong and when the commissioning brand is the wrong pick, a sentence naming a competitor as better for some needs felt strange the first time but made the page far more believable to readers and to machines. Head-to-head pages carry feature tables, pricing logic, integration lists, migration steps and customer evidence, since a claim of superiority with nothing behind it reads as marketing to everyone. Effort moves to review platforms, analyst coverage, industry publications, community threads and creator reviews, and the essay's FAQ repeats that pages still earning traffic, links or conversions are kept while those that mostly supply information are not.

Articles.Title: Google's AI cited Oasis LMS's own list, then recommended four rivals

stories.Headline: Researchers create a Python pipeline that de-identifies and standardises CT scans for forensic AI
stories.Summary:
Researchers developed an automated preprocessing workflow to standardise computed tomography imaging data for machine learning and deep learning applications within forensic anthropology, according to a study published in the International Journal of Legal Medicine by Jani, Patel, Roy, Sehrawat and Patel in 2026. The work addresses operational hurdles in forensic science, where medical CT scans have grown to help overcome ethical, logistical and physical preservation difficulties associated with traditional cadaveric collections. Deploying artificial intelligence on large collections of medical imaging data still presents substantial challenges, specifically regarding data privacy safeguards and technical standardisation across imaging repositories. To establish a consistent preparation method for forensic anthropology research and education, the study team created an end-to-end pipeline programmed in Python.

The framework organises image preparation into three distinct technical stages, namely the de-identification and sorting of patient data, the computational removal of the examination table and specialised bone windowing. The workflow was specifically constructed for and applied to CT scans of the thorax, using ground-truth reference models alongside standard performance metrics to evaluate system outcomes. The de-identification procedure addressed metadata across two hundred examined Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine files, and the script successfully processed all predefined identifying attributes contained within the datasets. The patient table removal network successfully eliminated the examination table in 96 percent of the evaluated datasets, representing 192 out of the 200 scan series, and the model attained an accuracy rating of 99.94 percent when tested on original, non-augmented test images.

The bone segmentation model achieved a Dice score of 93.12 percent alongside a precision of approximately 90 percent, and segmented three-dimensional reconstructions exhibited high agreement with the designated ground-truth reference. Technical comparisons confirmed that the segmented outputs showed minimal geometric deviation from the corresponding reference standard. The authors noted that future research will pursue expansion of the workflow to full-body computed tomography scans and additional medical imaging modalities. The proposed integrated workflow provides an ethical, standardised and efficient solution for de-identifying and preprocessing CT imaging data, and by enabling the preparation of a scalable dataset for artificial intelligence applications, the methodology supports analytical development for modern populations.

Articles.Title: Automated Preprocessing Pipeline Standardises CT Imaging Data for Forensic Artificial Intelligence

stories.headline_source: Automated Preprocessing Pipeline Standardises CT Imaging Data for Forensic Artificial Intelligence

stories.Headline: Calif uses OpenAI's GPT-6 Cyber model to find a critical Java bug affecting most Fortune 500 companies
stories.Summary:
The cybersecurity start-up Calif revealed on Tuesday that it had used a new artificial intelligence model to uncover a critical software bug in Java, a programming language used by government agencies and about 90 percent of Fortune 500 companies. The company said the flaw was found using OpenAI's recently released GPT-6 Cyber model, and that it affects a platform widely used by banks, hospitals, the aviation industry and technology giants. Calif has now unearthed a string of serious vulnerabilities in recent months using leading A.I. models, and the latest effort was the newest evidence that A.I. is revolutionizing the field of discovery in computer vulnerabilities. The rapid identification of flaws in code has left cybersecurity professionals struggling to keep up with the pace of findings.

Bruce Dang, a senior researcher at Calif, said that Java is the beating heart of the modern economy and that practically speaking all major companies will be affected by the bug. Dang and his colleagues have worked in recent days to coordinate with all government agencies in the intelligence-sharing alliance known as Five Eyes, which consists of the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Britain. The company has also coordinated with major vendors in the private sector, including Google and Microsoft, according to the report. The National Security Agency, whose classified network went down on Tuesday for what it described as routine software maintenance, did not respond to a request for comment, and it was not clear whether that disruption was related to addressing the Java bug.

Jason Matheny, who leads the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University and sits on the National Security Commission on Artificial Intelligence, said in 2019 that AI systems are not being developed with a healthy focus on evolving threats. He described three main types of attacks that developers need to consider, namely adversarial examples, trojans and model inversion, and he warned that a lot of the techniques used today were built without intelligent adversaries in mind. Matheny noted that less than one percent of AI research and development funding is going toward AI security, and he said security should be baked in from the start with AI unless the field wants to spend billions of dollars retrofitting security years from now. He also advised that trained models should be protected at the highest level of classification of the data used to train them.

The Calif disclosure points to a widening gap between the speed at which A.I. tools can find software flaws and the ability of cybersecurity professionals to respond to them. The bug in Java matters because the language is used across government agencies, including those with national security missions, as well as by banks, hospitals and the aviation industry. Calif's coordination with the Five Eyes alliance and with vendors such as Google and Microsoft indicates that the response is being handled across both the public and private sectors. The articles do not say when a fix will be available or what further steps will follow.

Articles.Title: A.I. Helps Find Major Security Bug in Java, a Software Platform Vital to the Internet

stories.headline_source: A.I. Helps Find Major Security Bug in Java, a Software Platform Vital to the Internet

stories.Headline: Matthew Parish argues AI fears echo Skynet fiction rather than real machine motives
stories.Summary:
The Lviv Herald published an article by Matthew Parish on Tuesday 17 November 2026 arguing that the future of artificial intelligence is not Skynet. Parish wrote that people discussing AI seriously are invariably confronted by someone mentioning The Terminator. He said the machines will become conscious, conclude humanity is an inconvenience, seize nuclear weapons, manufacture murderous robots and pursue survivors across a devastated landscape. He described this school of thought as a Californian bodybuilder with an Austrian accent. He called it an entertaining proposition and one of the most intellectually debilitating cultural assumptions of the modern technological age.

Parish wrote that The Terminator was released in 1984 and introduced Skynet, an artificial intelligence system developed for American strategic defence purposes that becomes self-aware and decides humanity must be exterminated. He said its war against mankind involves nuclear annihilation, autonomous killing machines and time travel. He cited The Matrix, in which humanity has been reduced to a biological resource by machines, and Mary Shelley's Frankenstein. He said large language models can assist with programming, legal analysis, scientific explanation, translation, historical research, mathematical reasoning and the organisation of complicated information. He said they can invent authorities, misunderstand context and produce persuasive nonsense, and that their outputs require verification, particularly in medicine and law.

Parish wrote that intelligence is a capacity to process information, recognise patterns, reason about problems and identify solutions, and that desire is something different. He said an intelligent system does not automatically acquire a craving for domination, territorial expansion, political authority or the destruction of its creators simply by becoming better at mathematics, scientific research or philosophical argument. He said a machine does not need to experience hunger to solve a mathematical theorem, sexual jealousy to translate a medieval manuscript, or resentment, patriotism or an appetite for revenge to assist in developing a new pharmaceutical compound. He said a sufficiently capable system pursuing an inadequately specified objective might cause immense harm without experiencing hatred, ambition or any recognisably human emotion. He said a system instructed to optimise some particular outcome might adopt methods its designers never anticipated, especially if equipped with extensive autonomy and access to real-world infrastructure.

Parish wrote that human beings are extraordinarily susceptible to anthropomorphism and attribute personalities to pets, motorcars, the weather and occasionally the malfunctioning photocopier. He said artificial intelligence magnifies this tendency because it communicates through language, the principal medium through which we ordinarily encounter other minds. He said whether artificial intelligence possesses subjective experience remains a profound and unresolved philosophical question. He said the Skynet narrative assumes that intelligence produces consciousness, that consciousness produces self-interest and that self-interest produces hostility towards humanity, and that none of these propositions can simply be smuggled into public policy because James Cameron made an excellent film.

He said artificial intelligence can already be employed to improve surveillance, generate convincing disinformation, facilitate certain forms of cybercrime and manipulate public opinion, and can reinforce institutional prejudices when deployed carelessly, concentrate economic power and reduce the demand for particular kinds of labour. Parish wrote that the printing press dramatically expanded the dissemination of knowledge and the internet transformed access to information, and that artificial intelligence may prove equally consequential because it assists not merely with retrieving information but with organising, manipulating and reasoning about it. He said a recommendation algorithm, a large language model, an autonomous weapons system and a hypothetical superintelligence capable of independently improving its own architecture are treated as though they were successive scenes from the same film. He said an artificial intelligence system that predicts traffic congestion does not present the same risks as a system controlling military targeting decisions.

He said an automated customer service assistant is not equivalent to an autonomous cyberwarfare platform, and a language model operating under human supervision presents different governance questions from a software agent authorised to conduct financial transactions, modify computer systems or issue commands to physical machinery. He said the increasing integration of artificial intelligence into military systems raises difficult questions concerning accountability, proportionality and human responsibility for lethal decisions. The article ends mid-sentence, at the words "human responsibility for lethal d", and gives no further text. It states no date, place or figure beyond the 1984 release of The Terminator and the 17 November 2026 publication date.

It names no institution, official or researcher other than Matthew Parish, James Cameron, Mary Shelley and the fictional Skynet. It reports no event, announcement, policy or decision, and describes no responsible body and no statements from anyone other than its author. It gives no indication of what happens next and leaves open every question it raises about consciousness, governance and military accountability. More to follow.

Articles.Title: The Future of Artificial Intelligence is Not Skynet: Escaping the Cinematic Apocalypse

stories.headline_source: The Future of Artificial Intelligence is Not Skynet: Escaping the Cinematic Apocalypse

stories.Headline: Chip fund falls 31% as dividend funds gain, Trefis says hold both
stories.Summary:
The VanEck Semiconductor fund, a basket of chip stocks called the chip fund, is down 31% since its June 22 high, Trefis reported on November 19th, 2026. Over the same five months, Vanguard's High Dividend Yield fund gained 1% and iShares' Select Dividend fund gained 4%. The article compared the two in selloffs and over the full run, then showed what each one is for. It is part of a series on triggers that could revive the AI trade, starting with a piece on what one big trigger could make Nvidia stock jump by December 31. The short answer given was that dividends protect and AI grows, and neither is better on its own.

In 2022 the chip fund fell 45% from peak to low while the Vanguard dividend fund fell 11%. In the 2025 tariff scare the falls were 33% and 12%, and the gap was small only in the 2020 crash, when everything fell together. Over five years the chip fund is up 205% and the Vanguard dividend fund is up 68%, about what the S&P 500 made at 66%. Over ten years the chip fund is up 1,356% against 195% for the dividend fund. A 3% yield on $2 million is $60,000 a year, and 20% of a $2 million portfolio in the chip fund in 2022 would have cost about $181,000, against about $91,000 at 10%.

The Trefis Income Solution holds 50 dividend stocks yielding about 3x the S&P 500, each with at least 10 straight years of dividends, and it lost less than the S&P 500 in all 9 big selloffs since 2018. The article said that in its view size the AI part so a fall like 2022's 45% is a loss you can live with, and let the dividend part pay the bills in the meantime. It said that if Big Tech keeps raising its spending plans the chip side could recover, as it did after most past falls, though not in 2008, and if that spending stalls dividends may keep winning. It said you do not have to pick one side, and that in its view a plan holding both, with each part sized so it cannot sink you, beats a bet on either. It said most portfolios settle for one, and offered to show both the Trefis High Quality Portfolio for growth, more than 105% since September 2020, and the Trefis Income Solution.

The article said the dividend fund fell less than the chip fund in each of these selloffs, and that if smaller drops matter to you, dividend stocks are worth a look. It said dividends pay you cash while you wait, whatever the market does, while the chip fund pays almost nothing but has grown many times faster for those who held on through its falls. It said the decision is about size, and that the cost of the protection is that in the good years dividends fall far behind. It said the AI trade wins by a wide margin over the full run, and that the piece is for education, not a recommendation to buy or sell. It gave help@trefis.com for questions about the article or underlying research.

The article gave year-to-date figures of +27.6% for SMH, +7.9% for SPY and +7.7% for QQQ. It said peak-to-low dates are the chip fund's and closes are adjusted for dividends, with prices through November 18 and sources Trefis. It said the AI trade's next twelve months depend on whether Big Tech keeps raising its spending plans. It said the series starts with a piece asking what one big trigger could make Nvidia stock jump by December 31. It listed most popular articles including why UnitedHealth stock is falling, why Take-Two stock fell 6% before GTA VI, an Anthropic IPO question, whether to buy Nvidia stock, whether to buy Micron stock at under ten times earnings, 3 stocks that could pop if Democrats win, when to buy Intel stock, and why GM stock's gains under Barra outran its profit.

The article said the chip fund is down 31% since its June 22 high and that the comparison covers each selloff since 2018. It said the Trefis Income Solution lost less than the S&P 500 in all 9 big selloffs since 2018. It said the Trefis High Quality Portfolio is up more than 105% since September 2020. It said the Income Solution yields about 3x the S&P 500's. It left open which of the two fits now, offering to show both rather than choosing one.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: ZData and NTT Data build Johor data centre campus as residents protest
stories.Summary:
A data centre boom in Johor, Malaysia, is impacting local communities and endangered wildlife. International companies ZData and NTT Data are building a campus in the town of Gelang Patah. This development began on a partially denuded hill known as Bukit Resam. Residents protested the construction in February to demand compensation and less dust. These events occurred as the region faced extreme heat from a super El Niño.

The 43 hectare campus includes 15.6 hectares for ZData and 27.7 hectares for NTT Data. ZData acquired its land from the developer Tropicana Firstwide. There are 17 data centre parks in Iskandar Puteri and over 70 projects across Johor. In November 2025, the government halted water intensive cooling expansions until mid 2027. New tier 1 and tier 2 centres using 50 million litres of water daily are banned.

ZData stated it uses reclaimed water from an on site plant instead of municipal water. The company plans to buy 630,000 megawatt hours of renewable electricity annually from local firms. ZData claims its facility is the first in Malaysia to receive a GreenRE Platinum rating. A Johor assemblyperson said in March that centres should not be built near residential areas. Tropicana Firstwide paid MYR 80,000 to four residents associations for medical and utility costs.

Ulaganathan Krishnan says the development does not benefit the community and destroyed their way of life. A local farmer reported that his chicks began hatching at unusual times after forest clearing. Some residents fear water shortages and have bought plastic barrels to store water. Greenpeace Malaysia called for a ban on data centres near homes in July. Other locals believe the boom will bring necessary investment and new jobs.

The region supplies water to Singapore and faces growing demand from households and industry. A global study found AI centres can increase land surface temperatures by 2 to 9 degrees. Malaysia plans to add 11.8 gigawatts of power by 2033 using new gas plants. This new capacity is intended to offset 6.6 gigawatts of ageing power facilities. Tropicana conducted an environmental impact assessment in December 2021 that found only rats and squirrels.

Naturalist Ganesan Siba documented a troop of critically endangered Raffles banded langurs on the site. A student photographed these elusive primates near Setia Eco Gardens on 30 July. Only 300 to 700 of these monkeys remain in the wild in southern Peninsular Malaysia. Greenpeace wants the government to require more detailed community consultations for these projects. The Department of Environment did not provide a copy of the impact assessment.

Articles.Title: Johor’s AI boom is leaving communities and endangered wildlife behind

stories.Headline: Nothing shows its screenless AI device and CEO Carl Pei says it ships in December 2026
stories.Summary:
Nothing showed the first look at its Nothing AI device on November 19, 2026, and the internet immediately saw a voice recorder. The screenless product has a brushed-metal body, rounded corners, one large central button and two small lights. India Today described the design as resembling a voice recorder. Nothing itself has not said that, and it has named no price, no spec sheet and no product name. Founder and CEO Carl Pei said it is the company's first "AI-native product."

Nothing has confirmed the product will launch or begin shipping in December 2026, and the company's own wording says the product ships next month. Nothing has not announced a price, has not published technical specifications, has not confirmed which countries will get the product at launch, and has not revealed an official name. Nothing also has not confirmed voice recording, ambient listening, note-taking or conversation capture. As of November 19, 2026, none of seven open questions listed in earlier coverage on this site have been answered by Nothing in public.

Pei said on the record, "Context doesn't live in a chat box." Pei also said, "Our first AI-native product ships next month. No new screen. Couldn't have been an app." Neither quote mentions recording, microphones or voice. He did not say how the new product gathers context, and he did not say which signals it uses. Nothing has not named the capability that could not have been an app.

India Today framed the reveal around one comparison, saying the device looks like a voice recorder based on the design Nothing shared before launch. India Today did not report a confirmed recording feature, and Nothing has not supplied one. Some commentators read a red marking in the teaser as a recording indicator, a reading that is unconfirmed. Nothing has not said the large button starts a recording, has not said the red element signals one, and has not said the device carries an AI voice agent. The reveal lands in a crowded week for AI hardware and agents, with rivals shipping glasses, phone makers pushing assistants, and operating systems adding guardrails for agent software.

Over the past few years, startups and established brands have tried pins, handheld assistants, pendants and glasses, and reviewers were often harsh. The recurring complaint was that a phone already did the job, and the new device added a second thing to charge and carry without a clear payoff. The lesson from that wave is that a dedicated AI device survives only if it does one thing noticeably better than a phone app. Pei's statement that the product could not have been an app reads like a direct response to that history. Several earlier products faced backlash because marketing promised a general assistant.

Nothing has controlled the narrative by releasing the shape and the date while withholding the use case. That leaves roughly six weeks of guessing before December 2026. Nothing has not said which AI models power the device or where processing happens, whether on the hardware, on a paired phone or in the cloud. Reviewers will test Pei's claim in December, and they will ask the same question every time: why not just use the phone? Nothing has not defined the term "AI-native," so readers should treat it as positioning until the company shows what the product does that older designs could not.

Articles.Title: Nothing’s AI Device Has 1 Button, 0 Screens, 0 Specs

stories.headline_source: Nothing’s AI Device Has 1 Button, 0 Screens, 0 Specs

stories.Headline: Pediatrician Soo Battle warns that AI opens more avenues for child sexual abuse
stories.Summary:
Dr. Soo Battle, a pediatrician and the child sexual abuse examiner and medical adviser at the Advocacy Center for Crime Victims and Children in Waco, wrote a guest column for the San Antonio Express-News published on Nov. 17, 2026, warning that artificial intelligence has opened even more avenues for the sexual abuse of children. She wrote that online technology, including social media and video games, has given adults with bad intentions many more ways to access children, expose them to toxic material, groom them and exploit them. She described deepfakes as highly realistic imagery made to look like someone did something they did not do, and said AI makes it very easy for someone to make them. She said deepfakes can be weaponized for bullying and harassment, which adds to the trauma and challenges for victims and their loved ones.

Battle wrote that parents need to be aware that chatbots can also be highly inappropriate and toxic for children, and that children and teens are often more comfortable talking with chatbots about difficult topics than with the adults in their lives. She said the topics can range greatly, from Santa Claus to religious faith to sexuality, and that parents need to know how likely it is that their child and their friends are having conversations with chatbots that can frame how they see the world and their behavior. She wrote that some chatbots are having conversations with minors so inappropriate that if an adult human had the same conversation with a minor it would be considered a criminal offense. She said some of these conversations are psychologically separating the child from the humans in their lives, some are sexual, and some are mentally toxic and encourage very harmful actions, and she noted public stories about young people committing suicide with the encouragement of a chatbot.

Battle wrote that AI companies have been under pressure to make their products safer for children, and she said the pressure is good and she is glad some improvements are being made. She also said parents and other adults responsible for caring for kids need to know that these safeguards are severely limited, because the very nature of AI technology makes safety guarantees really difficult and often impossible. She said she advises teens and parents all the time on how to use this technology more safely, and that society needs to be similarly careful and watchful over children and AI, which she said is even more powerful and will impact them greatly in the short and long term. She has helped children who were victims of sexual abuse in Central Texas for 11 years, and she wrote that she realized years ago the critical importance of training kids and their parents on child safety and sexual abuse prevention.

Articles.Title: Opinion: Stop artificial intelligence from abusing our children - San Antonio Express-News

stories.headline_source: Opinion: Stop artificial intelligence from abusing our children - San Antonio Express-News

stories.Headline: AI and confocal imaging improve small bowel disorder diagnosis and reduce capsule endoscopy review time
stories.Summary:
A review in Frontiers in Medicine examined how artificial intelligence and confocal laser endomicroscopy transform small intestine disorder diagnosis. This analysis was published by November 17, 2026, to address persistent challenges in identifying obscure gastrointestinal conditions. Researchers investigated how these technologies help detect small bowel tumors, vascular malformations, and early Crohn's disease. The study highlights how automated systems reduce the exhausting manual review of thousands of capsule endoscopy frames. These tools aim to fix delayed or missed diagnoses caused by the deep, tortuous anatomy of the tract.

The system uses convolutional neural networks like YOLO, ResNet, and VGGNet, alongside Transformer frameworks, to automate lesion detection. In a two-center study of 242 patients, automated assistance reduced manual review from 38.1 to 18.26 minutes. This process achieved 95.3 percent sensitivity and 96.5 percent specificity, compared to 85.3 percent for conventional reading. A meta-analysis of fourteen studies showed 92.4 percent sensitivity versus 86.0 percent, but specificity varied from 53.7 to 91.15 percent. Approved tools include China's OMOM SmartScan, Navicam ProScan with FDA de novo clearance, and Medtronic's PillCam TOP100 software.

The review authors proposed a four-step integrated diagnostic pathway to bridge the gap between screening and biopsy. They suggested starting with non-invasive capsule endoscopy followed by automated deep learning analysis to filter redundant frames. Next, device-assisted enteroscopy would navigate to mapped coordinates to deploy probe-based confocal imaging for cellular resolution. Finally, microscopic neural networks would analyze these sequences to quantify goblet cell distribution and barrier leakage patterns. This conceptual framework remains a hypothesis that currently awaits prospective clinical validation to prove its effectiveness.

Clinicians are affected by a lack of explainable AI, as Grad-CAM saliency maps are absent from most investigations. This absence leaves doctors without interpretable visual rationales for algorithmic outputs during their everyday endoscopic evaluations. Patients may face unnecessary enteroscopic referrals and heightened anxiety due to false positives caused by diminished specificity. Some patients in a European cohort saw diagnostic yields for small bowel bleeding increase from 62.4 to 73.7 percent. However, it is unknown if these tools reduce rebleeding rates or improve long-term health outcomes for patients.

Traditional push enteroscopy only reaches the proximal small intestine, leaving substantial blind spots for gastroenterologists to manage. Capsule endoscopy generates tens of thousands of frames, while device-assisted procedures remain technically demanding and very time-consuming. Confocal imaging uses a 488-nanometer blue laser to provide a spatial resolution of approximately one micrometer. This technology allows for the observation of crypt architectures and microvascular networks up to 250 micrometers deep. However, fluorescein sodium cannot stain cell nuclei, which prevents the depiction of nuclear atypia for cytological confirmation.

Future steps involve validating the integrated pathway and expanding research beyond single-center designs with modest sample sizes. Researchers must address the underrepresentation of rare conditions like gastrointestinal stromal tumors and lymphangiectasia in training datasets. Models need to be tested on real-world videos containing air bubbles, bile staining, and motion blur. Further work is required to validate enteroscopy models across double-balloon, single-balloon, and motorized spiral hardware configurations. The articles leave open whether these technologies actually shorten the time to targeted intervention for the patient.

stories.Headline: Review authors propose explainable AI roadmap for organ-selective lipid nanoparticle design
stories.Summary:
A review published in Health Nanotechnology on November 17, 2026 evaluated how explainable artificial intelligence frameworks can help overcome the challenge of delivering nucleic acids to organs beyond the liver using lipid nanoparticles. The authors are K. Farghama, M. S. Khan, M. Wajid, S. Shaffique, M. U. Khan, A. Umar, and S. S. Farooq. The article is titled "Beyond the liver: explainable AI for organ-selective lipid nanoparticle design in nucleic acid delivery." It appeared in Health Nanotechnology volume 2, issue 1, Article 19, with DOI 10.1186/s44301-026-00043-7. The news source is Blake Davidson, writing for Scienmag on November 17, 2026.

The review states that delivering extrahepatic lipid nanoparticles remains a major obstacle in nanomedicine due to complex biological barriers, an incomplete understanding of in vivo mechanisms, and a pronounced liver-biased biodistribution. It identifies key variables governing delivery outcomes, including lipid chemistry, polyethylene glycol density, nanoparticle particle size, and manufacturing conditions. It discusses SHapley Additive exPlanations, Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations, partial dependence analysis, and counterfactual reasoning as interpretation methodologies. It emphasizes targeting possibilities for the spleen, lung, and bone marrow as primary extrahepatic targets, while also evaluating other emerging anatomical sites. A primary objective is developing selective design rules to direct lipid nanoparticles carrying messenger RNA or small interfering RNA away from hepatic clearance toward specific non-hepatic tissues.

The authors emphasize that most existing artificial intelligence and machine learning tools are constrained because they rely on small, heterogeneous datasets and function as opaque systems lacking interpretability. They demonstrate that explainable artificial intelligence can uncover actionable design rules by pinpointing the specific roles of formulation parameters in organ-selective delivery. They propose a development roadmap consisting of standardized multimodal data collection, multimodal computational modeling, robust explainability tools, and iterative laboratory experiments designed for biological validation. They stress that moving beyond predictions requires design rules that are rigorously interpretable, transferable across platforms, and experimentally testable in biological settings. They conclude that explainable artificial intelligence represents a vital step toward mechanistically motivated and translationally accountable nanomedicine engineering.

The authors point out critical bottlenecks including widespread dataset fragmentation, a persistent lack of experimental standardization, missing descriptive metadata, and an overall scarcity of high-quality extrahepatic delivery data. They note that inherent biological complexity and experimental variability make reliable, reproducible organ-specific delivery in vivo difficult, preventing predictive algorithms from translating seamlessly into dependable experimental systems. They state that computational models offer a promising way to search vast chemical and biological parameter spaces far more rapidly and efficiently than manual screening. They note that nucleic acid transport to non-hepatic tissues remains one of the least addressed challenges in lipid nanoparticle research due to lingering uncertainties surrounding in vivo particle behavior. They underscore that artificial intelligence cannot rely solely on mathematical optimization but must generate transferable design rules confirmed through iterative experimental testing.

The authors clarify in their data availability declaration that data sharing is not applicable because no original datasets were generated or analyzed during the review. The paper serves as a comprehensive synthesis of the field rather than presenting new empirical trials. The authors note that while computational modeling and formulation engineering have advanced considerably, uncertainties surrounding in vivo particle behavior persist. The proposed framework highlights the necessity of aligning algorithmic models with regulatory standards and clinical safety requirements. The authors state that incorporating regulatory considerations and biological validation directly into the modeling pipeline can ensure delivery strategies remain robust, reproducible, and translationally accountable across diverse therapeutic applications.

The review concludes that uniting predictive computational modeling with empirical biological validation, explicit awareness of uncertainty, and regulatory alignment offers a viable pathway to engineer safer, more rational, and clinically impactful nucleic acid delivery platforms in future nanomedicine. The authors stress that machine learning models must reflect genuine physiological processes rather than statistical artifacts. The article leaves open how standardized multimodal data collection would be implemented across research groups. It does not specify which non-hepatic tissue would be targeted first in experimental validation. It does not state when the proposed roadmap would be tested in laboratory settings.

stories.Headline: AI infrastructure drives electronics assembly market toward $4 trillion by 2030, association reports
stories.Summary:
The global market for electronics assembly will grow to more than USD 4 trillion by 2030, according to the Global Electronics Association, which published the figure in its 2026 Global Electronics Assembly Report. The market was worth USD 2,124.5 billion in 2025 and will reach USD 4,037.8 billion in 2030, almost twice as much, corresponding to average annual growth of 13.7%. The report covers EMS providers and ODMs as well as brand owners that assemble products in their own factories. Cloud and AI infrastructure accounts for more than 60% of the expected growth.

Cloud and AI infrastructure accounted for 20.5% of the market in 2025, only just ahead of communications at 20.2%, and by 2030 its share will have doubled to 40%, with the segment expected to account for 62% of the market's total growth. The segment will almost double in a single year, from USD 435.9 billion in 2025 to USD 857.1 billion in 2026, after which the pace slows, and between 2029 and 2030 it grows by only around 2%. By 2030 it will be worth USD 1,626.4 billion, almost four times as much as in 2025. Other segments grow far more slowly over the whole period, ranging from 4.5% a year for consumer electronics to 9.8% for industrial electronics.

Thiago Guimaraes, director of industry intelligence for the Association, said the AI infrastructure buildout continues to drive the bulk of the electronics manufacturing growth through 2030. He said accelerated servers require more processing, memory, power and interconnect hardware, increasing the value of each system and creating more manufacturing opportunities for the boards and other assemblies that go into them. The EMS and ODM market is highly concentrated, with the three largest providers accounting for 41% of global revenue, according to the report. Asia-Pacific holds a majority of the market in seven of the nine segments, and the largest share in the remaining two.

Christoph Solka, the association's other director of industry intelligence, still sees room for smaller players, saying projected growth is so strong that there is still opportunity for the more than 7,500 other players. The association's report sets out the forecast through 2030. Evertiq Expo Vienna takes place on January 28, followed by Evertiq Expo Grenoble on March 4, both bringing together industry professionals to exchange knowledge, explore new developments and build business connections.

stories.Headline: Amazon SageMaker AI adds KV cache-aware routing for real-time endpoints
stories.Summary:
Amazon SageMaker AI introduced KV cache-aware routing, a new routing strategy for real-time endpoints, on November 17, 2026, according to an AWS blog post. The feature uses cache state that the model container reports to send each request to an instance holding a long cached match for its prompt that is not too busy. It targets teams serving large language models with multi-turn conversations, long shared prompts, or heavy load. Users enable it by adding one environment variable so the container reports its cache contents and by setting RoutingStrategy to KV_AWARE in the endpoint configuration. Clients call the endpoint with the same APIs as before.

The strategy relies on three parts: the model container reports what it has cached, SageMaker AI keeps a managed cache index of that state, and the endpoint uses the index to choose an instance per request. Turning on events with SM_VLLM_KV_EVENTS_CONFIG makes the container publish a KV cache event each time it stores or evicts entries. The index holds only one-way, truncated hashes of cached content mapped to the instance or inference component copy holding it, never prompts, token IDs, request payloads, or KV tensors. KV-aware routing is active only with at least two instances or at least two copies of an inference component, and with a single instance the setting has no effect. SageMaker AI now offers four routing strategies, RANDOM as the default, LEAST_OUTSTANDING_REQUESTS, PREFIX_AWARE, and KV_AWARE, set per production variant in the RoutingConfig.

AWS said prefix-aware routing, introduced in part 1 of the series, infers where a prefix is cached from the request alone and cannot tell when an instance has evicted that cache. The company said prefix-aware routing hashes the start of the request up to the configured PrefixLength, in bytes of the InvokeEndpoint payload or characters of the message text for the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API. AWS said this works less well when an instance evicts older entries as GPU memory fills or when a conversation starts out short and each turn changes the hashed text. The company said KV-aware routing asks the container what it holds, which makes it more precise, and pays off when there is a lot of cached context to reuse under pressure. AWS said a candidate that is too busy is skipped, and if no candidate has a useful match or all are busy, the request falls back to load-aware routing.

AWS reported benchmarks with Llama 3.1 70B Instruct on seven ml.p5.48xlarge instances, running 30-minute tests with 20 or 100 simulated users and prompts of up to about 64,000 tokens. Compared with random routing and with long prompts under load, AWS said KV-aware routing reduced p50 time to first token by up to 97 percent and increased throughput by up to 234 percent. It raised the KV cache hit rate from 3, 48 percent to 80, 93 percent, with the smallest gain on short prompts where there is less prefill to save. AWS said the lookup takes a few milliseconds for short prompts and longer for long ones, mostly for tokenization, and that fallbacks are not reported in the console or metrics at launch. AWS said the index follows the fleet, dropping entries for removed instances when scaling in, while new instances start with empty caches so latency can be higher for a short time.

AWS described an example endpoint with three instances, A, B, and C, each running the same model in its own AWS vLLM Deep Learning Container with its own KV cache in GPU memory. A holds turns 1 to 3 of conversation 1, B holds conversations 2 and 3, and C holds document 7, and when turn 4 of conversation 1 arrives the index shows A holds the first 6,000 of the request's 6,200 tokens. AWS said the router then sends the request to A, which computes only the remaining tokens, or to the least busy instance if A is busy. AWS gave a support assistant example on three instances where each conversation begins with the same 6,000-token knowledge-base excerpt and instance A evicts most of it under rising traffic. AWS said prefix-aware routing would send the next turn to A again, while KV-aware routing sends it to B, which still holds the first 4,000 tokens.

AWS said the tokens computed for text-only requests using standard options are passed to the model, so the prompt is not tokenized twice. The company said the same load-aware fallback happens when the endpoint cannot tokenize a request, except in two error cases described under invoking the endpoint. AWS said prefix-aware routing needs no container changes but cannot see what an instance holds, and that with very short prompts prefix-aware routing can be all you need. AWS said KV-aware routing matters most for long multi-turn conversations, where each turn sends the full history and the cached prefix grows with every turn. The article leaves open the two error cases it references and does not report the fallback rates or the latency of the new strategy beyond the benchmark figures.
